en: Auspiciousness.

The Kramadīpikā: A Treatise on the Scriptures Devoted to the Description of the Worship of the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by the commentary composed by Vidyāvinoda Śrī Govinda Bhaṭṭācārya. Chapter One.
Eager for the pleasure of playing the flute,
his chest anointed with divine fragrance,
he captivates the hearts and wealth of the cowherd women.
I meditate upon a certain son of the cowherds.

At the outset, for the purpose of instructing his disciples, he composes an auspicious invocation—preceded by the recollection of the chosen deity—which is the unique cause for the removal of the evil that obstructs the work he intends to begin, and whose duty is enjoined by the Vedic revelation inferred from the practice of the distinguished (*viśiṣṭa-śiṣṭa*).
He does so under the guise of a benediction, beginning with the words "Kalāt-tamāyā... and so forth.
Having assumed a form through a mere fraction of Māyā taken from His own potency,
charming with the sound of His flute resonating in measured tones,
He dwells within the heart, agitating the three worlds.
May the beloved of the cowherd women bring you prosperity!
The construction is as follows: "May the beloved of the gopī-jana be for your *śrī*, that is, for your prosperity.
He is the beloved—the master—of the *gopī-jana*, the community of cowherd women.

And thus, the sense is: if he is the beloved even of the *gopī-jana* who are unaware of the intricacies of formal etiquette, how much more so is he the beloved of the spiritual practitioner (*sādhaka*) who is skilled in the performance of every mode of worship?
Alternatively, the meaning is that the *gopī* is *prakṛti* (nature) and the people are the *mahat-tattva* and so forth, while He is their "beloved," meaning their impeller.

Of what nature is He? He is one by whom a form (*mūrti*) has been assumed through even a slight trace (*lava*) of *māyā*—which, though inherent (*adhyasta*) in Himself as His own essence consisting of knowledge (*jñāna-svarūpa*), has been acquired (*prāpta*) and is characterized by the nature of projection (*vikṣepa*).
By this it is implied that even in connection with a body, there is no lapse in His awareness of His own true nature, because the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) lacks authority over Him.
Alternatively, *kalā* means "binding";

thus, he is one who has assumed a form consisting of a mere trace of *māyā*, which is accepted for the purpose of setting in motion the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) that is characterized by bondage. As it is said: "By means of water, he emitted living beings upon the earth."

Alternatively, he declares the seed-syllable of Kāma, which is the form of the *saṃmohana* mantra and the seed of all Gopāla mantras, as "kala. Here, "ka" and "la" are *kalau*; by these two, the *māyā* (the letter *i*) and the *lavaka* (the anusvāra) are "attau," meaning taken up or joined. He is thus described as one by whom the form of the seed-syllable has been "āttā," or accepted, through those two. In the word "kala," the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is one who is delightful by the sound of a flute—a bamboo pipe that resounds with a *kala* sound, meaning an indistinct yet sweet resonance; thus, he is "one whose flute sounds sweetly" (*kala-kvaṇad-veṇu*).
By means of its melody, he is delightful, which means he bestows all forms of happiness.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is "residing in the heart," meaning he is situated within the lotus of the heart; that is to say, he is to be meditated upon in the heart.
Alternatively, it means he is situated in the hearts of all living beings in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin).
Doing what? The "trilokī" is the collection of the three worlds;
"trailokyam vyākulayan" means making the three worlds agitated—rendering them devoid of discernment regarding their duties and deluding them through illusion (māyā).
As it is said in the Gītā:
"The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings to revolve by His illusory power (māyā), as if they were mounted on a machine. Regarding this,

the author of the *Laghudīpikā* indicates that the ten-syllable mantra, accompanied by its seed-syllable, is suggested here by the phrases "having taken away [the world] by His portion" (*kalātta*) and "beloved of the cowherd women" (*gopījanavallabha*).
By the words beginning with "kala-kvaṇat," meditation (dhyāna) is indicated;
and by the phrase "agitating the three worlds," the ritual applications for subjugation (vaśya) and so forth are indicated—thus he says. (KrdC 1.1)
He declares his intention to perform [the work] preceded by a salutation to the Guru: "Having bowed my head to the honored particles of dust arising from the two lotus-feet of the Guru..."
Having analyzed here what was spoken by Nārada and others, I shall describe the ritual procedure for the worship of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.

In this treatise, having analyzed—that is, having performed a detailed investigation—I shall describe the method of worshiping Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, including the procedures for ritual offerings, fire oblations, and so forth, until its conclusion, as that is currently underway. Furthermore, by doing so, the superiority of my own work over ancient texts is demonstrated.
Of what nature is it? It is that which was proclaimed by Nārada, Gautama, and others.
The sense is that by this, the independence of his own statement is refuted.

Having done what? Having bowed down to those particles of dust—those tiny specks of pollen—which have been honored and worshipped with the head, that is, the crown of the head; and how are they described? They are those arising from the pair of lotuses, which is the very pair of feet of the Guru.
By this, the excellence of devotion toward the guru and the husband is indicated;
likewise, it is also indicated that meditation upon the guru should be performed upon the head. (KrdC 1.2)
He establishes the preliminary context to declare the superiority of the Gopāla-mantra over other mantras:
[It is superior] for those born of the four castes— Kṣatriyas, Suras (Brāhmaṇas), Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—
and for those belonging to the four stages of life— ascetics, forest-dwellers, householders, and students.
For among the Manvantaras, the fruit of recitation, oblation, sacrifice, and so forth, indeed ripens for someone in some way or another.

For, among the various types of mantras other than the Gopāla-mantra, some mantra has been purified by means of [the prescribed] number of recitations (*japa*) and so forth; and among the castes beginning with the *kṣiti-sura* (brahmins), among the stages of life (*āśrama*) beginning with the forest-dwelling sages—and by the word "and" (*ca*), among women—some person, by virtue of their fortune, [attains success] through *japa*, *homa*, and so forth (the word "etc. indicating other such rites).
The construction is as follows: "the acceptance of libations and so forth bears fruit," meaning it bestows a result.
Regarding this, a certain "earth-god" (kṣitisura)—that is, a Brahmin—maintains that the word *hi* here functions as a particle of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
The *nṛpa* is a Kṣatriya;
the *viṭ* is a Vaiśya;
and the fourth is a Śūdra.
The sage (muni) is the ascetic (yati);
the forest-dweller is the hermit (vānaprastha);
the householder is one who has taken a wife.
A *varṇin* is one who observes the vow of celibacy (*brahmacārī*).
Now he declares the efficacy of the Gopāla mantra for all:
"Among all castes, as well as among all stages of life, among women, and among those of various names and birth-stars;"
This mantra of Gopālaka swiftly bestows all desired fruits.

This ten-syllable Gopāla mantra, which will be described hereafter, is presented first as being independent of any calculation regarding the *siddha* and other classes; it does not refer to the entire group of mantras concerning Gopāla, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). "A twice-born man who gives a mantra joined with *svāhā* and the *praṇava* to a Śūdra shall go to hell, and the twice-born man is born as a Śūdra."

This is because it contradicts scripture and because it would result in [the fault of] metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). [The Lord is] the one who bestows immediately, that is, quite suddenly, the desired fruits intended by [the devotees] among all the castes (*varṇa*).

The meaning is: even though they exist among all castes beginning with the Brahmins, in all stages of life beginning with the student (brahmacārin), among women, those born under various names and asterisms, and those with various kinds of names, as well as those born under various kinds of birth-asterisms. KrdC 1.4.
Even this being so, he reveals that the mantra should be given to one who is intent upon the service of the Guru's feet:
"Surely, devotion arises directly through the falling glance of Acyuta; this is the cause."
Therefore, one who possesses devotion toward Hari and the Guru is qualified for the attainment of those four fruits.

Since it is indeed certain that devotion to the glance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s merciful look—attained through the falling of Acyuta’s sidelong glance—is the direct and ultimate cause, for that reason, a person endowed with devotion becomes qualified for initiation and so forth in order to attain those four fruits; that is to say, for the sake of obtaining the four well-known human goals (puruṣārthas), beginning with dharma. This is the meaning.
By this, it is indicated that meditation should be performed by means of the non-duality of the Guru and the deity.
Now he describes the sequence of worship:

having bathed, wearing clean, pure, and fine garments, with his feet, hands, and face washed, having sipped water for purification (ācamana), with hands marked by the pavitra and sealed, and radiant with white vertical marks (ūrdhva-puṇḍra);
Facing the eastern direction, having assumed either the very firm lotus posture (padmāsana) or the auspicious posture (svastika),
one should sit and, with palms joined in reverence, pay homage to one's own gurus and then to Gaṇādhipa.
"Bathed" means according to the procedure taught in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, though some say it may also be according to the procedure taught in the *Āgamas*.
"In spotless, pure, washed, and fine garments" refers to one who possesses such clothes.
"Having washed" means having cleansed one's hands, feet, and face.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the procedure prescribed in the *Smṛti*,

he— being "with the *pavitra*" (meaning accompanied by the *pavitra* ring), with hands joined by the *mudrā*, and in the reading "supavitra," marked and bound by a most beautiful *pavitra*— is radiant with the *tilaka*. Facing the eastern direction, that is, facing the east.

In this context, since facing east is explicitly mentioned, facing east is primary; however, in its absence, one should face north, for at night all worship requires facing north, as it is stated likewise in the Purāṇas.
Immediately thereafter, having assumed either the lotus posture (padmāsana) or the auspicious posture (svastika) in such a way that it is very firm—of these, the lotus posture is well known.
As for the characteristic of the *svastika*: having placed both soles of the feet properly between the knees and the thighs, sitting with the body straight— this they call the *svastika*.

Seated and having taken his place, he should salute his own gurus and Gaṇeśa. Now, the word *atho* has the sense of "and," implying an unmentioned inclusion; by this, one should also salute Durgā in front and Kṣetrapāla behind. This is stated in the *Gautamīya*: "The guru on the left, Gaṇeśa on the right, Durgā in front, and the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati) behind."
And the preliminary practice is: *guṃ* obeisance to Guru; *gaṃ* obeisance to Gaṇapati;
*duṃ* obeisance to Durgā.
*Kṣeṃ*, salutation to Kṣetrapāla. "With joined palms" means having formed the hollow of the hands in the gesture of reverence (*añjali-puṭa*).
In this regard, one should understand according to the sequence stated in the *Śāradā-tilaka*: the placement of the articles of worship on the right and the placement of the water-jar on the left.
On the back [of the altar] is the placement of the hand-washing vessel; in front is the placement of implements such as the lamp and the fly-whisk. // KrdC_1.6 //
He states the ritual action to be performed prior to the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*): "Then, having purified his two hands with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*),
[he performs] the triple clapping of the palms (*tritāla*), the binding of the directions (*dig-bandha*), and the fire-pavilion (*hutāśa-śālā*)."
Having thus fashioned this limb consisting of the elements,
one of pure intellect should purify it in due order.

Thereafter, immediately following that, one of pure intellect—that is, one of clear mind—should purify this limb, which is the body composed of the five great elements such as earth and so forth, which consist of the nature of the elements (bhūtātmaka); the meaning is that one should make it consist of the nature of the deity (devatātmaka), because of the scriptural statement: "One who is not a god should not worship a god."
Gradually, in the manner that will be described:

having done what? Having purified both hands with perfume and flowers using the *astra-mantra* itself—namely, "Astrāya Phaṭ"—or indeed with the *astra-mantra* that is a limb of that [specific] mantra, and having performed the ritual placement (*kara-nyāsa*) on the hands, one should perform three successive claps (*tāla*) upward using the *astra-mantra* itself.
Thus it is said in the *Śāradā*: "Having performed the ritual placement of the hands (*kara-nyāsa*), one should then perform the three claps.

Immediately thereafter, having performed the binding of the ten directions (*dig-bandhana*) with the *astra-mantra* by means of a snap of the fingers, and having fashioned a wall of fire (*vahni-prākāra*) around oneself in the form of an encircling water using the *astra-mantra*, the traditional practice (*sampradāya*) here is as follows: [one should draw] the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which resides in the pericarp of the heart-lotus and resembles the flame of a lamp, by means of the mantra "Haṃsa."

Having joined [the self] with the Supreme Self residing in the thousand-petaled lotus above the head via the path of the *suṣumṇā*, and having visualized the twenty-five principles beginning with earth as dissolved therein, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*).

He describes the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*): One should first meditate upon the seed-syllable of the ever-moving [wind], accompanied by the *lavaka*, which is smoke-colored at the mouth of the *iḍā* and has the power to dry up all the worlds.
Having filled his entire body with that pervasive form and having completely dried it up,
he should then release the breath into the path of the sun’s rays.

The practitioner, the seeker of mantra, should first of all visualize at the mouth of the *iḍā*, in the left nostril, the seed-syllable of the wind, the form "yaṃ," which is accompanied by the nasal drop (*bindu*) and the *salava* (the vowel *a*), and which is the seed of the constant movement.
Of what nature is it? Smoke-colored, that is, black in hue.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "sakala" (possessing parts).

The meaning is as follows: one should recite the seed-syllable of air (*vāyu-bīja*) sixteen times while inhaling air through the left nostril, thereby drying up the body composed of the five elements.

Immediately thereafter, having filled one's entire body with that wind consisting of the seed-syllable—which possesses an expanded form and a vast body—one should contemplate the unification of the internal bodily air with the external air, and thus bring it to a state of complete desiccation.

Having recited the seed-syllable of wind (yaṃ) sixty-four times with the breath retained (kumbhaka), one should release the wind by exhaling through the right nostril via the *piṅgalā* channel along the path of the sun; the meaning is that while reciting the seed-syllable of wind thirty-two times, one should emit or abandon the air. // KrdC_1.8 //
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable as red and its vital breath dissolved within that very path,
one should fill the body with fire and burn it from the left side.
One should release the breath along with the ashes outward.

Having visualized the seed-syllable *raṃ*— the seed of fire (*āśuśukṣaṇi*) which is ruddy, meaning red in color— as being dissolved and joined with the wind (*māruta*) along that very path of the sky-gem (*kha-maṇi*), the sun, through the right nostril; then, having performed inhalation (*pūraka*) by filling [with air] while reciting that seed-syllable sixteen times, one should subsequently perform retention (*kumbhaka*) while reciting the *raṃ*-seed fourfold.

Having completely incinerated the body in Japan, one should then recite "Ram" thirty-two times; the meaning is that one should release the breath along with the ashes through the left nostril by way of the *iḍā* channel. (KrdC 1.9)
He shows its production: "Then,
let it lead the moon on the forehead— the extremely pure moon— by way of the path of the nectar-rayed [moon], from there [to the syllable] consisting of all the letters."
Having caused the subsequent *japā* vowels to descend, one should fashion with them the entire body; then, this face, hands, and limbs [should be formed] by means of a rain from a flood of nectar.

Beyond that, the letter *ṭha*—which follows *ṭa* (*ṭa-para*)—is exceedingly pure and white; one should lead or cause that moon-seed (*candra-bīja*), which has the form of the nectar-rayed moon, to reach the moon on the forehead—the moon situated in the *brahma-randhra*—by means of the left nostril through sixteen recitations.
Now, one might ask: "Since the entire body has been burnt away, how can the moon-seed be led by way of the path of the nectar-rayed moon? To this, we say: No.

Because that which was previously mentioned consists of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), immediately thereafter—from *amutaḥ*, meaning from the nectar-rayed one, the moon on the forehead, the moon situated at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-randhra*)—there arises a rain of the collection of nectars consisting of all phonemes, that is, consisting of the *mātṛkā*. "The letter following *la*" refers to the letter *va*; this is the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, and by its recitation [the rain falls].

Having caused [the seed-syllable] to descend and arise by reciting it sixty-four times during the *kumbhaka* (retention) breath, one should thus construct and fashion this entire body by means of a rain consisting of the *mātṛkā* letters.
Of what nature is it? It is a body (*vapuḥ*) comprising the faces, hands, and limbs—where "face," "hand," and "limb" refer to the various constituent parts (*avayava*).
Regarding the reading "wherein that [body] is thus enriched with face and hands," the meaning is that it is enriched with a face and enriched with hands.

Immediately thereafter, one should exhale the breath through the right nostril while reciting the yellow-colored earth-seed syllable *laṃ* thirty-two times, and contemplate that body as being clearly perceived.

Following that, according to the oral tradition (*sampradāya*), one should bring the life-force (*jīva*) from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-randhra*) to the heart-lotus by means of the self-mantra "so 'ham" (I am That). KrdC 1.10.
Now he demonstrates the placement of the *mātṛkā* (the alphabet):
one should place [the letters] in sequence upon the head, face, forehead, eyes, ears, nose, cheeks, the two lips, and the head and mouth.
Then, with care, one should apply [the mantras] beginning with *ya* to the joints of the arms and legs,
to their tips, and to the two sides, the back, the navel, and the abdomen.
A wise person should daily recite [the mantras] located in the heart, armpits, nape of the neck, roots of the hands, both feet, belly, and mouth,
following this sequence beginning with the heart.
Perform the ritual placement for the sake of accomplishing the pure body.

In this context, the word "head" (*śiras*) is indicative of the forehead, as seen in the *Śāradādarśa* where it says "the forehead and face are covered," and because otherwise there would result the placement of two syllables in a single location. The compound "the circle of the face" (*vadana-vṛtta*) refers to the facial orb; the analysis of the compound is: "the pair consisting of the eyes, ears, nose, cheeks, lips, and teeth.
The term "pair" (*dvaya*) is to be connected everywhere, including with each member beginning with the eyes.
In the aforementioned locations— the palate (*ghoṇā*), the nose (*nāsikā*), and the two rows of teeth (*dad-dvaye*)— one should sequentially place the sixteen vowels (*acaḥ*) one syllable at a time,
as well as the consonants (*halas*) beginning with *ka*; there, one should respectfully place the twenty consonants beginning with *ka*.

One should respectfully place [the syllables] at the joints of the hands and feet and at their tips. Immediately thereafter, one should place the five syllables beginning with *ya* on the two sides, the back, the navel, and the abdomen— that is, on the back, navel, and abdomen together with the pair of sides— and subsequently, by this method to be described, the [syllables] beginning with *ya*.

One should perform the daily placement (nyāsa) every day, starting from the heart, upon the syllables located at the positions beginning with the heart, as well as on the two hands, feet, belly, and mouth; this should be done so that the heart comes first.

Although the words "two hands, feet, etc. form a compound with the preceding word "all," they are not compounded here with the adverbial phrase "starting from the heart" because of its dependency; however, this should be understood as a case where the dependency involves elements of equal importance.
"For the sake of accomplishing a pure body" means for the purpose of bringing about a pure physical form. (KrdC 1.11–12)
Having thus fashioned a body with fifty times a hundred [letters],
together with those beautified by the half-moon (the *visarga*) and the moon (the letter *sa*),
and having arranged them in conjunction with the forms headed by Keśava;
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in sequence, together with the powers (śaktis) such as Fame (kīrti) and the rest.
Now I shall describe the forms and powers of the vowels, which consist of all the worlds:
Keśavakīrti and Nārāyaṇakānti.
Likewise, Mādhava and Tuṣṭi.

In the manner thus described, having fashioned the body—the physical form—with fifty letters (the half of a hundred), one should thereafter arrange those same fifty letters together with the "lords of the night" accompanied by the *visarga*; that is to say, together with the half-moon (*ardha-kṣapeśa*), meaning together with the *anusvāra*.

With those accompanied by the *visarga*—meaning together with the *visarga*—and with those "beautified," meaning together with both the *anusvāra* and the *visarga*, one should place them at the beginning in that manner.

For the purpose of accomplishing the body through purification, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the *mātṛkā* letters; immediately thereafter, one should place the letters beginning with "aṃ namaḥ" and ending with "kṣaṃ namaḥ," as well as those beginning with "aḥ namaḥ" and ending with "kṣaḥ namaḥ," in those very locations of the *mātṛkā*—the forehead and so forth. This is the meaning.

Thus, the fourfold *mātṛkā*-arrangement has been described. Now, one might ask: how can it be said to consist of "fifty letters" (*arṇa-śatārdhaka*), given that there are only fifty-one phonemes? It is replied: because two syllables are unified by means of the letter *kṣa*, or because two *la*-sounds are unified by means of the letter *la*.

Alternatively, since the context establishes that the intended meaning is the number fifty-one based on worldly convention, the venerable Śrī Premānanda Bhaṭṭācārya-Śiromaṇi maintains in his *Prapañcasāra-vivaraṇa* that the number "fifty-one" (ka-pañcāśat) refers specifically to the fifty letters.

However, in reality, the phrase "the half of a hundred letters and *ka*" (*arṇa-śatārdhaṃ ca ka*) means "that which consists of the half of a hundred letters plus *ka*," whereby the total number of syllables arrives at fifty-one.
Alternatively, the word "half" (ardha) refers to an unequal division.
He states the ritual placement of Keśava: "having placed [the syllables] as 'Keśava'.

Those forms for which Keśava is the precursor—that is, the first—are the forms beginning with Keśava; and thus, together with these forms beginning with Keśava, they are joined with the powers beginning with Kīrti.
And the placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed with the letters of the *mātṛkā* in the aforementioned locations, beginning with the forehead, in their proper sequence.

Govinda is endowed with nourishment (puṣṭi), Viṣṇu with steadfastness (dhṛti), and Sūdana with honey (madhu) and so forth; Trivikrama is peace (śānti), Vāmana is joined with action (kriyā), and [Pradyumna] is endowed with compassion (dayā).
And *sūdana* means "the destroyer of honey" (*madhu*), that is to say, *Madhusūdana*.
Medhā is joined with Śrīdhara, and Hṛṣīkeśa is joined with Harṣā;
Ambujnābha is joined with Śraddhā, and likewise Dāmodara is joined with Lajjā.
Hṛṣīkanātha means the Lord of the senses;
Ambujanābha means the one whose navel is a lotus.
Lakṣmī with Vāsudeva; Saṅkarṣaṇa joined with Sarasvatī;
Prādyumna accompanied by Prīti; and Aniruddha with Rati—these [deities] are endowed with their respective consorts.
From *prādya* and *dyumna*, [the form] *pradyumna* is derived.
Cakrijayā, Gadidurgā, Śārṅginī endowed with splendor, Khaḍginī, Satyā, Śaṅkhinī, Caṇḍā, Halinī, Vāṇī, Musalī, Yugā, Balā, and Asiknī.
Śūlin, Vijyā, Pāśin, Virajā, Viśānvita, Ambuśī, Bhūyas, Vimada, Mukundayuktā, Nandaja, Sunandaja, Smṛti, and Nandiyuta.
Then Nara-ṛddhi, Naraka-jit, Asamṛddhi, Śuddhi, Yugha, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Buddhiyuta,
Satyayutabhakti, Matiyukta, and then Śauri.

Through *kṣamā* (patience) she is Śūrā; through *ramā* she is Janārdanī; she is the bearer of clouds and the earth (*megha-bhū-dharā*), she is the one who moistens (*kledinī*), she is endowed with the primordial form of the universe (*viśvādya-mūrti-yuktā*), she is the wet one (*klinnā*), she is united with Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise she is the giver of wealth (*vasudā*). (Kṛd 1.21)
*Kledī* means *kledinī*; it is stated thus for fear of breaking the meter (*chanda-bhaṅga*). *Viśvādimūrtiḥ* means *viśvamūrtiḥ*. // KrdC_1.18–21 //
And Puruṣottama, Vasudhā, Varā accompanied by Balānuja, Bhūyas, Parāyaṇa, Bālā, Sūkṣmā, Vṛṣaghnī, and Sandhyā. Kṛd 1.22.
Savṛṣā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Varāhī, Niśā, Vimalā, Amoghā,
Narasiṃhā, and Vidyut— these are proclaimed as the forms of the ploughs (halas), joined with their respective Śaktis.
The word division is *amogha* (unfailing) and *iti*.
He demonstrates the method for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the previously mentioned forms, such as Keśava, and powers, such as Kīrti:
having uttered the syllables together with half-moons, one places the forms and powers in front, ending with the dative case (*ṅe*) and adding the word of salutation (*nati*).
Having spoken thus, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seven elements beginning with *yā*,
as well as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and even the wrath (*krodha*) within oneself at the end.

First, having stated the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, [the author asks] what kind of letters? "Accompanied by the crescent moon," meaning with the bindu (*anusvāra*). Immediately thereafter, he mentions the forms (*mūrti*) beginning with Keśava and the powers (*śakti*) beginning with Kīrti, ending in the dative case (*ṅe*). This applies to both [the letters and the names]. However, that is not heart-grasping due to its laboriousness; therefore, for the sake of brevity: *aṃ keśavāya kīrtyai namaḥ*.

Thus, in the usage "to Keśava" (*keśavāya*), the dative case is untenable because of the absence of connection with the word *namaḥ*; for it does not occur that one says "salutation to Viṣṇu, to Sūrya" (*viṣṇave sūryāya namaḥ*).
Rather, it occurs as "salutation to Viṣṇu, salutation to Sūrya" (*viṣṇave namaḥ sūryāya namaḥ*)—and likewise, "salutation to Keśava, salutation to Kīrti."

There is the possibility of a double application [of the word] in both cases, or the particle *ca* should be supplied in both places for the purpose of indicating a conjunction (*samuccaya*), as in the expression "for prosperity and for immortality" (*sa śriye cāmṛtāya ca*). Likewise, there is the possibility of a double application of the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*) for the sake of connecting them with both [names].
However, in the usage "Oṃ, obeisance to Keśava and Kīrti," these faults do not occur, because of the force of the copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*).

Since the possibility of connecting the dative case-meaning and the possibility of connecting the phonemes (*varṇa*) arise only when [the two deities] exist in a state of association, as in the case of Agni and Soma, their status as a dual deity (*devatātva*) belongs to them while they remain associated.
How, then, is the ritual application (*kārya*) regarding the skin and so forth in the *yājyā* verses to be understood?
It is said: "Salutation to Him who is the self of the skin, by means of Puruṣottama and Vasudhā."
"Raṃ, obeisance to the blood-self with the two [syllables] 'bali' and 'parā'";
such is the form [of the mantra], because it is stated as such by the author of the *Mantramuktāvalī*.

However, in the *Prapañcasāravivaraṇa*, Paramānanda Bhaṭṭācārya states that there is no fault here because the word "ātmane" is a nipāta (indeclinable) that functions as a substitute for a case-inflected noun (*sub-anta-pratirūpaka*).

Thus, the formulation "Oṃ, obeisance to Keśava and Kīrti" is the one accepted by the authors of the *Mantramuktāvalī*, the *Laghudīpikā*, Tripāṭhī Rudropādhyāya, Vidyādharācārya, and Paramānanda Bhaṭṭācārya; whereas the formulation "Oṃ, obeisance to Keśava and to Kīrti" is the one accepted by Padmapādācārya and others.
Having understood this according to the tradition of one's own guru, [one should proceed].
"One should perform the ritual practice.

Regarding this very point, he states a specific method of deposition (*nyāsa*): "with the letters beginning with *ya*" means together with the ten syllables starting with the letter *y*; [one should deposit] the seven constituents (*dhātu*)—namely skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—with the word *ātmane antaḥ*, that is, ending with the word *ātmane*.

The meaning is that one should place those [deities] who have [the aforementioned attributes] at the end—that is, one should deposit the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and anger within oneself in their respective locations, such as the heart and so forth.
There is also an alternative reading: *prāṇaṃ śaktim* (the vital breath as power).
Regarding the meditation for the *Keśavādi* nyāsa, he says "rising," etc.:
[He is] possessed of the splendor of a hundred rising suns, white as molten gold,
and attended on both sides by the Daughter of the Ocean and the Mother of the Universe.
I bow to Viṣṇu, who is adorned with various ornaments shining with diverse jewels, who wears yellow garments, and who holds a conch, a lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, and a discus in his hands.
I bow to Viṣṇu.

Of what nature? To him whose radiance and brilliance are like that of the hundred suns rising—that is, going toward their ascent—and who is fair-complexioned like gold placed in the midst of a blazing fire.
Furthermore, of what nature was it on both sides? It was attended and served on both the right and left sides by the daughter of the ocean, Lakṣmī, as well as by Pṛthivī, the mother of the universe.
Again, of what nature was it? It was beautified by various kinds of jewels, that is, it had ornaments of many diverse types.
Furthermore, of what kind is he?
"Āpīta" means one whose garment is yellowed in a complete manner.
Furthermore, of what kind is he?
One whose hands hold these—conch (śaṅkha), lotus (padma), lily (kamala), the Kaumodakī mace (gadā), and the discus (cakra).
Here it should be understood that they are arranged in order from top to bottom, with the conch and lotus on the left side and the mace and discus on the right side. (KrdC 1.25)
He states the fruit of meditation (dhyāna) and ritual placement (nyāsa): "Having meditated thus...
Having meditated thus upon the Supreme Person, one who performs the ritual placement day by day with syllables joined to Keśava and the others;
May he be long nourished by intelligence, longevity, mindfulness, fortitude, fame, splendor, fortune, and good luck.

Having thus meditated upon Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, in the manner described, the man who daily and every day performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the letters of the alphabet accompanied by [the names] Keśava and the others, becomes for a long time—over a great duration—augmented and nourished by wisdom and the rest. Wisdom (*medhā*) is the intellect endowed with retentive power;
longevity (*āyus*) is life; memory (*smṛti*) is recollection; fortitude (*dhṛti*) is steadfastness; fame (*kīrti*) is the narration of one's excellent deeds; and splendor (*kānti*) is beauty.
Lakṣmī is sovereignty, good fortune, and being beloved by all.

He states a particular method of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the words "this very one": "The wise person who follows this very procedure, preceded by *Ramā* (the goddess Lakṣmī), shall attain [success]."
Having reached the vast expanse of the waters,
he returns once more at the end to the green [earth].

That wise man who worships according to this very method—the manner of the *nyāsa* of Keśava and others—beginning with the seed-syllable of Śrī preceded by Ramā, shall attain and obtain great and vast prosperity (*ramā*) in this world; furthermore, at the end, at the conclusion, he goes to, that is, attains, the state of Hari, meaning the nature of Viṣṇu. (KrdC 1.27)
He demonstrates the deposition of the principles (tattva-nyāsa) with the words "thus, having become Acyuta," and so forth:
"Thus, having made his body [one] with Acyuta, he should perform the deposition of the principles,
preceded by the syllable *ma* and accompanied by the obeisance (*naty*) to the supreme syllable."
May he further, for the sake of others and for himself, sequentially extract the mantras of reality from that very source until they are completely perfected.

Thus, having made his body immutable (acyutīkṛta-tanuḥ) in the manner previously described—that is, having attained the body of Viṣṇu—one should perform the deposition of the principles (tattva-nyāsa) in the manner that will be explained. He shows the method: "ma-pūrva" means that which has "ma" as its first [syllable].
"Ka-para" means that which has "ka" as its final [letter].
"Accompanied by *nati*" means accompanied by the word *namaḥ*.
Thus, each individual syllable, from the letter *ma* onwards in reverse order up to the letter *ka*, is joined with the word *namaḥ*.

Having first [uttered the syllable] *bhūyaḥ*, then having given the word *parāya*, then having given the name of those principles (*tattva*) which is to be described as non-dual (*advaya*), then having given the word *ātmane*, then having given the word *namaḥ* at the end with the suffix *-natya*, let him extract the *tattva-mantras* in their proper sequence. (KrdC 1.28)

Now he shows the names, the placement, and the locations of the principles (tattvas): the practitioner of mantra, having joined the seed-syllable and the vital breath (prāṇa) within the entire body, should place the intellect (mati), ego (ahaṅkāra), and mind (manas) in the center.

Then, [one should worship] the group of qualities preceded by the word "śabda" in the mouth, heart, secret place, and feet; and then the group beginning with the agent (kartṛ) situated in the ear and so forth.
Having joined the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the mantra that pervades the entire body and all its limbs, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with them;
the meaning is that one should place these two— namely, *maṃ namaḥ parāya jīvātmane namaḥ* and *bhaṃ namaḥ parāya prāṇātmane namaḥ*— upon the whole body.

Having thus bestowed the *tattva* word, some perform its application by saying, "Oṃ, salutation to the supreme *jīva-tattva*-self, salutation. This is not correct, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence; for if it were so, the application of the word *mūrti* would also follow in the *mūrti-pañjara-nyāsa*.
In this context, it should be understood that the addition of the nasal dot (*bindu*) to the *makara* and other signs is known through oral tradition (*sampradāya*).

Having applied the mind (*mati*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*) within the heart by means of the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should likewise perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). The meaning is that he should place these three in the heart with the following:
"Baṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the mind; Phaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the ego; Paṃ, obeisance to the supreme self of the mind. Thus one should perform the placement in the heart.

Immediately thereafter, having joined the aggregate of qualities—consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—together with sound itself into the five locations of the mouth, heart, secret place, feet, and [the head], one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by means of that mantra; thus, for example: *namaḥ parāya rūpātmane namaḥ* at the heart.
The meaning is that one should assign "thaṃ namaḥ parāya rasātmane namaḥ" to the secret place (guhya),

and "taṃ namaḥ parāya gandhātmane namaḥ" to the two feet. Thereafter, one should assign [the mantras] corresponding to the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose— which reside in the ears and so forth— to the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose.

One should place [the syllables] in such a way that they remain as they are; thus: "Ṇaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of hearing, obeisance"—on the two ears; "Ḍhaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of touch, obeisance"—on the skin; "Ḍaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme One, the essence of sight, obeisance"—on the two eyes.
One should perform the placement [of mantras] as follows: "Ṭhaṃ, obeisance to the supreme one; obeisance to the self of the tongue" on the tongue;
and "Ṭaṃ, obeisance to the supreme one; obeisance to the self of the nose" on the two nostrils. (KrdC 1.29)
Regarding "beginning with speech":

one should place the group of faculties beginning with speech in their respective abodes of the self—namely, the space [element] and so forth—in the head, the mouth, the heart, the crown of the head, and the two feet; and the lotus of the heart in the heart.

The knower of mantras should dwell in the syllables of the sun, the moon, the lord of stars, and the fires— namely two, six, eight, four, ten, and three— which pervade the [respective] digits (kalās), as well as those of the elements and the Vasus.

Having applied the pentad of organs of action—consisting of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—to the mantra, one should assign them to their respective abodes in the self: the mouth, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
Thus: "Aṃ, obeisance to the supreme one; obeisance to the self of speech" in the mouth;
"Jhaṃ, obeisance to the supreme one; obeisance to the self of the hands" in the two hands.
The meaning is that one should perform the placement (vinyāsa) as follows: with "jaṃ namaḥ parāya pādātmane namaḥ" on the two feet;
with "chaṃ namaḥ parāya pāyv-ātmane namaḥ" on the anus; and with "caṃ namaḥ parāya upasthātmane namaḥ" on the generative organ.

Having applied the group beginning with space—consisting of space, air, fire, water, and earth—to the mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, the generative organ, and the feet.
Thus: "Ṅaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self, obeisance to the space-self" on the head;
"Dhaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self, obeisance to the air-self" on the mouth.

The meaning is that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: "Gaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, salutation to the self of fire" at the heart; "Khaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, salutation to the self of water" at the *liṅga*; and "Kaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, salutation to the self of earth" at the feet.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "the heart-lotus" (*hṛt-puṇḍarīkam*) is as follows: the heart-lotus, and likewise the orbs of the fires—the mandalas of the sun, moon, and fire—arise from the rising of the sun; these three are pervaded by twelve, sixteen, and ten digits (*kalās*), because they are composed of the elements [five], the Vasus [eight], the sages [seven], and the eyes [two], which correspond to the syllables.
From the letter *ya*, take the fifth letter among the true letters (*bhūta-varṇa*), which is *śa*; the eighth letter, which is *ha*;
the seventh letter among the sages (*muni-varṇa*), which is *sa*; and the second letter among the eyes (*akṣi-varṇa*), which is *ra*.
Having joined these together in the mantra, one should place them upon the heart.
And thus: *Śaṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, who is the self of the lotus-heart;
*Haṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, who is the self of the solar disc pervaded by twelve digits;
*Saṃ*, salutation to the Supreme, who is the self of the lunar disc pervaded by sixteen digits.
One should perform the fourfold placement upon the heart with the mantra: *raṃ namaḥ parāya daśakalāvyāptavahnimaṇḍalātmane namaḥ*.

Then, for the sake of the power of the places situated in the locations beginning with space, the aspirant who seeks the goal should place the *sarvahatī-upaniṣad* upon the *parameṣṭhin* and *puruṣa*, which are the universal cessations (*viśvanivṛtti*). This is the *salāva*. (Krd 1.31)

Immediately thereafter, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables corresponding to the locations beginning with space (ākāśa), accompanied by the secret (*rahasya*) Upaniṣadic terms *parameṣṭhin*, *puruṣa*, *viśva*, *nivṛtti*, and *sarva*.

Regarding the phrase "with the six, the letter *ṣa*, the letter *ra*, and the letters of power": the letter *ṣa* [is mentioned]; and by the word "near" (*upa*), the letters *ya* and *la* situated near the letter *ra* are indicated—namely, the letter *va* and the letter *la*.
One should place these, together with the nasal dot (*salavaka*), at the respective locations.
One should assign the elements beginning with space to the places of assignment: on the head, the mouth, the heart, the genitals, and the two feet.
Regarding this very point, he states the distinction: "Vāsudeva," etc.
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Nārāyaṇa are respectively joined with Parameṣṭhin and the others. (Kṛd 1.32)

Gradually and in due order, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Vāsudeva and the others together with Parameṣṭhin and the rest; thus: "Oṃ *ṣaṃ*! Salutation to the supreme Vāsudeva, the self of Parameṣṭhin—salutation! on the head; "Oṃ *yaṃ*! Salutation to the supreme Saṅkarṣaṇa, the self of Puruṣa—salutation! on the mouth; "Oṃ *laṃ*! Salutation to the supreme Pradyumna, the self of Viśva—salutation! on the heart.
"Vaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Aniruddha, obeisance to the Self of Nivṛtti"—thus at the *liṅga*; "Laṃ, obeisance"—thus at the heart;
"Vaṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Aniruddha, obeisance to the Self of Nivṛtti"—thus at the *liṅga*.
"Laṃ, obeisance to the supreme Nārāyaṇa, the Self of all; obeisance"—this is the meaning: one should thus place [the mantra] upon the two feet.
However, some perform the application of Vāsudeva and the others immediately after Parameṣṭhin and the rest.

Then, the knower of that [method] should place the essence of *kopa* (the letter *ka*) joined with the *kṣāra* (the letter *ra*) and the *bindu* (the nasal dot), forming *nṛsiṃha*, upon all the limbs in sequence;
thus is described the placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of the principles (*tattva*).
The suffix *svā* occurs after verbal roots such as *nikṛt*, *viśvamūrti*, and others.

Then, immediately after that, in due order according to the sequence of the guru’s instruction, one who knows that— that is, one who knows the seed-syllable (bīja) of Nṛsiṃha— should join the "destructive" elements (kṣarau), namely the letter *kṣa*, the letter *r*, and the vowel *au* (forming *kṣrau*), together with the nasal drop (*bindu*), as well as the essence of wrath (*kopa-tattva*) and Nṛsiṃha, into the mantra, and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon all the limbs.
And likewise, the meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on all limbs with the mantra: *kṣrauṃ namaḥ parāya nṛsiṃhāya kopātmane namaḥ*.
He concludes the placement of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*): "In the manner described, the placement consisting of the principles has been explained.
Of what nature is it? Some say it is that which effects the presence of Kṛṣṇa in the images and so forth, such as those having the universal form (*viśva-mūrti*).
*Bimba* means an image, *pratimā* a statue, and *mūrti* a form; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of everything such as jewels, mantras, and the like.
The meaning is that Hari establishes his presence (*sānnidhya*) within these.
In some places, the reading is *kvacin martyādiṣu* ("in certain [objects] such as mortals, etc.").
He states the purpose of this nyāsa as follows: "Thus performed.
Thus performed, one certainly becomes authorized for the recitation and other rites of all Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Having joined the reality of the wind with the mantra, one should perform the reality here; this person desires to mutter the mantra.

When the *tattva-nyāsa* has been performed, one certainly and definitely becomes authorized; the meaning is that this applies not only to the recitation of mantras related to Gopāla, but also to the recitation (*japa*) and other rites of all Vaiṣṇava mantras. Now he describes the method of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), saying: "the restraint of the vital air" (*pavana-saṃyamana*).

The meaning is that this practitioner should perform—that is, carry out—restraint of the breath (prāṇāyāma), which is the control of the vital air (pavana-saṃyamana), by means of whichever mantra he desires to recite here on the plane of worldly activity.
Regarding this very point, he states another method: "Or else," [referring to] the Hari-mantras among all [mantras].

In the procedures for recitation (japa), a person of pure intellect should practice the restraint of the vital breaths (marut) according to the rule, using the root mantra and repeating it as many times as there are principles (tattvas).
"By the root mantra" means by the *mūla-mantra*; some say it refers to the ten-syllable mantra that will be described hereafter.
However, in reality, it refers to the seven-syllable *gopījana-vallabha* mantra, because that alone is designated as the *mūla-mantra*.
Since there is no other purpose for that statement, some maintain that the enumeration of the principles (tattva-saṅkhyā) occurs twenty-eight times and twenty-four times respectively. (KrdC 1.35)
The wise have prescribed that triad both before and after the recitation;
he who performs these sixteen here is a sun among men.
Indeed, within a month, that swan becomes fully perfected.
The wise have prescribed those three—namely, the three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) consisting of exhalation and so forth—at the beginning and at the end of the recitation;
some say they are the three [limbs] beginning with exhalation (recaka).
Because these are ancillaries to the recitation, this [set of three] is shown at its beginning and its end.
Sanātana says: "Before" (purataḥ), "at the beginning" (ādau), and "after" (parataḥ), "at the end" (ante)—these refer to the timing for the breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
These three constitute the number "three" for the breath-restraints.
The person who practices sixteen breath-restraints every day, that is, daily.
Month by month, he is purified from sin and evil; he becomes pure—this is the general fruit.
Furthermore, everything else has already been written above.
(Hari-bhakti-vilāsa 5.132) Right here, he states another method with the words "or else" (athavā): "Or else,
O limb, [attain] birth through this well-restrained [practice]..."
In all rites involving the recitation of the name of Kṛṣṇa,
one should practice and perform them seven times with a single repetition, which removes all sins. (Krd 1.37)

"Kṛtī" refers to the *kṛti* meter, which consists of twenty syllables; thus, "seven times *kṛtī*" means where there is one [verse] consisting of that [meter], repeated seven times. Alternatively, "seven *kṛtis*" joined together (*sahitāni*) means twenty-eight times in both cases. In all practices of reciting the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, one should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the *aṅga-janma-manu*, which is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*).
The meaning is that first there is one, then seven, then twenty, and then, upon mastery through practice, twenty-eight times.

However, some say the intended sense is that first there are seven, then twenty, then one, and then twenty-eight times by way of the sequence of practice; as for that, he alone should be questioned regarding the authority for such a view.

He describes the method of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of a specific mantra with the words "twenty-eight" (*aṣṭāviṃśati*). One of well-restrained mind should not restrain the vital air while reciting a ten-syllable mantra twenty-eight times, which yields the desired fruit; however, if [the goal is] eight [restraints], one should do so with the ten-syllable mantra.

Practicing without interruption, a man who is not distracted should perform the application of the vital breath (prāṇa-yoga), preceded by exhalation (recaka), while muttering another [mantra] according to its syllables. Krd 1.38.

One of firm resolve and pure intellect, while reciting the ten-syllable mantra consisting of twenty-eight counts, should offer [the breath] and perform *prāṇāyāma*. What kind of ten-syllable [mantra]? One that grants desired fruits—that is, one that grants the fruit according to one's own intention.
In that regard, by reciting the ten-syllable mantra four times, there is exhalation (*recaka*).
The traditional teaching of the Guru is that one should perform *pūraka* (inhalation) with eight recitations and *kumbhaka* (retention) with sixteen recitations.
The remaining point is that if the *prāṇāyāma* is performed with an eighteen-syllable mantra,
then according to the traditional teaching of the Guru, one should perform the *prāṇāyāma* by practicing twelve recitations on Sundays.
If the breath control (prāṇāyāma) is performed with different mantras than those previously mentioned,
then one should perform the recitation (japa) according to the syllables, in accordance with the relative length of the mantra-syllables.
The meaning here is that one should recite many times with mantras of few syllables, and few times with mantras of many syllables.
Of what sort? A practitioner (*sādhaka*), meaning one skilled in the practices known as exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*).
Regarding this, Rudradhara states that "those who are proficient in those two—the inhalation and retention—which are the preliminary actions for exhalation, which is the act of abandonment."

This [objection] is indeed to be considered; for even so, because skill in *recaka* (exhalation) has not been attained, and because this work follows the *Prapañcasāra*, it conforms to the texts of Śāradā. (KrdC 1.38)
Now he shows the method of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the words "one should exhale the wind": one should exhale the wind through the right [nostril],
fill [the lungs] through the left, and again through the middle channel (madhya-nāḍī).
One should maintain the three [breath-controls] beginning with exhalation as described; they consist of the measures (mātrā) known as Kalā, Danta, and Vidyā.

A skillful and discerning person should exhale—meaning release—the vital air (māruta) through the right channel (dakṣiṇa-nāḍī) by means of skill (dakṣayā); likewise, he should inhale—that is, fill—the released air through the left channel (vāma-nāḍī), and hold the vital air through the central channel (suṣumṇā). In this manner, the triad known as exhalation and so forth—namely the threefold set called *recaka*, *pūraka*, and *kumbhaka*—is proclaimed and explained.
He states the limit of time for the exhalations (recaka) and so forth: "until sixteen and thirty-two. There are sixteen *kalās* and thirty-two teeth (*danta*).
The meaning is that the *vidyās* consist of sixty-four forms, which signifies that they are composed of that same number of *mātrās*.

Regarding this, Bhairava Tripāṭhin states: where *prāṇāyāma* is performed by counting mantras, the time for the *kumbhaka* alone is specified; in that case, one should perform the recitation of the mantra according to the count of the *prāṇāyāmas* through the process of breath practice. However, he says that in the case of exhalation (*recaka*), the counting of the exhalations and so forth should be performed.

By the word *mātra*, the time for touching each of the three joints of the fingers beginning with the little finger on the left thumb is indicated, as well as the time for touching the circle of the left knee clockwise with the left hand.

Regarding this, Rudropādhyāya has stated: "Although exhalation (*recaka*) is mentioned first here and inhalation (*pūraka*) immediately after it, nevertheless, inhalation should be understood as first and retention (*kumbhaka*) as subsequent."

Since there is a relinquishing of that which has been grasped as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), that which is stated in reverse order is for the sake of concealment; thus, even [the sequence] *kalā*, *danta*, and so forth, should be understood in reverse order. This is because of the view of the *Śāradā* Tantra, which states: "One should draw up the wind through the *iḍā*," and so on.

Thus, it is also shown that retention (*dhāraṇa*) occurs with four counts held and release (*tyāga*) with half of that; however, this is not so, because this text follows the *Prapañcasāra*, which adheres to the tradition of Śāradā, and since the *Prapañcasāra* speaks only of exhalation (*recaka*) and so forth, whereas inhalation (*pūraka*) and so forth pertain to breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) as included within the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*).
Regarding what was said—that there is a release of what has been held—it is replied that here too, the natural holding of the breath is intended.
Otherwise, [the body] would fall [to pieces] due to its being composed of the elements (*sattva*).
As for the statement that the teaching was given in reverse order for the sake of concealment, that is incorrect;
for it is appropriate to explain the portion concerning the ritual practice (*anuṣṭhāna*) that is distinct from the mantra by way of the straightforward path alone.
As for what was stated—that retention is performed by holding [the breath] with four fingers and release with half of that—that too is incorrect due to a lack of authoritative evidence.
Furthermore, a restriction regarding the fingers in *prāṇāyāma* is also taught in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, as follows:
"The holding of the nostril-passage with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb..."
"That is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*, excluding the index finger and the middle finger. (KrdC 1.39)
Sanātana, corroborating that very point with the statement from the *Kramadīpikā*, shows a certain distinction therein with the words "one should exhale" (*recayet*).
By "the right" (*dakṣayā*), he means by the right channel (*dakṣiṇa-nāḍyā*); "the right person" (*dakṣaḥ*) refers to a wise man (*vidvān janaḥ*).
One should hold [the breath] through the central channel, the *suṣumṇā*.

In this way, there are three [stages] known as exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*). Regarding these three—exhalation and so forth—he states the duration for each in sequence: sixteen *kalās*.
The teeth are thirty-two;
the sciences are sixty-four; the meaning is that [the mantra] consists of that many *mātrās*.
A *mātrā* is the duration of contact with each of the three joints of the fingers, starting from the left little finger up to the thumb.
Or it is the time of touching the circle of the left knee with the left hand while moving clockwise;
regarding that as well, a restriction of the fingers has been stated: "The holding of the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb."
"That is to be known as *prāṇāyāma* when [performed] without the index and middle fingers.
Thus, in those aforementioned *prāṇāyāmas*, the number was stated for the exhalations (*recaka*) and so forth;
however, the distinction here is that it refers to "these *prāṇāyāmas*."
[In *Hari-bhakti-vilāsa* 5.131],

concluding the subject at hand, he demonstrates the conceptualization of the *pīṭha* within the body for the purpose of the sacrifice of the self, beginning with the words "having performed *prāṇāyāma*":
"Having performed *prāṇāyāma*, one should then conceive of the *yoga-pīṭha* by means of one's own body."

One should assign the Foundation Power (Ādhāra-śakti), Primordial Nature (Prakṛti), the Tortoise, the Earth, the Ocean of Milk, and Śvetadvīpa; then the Great Pavilion, resplendent with jewels and honored by the Great One, and the Kalpa-tree— furthermore, in the region of the heart, in the two shoulders, the two thighs, the two faces, and the pair of sides of the waist.
One should place dharma and so forth, as well as adharma and so forth, upon the four limbs beginning with the feet; then, in the heart, the remaining mantra,
together with the sun, moon, and fire joined with the portions of the *praṇava*.
The qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas are [revealed] by the vowels that are to be tasted.

Having thus performed *prāṇāyāma* in the manner previously described, immediately thereafter, one should fashion the sacrificial pedestal (*yāga-pīṭha*), that is, the seat of worship (*pūjā-pīṭha*), with one’s own body, one’s own physical form. He states the method of this mental construction as follows: "One should install" (*nyased*).
One should install [the deities] in the region of the heart, from the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*) up to the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpa-vṛkṣa*).

Kamaṭha is the tortoise, Śeṣa is Ananta, and the Kṣīra-sindhu is the Ocean of Milk; that great pavilion (mahā-maṇḍapa) which is resplendent with jewels is the "Jewel-Pavilion" (ratna-maṇḍapa). Thus, one should place the ninefold [set] in the heart, meaning: "Obeisance to the Support-Energy (ādhāra-śakti)," and "Obeisance to Prakṛti."
Immediately thereafter, one should place the four limbs and members—beginning with Dharma and beginning with Adharma—upon the two shoulders, the two raised faces, and the pair of hips and sides.
The term "four limbs and members" (*pāda-gātra-catuṣṭayam*) is to be connected to both [the shoulders and the faces].
The "four limbs" (*pāda-catuṣṭayam*) and the "four members" (*gātra-catuṣṭayam*) refer to the four limbs consisting of the forms of Dharma, Knowledge, Dispassion, and Sovereignty (*dharmādi*).
One should place [the syllables] on the two shoulders and on the two upper arms with "Homage to Dharma," and on the right thigh;
thus one should arrange them in a clockwise sequence,
because the *Śāradā-tilaka* shows the order as being on the face, the sides, and the sides of the navel.
And this is also the view of Bhairava Tripāṭhin.
Regarding these [mantras], the Vidyādhara Ācāryas maintain that they follow the very order in which they were heard.
Immediately thereafter follows the remainder: Ananta, the lotus (abja), the sun, moon, and fire—the solar, lunar, and fiery mandalas.
Of what sort? They are joined with the parts of the *praṇava*. The "parts" (*aṃśāḥ*) of the *praṇava*, which is the syllable *oṃ*, are its components:

the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*. They are joined with, or accompanied by, these. In this context, one should understand from the tradition that they are initially accompanied by the *praṇava* part together with the nasal bindu (*anusvāra*).

Together with the initial letters of each [element] accompanied by the bindu—that is, their respective first letters—the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are thus [represented]. And so, in the heart-lotus: *anantāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Ananta).
Salutation to Padma;
aṃ, salutation to the self of the solar maṇḍala pervaded by twelve kalās; uṃ, salutation to the self of the lunar maṇḍala pervaded by sixteen kalās.
Maṃ, obeisance to the one whose nature is the fire-maṇḍala pervaded by ten digits;
saṃ, obeisance to sattva; raṃ, obeisance to rajas.
Homage to that Tamasā. KṛdC 1.40–41.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the triad beginning with the Self (ātman) together with the seed-syllable of the Self, using portions of ether, fire, and māyā; and having likewise placed the Knower of Wisdom (jñānātmā) in the eight directions surrounding the center, as well as the nine Śaktis in the middle; one should then duly place the seat-mantra (pīṭha-anu) there, situated in the center of its pericarp.
One should contemplate that which is named the immortal, the eternal bliss, consciousness, and light.
The triad beginning with the Self—namely the Self (ātman), the Inner Self (antarātman), and the Supreme Self (paramātman)—is the object to be characterized.

Of what nature is it? The Vidyādhara Ācāryas maintain that it is "accompanied by the primordial seed" (*ādi-bīja-sahita*), meaning accompanied by its own respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the form of their initial letters, together with the nasal bindu (*sa-bindu*).
The Tripāṭhins, however, hold that "the primordial" (*ādi*) refers to the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), and that [the triad] is accompanied by that.
The sky is the letter *ha*;
fire is the *repha*;
and *māyā* is the long *ī*.
*Lava* is the *bindu*.
Together with these, one should place the *jñānātman* (the self of knowledge), accompanied by the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī, in the heart-lotus; this is the connection with what precedes.
Thus: *Āṃ, obeisance to the Self*.
Aṃ, salutation to the inner self (antarātman). Paṃ, salutation to the supreme self (paramātman). Hrīṃ, salutation to the self of knowledge (jñānātman).
Thus one should place [the mantra] in the heart.
Immediately thereafter, one should place the nine Śaktis, beginning with Vimalā and Utkarṣiṇī, in a clockwise direction throughout the eight directions and in the center upon the pericarp (karṇikā).
On the filaments (kesara) of the lotus, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, [one should say]: "Salutation to Vimalā."
Homage to Utkarṣiṇī.
Homage to Jñānā. Homage to Kriyā. Homage to Yogā.
Homage to Prahvā. Homage to Satyā.
Homage to Īśānā.
One should place [the mantra] "namo 'nugrahāyai" upon the pericarp (karṇikā),
and the seat-mantra (pīṭha-mantra) should also be placed there.

Upon this, one should place the seat-mantra (pīṭha-mantra) to be spoken hereafter: "Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed Viṣṇu, the self of all beings, Vāsudeva; salutation to the self of the seat which is the simultaneous union of all selves. One should meditate upon that abode, the consciousness of Brahman well-known in all the Upaniṣads, on the seat of the aforementioned form, according to the rules and by the path taught by the Guru.
Of what nature is it? It means situated in the center of its pericarp, that is, located in the middle of the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
Having described the form useful for this meditation, he states its innate (svābhāvika) form.
Of what nature is it? "Eternal" (nitya) means indestructible consciousness, whose essential nature is self-luminous.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It means that it is the nectar, which is the pure essential nature (*śuddha-svarūpa*).
In that [state], all mantras, beginning with the Support-Power (*ādhāra-śakti*), reside.
The mantras should be understood according to tradition as beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ), ending in the dative case, and concluding with *namaḥ*.
He shows the powers of the seats (pīṭha-śaktis):
"Vimalā, Utkarṣaṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā are the powers; likewise Prahvī, Satyā, Īśānā, and the ninth is Anugrā. (Krd 1.43)
"Purification" (vimalā). // KrdC_1.43 //
He extracts the *pīṭha*-mantra with the words beginning with "the *tāra*" and so forth:

"In this way, the heart is the Lord Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings, accompanied by all; [the names] ending in the dative case (ṅe) along with Vāsudeva, joined with the word 'sarvātman', and the conjunction. (Kṛd 1.44)
The syllable following the yoga-limit is *padma*, followed by the locative case-ending *-ṅe* and a prostration (*nati*) at the end;
this is the manifest Great Mantra of the Seat (*pīṭha*), which is sufficient for all rites of worship.
*Tāra* is *praṇava* (OM);
*hṛdayam* is *namaḥ*;
and "Bhagavān" as well as "Viṣṇu" are accompanied by all [the preceding terms], joined with every word, ending with "Bhūtātmā," meaning the Self of all beings.

These three, together with Vāsudeva—making four including Vāsudeva—should each be formed with the dative case-ending (ṅe). Furthermore, there is the "union with the Universal Self" (*sarvātma-yuta*), which is the essential form *sarvātma-saṃyoga*. At the limit of the yoga, following the word "yoga," the essential forms are "padma-padma. Then follows the "Self of the Seat" (*pīṭhātmā*) joined with the dative ending, i.e., the Self of the Seat in the dative case;
at the end of this is the salutation, the word *namaḥ*.
"He brings forth the *pīṭha*" means that this *pīṭha-mahāmantra* has been stated or taught.
Of what nature is it? It is sufficient—that is, capable—for *saparyās*, which are acts of worship (*pūjā*). // KrdC_1.44-45 //
Sanātana says: "Tāra" is the Praṇava;
then the word "hṛdayaṃ namaḥ"; and then "bhagavān" and "viṣṇuḥ."
"Pervaded by all" (*sarvānvitaḥ*) means "endowed with all words" (*sarva-śabda-yuktaḥ*), and "the self of beings" (*bhūtātmā*) means "the self of all beings" (*sarva-bhūtātmā*).
These three, together with Vāsudeva—meaning accompanied by Vāsudeva—are each in the dative case (ending in *ṅe*).
Consequently, the neuter form *sarvātma-saṃyogam* ("union with the self of all") is used because it is joined with [the word] *sarvātmanā*; this neuter usage is an archaic (Vedic) feature.
And then, at the conclusion of the yoga, there is the "lotus," meaning the yoga-lotus (*yoga-padma*).
At the end of that is the word for the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), ending in the dative case (marked by *ṅe*).
And at the end of that is the salutation, the word *namaḥ*.
Thus, it is established: "Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, the self of all beings, Vāsudeva, the self of the lotus-throne of the yoga of union with the self of all; salutation.
And likewise in the Śāradā-tilaka:
"One should say 'Salutation to the Blessed One,' and then utter the word 'Viṣṇu'."
Then one should say, "To Vāsudeva, the self of all beings."
"Then, from the word *sarvātmasaṃyoga*, the word *yogapadma* follows; this mantra, beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *hṛt* (namaḥ), is said to be for the *pīṭha*-self.
Thus it is stated in the Sanatkumāra-kalpa.
Having uttered the word *oṃ namaḥ*, and likewise the word *bhagavate*,
having spoken the word *vāsudevāya*, and similarly the word *sarvātmane*.
Having uttered "saṃyogayoga," one likewise utters the word for the self of the seat (pīṭhātmane);
joined with the wife of fire (svāhā), this is declared to be the seat-mantra (pīṭha-mantra).
Thus [Ha.bha.vi. 5.144-5].
He demonstrates the purification of the hands with the words beginning "of the two hands," having arranged the pair of hands.
From the path being contemplated as consisting of mantra,
one should effect with the syllables of the mantra that entire,
supreme, and unsurpassed light of Hari.

Having pervaded the pair of hands according to the method to be described— beginning from "having pervaded" up to the end of the rule "in the hand"— one should, by means of the syllables of the mantra in the manner that will be stated,

fashion (vidhāya) and create (kṛtvā) the nature of the mantra (mantrātmaka), which is the essence of the mantra; then, with these two hands, [one should perform] everything previously mentioned and to be mentioned.
And one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*), worship (*pūjā*), and so forth;
he states the reason for the purification of the syllables of the mantra by means of the letter *ka* with the words "the supreme," etc.
The meaning is that the syllables of that mantra are the supreme nature of the splendor (*tejas*) of Hari Kṛṣṇa.
Of what nature is it? Furthermore, "unsurpassed" (anuttama) means that there is nothing superior to it; such is the meaning.
The phrase "one should perform the whole" (sakalaṃ vidadhīta) should also be applied to the subsequent part according to the maxim of the crow's eye (the single pupil serving both sockets).

Thus, the author of the *Laghudīpikā* explains: "One should make that unsurpassed light—the splendor (*tejas*) of Hari—residing in the lotus of the heart, 'whole' (*sakala*), that is, endowed with parts, by means of the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa*)."
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Kramadīpikā* composed by the venerable Keśavācārya.

**The Second Chapter** In order to extract the mantra indicated by the words "having placed the pair of hands," etc., [the author] first praises the ten-syllable and eighteen-syllable mantras, which are the foremost among the Gopāla-mantras: "I shall speak..."
"Manum":
I shall speak of Manu, whose nature is renowned throughout the three worlds,
and who is sought after by sages possessing an undiminished store of merit.
It has the lord of birds as its emblem, bestows wealth, virtue, desire,
and liberation, and is skilled in performing all ritual actions.
I shall speak and extract the mantra.
Of what kind? It is one whose majesty—that is, its power—is celebrated and renowned throughout the three worlds.
Furthermore, of what kind?
It is that which is to be sought after, to be investigated, by sages desiring liberation.
By what kind of sages?
By those whose accumulation of merit—that is, the collection of well-performed deeds—is unexhausted and complete.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is "pakṣīndra-ketu," meaning that which has the Lord of Birds, Garuḍa, as its emblem (ketu) or insignia; that is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the work concerns Him—that is, it expounds upon Him.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?

"Vastu" means "vasu," which is wealth; thus, the meaning is that it bestows the fourfold aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "sakala," meaning skillful in bringing all [actions] under its control without exception. (KrdC 2.1)
This most secret [teaching] is like a fire for the heap of cotton that is ignorance; it bestows sovereignty of speech upon men,
removes misfortune, and destroys poison and untimely death.
The sole cause for warding off planetary influences, diseases, and other such afflictions.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is extremely secret.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
"Abodha" means ignorance, which is of the nature of false knowledge; that itself is a mass of cotton-wool.
In this context, "blazing" means like fire, which destroys all ignorance;
what is it further like?
It bestows upon men—that is, upon practitioners—the sovereignty of speech, granting mastery over words.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is the remover of misfortune, meaning that which wards off the undesirable things that bring about suffering.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?

It is the sole, peerless cause and means for warding off such inauspicious things as stationary and mobile poisons, untimely death, premature demise, the malefic influence of the nine planets, and diseases consisting of physical ailments produced by wind, bile, and so forth. (KrdC 2.2)
It bestows victory in battle, grants fearlessness in the forest,
provides easy deliverance when crossing on water,
and increases men, horses, chariots, and elephants.
[He bestows] sons, cattle, land, wealth, and grain.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It bestows victory in the great battle;
in the forest, it grants fearlessness, removing all dread.

In a flood of water, it provides water for crossing; in a forest, it grants a means for easy passage. Likewise, the horse is the provider of growth for men, as well as for chariots, elephants, and other vehicles;
it bestows sons and other blessings, and produces an abundance of strength, heroism, valor, intelligence, excellent voice, complexion, luster, and good fortune.
It is the jewel of ten million cosmic eggs, the bestower of the eight primary qualities; what more need be said? It is the subduer of all.
*Balam* is bodily capacity; *vīryam* is semen or power;
*śauryam* is the splendor that overcomes others;
the collection (*nicaya*) of these is their aggregate.
*Pratibhā* is the intellect in the form of intuitive flash; *svara* is sound;
*varṇa* is [complexion] such as whiteness and so forth;
*kānti* is luster. Thus, *pratibhā-svara-varṇa-kānti* is a single compound word, and likewise, there is *pratibhā-svara-varṇa-kānti*.
"Resplendent with the beauty of his complexion" means that he is the one who causes their good fortune— that is, the one who makes them worthy of the respect of all the world— and thus the giver.
Furthermore, "by whom the millions of shaken and agitated cosmic eggs [were stirred]" means that he is the one who deludes the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).

Furthermore, "bestowing the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇimā*" means bestowing the eight qualities known as *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *garimā*, *mahimā*, *īśitva*, *vaśitva*, *prākāmya*, and *prāpti*.
Furthermore, what more need be said?
"Bestowing everything in this world" means bestowing all desired objects. // KrdC_2.4 //
Now, he extracts the king of mantras consisting of ten syllables with the verse beginning "Śārṅgī," and so forth:
"Śārṅgī, he who has curved tusks (A), the letter beyond [the first] (Ū), joined with the eye of Rāmā (Ī)—this is the second syllable;
Śūlin (E), Sauri (S), Bāla (B), and the two following Balānuja (M and A)—these are then the four syllables. (Krd 2.5)
The fourth [letter] is Śūra, followed by Sānana; it is Āvṛtta, Suśobha, and the eighth is Agnisakha.
Having extracted that pair of syllables beloved by him, one should likewise extract the mantra situated above that. (Kṛd 2.6)

The letter *ga* is [the word] *śārṅgī*. Of what nature is this? It is accompanied by the upper tooth (*sottaradanta*). Being placed in the row of upper teeth, the upper tooth is the vowel *o*; together with that, the first syllable is extracted. The letter *pa* is *śūra*. Of what nature is this? It is joined with the left eye (*vāmākṣiyuk*). The left eye is the fourth vowel; together with that, the second syllable is extracted.

The four syllables are stated again in sequence: the "thorn" (śūlin) is the letter *ja*; the "child" (bāla) is the letter *ba*; the two younger brothers of Bala (the letters *la*) joined with two *la*s form the essential nature *lla*. Thus the four syllables are extracted; "the fourth of the hero" (*śūra-turīya*) refers to the fourth [consonant] of the hero, which is the letter *pa*.
What is this "sānanavṛtta"? It is that which exists together with the form of the *ānanavṛtta*; thus, it is the seventh [syllable] of the mantra, meaning it becomes the seventh of the mantra.
The eighth is the wind, the friend of fire—that is to say, the letter *ya*.
Accordingly, it should be understood that the eighth phoneme of the mantra is *ya*.

Above that, the pair of syllables of his beloved, distinguished by the sequence of colors previously mentioned, together with the two syllables *svāhā* as their essential form—thus are the two syllables extracted. (KrdC 2.5–6)
It has been revealed:
"This ten-syllable mantra of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) has been made manifest;
it especially increases devotion to His pair of lotus feet. (Krd 2.7)

This ten-syllable mantra of Śrī Gopālaka, the enemy of Madhu, has been extracted. Of what nature is it? Specifically, it is especially a promoter of devotion to the pair of lotus feet; the meaning is that it causes the increase of that devotion—understood as the knowledge of Him as the object of worship—toward the pair of lotus feet of Śrī Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. (KrdC 2.7)
He shows the seer and other [components] of the mantra: "Nārada" means that the sage of this [mantra] is celebrated as Nārada; the meter is stated by the sages to be Virāj.
The son of Nanda-gopa, who brings auspiciousness to all the worlds and to the deities, has been proclaimed.
The sage (ṛṣi) of this aforementioned mantra is proclaimed and declared to be Nārada;
the meter (chandas) is said to be Virāṭ by the sages such as Gautama and others;
and the deity is said to be Śrī Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the son of the cowherd Nanda.
Of what nature is he? He is the auspiciousness of all the worlds, the cause of the welfare of all people.
By this, it is indicated in the *Prapañcasāra* that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed on the head, the tongue, and the heart of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and others respectively;
for such is the injunction, and the practical application (*prayoga*) of the ten-syllable Gopāla mantra is as follows: "Obeisance to the seer Nārada" on the head.
"Salutation to the Virāṭ meter at the mouth;
salutation to the deity Śrī Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa at the heart"—thus is [the mantra].
Of this mantra, Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi).
Some maintain that this should be applied in the same way to *chanda* and the deity as well.

Now he shows the five limbs of this mantra with the words beginning "the limbs": "The five limbs [are formed] by the wheels accompanied by the beloved of the consumer of oblations (Agni), which are appropriately placed upon the mouth, the circle, and the rest."
And here, those [names] called Trailokyarakṣaṇayuja and Asurāntaka,
along with the preceding one, have been stated with their case-endings applied.
"Namah" at the heart, "Śivāya" (the beloved of Agni) with "Vaṣaṭ" at the head, "Hūm" situated at the armor,
and "Phaṭ" as the weapon— thus the five limbs are declared.
If [the mantra] ending with the fourth case and the word *vauṣaṭ* is uttered at the eyes; // Krd_2.10 //

In this scripture, five limbs (aṅgas) of that [mantra] are taught. What are they? Regarding this, it says: "Bowing in the heart. This means that "bowing in the heart" is the word *namaḥ*; "on the head, the beloved of Pāvaka" is *svāhā* together with *vaṣaṭ*, meaning the *śikhā* limb accompanied by the word *vaṣaṭ*.
"Hum" means "also situated in the armor," that is, in the *kavaca*; "hum" also means "situated in the foot.
