"Sa-phaṭ" means the weapon-mantra (*astra*) accompanied by the word "phaṭ. In this manner, the five limbs (*aṅga-pañcaka*) are declared and described so as to be with the dative case; and with the dative case, the application of the heart and the other limbs must be performed.
With what [discs]? With discs that possess the sounds "cakra.

Of what kind? Those endowed individually with "mukha," "vṛtta," "vi," and "su"—that is, endowed with these as their respective forms. Even though it is engaged in the protection of the three worlds, [it is] the protection of the three worlds... by means of those [discs].
Because it joins [them], it is called *yuga*; thus, even with such a *cakra*, one should perform the syntactical connection by varying it as "with *cakras*" due to the word "api.
And so, "with the *cakra*" means with the one previously mentioned called Asurāntaka.
And [the word] "ca" (and) is used as a conjunction.
Furthermore, by what kind [of words]? By those joined with case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Since the fourth case (*caturthī*) is the one under discussion, the connection of this word must also be analyzed separately: "if there is a placement of the two *dṛś* [words] in some mantra. If, in a certain mantra, there is a placement of the two *dṛś* [words], then in that case—
"Vauṣaṭ" is uttered;
it is said that here the phrase "to the wheel of flames" (jvālā-cakrāya) should also be joined, according to the author of the *Laghudīpikā*.
And the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: "To the wheel, svāhā! To the heart, namaḥ!"
Svāhā to the wheel of expansion; svāhā to the head; svāhā to the excellent wheel; vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
svāhā to the wheel that protects the three worlds; huṃ to the armor; svāhā to the wheel of flames; vauṣaṭ to the two eyes; svāhā to the wheel that destroys the asuras; phaṭ to the weapon.

Regarding the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limb-mantras (*aṅga-mantra*) upon the fingers, at the end of each respective limb-mantra, one should apply: "Oṃ [mantra] to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; to the two index fingers, *svāhā*," and so forth.
In another scripture (*āgama*), it is stated: "Hrīṃ to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; Hrīṃ to the two index fingers, *svāhā*."

Because of the observation of the word "tataḥ" and so forth, some maintain that the applications such as "to the heart, namaḥ" (hṛdayāya namaḥ) and so on should be considered for the thumb and other limbs, since they do not denote a meaning inherent [in those limbs] and because there is a lack of authoritative evidence. Others, however, say that the teachers [hold] that by means of the ritual placements (nyāsa), the mantra for the limbs as heard in the text itself is extended (atideśa) to the fingers. KrdC 2.9–10.
He shows the ten limbs:
the set of ten limbs is proclaimed as being endowed with the ten mantra-syllables, each accompanied by a crescent moon, and ending with "namas."
Then, one should apply the mantras for the heart, head, crest, armor, the two sides, the hips, the back, and the top of the head.

The ten limbs are proclaimed and described as being accompanied by the syllables of the mantra, ending with "namas," joined with the crescent moon (the anusvāra). They say the locations are: the heart, the head, the crown of the head, and after that, the well-known crest-lock (śikhā), the armor (tanutra or kavaca), and the weapon (astra) in the ten directions, together with the two sides, the waist, the back, and the top of the head.
The meaning is "as previously stated.
According to those who follow the three-part recension (*tripāṭhin*), the *kaṭi* (waist) is below the navel.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is: *goṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *pīṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth. (KrdC 2.11)

Now, with the words "I shall speak," and so forth, he demonstrates the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the power (*śakti*), the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-devatā*), the nature (*prakṛti*), and the application (*viniyoga*) of this mantra:
"I shall speak the seed of this mantra;
[it is] *cakrī* or *śakrī*, ignited by the left eye."
This is taught as the seed-mantra of Sa-Pradyumna;
this Mantra-Pradyumna is the deluder of the world.

I shall state the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of this previously mentioned mantra, together with its powers (*śakti*), the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), and so forth. He states the seed-syllable: "Cakrī" refers to the letter *ka*.
Of what nature is this? It is joined with "Śakrī," where "Śakra" is the letter *la*. Furthermore, of what nature is it?
"Blazing with the left eye" means accompanied by the left eye, which is the fourth vowel;
furthermore, of what nature is it?
"With Pradyumna"—Pradyumna is the bindu—and thus it is established as being "with Cakrī."
This is declared to be his seed-syllable;
the meaning is that this very mantra is Prādyumna.
Of what nature is it? It is the deluder of the world and the subjugator of the universe. (KrdC 2.12)
He speaks of the power (śakti): "Haṃsa.
Haṃsa is the fat (medas), endowed with a curved movement;
that [power] is the boar (potrī), possessed of eyes and so forth, consisting of four syllables.
She is declared by all the hosts of gods to be Śakti,
the beloved of Agni, who grants the desires of her worshippers.
The *haṃsa* is the syllable *sa*.

Of what nature is it? It is joined with and connected to the *medas*, which is the syllable *va*, and the *vaktravṛtta*, which is the syllable *ā*; likewise, there is the *pautrī*, which is the syllable *ha*.
Of what nature is it? It is endowed with the *netrādi*, which is the syllable *ā*.

And thus, "svāhā" is established; this power (śakti), consisting of two syllables, is said to have four phonemes (yugārṇa). Likewise, she is the beloved of Fire. Of what nature is she? She is the "bestower of desires," granting whatever is wished for. Of what kind of Fire? Of him who is to be "venerated by the hosts of gods," that is, worshipped by the assemblies of all the deities. (KrdC 2.13)
He states the application: "As for application"—
in the case of the mantra's application toward the four aims of human life,
Kṛṣṇa is said to be the *prakṛti* (primordial nature), and Durgā is the presiding deity.
The meaning is that this mantra is applied (*viniyoga*) for the sake of accomplishing the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) means the fundamental cause, the producer of the mantra, or the very essence of the mantra. He states the presiding deity: "the presiding deity of Durgā. (KrdC 2.14)
He states the meaning of the mantra with the words beginning "gopāyati" (she protects):
she is called *gopī* because she protects this entire world, protecting the Supreme Person (*para-pumān*).
That which is born from that *prakṛti* is *jana*, consisting of the elements beginning with water and ending with earth.

This [word] "gopāla" means that which protects (*gopāyati*) and guards this entire world, differentiated by name and form, because it is its cause; here the suffix *āya* is used in its own sense (denoting the agent).
Likewise, it "protects" the Supreme Person, whose nature is Brahman—eternally pure, awakened, and consisting of spoken bliss and non-duality;

according to the etymology of the root *gup* in the senses of protecting and censuring, it refers to that which takes as its object [Brahman] through the state of being unknown, [extending] from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the earth.
The entire collection of effects, beginning with the principle of Mahat and ending with earth, is called "the person" (jana).
The light that is dense bliss and untainted, which has taken refuge in these two cowherd women through its pervasive movement by means of the wind, is taught as the Beloved.
"By *svāhā*, I cause myself to go"—this [is for] that which is not the radiance;
he who is the Lord of cause and effect, the Supreme Self—such is the mind of this Acyuta, whose oneness is with the Unfallen. (Kṛd 2.17)

Because He is the inner controller (antaryāmin) who impels and governs these two cowherd women— along with their ignorance and its effects— by means of His own activity, and because He is their refuge, presiding over them through His pervasion as the all-encompassing one, He is taught and declared to be their Beloved Lord.
The supreme light is the consciousness of Brahman.
Of what nature is that light?
Its singular essential nature is intense bliss, the unsurpassed bliss.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?

It is "nirañjana," free from the turbidity of *māyā*. "Svāhā" means: I cause my own self—the individual soul (*jīva*) in its singular essence—to go toward, to be offered to, and to attain identity with that Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is one's own splendor (*svatejas*) and whose nature is self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśacidrūpa*). This is the meaning of the word *svāhā*.
The first word "iti" serves to introduce the word "svāhā," while the second "iti" indicates the manner [of the offering]. To the question "to whom? it says: "to him who... (yaḥ).

He who is the Lord, the Master, and the Sustainer of cause and effect, as well as of the people and their natures— namely, the Supreme Self (paramātman) because of His being consciousness free from limiting adjuncts— in this manner, for this worshiper, there arises oneness with Acyuta, that is, non-difference from Acyuta.
He states the meaning in another way: "Or else" (*athavā*).

Or else, "the Gopī-jana" refers to the entire collection of powers (*śakti*) of the forest of the whole world; its Lord (*svāmī*), who is non-different from Himself, is indicated as the Beloved (*vallabha*). (Krd 2.18)

Alternatively, by the term *gopījana*, the entire collection of powers for protecting the whole universe is expressed. Therein, the word *gopī* denotes power (*śakti*), and the word *jana* denotes its multitude.

The meaning is that, because of the intended non-difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), the Lord— who is non-different from and not distinct from that collection of powers— is clearly designated and declared as the "ruler," the "controller," the "substratum," and the "beloved. The meaning of the word *svāhā*, however, should be understood exactly as previously stated.

The author of the *Laghudīpikā*, however, explains: "The collection of powers for preservation (*avana*); 'preservation' means stability; therein, the 'collection of powers' refers to the assemblage of causal powers, such as the group beginning with Jagatpālinī.

And it has been stated by the great ones: "Those [powers] beginning with Jagatpālinī are declared to be the *kalās* for the sake of stability. The meaning is that its master is the leader (*nāyaka*). (KrdC 2.18)
He states the meaning by way of another method: "Or else (*athavā*)":

"Or else, for the sake of the beloved of the young women of Vraja, I offer myself and my own [possessions] as well; thus one should offer everything into the Brahman, which is the assembly of the wise, for the attainment of all prosperity. (Krd 2.19)

The *gopī-jana*—the community of cowherd women—is his beloved, the object of his unsurpassed love; for him, the lover of the young women of Vraja, the cowherd beauties, the giver of joy to their hearts, I offer myself with the cry of *svāhā*.

What of myself? And what of my own friends and others? In this manner, one should surrender everything to the Supreme Lord of lords, the Brahman-with-attributes who sets the cycle of worldly existence in motion.
For what purpose? For the sake of all prosperity and for the attainment of all sovereignty. (KṛdC 2.19)
In order to extract the mantra of eighteen syllables, he first analyzes and demonstrates the two words *kṛṣṇa* and *govinda*, which are contained within it, beginning with the word *kṛṣ*:
"The word *kṛṣ* has the meaning of existence (*sattā*), and *ṇa* consists of bliss; therefore, [the name] is *kṛṣṇa*."
Because he draws away the sins of his devotees and because his body consists of mantras, he possesses that very color.
Because he is the denoter of the word "cow" (go), Govinda is known through that [word];
because he knows the mass of words, he is Govinda.
And also from the tending of cows. (Kṛd 2.21)
The word *kṛṣ* has the meaning of "existence" (*sattā*). It is capable [of expressing that] there.
Some maintain that in the rule *kṛṣ sattāyām*, the form ending in *kvip* denotes existence.

The *kṛt* and the *ṇa*: the letter *ṇa* consists of bliss (*ānanda*) and expresses bliss. According to some, this is because the root *nand*, meaning "bliss," is being cited by means of its partial mention (*ekadeśagrahaṇa*).
Thus, when a *dvandva* compound is formed, and the initial vowel is elided (*ādyaci-lopa*), the meaning is that Kṛṣṇa is eternal bliss (*sadānanda*).
He explains the word *kṛṣṇa* by another method: "Because he draws away (*karṣaṇāt*) the sins (*agha*) of the devotees—that is, because he cleanses their evil—he is *kṛṣṇa*.

Regarding the reading "because of drawing away the devotees and so forth" (*bhaktādi-karṣaṇāt*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes non-devotees; the meaning is that "drawing away the devotee" is leading him to his own abode, while "drawing away the non-devotee" is leading him to hell.
He states another etymology: "tad-varṇa... (of that color).
He is called "Kṛṣṇa" because his body is black in color; or, by the intended expression of non-difference between the signifier and the signified, he is the mantra-body.
Regarding the word "go" and so forth:
*go* means knowledge (*jñāna*).

Because the word "go" (cow) signifies speech and signifies knowledge, he is Govinda, since by that knowledge he is perceived, attained, and known. He states another derivation for the root *vid*, meaning "to obtain," namely: "he knows. Here, the word "go" signifies sound.
The root *vid* means "to know.
He is Govinda because he knows (*vindati*) the *go*, which is the mass of sounds, the collection of words, or the *mātṛkā*.
He states another interpretation: he is Govinda because of his investigation (*vicāraṇa*) of the *go*, that is, his investigation of the word "cow" (*go-śabda*).
Alternatively, "gāvaḥ" refers to the senses; because He directs them toward their respective specific objects through His discernment, He is Govinda.
Or, "gāvaḥ" refers to specific types of cattle;
and thus the Śruti says: "Cattle are both two-footed and four-footed."
He is Govinda because he moves about or acts among their various merits and demerits;
or else, he is Govinda because he protects the *gāvaḥ*, which are a specific kind of cattle.
The particle *api* is used in the sense of *ca* (and).
Now he extracts the mantra:
these [syllables] in sequence, preceded by the seed-syllable of Manmatha, followed by the fourth case-ending from the mantra, and then after that.
If these eighteen syllables should exist, they would be the best of mantras, more secret than the secret, this very wish-fulfilling gem.
These two names known as Kṛṣṇa and Govinda, when placed in sequence with the dative case— that is, each joined with the fourth (dative) case—

following the previously mentioned ten-syllable Gopāla mantra, after the first seed-syllable of Manmatha and immediately after the seed-syllable of Kāma; if these two should thus occur, then this becomes the eighteen-syllable, most excellent mantra.
By the power of this very [mantra], some desire the inclusion of the Kāma-bīja even in the ten-syllable [mantra].
Of what nature is it? It is more secret than the secret;
it is the secret even among secrets.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
The meaning is that he is the bestower of desired objects by the mere thought of them. // KrdC_2.22 //
He also states the seer and so forth: "The former," etc.
The virtuous declare that for this [mantra], the sage and deity are those previously indicated, while its meter is Gāyatrī.
Its limbs consist of groups of four syllables of the mantra, ending with the armor (varma), and the weapon (astra) consists of two syllables. (Kṛd 2.23)

The sage and deity of this mantra are to be understood as those previously indicated in connection with the first mantra. Furthermore, the wise declare that its meter is *gāyatrī*. Regarding the "limbs," by taking four groups of four syllables from among the letters of the mantra—thus forming sixteen syllables—one obtains four [sections] ending with the armor (*varma*), that is, concluding with the *kavaca*.
The limbs are as follows:
the remainder is the *yugārṇa* (four-syllable) mantra; the two syllables known as the *astra* (weapon) constitute the limb.
And the ritual application (*prayoga*) is: *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *govindāya śirase svāhā*.
Vaṣaṭ to the crest-jewel of the cowherd women; Huṃ to the armor of the Beloved;
Svāhā Phaṭ to the weapon.
He states the seed-syllable and so forth: "The seed," he says.

"The seed is power (*śakti*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and also application (*viniyoga*), as before; now I shall declare the placement (*nyāsa*) that effects all accomplishments, which fulfills the desire of the one who preceded him. (Krd 2.24)

The meaning is that the seed (*bīja*), power (*śakti*), nature (*prakṛti*), and application (*viniyoga*) of this mantra are to be understood here as well, being the same as those previously stated for the former mantra.

Regarding the phrase "of the one before that": immediately thereafter, he makes the formal promise, "I shall now describe the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) which brings about all accomplishments and bestows every success for the ten-syllable Gopāla mantra"; he then describes the sequence of the placement for the ten-syllable mantra with the words "having pervaded," etc.
Having pervaded the meaning within the two hands, the wise one should perform the placement (nyāsa) with the syllables situated between the pair of *tāras*,
with the *tāra* constricted on the outer and inner sides.
It should be performed with heart-pleasing ornaments of bindus.
Immediately thereafter, the wise and learned practitioner should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the syllables of the root mantra.

Having done what? Having pervaded—that is, having performed the placement as a pervasive covering—the root mantra within the two hands, as well as on the outside of the hands, on the backs of the hands, and likewise on the sides of the hands.
Of what kind of mantra?
"Enclosed by *tāra* and encapsulated by the *praṇava*" means:
by what kind of syllables? By those situated between a pair of *tāras*, that is, placed in the middle of two *praṇavas*.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?

"Adorned with bindus" means those whose head-ornament is the *bindu*, that is to say, accompanied by the *anusvāra*. Furthermore, of what kind? "Heart-pleasing through the heart," meaning accompanied by the word "namas" which is pleasing to the heart (*hārdena*) and beautiful (*hṛdyaiḥ*).
And the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *Oṃ goṃ oṃ namaḥ* on the three joints of the right thumb; *Oṃ pīṃ oṃ namaḥ* on the index finger, and so forth;
*Oṃ llaṃ oṃ namaḥ* on the left little finger, and so forth. (KrdC 2.25)
He states the locations for the placement of the aforementioned syllables with the words beginning "on the branches" (*śākhāsu*):

"On the ten branches, let the one of pure intellect place three joints each, starting from the right thumb and ending with the left thumb; thus is the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) residing in the hand described."

The posture with both hands preceded by the two thumbs is for maintenance; the withdrawal is preceded by the left [hand], ending at the right thumb—these three also produce the effect accompanied by maintenance.
Having separated the ten fingers into branches, one should recite three syllables over each joint, thus pervading the three joints;

however, according to Tripāṭhin, "three joints" means that one should recite separately over each of the three joints and also separately on the tips of the fingers. Thus they say: at the first joint *oṃ*, at the second *oṃ*, at the third *oṃ*, and at the tip of the finger *namaḥ*; and so it is elsewhere as well.

A person of clear intellect—one whose mind is stainless—should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) such that it begins with the right thumb and ends with the left thumb; that is, the left thumb should be at the conclusion, at the end of the placement.
In this way, the "creation residing in the hand" is described; the meaning is that the method for performing the creation-placement (*sṛṣṭi-nyāsa*) upon the hands has been explained.

The *sthiti* (establishment) placement begins with the pair of thumbs: having placed [the mantras] on the fingers from the thumb to the little finger in the right hand, one should likewise place them on the fingers from the thumb to the little finger in the left hand; this is called the *sthiti-nyāsa*. The *saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) begins with the left and ends with the right: starting from the left thumb and ending with the right thumb, this is called the *saṃhāra-nyāsa*.

The meaning is that this triad—consisting of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—produces all three; and the "fivefold deposition of creation and so forth" refers to the task associated with maintenance.
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (thence):
thence, following the sequence of maintenance, the wise one should perform the ten-limbed depositions.
Likewise, that fivefold limb [of the mantra] is prescribed as the ritual procedure for the hand.

Then, immediately after that, according to the sequence of placement—that is, by the method of placing [the mantras]—the wise one, the learned one, should place the ten limbs (*daśāṅgakāni*), namely the ten limbs of the previously mentioned mantra, upon the ten fingers.

"In that same way" means by that same manner, according to the sequence of placement; he should place those five limbs—the previously mentioned pentad, the aforementioned five limbs—upon the ten fingers. Thus concludes the ritual procedure consisting of the placement upon the hands (*kara-nyāsa*).
And thus, this method or manner is proclaimed—that is, described—as being in the two hands (kara). This is the meaning. // KrdC_2.27 //

Showing the specific method of the *mātṛkā*-nyāsa and stating the *tattva*-nyāsa in sequence, he says: "O Lord of Mantras, having performed the placement with the letters of the Mother [alphabet] encapsulated by the mantra, together with the *bindu*, as before."
And there are ten principles (tattvas) which possess the phonemes of the mantras, due to the distinction between the paths of the subtle withdrawal and emanation.

Then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) on the forehead and other parts as before— using the letters of the Mātṛkā combined with the ten-syllable mantra (daśārṇa), along with the bindus and anusvāras— the practitioner should subsequently, after completing this specific Mātṛkā-nyāsa,
place the ten principles (tattvas) that are about to be described.
Of what kind are those [mantras] that possess the phonemes of mantra, being endowed with the syllables of mantra?

How should one arrange the ten principles (*tattva*)? To this he says: "By way of the distinction between dissolution (*saṃhṛti*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*)," meaning first by the sequence of dissolution and immediately thereafter by the sequence of emanation. (KrdC 2.28)
He shows the manner of dissolution and creation with the words "saṃhṛtau": "When the dissolution has occurred, the best of men, having entered [the state of] dissolution,
returns to the path of creation."
The extraction of these [roots] is indeed as previously stated;
now I shall describe the procedure for their grammatical assignment (*nyāsa*).

That best of men, the most excellent of men, just as he was followed in the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra) during the placement of withdrawal, so too should he return in the path of creation during the placement of the creator; that is, he should be the reverse of that [process]. He states the method of extraction (uddhāra): "Extraction" (uddhṛti), etc.

The meaning is as follows: "the extraction" (*uddhāra*) of these principles (*tattva*s), which is their definitive removal (*niścayena uddhṛtiḥ*), is to be performed "as previously stated," that is, according to the method described earlier in the *Tattvanyāsa*. One should extract the mantras of the principles in sequence, beginning with the word "obeisance" (*namaḥ*) for the Supreme (*parāya*) and ending with "obeisance" (*namas*) for the Self (*ātmane*). The phrase "now I shall state the *nyāsa*" means that at this point I am providing the names of the principles related to the *nyāsa* as well as the description of their respective locations. (KrdC 2.29)

He states the names of the principles (tattvas): "Earth," and so forth. Earth, water, fire, air, ether, ego (garva), the great one (mahat), nature (prakṛti), and spirit (puruṣa)—these are the principles; now, the supreme (para).

One should then perform the placement (nyāsa) of the feet, the anus, the heart, the mouth, and the head—five in total—with two in the middle and three pervading the whole; thereafter, one should perform it in the reverse order.
Mahī is the earth;
salilaṃ is water;
pāvakaḥ is fire.
Anila is wind;
viyat is space;
and garva is egoism.

The Great (mahān) is the principle of the Great (mahat-tattva); [so too are] primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), and the Supreme (para). These principles, beginning with earth, are what is denoted by the term "tattva."
He states the locations for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): "Now," meaning immediately thereafter, one should perform the placement of the five principles (*tattva*), beginning with earth.
Where? Upon the feet, the anus, the heart, and the mouth; that is, over the two feet.
In the two eyes, in the linga,
in the heart,
and in the mouth.
On the head;

in the middle [of the body], in the sense of the locative case (adhi-saptamī), in the heart—there one should perform the placement of the two principles or the three, which pervade all parts and extend over all limbs. Then, immediately after that, by way of reversal—that is, by the method opposite to the aforementioned sequence of withdrawal—one should perform the placement.

And the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: beginning with "Oṃ Goṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Earth-Self, obeisance," on the two feet, and ending with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Supreme Self, obeisance," this is the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). Beginning again with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Supreme Self, obeisance," [the emission begins]. Oṃ...
"Goṃ, salutation to the supreme [element], salutation to the self of earth on the two feet"—this is the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa*.
In the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa*, there are three [principles] for the entire body:
Mahat and Ahaṅkāra in the heart, and Ākāśa in the head.
The [elements] of air, fire, water, and earth are to be known as being located in the mouth, heart, the linga, and the two feet, respectively;
however, some desire their placement within the words of the *tattvas*, which is to be considered. (KrdC 2.30)
"This is most secret": this placement (nyāsa), perfected by the ten principles (tattvas), has been fully explained;
it should also be performed by the virtuous upon other Gopāla mantras for the swift attainment of results. (Krd 2.31)

This placement (nyāsa) has been declared and described by the virtuous scholars; it should be performed for other Gopāla mantras as well, even those extracted from mantras other than the ten-syllabled one. Of what nature is it? It is most secret, being exceedingly concealed.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
"Refined by the ten principles" (tattva-daśaka-parikptaḥ) means refined—that is, opened up—by the ten principles (tattva-daśaka).
For what purpose? "For the swift attainment of the fruit," that is, for the rapid acquisition of the result. (KrdC 2.31)
He states another method of ritual placement (nyāsa): "From the hair to the feet," etc.
Then, one should place the excellent mantra upon the body with both arms, fixed between the eyebrows, extending from the hair down to the feet.
One should likewise place the syllables three times on the crown of the head, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the mouth, the heart, the navel, the genitals, the knees, and the feet.

Immediately thereafter, with both arms and hands, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) three times upon one's own body, from the hair to the feet— that is, from the head down to the feet— of the ten-syllabled Gopāla-mantra, the most excellent of mantras, which is encased by the *dhruva* (the syllable *oṃ*) and encased by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*).
Thus say the Vidyādhara teachers, Tripāṭhī and others.
According to their opinion, the reading is "from the hair to the feet.
Now, he describes the placement of the mantra syllables according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, beginning with the words "on the head" and so forth.
Thus, one should place the ten syllables, enclosed by the *praṇava* (oṃ), in the locations to be described, starting from the head.
He states the locations: "on the head," meaning on the crown;

"in the eyes," meaning in both eyes, there is only one syllable; "in the ears," meaning in both ears, here too there is only one; "in the nose," meaning in the pair of nostrils, there too there is only one; the mouth, the heart, the belly, the auspicious *liṅga*, and in the two knees, there is one.
The meaning is that one should arrange ten syllables in these ten places, with one [syllable] in each of the two feet. (KrdC 2.32)
This emanation has been described by the learned; likewise, the maintenance of the body from the heart to the mouth has been declared by the sages;
and the dissolution from the feet to the head—this is the triad.
And one should fashion creation and, following that, maintenance.
The meaning is that this creation was taught by the learned ones who know the scriptures (*āgama*).

As for the "establishment" (*sthiti*), which is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), it was declared by the sages such as Nārada and others to extend from the heart to the mouth—that is, described starting from the heart and ending at the mouth.

Regarding the sequence there, it is: heart, belly, genitals, knees, feet, head, eyes, ears, nose, and mouth; and the dissolution (*saṃhāra*) should be performed starting from the feet and ending at the head.

In that regard, one should arrange these three—the mantra syllables to be given in reverse order—and subsequently, after the performance of this triad, one should again arrange the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and the maintenance (*sthiti*).
Thus, the meaning is that the five placements (*nyāsa*) are to be performed.
The practical application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *goṃ namaḥ*, *pīṃ namaḥ*, and so forth. //33//
He shows what constitutes the end of renunciation for those belonging to the various stages of life (āśrama): "Renunciation," he says.
They declare that this renunciation is ordained for mendicants (maskarin) and forest-dwellers (vaikhānasa) as ending in withdrawal (saṃhāra);
for householders (gṛhamedhin), it ends in maintenance (sthiti); and for those following the [caste] orders (varṇin), it ends in emanation (sṛṣṭi). KRD 2.34.

This assignment (nyāsa) is prescribed for the Maskarins and Vaikhānasas as ending with withdrawal; a Maskarin is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a Vaikhānasa is a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), meaning that these two must perform the threefold assignment.
For householders (gṛhamedhin), this assignment is prescribed as ending with maintenance.
The meaning is that householders likewise must perform five renunciations (*nyāsa*).
For those belonging to the [student] caste (*varṇin*), namely for celibate students (*brahmacārin*), this renunciation is ordained to last until the end of creation;
thus, the meaning is that celibate students must perform four renunciations.
Thus, the ancient masters who are conversant with the scriptures have declared the aforementioned collection of meanings; this is the ellipsis. (KrdC 2.34)
Regarding "vairāgye":
some teachers say that for a householder endowed with dispassion (*vairāgya*), there is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*);
for one who dwells in the forest possessing innate knowledge (*sahajāna*), there is maintenance (*sthiti*); and for those seeking learning, there is emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). (Kṛd 2.35)

Some teachers state that for a householder endowed with dispassion (*vairāgya*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) extends up to the end of *saṃhāra*. Furthermore, they say that for one who dwells in the forest as a forest-dweller (*vanavāsin*) together with a wife, the placement extends up to the end of *sthiti*.
Likewise, for students of knowledge (*vidyārthin*) other than celibate students (*brahmacārin*), the placement extends up to the end of *sṛṣṭi*; such is the meaning. (KrdC 2.35)

He demonstrates the rule for the placement of syllables on the fingers, beginning with the words "on the head" (*śirasi*) and so forth: "That middle finger which is prescribed for the head is used for the eye when joined with the index finger; for the ear it is without the thumb; and for the [other] ear it is joined with the ring finger."

All [the fingers] are placed on the face; the index finger is superior when placed on the heart; the middle finger joined with the first-born (thumb) is placed on the navel; and the ring finger is placed on the ears, O Śivā.
Those same fingers [are placed] on the two knees, but with the thumbs on the two feet;
there may be an exchange between the positions and the syllables, but not between the fingers and the positions.

The middle finger is placed upon the head—that is, on the crown of the head—as a means of performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*); thus, the meaning is that the placement should be performed on the head with the middle finger.
That same middle finger, joined with the index finger, is placed upon the eyes—the pair of eyes;
likewise, the placement of the two eyes should be performed with both the middle and index fingers.
In the ears, that is, in the pair of auditory organs, all the fingers except the thumb are prescribed;
in the nose, that is, in the pair of nostrils, the ring finger (upakaniṣṭhakā), accompanied by the thumb—that is, joined with the thumb—is prescribed;
and in the mouth, all the fingers are prescribed.
In the heart, the *sajyāyasī* [mudrā] is formed with the thumb and index finger together with the *jyeṣṭhā*.
At the navel and the abdomen, it is indicated by the term "nābhi"; thus says Vidhyadhara.
The *Laghudīpikā* and other works maintain that the primary meaning of the term "nābhi" applies here as well.
The middle finger is prescribed joined with the first-born (the index finger) and joined with the thumb;
some say that regarding the Śiva-liṅga, it is prescribed in such a way that the middle finger with the thumb is positioned as it would be in the belly.
Regarding the reading "śravo vihitāḥ śive," the meaning is that those [fingers] on the pair of ears which are devoid of the thumbs are prescribed for Śiva.
Regarding the knees, those same fingers—meaning all the fingers excluding the thumbs—are prescribed.
On the two feet, all the fingers including the thumbs are prescribed.
By the phrase "of the place and the vowel" and so forth, there occurs an exchange—that is, a reversal—between the location and the syllable.
For example: *goṃ* is at the head during emission (*sṛṣṭi*), and at the heart during maintenance (*sthiti*).
"In the withdrawal [of the fingers], the placement is on the feet.
Thus, there is no reversal regarding the positions of the fingers;
rather, the meaning is that in creation, maintenance, or withdrawal, the placement should be performed with whichever finger was prescribed for whichever position. // KrdC_2.36-37 //

Now he speaks of the placement (nyāsa) known as the "Cage of Sovereign Power" (vibhūti-pañjara), saying: "I shall speak"—namely, I shall speak another supreme placement called Bhūti, which bestows prosperity, consists of ten repetitions of the mantra, and is most secret even from the best of practitioners. (Krd 2.38)
Furthermore, I shall speak—that is, I shall tell—of that which is called *bhūti*, meaning its name is *bhūti*.
Of what nature is it? It is the "best of nyāsas," meaning the most excellent among nyāsas;
moreover, it is "wealth-producing," meaning it bestows sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
Furthermore, it consists of ten recitations of the mantra, structured with ten enclosures of the mantra;
moreover, it is most secret and exceedingly hidden from even the best of practitioners. (KrdC 2.38)
He states the locations for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the verse beginning "In the foundation" (*ādhāra*), etc.: in the foundation,
the banner, the navel, the heart, the throat, the mouth, the two shoulders, the two thighs,
the neck, the navel, the belly, the heart, the pair of breasts, the two sides, the back, and the hips.

[The suffix *ka*] occurs after [the words] *kāya*, *akṣi*, *śruti*, *kapola*, *kara*, *pāda*, *sandhi*, *agra*, and *śākhā*, when they denote the directions beginning with the east (such as the right side), as well as after *mūrdhan*, *sakala*, *doṣan*, and *sakthi*.
One should place the syllables arising from the *manu* in the head, eyes, mouth, throat, heart, navel, root (kanda), anus, knees,
and feet; likewise, one should place them in the ears, cheeks, shoulders, breasts, and sides.
[The suffix *kvip* is applied] after words ending in *sphic*, *ūru*, *sthala*, *jānu*, *jaṅghā*, and *aṅghri*.
The base of the phallus is the triangle located at the root, the *mūlādhāra* station;
the banner is the penis;
and the navel, heart, throat, mouth, and both shoulders and thighs [are the stations].
Among these, there is a single repetition.
According to the author of the *Laghu-dīpikā*, "kandharā," "ghāṭā," "kandharā," and "kaṇṭha" [are synonyms for the neck].
The navel, the belly, the heart, the pair of breasts, and the two teats.
"Pārśva" refers to the pair of sides;
"apara" refers to the region of the back;
"śroṇi" refers to the region of the hips.
*Śroṇiḥ* means the hip.
According to those who follow the three-fold recension (*tripāṭhin*), *aparaṃ śroṇyāḥ* means the posterior part of the hip.
In these cases, there is a second repetition.
The head is *kaṃ*;
the mouth is *āsyaṃ*;
the eyes are the pair of *akṣiṇī*.
The two ears are the *śrutī*;
"na" refers to the two nostrils and the two cheeks; among these, there is the third movement (*vṛtti*).
Regarding "kara-pada," there are four joints in each of the hands and feet, as well as [the movements] at the joints, on the tips of the fingers, and on the fingers themselves.
Here, the fourth function is in the right hand;
likewise, the fifth function is in the left hand. Thus there are two positions, whereas for the Vidyadhara, however, there is a single function in both hands.
He says that there is one metrical form for both feet;
this is to be considered,
because it is not perceived as such from the root text.
In the joints of the feet, at the tips of the toes, and on the toes themselves—
here too, the sixth occurrence is in the right foot,
and the seventh occurrence is in the left foot.
Therefore, the followers of the Tripāṭhin school maintain that there are four placements for the hands and feet:

[one] in the middle of the head, [one] in the eastern and other directions [of the head], [one] on the entire head, and [one] on the entire skull in a clockwise manner as a pervasive placement; likewise, [one] on the two arms, and [one] on the two thighs at the base of the legs.
The eighth enclosure is for these two, the neck and the middle region;
there is one enclosure for the head in the directions starting from the east;
and there is one enclosure for the crown of the head and so forth—thus say the Vidyādhara teachers.
That is to be considered;
for likewise, by the natural force of the word, there is the perception of a single repetition with respect to the head and so forth.
"Head" (śiras) means the skull (mastaka).
*Akṣi* refers to the pair of eyes;
*āsya* is the mouth;
*kaṇṭha* is the throat.
The heart;
the *tuṇḍa* is the abdomen;
the *kanda* is the *mūlādhāra*.
According to the followers of the Tripāṭhin tradition, "svādhiṣṭhāna" refers to the anus,
the penis,
and the knee.
"Prapada" refers to the pair of feet; among these [locations], there is the ninth repetition.
[It is also applied] to the pair of ears and the pair of cheeks.
On the two shoulders;
on the two breasts;
on the two sides.
On the pair of buttocks, that is, the pair of hips;
likewise on the pair of thighs, knees, shanks, and feet— in these,
there is the tenth repetition.
In this manner, that is, by this method, one should place the syllables related to the mantra originating from the mind.
And the ritual application is as follows: *goṃ* namaḥ at the *mūlādhāra*, *pīṃ* namaḥ at the *liṅga*.
"Jaṃ namaḥ nābhau," and so forth. (KrdC 2.39–40)
He states the fruit of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the words "Thus":
"Thus has been described the *Vibhūtipañjara*, which bestows all happiness, wealth, dharma, and liberation."
It delights the minds of young women and increases devotion to the lotus feet of Hari.
In this manner, the "Cage of Abundances" (Vibhūti-pañjara) has been described.
Of what nature is it? It bestows all happiness, wealth, dharma, and liberation—that is, it grants the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha).
Furthermore, it delights the minds of both men and young women; it not only pleases everyone, but gladdens the hearts of both males and females.
Rather, it increases devotion to the lotus-feet of Hari.
He states the ritual placement of the body-cage (*mūrti-pañjara-nyāsa*) with the words "for manifestation" (*sphūrtaye*): "Now, for the manifestation of this mantra, the body-cage is proclaimed;
it destroys affliction, seizing spirits, and poison, and bestows fame, prosperity, beauty, and nourishment. (Kṛd 2.42)

Immediately following this, for the purpose of manifesting and inflaming this ten-syllable mantra, the "Cage of Forms" (mūrti-pañjara) is proclaimed. Of what nature is it? *Ārti* is suffering or affliction;
*graha* is the inauspiciousness produced by planetary influences (*graha*), including both stationary and mobile poisons (*viṣa*).
"Arīḥ" means an enemy;
the meaning is "one who slays them.
Furthermore, of what kind [is he]?
It bestows fame and so forth. "Fame" (kīrti) means renown; it is so called because it bestows fortune (śrī), which is prosperity, beauty, nourishment, and strength. (KrdC 2.42)
Now he sets forth the ritual placement (nyāsa): "Keśava and so forth"—
[one should place] the six pairs of forms beginning with Keśava,
preceded by Dhātṛ, [and] the suns ending with "namas."
One should sequentially arrange the twelve vowels, which are the syllables of existence, excluding the neuter letters.
Together with Keśava and the others—the deities of the six previously mentioned yugas—one should sequentially assign Dhātṛ and the preceding [deities] along with Mihira.
Of what kind are they? They end with "namaḥ," meaning their names conclude with the word "namaḥ.
Furthermore, together with whom?
"Along with the twelve syllables of existence"—that is, together with the twelve syllables belonging to the twelve-syllable mantra that will be described hereafter.
This is what is meant: first the vowels, and then the word *namaḥ*.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *oṃ aṃ oṃ keśava-dhātṛbhyāṃ namaḥ*;
according to the followers of Tripāṭhin, it is *oṃ aṃ oṃ keśava-dhātre namaḥ*. (KrdC 2.43)
Now, regarding the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the cage of forms (mūrti-pañjara), he states the locations for the placement: "In the belly of the forehead,
the heart, the throat, the hollow of the navel,
on the left and the other side, at the end of the arm, and in the neck."
Likewise, on the three left [arms], the back,
and the crown of the head, he should [place] the mantra consisting of twelve syllables.
On the forehead,
on the belly, and on the heart.
"At the base of the throat-pit" means in the neck.
"On the other than the left" means the right side; that is, at the end of the right arm and in the throat.
"In the three on the left" means on the left side, at the end of the left arm, and in the throat.
On the back, at the hump;
furthermore, even if the reading is *anva*, this same meaning is to be understood.
Likewise, in that manner, one should place the twelve-syllable mantra (*manu*) consisting of six pairs of phonemes upon the head—this is the meaning. (KrdC 2.44)

He states the purpose of the complete mantra-deposition (nyāsa) on the head with the words beginning "caitanya": Vāsudeva, whose body is the nectar of consciousness, who possesses the brilliance of ten million suns, and who resides upon the crown of the head, [pervades] the entire body.
The milk of the breast, as if sprinkled with pure white milk,
pervades it, strewn with the manifest syllables of the mantra.
That well-known Vāsudeva, being situated at the head—that is, residing upon the crown—pervades the entire body with his own splendor; this is the meaning.
Of what nature is Vāsudeva? He is one whose very body is the nectar of consciousness (caitanyāmṛta).
Alternatively, he is one whose body is that very consciousness which is self-luminous, immortal, and liberation itself.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is one whose splendor is like ten million suns.
Of what sort is the body?
It is "filled with manifested mantra-syllables," meaning it is pervaded by those manifested mantra-syllables arising from the twelve syllables.
Like what? Like the milk from the udder poured—that is, cast—into "pure water," that is, into very clear liquid. (KrdC 2.45)
He summarizes what arises from the deposition of the body with the words "creation and maintenance":
creation and maintenance consist of the pair of ten and five limbs, the triad beginning with the Sage (muni), and [the others] in the throat and heart.
Having performed the placement and having tied the knots, one should further bind the ten directions with mudrās.
Rudradhara maintains that the verse beginning with "sṛṣṭi-sthiti" shows the preliminary rite for the Mūrtipañjara;
however, this is to be considered,
because there is no authoritative evidence for it therein.

Having first performed the creation and maintenance [stages] as previously stated with "on the crown," "on the eyes," and so forth, one should again perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's own body; that is to say, having performed the placement of the pair of ten-limbed and five-limbed [mantras], one should place the triad beginning with the seer (*ṛṣi*) on the mouth and the heart.
Then, having formed and bound the mudrā to be described, the ten directions must once again be bound.
The meaning is: "by means of the mantra to be stated hereafter," namely, *oṃ sudarśanāyāstrāya phaṭ*.

He states the extraction of the twelve-syllable mantra with the words beginning with "Tāram": Tāra (Oṃ), Hārda (Namaḥ), Viśvamūrti (Viṣṇave), Śārṅgin (Śārṅgiṇe), and Māṃsānta (Māṃsāya); these are the excellent deities situated between Vāyu (Ya) and Ma (Ma).
This excellent mantra, consisting of six pairs of syllables, is said to be the manifest and easily accessible gateway to the city of liberation.
*Tāram* is the *praṇava* (OM).
*Hārda* is the heart, which extends as far as the word *namaḥ*.
*Viśvamūrtiḥ* is the syllable *bha*.
The syllable *ga* is [the letter] Śārṅgin;
at the end of *māṃsa* is the syllable *la*;
its end is the syllable *va*.
*Te* is its own form;
*vā* is its own form;
*ya* is its own form.
Between those two [names], *sudeva* and *su-deva*, there are three syllables;
thus, the twelve-syllable mantra, consisting of six pairs of letters, well-known as "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya," is declared and described as the most excellent of mantras.
Of what nature is it? It is the easily accessible gate, meaning the easy means, for the city of liberation (*mokṣa-purī*) directly and without mediation. (KrdC 2.47)
He reveals the twelve Adityas with the words beginning "Dhātṛ-Aryaman":
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśu, Bhaga, Vivasvat,
Indra, Pūṣan, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu are declared to be the rays (Bhānus).
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśu, Bhaga, Vivasvat, Indra, Pūṣan, Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu—these are declared to be the twelve rays.

Now he describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the eighteen-syllable mantra, beginning with "Then, O Yuga... and so forth: "Then, indeed, I shall describe the ritual placement of my eighteen-syllable mantra;
let one perform the five-limbed [placement] on the two hands and on the five fingers."

Having extended [the mantra] three times along the body according to the person, one should then respectfully assign the letters of the human alphabet once together with the *praṇava*, and subsequently the words as well.
Furthermore, in the compound *yugarandhrārṇasya*, the word *randhra* is placed last because it is a *rājadanta* (dental) compound.
*Yugarandhra* refers to the number of syllables [in a verse] where there is a "pair of apertures" (*yugarandhra*); that is *yugarandhrārṇa*. Its [value] is nine, for *randhra* signifies nine.
Thus, there is the formal promise: "I shall state—meaning, I will explain—the *nyāsa*, which is the ritual placement, of the eighteen-syllable mantra.
One should perform the hand-placement (*kara-nyāsa*) by assigning the five previously mentioned limbs to the five fingers of both hands using the syllables of the mantra;
the placement of the weapon (*astra-nyāsa*) is to be understood as being on the little finger.
Immediately thereafter, having focused upon the body and having pervaded the mantra by reciting it three times,

and having again placed the *praṇava* once, one should then place the letters of the human script— the syllables of the mantra. Furthermore, immediately after that, the five words should be placed with due reverence.
He states the locations for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra-syllables as "in *kaca* and *bhuvi*":

in *kaca* and *bhuvi*— that is, on the forehead, between the two eyebrows, in the pair of ears, the eyes, the pair [of nostrils], the mouth, the neck, the heart, the navel, the hips, and in both groins.
The one of cool intellect should place the syllables on the knees and feet; he should certainly fix the five words upon the head, the two eyes, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and the feet.
The "place of origin" (*bhū*) for hair (*kaca*), that is, the head;
there, [specifically] on the forehead, between the pair of eyebrows—that is, in the middle of the brows—and not on the pair of ears, nor on the pair of eyes, nor on the pair of nostrils;
[and further] on the face, the neck, the heart, the navel, and both hips, namely the left hip and the right hip.
In the two eyes, the two lingas,
as well as in the two knees and the two feet, one of cool intellect and stainless mind should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the syllables associated with the mantra.
Here, one should place one syllable on the two knees;
one should place one syllable on the two feet;
likewise, one should certainly place [the remaining syllable] on the head and the crown.
He states the locations for the placement of the five words: "the two eyes," and so forth.

One should place—that is, install—the five words associated with the mantra, beginning with *klīṃ* as the first, while the others are clear; these should be placed upon the pair of eyes, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and the feet. (KrdC 2.50)
Regarding "the five limbs":

one should again assign the five limbs, as well as the sages and all other [deities], which are identical to what was stated previously. Now I shall describe the mudrās that are to be bound for the mantras.
Furthermore, one should again place the five limbs upon the body;
likewise, the sages and so forth, the seers and so forth;
and all other groups, such as Keśava and the rest, are exactly the same as previously described.

Regarding this, the author of the *Laghudīpikā* states that there is a specific rule of double repetition for the mantra during the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) of the ten principles (*tattva*) and so forth.

Now, immediately following this, I shall describe—that is, I will speak of—the mudrās which are to be bound, meaning those which should be formed, belonging to the two mantras consisting of ten and eighteen syllables respectively. (KrdC 2.51)
He demonstrates the mudrās for the placement of the limbs, beginning with the heart and so forth: "Without the thumbs," and so on.
With the fingers of the hand straight and without the thumbs, there shall be the mudrā for the heart and for the head.
Indeed, the fist with the thumbs pointing downward is for the crest-lock (śikhā);
the fingers of both hands should be [extended] for the armor (varman).
The sound produced by the thumbs and index fingers of both arms raised with the *nārāca* fist is declared to be the *astra-mudrā*, which is applied in all directions.
Where the index and middle fingers are the two eyes.
The fingers, being without thumbs—that is, lacking thumbs—and straight rather than crooked, shall form a mudrā at the heart;
and those same [fingers] should be known as the mudrā at the head, that is, on the crown.
"Khalu" indicates certainty.
The fist with the thumbs pointing downward—that is, a fist formed such that the thumbs are at the bottom—becomes the *mudrā* for the topknot (*śikhā*).

For the armor (*varman* or *kavaca*), the fingers of both hands [joined together] constitute the *mudrā*, as denoted by the term *mudrā*. Sound (*dhvani*) or voice is said to be the weapon (*astra*) *mudrā*.
Of what nature is the sound?
It is that which arises from the two thumbs and index fingers as the instruments, belonging to the pair of arms raised by the fists like iron arrows (nārāca) or shafts (bāṇa).
Furthermore, of what kind is it?

Wherever the two syllables *akṣiṇī* (eyes) occur in a mantra as a constituent part of the "eye," there the mudrā consists of the index and middle fingers joined together, extending widely and fixed in all ten directions.
Regarding the flute mudrā, he says: "On the lip...
On the lip, the left thumb is joined;
its little finger is joined with the right thumb, and that [right] little finger is extended. (Krd 2.54)
The index, middle, and ring fingers slightly contracted and moved are here called the flute mudrā; it is well-guarded and dear to Hari.
The connection should be made such that the thumb of the left hand touches the lower lip.
That fifth finger of the left hand, which is the little finger, should be joined with the right thumb—that is, it should be bound to the right-hand thumb.
That little finger [of the right hand], being the little finger of the right hand, should be extended and kept straight.
The index, middle, and ring fingers of both hands should be slightly contracted and moved;
thus is the *veṇu-mudrā* described in this scripture, which is well-guarded and extremely secret in other texts, for it is the beloved consort of Hari, the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (KrdC 2.54–55)
"They are not mentioned":
they are not mentioned here because they are already well-known—namely, the garland (*mālā*), the *śrīvatsa*, and the *kaustubha*.
It is said that among the seals of Acyuta, the seal shaped like a *bilva* fruit is [the one referred to]. (Krd 2.56)

The mudrās of the garland (*mālā*), the *śrīvatsa*, and the *kaustubha* are not described by me, the author of this work, because they are well known; the implication is that only what is not well known is revealed here.
For this very reason, the gesture of representing a forest garland (*vanamālā*) on the neck is the *vanamālā-mudrā*.
To perform it, one should join the little finger and index finger of the right hand, which is facing downward, with the left index and little fingers which are turned upward.

Placing the two fingers—the ring finger and the middle finger—of the right hand upon the thumb of the left hand, one should position the middle and ring fingers of the left hand beneath the thumb of the right hand; this is the Śrīvatsa mudrā.
Then, pressing the right little finger with the left little finger, and pressing the right index finger with the left ring finger.
Having placed the three remaining left fingers above, one should join the faces of the three fingers of the right hand together with the left index finger; this is the Kaustubha mudrā.
He describes the *bilva-mudrā*: "The thumb," and so forth.
Having bound the left thumb, held upright, with the thumb of the other hand and pressed its tip with the fingers as well, likewise with the fingers of the left hand.
Having bound it firmly, one of pure intellect should place it upon the heart while reciting the seed-syllable of Māra;
this ring called Bilva has been clearly described here, and it should be kept secret by those who know the ritual procedure.

The left thumb should be raised like a staff and made vertical, then lowered; immediately thereafter, having bound it with the thumb of the other hand, the right thumb should be placed across its seat—this is the meaning.
Having pressed and held the tip of that [left thumb] with the fingers of the right hand, those fingers of the right hand as well—
Alternatively, having bound it firmly with the fingers of the left hand as much as possible, one of pure intellect— that is, of purified mind—
should place it in the heart,
while uttering and pronouncing the seed-syllable of Māra, which is the seed-syllable of Kāma.
Thus, this [mudrā] called Bilvā has been clearly and explicitly described here in this treatise by those who know the ritual procedures and understand its methods; it should be kept secret.
He states the fruit of this [practice] with the words "By mind":

whatever has been performed here or even in the past by means of mind, speech, and body— whether unintentionally or intentionally— all that entire accumulation of evil deeds, he (the Lord) [destroys].
The person who knows this mudrā exhausts [all obstacles]; the hosts of gods bow down to him, and all people constantly come under his influence.

That person, knowing this mudrā, destroys— that is, removes— all that entire accumulation of evil deeds, the mass of sin, whether committed by mind, speech, or body, through negligence or through intention, and whether performed by day or by night.
Regarding the reading "whatever was performed here or even previously," the meaning is that which was performed in this life or in another birth.
Not only does it remove evil, but furthermore, the hosts of gods—the deities—bow down;
likewise, for this maker of the mudrā, the entire multitude of people always and at all times becomes submissive. This is the meaning. (KrdC_2.58)
Sanātana (Haribhakti-vilāsa 6.42):
This person, knowing this seal called *bilva*, destroys—that is, annihilates—the entire, complete multitude of his various evil deeds, the mass of sins.
Which [deeds]? Those performed here in this life and previously in a former birth, whether unintentionally through ignorance or intentionally through knowledge, by means of mind, speech, and body.

Regarding the reading *divārātrivihitam*, it means "performed by day and by night. The neuter gender of the pronoun *yat* (referring to *yat*) is due either to the poetic license (*svātantrya*) of the great poet or because it functions as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Alternatively, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "since it causes [them] to perish (*yat kṣapayati*), therefore they bow down (*tat tasmān namanti*)."
Furthermore, the characteristics of the mudrās have not been written down because they are secret.
Thus it has been said:
"A wise person should reveal the guru, but must never reveal the mantra."
"One should not show the rosary or the mudrā even to one's guru. And here, these are prescribed for the sake of understanding that [teaching]. Likewise, it is said in the Āgama:
The añjali formed with both hands by properly joining the palms together with flowers is declared by the best of teachers to be the āvāhanī mudrā.
When all [the fingers] are turned face downwards, it is called the *sthāpanī* (establishment) mudrā. With both fists joined together and the pair of thumbs raised,
this is designated as the *sannidhāna* (presence) mudrā by those who know the tantras.
That very [channel], when it contains the thumb, is proclaimed as "samīritā" (the restrained) during the process of suppression.
The sakalīkaraṇa is considered to be the arrangement of the limbs by means of the limbs themselves;
it consists of a fist formed with the left hand, with the index finger extended and pointing downward.
If this *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā* is rotated all around,
with all the little fingers and ring fingers facing one another once more;

Likewise, when the index and middle fingers form the *dhenu-mudrā*, it is proclaimed as such; with the thumbs interlaced and the other fingers of the hands extended, this is declared by the wise to be the *mahāmudrā* for the purpose of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*).
Holding the left thumb with the right fist,
one should join the four fingers behind that fist.
This is declared to be the conch mudrā in the ritual of worship for Vaiṣṇavas,
when the pair of thumbs and the pair of little fingers are turned toward one another.
If the other fingers are extended, then this is considered the *darśinī* [mudrā].
If the fingers are interlaced with one another and the two middle fingers are raised and joined together, then this mudrā is proclaimed as the *gadā*.
When the two hands are turned toward each other in the shape of a lotus, with the middle fingers and thumbs resting like the pericarp,
this is called the *padma* (lotus) mudrā; it is golden and has the middle fingers joined together.
The mudrā known as *bilva* is formed by touching the thumbs together.
But when the other [hand] is considered to be at the front of the left fist,
then this mudrā should be known by the wise as that named *muṣala*.
One should join the tip of the left index finger to the end of the middle finger;
then, one should extend both the left hand and the right hand.
Having applied [the hand] to the right shoulder like the launching of an arrow, one should then perform [the gesture] with the index finger and thumb; this is what is proclaimed.

The sages declare that the Śārṅga-mudrā should be displayed during the worship of Kṛṣṇa. Having pressed the two fingers, the little finger and the ring finger, with the right thumb, and having extended the remaining two fingers, it is proclaimed as the Khaḍga-mudrā.
Having formed a noose-like shape by joining the left thumb and forefinger,
one should take a fist with the right hand and extend the forefinger.
The practitioner of mantra should touch the base of the left thumb with that very [finger];
this is declared to be the *pāśa-mudrā* for the rite of worshiping Keśava.
Having slightly bent the index finger, one should press down with the remainder [of the fingers];
likewise, having grasped it with the right fist, one should display the goad.
Having joined the backs of the hands together, with the little fingers interlaced one over the other,
one should make the tips of the index fingers equal and likewise the tips of the little fingers.
Having slightly raised [the thumbs] and then extended the other two fingers like wings,
this is known as the Gāruḍī mudrā in the ritual for the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
There, with the little fingers and index fingers facing each other,
one should likewise press the middle and ring fingers with the thumbs.
One should carefully display at the heart the mudrā known as Śrīvatsa;
likewise, one should join the little fingers facing each other,
and similarly, the index and ring fingers, with the two hands placed back-to-back.
With the hands raised and joined to one another, with the fingers placed upon the chest,
one should join the left middle and index fingers at the wrist and then place them against the right.
This mudrā, known as the Kaustubha, is formed by placing the left thumb [on the right palm]; and in some traditions, it is said:
"The left ring finger is joined to the back of the right little finger."
The little finger is bound by the other [left hand], and likewise by the right index finger.
One should bind the left fingers at the base of the right thumb,
joining the right thumb and middle finger while keeping the other [left] fingers straight.
Four other mudrās, joined together, are known as the Kaustubha.

The left thumb is placed upon the lip; the little finger of that [left hand] is joined with the right thumb, while its little finger is extended. The index, middle, and ring fingers are slightly contracted and moved.
This is declared to be the Veṇu-mudrā, the well-guarded favorite of Hari.
Having extended a limb and touched its branch, O fair-faced one,
and then turning it forward, it is proclaimed as the Abhaya (Fearlessness) mudrā.
Having extended the right arm, one should place it upon the knee;
O Goddess, one should display the *prasṛta* [hand-gesture], which is the bestower of boons and the accomplisher of all aims.
With the two index fingers extended upward and downward respectively,
and expanding in sequence like a garland, this is proclaimed as the *vanamālā* (forest-garland) mudrā.

In the *Kramadīpikā* (2.57): Having raised the left thumb and pressed its tip with the thumb of the other hand, one should likewise press it with the fingers of that hand and the fingers of the left hand.

Having bound it firmly, one of pure intellect should place it upon the heart while reciting the seed-syllable of Māra; this seal known as Bilva has been clearly described here, and it must be kept secret by those who know the ritual procedure.
And in the Agastya-saṃhitā: "The mudrās for invoking, for establishing, for bringing near, as well as for firmly binding, and likewise for making [the deity] face [the worshipper]."
Likewise, there are the sakalī-karaṇī and the great mudrās;
and [the deities] Śaṅkha, Cakra, Gadā, Padma, Dhenuka, Bhaga, and Garuḍa.
One should display the Śrīvatsa, the forest garland, and the Yoni-mudrā.
The handful of flowers, brought from the *mūlādhāra* to the *dvādaśānta*,
is offered into images and other objects by means of the splendors residing in the three places.
O Sage, this is the invocation mudrā in the ritual of worship;
furthermore, it is taught that this same mudrā, when turned face down, is used for the rite of installation.
With both hands formed into fists by joining the raised thumbs,
this is the mudrā named Sannidhīkaraṇa, used in the rite of worshiping the deity.
That same [mudrā], with the thumbs tucked inside, is the *saṃnirodhinī*;
the pair of fists held palm-upward is considered the *sammukhīkaraṇī*.
The sakalīkaraṇī mudrā is likewise the placement of the limbs upon the limbs;
it consists of the two hands spread apart with the thumbs joined to one another.
This is declared to be the Mahāmudrā, which brings about the completion of what is deficient or excessive;
it is formed by placing the tips of the little fingers, ring fingers, and middle fingers within the space between the thumbs at the front.
With both hands, the middle fingers concealed and the fingers curled inward on all sides, this mudrā is called the Śaṅkhā, used for the worship of the gods.
But by mutually facing and interlacing the touch of the fingers with effort, O Sage, one should form the circle.
This is declared to be the *cakra-mudrā*; after that follows the *gadā-mudrā*, in which the fingers are joined facing one another with the middle fingers raised.
Then, O one whose wealth is austerity, having placed the two thumbs in the middle, one should properly form a circle with the hands by joining the fingers all around.
This is the lotus mudrā; after that, the cow (dhenu) mudrā.
Then, with the ring fingers, the little fingers, the two index fingers, and the two middle fingers, joined and facing one another, it is known as the kaustubha mudrā.
The little fingers are joined to one another and facing each other;
likewise, the left index finger is between the middle and ring fingers.
The left ring finger is touched by the index finger, adorned by the middle finger;
with the two thumbs alternately bent, this is the characteristic mudrā of the Kaustubha gem.
The little fingers are joined to one another and then separated in reverse;
with the thumbs placed underneath, this is the mudrā known as Garuḍa.
The two middle fingers and the ring fingers are placed between the thumb and the index finger;
the little fingers, the ring fingers, and the middle fingers of both hands are [extended], with the tips of the two index fingers [touching].
O Sage, this [mudrā] is the Śrīvatsa; from that, the Vanamālā [is formed]:
a fist with the little, ring, and middle fingers closed, and the index finger raised.

The *yoni-mudrā* is declared to be formed by the two index fingers raised over the head while the two hands are drawn together in a contracted position. This is the *paribhrāntā* gesture for the celestial dwellers.

"O Sage, the two ring fingers should be placed between the tips of the index finger and the thumb; the thumbs should rest at the base of the middle fingers—this is known as the mudrā recommended for worship. Thus [it is said]. He states the weapon mantra (astra-mantra) with the words "praṇava... and so forth.
Having uttered the *praṇava* (oṃ), the word *hṛdoḥ* at the end,
followed by *sudarśanaṃ* with the dative case-ending (*sudarsanāya*), and likewise the word *astraṃ* ending in *phaṭ*, one should perform the ritual application (*kalayet*) with this [mantra].
With the weapon-mudrā, Manu [protects] the ten directions.
The *praṇava* is *oṃkāraḥ*;

the *hṛt* is *namaḥ*. At the conclusion (*avasāne*) of these two, at the end, is the word *sudarśana* accompanied by the fourth case (*caturthī-vibhakti-sahita*), that is, the word *sudarśana* with the dative case; likewise, at the end of that is the word *astra* ending in the fourth case (*caturthy-anta*).

Furthermore, of what nature [is it]? Having uttered that which ends with *phaṭ*—that is, ending with the word *phaṭ*—one should, by means of this mantra (*amunā mantreṇa*) and with the *astra-mudrā*, "arrange the ten directions" (*daśa-haritaḥ kalpayet*), meaning one should perform the binding of the ten directions (*dig-bandhana*).
Thus, concluding the previously performed set of ritual placements (*nyāsa-jāta*), he indicates the meditation (*dhyāna*) to be described in the chapter on fire (*agni-paṭala*) with the word "iti."
Having thus performed the entire rite,
he [beheld] the unborn one who has a human form, who is sought by the Vedas, and who is skilled in the process of the creation and destruction of the world.
May he remember the beloved of the cowherd women.

In this manner, having performed and completed the entire ritual previously described, including all the *nyāsa*s and so forth, one should remember—that is, contemplate—Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of the cowherd women.
Of what nature is Kṛṣṇa? He who is capable of effecting the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is that which is to be sought through the Śrutis, that which is accessible through the Upaniṣads.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
Unborn (*aja*), meaning devoid of origination; furthermore, of what nature is he? He has a human form (*manu-vigraha*), which means a human body. // KrdC_2.60 //
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Kramadīpikā* composed by the venerable Keśavācārya.
**Chapter Three** Now he describes the meditation on the deity common to both mantras:
Then, there were trees with branches bent low by clusters of fresh sprouts and blossoming flowers from which honey-dripping nectar was released due to their manifest fragrance,
and which were entwined by graceful creepers of fully bloomed new clusters.
One of pure intellect should remember Śiva, cooled by the presence of Vṛndāvana.
Immediately thereafter, one of pure intellect and stainless mind should remember and contemplate Vṛndāvana.
Of what nature is it? It is cooled and made refreshing by trees. By what kind of trees?
It reveals its intense fragrance;
moreover, it is that in which the honeyed liquor has overflowed;
and furthermore, it is fully blossomed.

Moreover, by those [trees] whose branches were bent down by a profusion— that is, a multitude— of such flowers (*prasūna*) shining brilliantly with beauty as well as fresh sprouts; [in the alternative reading] "by those whose blossoming flowers were radiant and agitated by manifest fragrance," it means they were agitated, that is, pervaded on all sides, by a manifest fragrance.
And furthermore, the meaning is: such a flower as this, which is "matta-bhṛṅgollasan," that is, shining with intoxicated bees;
moreover, by what kind [of bees]?

By those whose activity is upon the *vallarī*—the lovely, charming tip of the creeper's branch—which is "praphulla-nava-mañjarī-lalita," that is, made beautiful by a blossoming, newly opened cluster of buds.
By those [feet] which possess movement;
furthermore, of what nature?
Auspicious, bestowing welfare. (KrdC 3.1)

Sanātana: These thirty-six verses that follow from here have been extracted from the *Śrī Hari-bhakti-vilāsa* and commented upon by the venerable master Śrī Sanātana Gosvāmī. Since his commentary here does not differ significantly from the one found there, it is not reproduced here; they should be consulted in that very work.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
Its interior is made resonant by the humming sounds emerging from wandering bees, which are charming as they savor the nectar of blossoming flowers.
It resounded here and there with birds such as pigeons, parrots, mynas, and cuckoos, and was agitated by the dancing of peacocks, the enemies of serpents.

Vṛndāvana has its interior made resonant by particular sounds—its inner space filled with humming. By what kind of sounds? By humming sounds that are charming and heart-stealing due to the tasting—that is, the licking—of the honey which is the nectar of the blossoming, fully opened flowers. Furthermore, by what kind of sounds?
It is frequented by wandering bees that have emerged from the mouths of those [bees] that have come forth from the *śilīmukha* flowers;
furthermore, how is Vṛndāvana? It is made resonant with sounds here and there by birds such as pigeons (*pārāvata*), parrots (*śuka*), mynas (*śārikā*), and cuckoos (*kokila*).
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is pervaded—that is, filled—with the agitation caused by the dancing of the peacock, which is the enemy of serpents. //2//
Furthermore, of what kind?
[It is] by means of those carrying the spray from the moving waves of the daughter of Kalinda,
and grey with the mass of pollen from the interiors of blossoming lotuses.
It was constantly attended by breezes that stirred the garments of the playful women of Vraja, whose passion had been kindled.
It is constantly and perpetually served by the Maruts, the winds.
By what kind of Maruts?
By those carrying the droplets—the drops of water—from the moving waves of the Yamunā, the daughter of Kalinda.
By this, the coolness of the wind is described.
Furthermore, of what kind [is it]?

"Vinidra" means blossomed; that which is the interior—the inner part—of the *sarasīruha*, the lotus, and by the mass of pollen (*rajaścaya*), the collection of dust therein, they are made greyish-white (*uddhūsaraiḥ*).
By this, their fragrance is described.
Furthermore, by what kind [of breezes]?
By those intent on fluttering—that is, capable of moving—the garments of the playful women of Vraja, those beautiful cowherd girls, whose passion (manobhava) was inflamed, meaning intensified.
By this, that which is to be honored has been stated. (KrdC 3.3)
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It has coral for its fresh sprouts, emeralds for its leaves, clusters of diamonds and pearls for its buds, and various fruits with the hue of lotuses.
One should meditate upon that wish-granting kalpa-tree, which is most massive, constantly served by all the seasons, and which rises even higher than that [palace].
Even within that [space], one should meditate upon a desire-tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) in the midst of Vṛndāvana.
Of what kind? Raised up, that is, lofty.
Again, of what kind?
"Thickest" means more massive.
Furthermore, of what kind?
That which has coral—meaning *vidruma*—as its very new sprout or *kisalaya*.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It is one whose covering or leaf is made of emerald, which is a specific type of gemstone.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
"Vajra" refers to diamonds and "mauktika" to pearls;
that which is a collection or multitude of these two constitutes the "koraka," or flower bud, therein. Furthermore, of what nature is it?

It is that which possesses the "lotus-love" (*kamala-rāga*), meaning it is a ruby (*padma-rāga-maṇi*) where various kinds of fruits are found. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is constantly attended to and always embraced by all the seasons—that is, by all six seasons.
By this, its being endowed with all flowers is shown. Furthermore, of what kind is it? It is "kāmadam," which bestows whatever is desired. (KrdC 3.4)
Below that [mountain], which sheds sprays of nectar, was a golden ground as radiant as the rising sun atop a range of peaks of fine gold,
with a floor of blazing jewels and brilliant with heaps of flower pollen.
Furthermore, the wise one, being unwearied, should again recollect [the deity] who is free from the sixfold arrows of passion.
The wise and learned person, being untiring and free from indolence,
should again remember and contemplate this golden ground beneath the wish-fulfilling tree.
Of what nature? "Suhe-ma" means that which possesses a beautiful row of golden peaks;
likewise, [she is] radiant like the sun risen from that eastern mountain, like the manifest sun.

Regarding the reading "dedīpyamānāṃ suhema-śikharācale 'py uditā," [it means] "shining brightly, arisen even on the mountain with beautiful golden peaks. On that mountain (*acale*)—that is, the peak (*parvate*)—where there is beautiful gold (*suhema*), the word *api* (even) is displaced in its order and should be understood immediately after the word *kanaka-sthalīm*.
Of what kind [of mountain] is this? [It is one where] nectar...?
Like a shower—that is, a falling mass—of that spray, which is a drop of nectar; thus, [he is] one who rains down a multitude of those drops of nectar.
Of what kind [is the ground]? Its surface is paved with blazing, swelling gems such as rubies and the like.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
She makes [the world] radiant with masses of flower-pollen;
furthermore, of what nature is she?
She is one from whom the six waves—namely desire, anger, and so forth, or hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death—have departed and been removed. (KrdC 3.5)

Having visualized an eight-petaled, reddish lotus upon a most magnificent yoga-throne set within a pavement of jewels, one should contemplate [the deity] in its center, possessing a splendor like that of the rising sun.
One should then meditate upon Mukunda, who is established in bliss.

In that golden city, upon its jeweled pavement—the ground surface set with gems—there stood a most vast and great seat of yoga (*yoga-pīṭha*). It was eight-petaled, having eight petals, and was reddish, crimson;
for this very reason, it resembled the rising sun.
