Having thus meditated upon the lotus, immediately thereafter, one should contemplate Mukunda Kṛṣṇa in the center of that eight-petaled lotus of reddish dawn-color. Of what nature? Seated in ease, comfortably seated; from this point on, he is the primordial progenitor of the lineage. (KṛdC 3.6)
Furthermore, of what kind?
Its luster is equal to a fresh blue lotus, resembling a mass of clouds made of crushed collyrium and the finest jewels.
O King, he possesses a mass of hair that is very glossy, dark blue, thick, and curled,
with a crest like the beautiful black plumage of a peacock.

Whose luster is equal to these: a jewel from the Sūtrāma mountain, a sapphire, crushed collyrium, split collyrium, ground kajjala, a mass of clouds, a multitude of clouds, and a freshly blossomed blue lotus;
what else is it like?

"Very glossy" (*susnigdha*) means very smooth and oily; "blue-black" (*nīla*), "dark" (*śyāma*), "thick" (*ghana*), "dense" (*nibiḍa*), "curled" (*kuñcita*), and "wavy" (*kuṭila*): [he is one] in whom there is a mass, that is, a collection, of such hair.
Furthermore, of what kind? "O King" (*rājan*):

he is one who has upon his crest (*cūḍā*) that which is shining (*rājat*), beautiful (*manojña*), and heart-stealing (*manohara*), namely the peacock's plume (*śikhaṇḍa*), the tail-feather of the peacock (*mayūra*). (KrdC 3.7)
Furthermore, of what kind?
One whose crest-jewel is fashioned like the son of the celestial tree (the mango) caressed by bees,
and whose ear-ornament is an upward-pointing fresh blue lotus.
With a forehead shining with a mark of yellow orpiment upon it, flickering amidst his dangling locks of hair, and adorned with a row of moving bees.
He by whom a crest-ornament was fashioned— that is, created— from the flowers of the celestial tree, the *pārijāta*, which were lovingly cherished and served with affection by the *rolamba* bees;
how else [described] is he?
He whose ear-ornament is that very same blooming fresh blue lotus used as an ear-pendant— upright and fully opened— is described as such.
Furthermore, of what kind is he?
He whose forehead—the surface of the brow—is radiant and beautiful with locks of hair that are playful and flickering, and upon which shines a tilaka-mark of yellow pigment (gorocanā);
furthermore, how is he?
He who possesses a row of moving eyebrows, like a line of trembling creepers. (KrdC 3.8)
Furthermore, of what sort is he? His face is as beautiful as the orb of the autumnal moon when it has reached its fullness; his large eyes are like lotus petals.
With his cheeks like mirrors, radiant with the rays from jeweled *makara*-shaped earrings, and possessing a high and beautiful nose; Kṛd_3.9.
Whose face was as lovely and captivating as the orb of the autumnal moon— full, complete, belonging to the autumn season, and with its dark spots removed—
and furthermore, whose eyes were large and wide like lotus petals?
Furthermore, of what kind?

"With jewels" means that which is shimmering—that is, shining—with the rays of those *makara-kuṇḍalas*, the ear-rings shaped like sea-monsters (*makara*); he whose cheeks are thus illuminated and radiant, and who is therefore like a mirror (*mukura*), is described as such.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
"Unnata" means one whose nose (*nāsā*) is elevated and charming; he is such, and [the text refers] to him.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? His lower lip is more beautiful than vermilion, and his limbs are illuminated by the splendor of a smile as radiant as the moon, the kunda flower, and the mandāra blossom.
His conch-like neck was radiant and captivating, adorned with a necklace fashioned from a collection of wild sprouts and flowers.

He whose lower lip is as charming as vermilion (sindūra) is described as such; furthermore, of what nature is he? "Indu-kunda..."—*indu* is the moon, *kunda* is the *kunda* flower, *mandāra* is the white *mandāra* tree or the *arka* flower.
Likewise, he was one by whom the quarters and directions were illuminated and beautified by the luster—that is, the radiance—of his gentle smile, which is a slight laugh.
Furthermore, of what kind was he?
He was one who possessed a mass of wild sprouts and flowers—that is, a collection of fresh shoots and blossoms produced from the forest.

He whose neck was radiant, shining, and captivating because of a necklace (*graiveyaka*)—an ornament for the throat—which had been fashioned and prepared by him; he whose throat was marked with three lines, such as he is described. (KrdC 3.10)
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
Its shoulders are adorned with festoons of *kapra* flowers hanging down, frequented by intoxicated bees.
His full chest is adorned with a series of necklaces and clusters of gems,
and he possesses the radiant Kaustubha jewel shining upon the expanse of his breast like the sun in the sky.

It was frequented and served by bees that were intoxicated, having drunk their fill of honey, as they wandered about; furthermore, it was adorned with a garland of such hanging *santānakas*—that is, a garland of flowers from the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*)—and thus its shoulders were well-decorated by that garland.
How else was it?
The *bhagaṇa*—meaning the collection of stars—is indeed a string of pearls (*hārāvalī*).

By that [collection], his chest—the broad and fleshy heart—is adorned and beautified; that very chest is the expanse of the sky (*vyoma-sthala*), the ground of the atmosphere. Upon it shines the Kaustubha gem, which is like the sun (*bhānu*); thus he is joined with that.
In this case, there is only the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) and not the figure of speech *upamā* (simile), because of the lack of a relationship between the host of stars and the sun.
And such being the case, the sense is that the beauty of both is attained at one and the same time. // KrdC_3.11 //
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is well-marked with the auspicious sign of the Śrīvatsa, has elevated shoulders, and possesses well-formed arms that are thick and reach down to his knees.
With a belly that is not sunken, a noble and deep navel,
and a line of body hair as beautiful as a swarm of female bees.

How is he further described? He is well-marked with the auspicious *śrīvatsa* sign, possesses elevated shoulders, and has well-formed arms that are thick and reach down to his knees; he has a deep, prominent belly and a noble, deep navel, and a line of body hair as beautiful as a swarm of female bees.
Furthermore, he is adorned with armlets and bracelets set with various jewels, which ripple like waves—
Adorned with necklaces, girdles, anklets,
and armlets, her slender body was encased in a cage of red unguents,
and her rounded hips were draped in yellow garments.
Constructed and joined with various gems such as sapphire (*indranīla*) and others,

there were armlets (*aṅgada*), bracelets (*bāhu-valaya*), as well as rings (*kaṅkaṇa*), bangles (*ūrmi*), signets (*mudrikā*), necklaces (*graiveya*— ornaments for the neck), and anklets (*nūpura*) together with small bells (*rasanā*) that encircle [the limbs] on all sides; and there was a waist-belt (*tunda-bandha*) for the purpose of binding the belly (*udara*).
He who possesses these ornaments, including a golden cord, is such;
how is he further described?
He is one whose slender body-stalk, like a painted vine, is made variegated with various colors by means of a divine, most excellent, fragrant powder—anointed with passion (anurāga).
Furthermore, of what kind was he?
He was one by whom the orb of the hips (*nitamba-bimba*) was completely encircled and enveloped with a garment that was "drunk"—that is, exceedingly yellow.
Although the use of the word *nitamba* for a woman's waist is seen in the lexicons (*kośa*), nevertheless, because it is equally charming, its use for a man's waist is not contradictory. (KrdC 3.13)
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It has beautiful thighs and knees, with well-proportioned and lovely shanks, and the grace of its elevated forefeet surpasses the splendor of a tortoise.
His beautiful lotus-feet are adorned with coverings of red toes that shine like rows of claws upon a ruby mirror.
He by whom the splendor and luster of a tortoise (*kūrma*) was disparaged and surpassed by his two forefeet—the tips of the feet—which were lovely, beautiful, elevated, and high;
furthermore, how was he?
By his rows of nails which shone and gleamed like mirrors fashioned from rubies (*māṇikya*). How did they shine? [They shone] thus.
He whose beautiful lotus-feet possess petals—namely, those very shining red toes—is thus described; [he is] him.
Furthermore, of what kind?
Delightful with the palms of his reddish hands and feet marked by the fish, goad, lotus stalk, thunderbolt, barley, lotus, and vajra.
Her bodily beauty, fashioned from the very essence of all loveliness,
surpassed the splendor of the body of the God of Love.

He who is delightful to all people because of his very red soles— soles that are perfectly marked with these: the fish (*matsya*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*) which is a specific type of weapon, the discus (*ari*), the conch (*dara*), the banner (*ketu*), the barley grain (*yava*), the lotus (*abja*), and the thunderbolt (*vajra*) which is triangular in shape like a lightning bolt.

Furthermore, of what sort is it? It is that by which the splendor of Manobhava, the god of love, is censured— that is, surpassed— by the beauty of her limbs, which is fashioned and composed from the collection of the essence, the most excellent portion, of loveliness (lāvaṇya).
That by which there is beauty of the body is thus described.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
By means of divine melodies set in motion by his fingers, which move restlessly within the holes of the flute filled by his lotus-like mouth.
It is an infinite ocean of the water of bliss, in which the continuous stream of the mental continuums of all sentient beings has been eternally melted away.

He by whom the continuous succession of the lineage of all living beings—of every creature—is perpetually and eternally made liquid, brought low, drawn out, and attracted; by what means? By those divine and sublime melodies produced and set in motion by the fingers of his hand, which flicker and move within the flute-holes—the openings of the bamboo—which are themselves filled by his lotus-like mouth.
The meaning is "by means of those sounds" (dhvanis), which are vowels.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? "Ananta..."—an ocean of immeasurable bliss. (KrdC 3.16)
Furthermore, of what sort was it?
[It was filled] with cows whose eyes were fixed upon his lotus-like face, and who moved slowly and languidly, stumbling under the weight of their udders.
Furthermore, it was surrounded by [the cows] whose remaining tips of grass were bitten off by their teeth and whose creeper-like tails were hanging down.
Immediately thereafter, [he saw the chariot] surrounded on all sides by cows.
Of what kind were they?
They were such that their eyes were fixed—meaning joined—upon the lotus-face of the Supreme Lord, which was like a lotus.
Furthermore, of what kind were they?
They were characterized by a slow and slight gait due to the stumbling caused by the weight of their breasts.
Furthermore, of what kind were they?
"By those [cows] whose remaining sprouts of grass—that is, the sprouts of grass left over from eating—have been bitten by the tips of their teeth;
and again, of what kind? By those whose creeper-like tails are *ālambinī*, that is, hanging down. (KrdC 3.17)
Furthermore, of what kind [is it]?
It is charming with frothy milk flowing from the pits of their mouths, which are filled by the sucking of breasts that are accompanied by a steady flow.
And even by the young calves, who pressed their pair of ears forward to listen to the charming, deep songs produced by the flute.
The phrase "surrounded by yearling calves" connects with what precedes it.

Of what kind were they? From the cavity of the mouth—that is, the opening of the face—which was full and motionless due to the sucking of the udder (the drawing of the breast with teeth and lips) accompanied by the flow of milk (*prasrava*). From that [cavity].
With those [milkmaids] who were charming and captivating because of the frothy milk that had overflowed and spilled;

and again, of what sort? "By means of the flute" (veṇu): by means of the flute (*vaṃśī*), they had their ears fixed high upon that enchanting, joy-inducing, and deep-toned (*mandra*) song (*gīti*) which had been set in motion and played. Thus, by them. (KrdC 3.18)
Furthermore, of what kind?
By the falling of the tips of their hooves, tossed about by the vigorous leaping and the impetuous striking of their heads against fresh horns.
With herds of young bulls and heifers whose dewlaps were thick with moisture and whose tails were held high; Kṛd 3.19.
A *vatsatara* is a three-year-old bull;
a *vatsatarī* is a three-year-old cow. With these groups or herds, [there is] that soft head upon which there is a fresh, newly grown horn.

In that context, "by those whose hoof-tips were unsteady and unsettled due to leaping— meaning moving here and there— caused by the agitation and excess of anger resulting from the blows and strikes of another fighting calf" means: by those [hooves] characterized in such a manner.
Furthermore, of what kind [are they]?
"Full," meaning very smooth or nourished.
Furthermore, of what kind?
Those whose necks possess such a dewlap (*sāsnā*)—that is, one characterized by an abundance of excellence—are "those [oxen]";
*sāsnā* refers to the dewlap on the neck.
Furthermore, of what kind were they?
With uplifted tails.
Furthermore, of what kind was it? It was filled with great bulls, exhausted by the heavy burden of their massive humps, who agitated the circle of the quarters with their lowing cries.
With their broad nostrils dilated by the nectar of the sound of the flute, which they drank in through their uplifted ears; // Krd_3.20 //
It was also surrounded by great bulls, oxen;
of what sort? By those whose circular array of directions—the collection of quarters—was agitated, that is, brought into a state of commotion, by the sound of *hambā*, a particular lowing noise.
Again, of what sort were they?
That very burden which is broad, excessive, and borne upon the hump—that is, the weight on the back—is what causes them to be weary and languid.
Furthermore, by what means?
By those ears which have been "stretched upward"—that is, held erect and raised—and by which [the sound] has been "drunk in," meaning heard with great intensity.

Those whose noses (*ghoṇā*) were uplifted—raised upward—expansive, clearly manifest, broad, and long by that nectar of sound, which is the nectar-like resonance of their lineage; they are such [persons]. (KrdC 3.20)
Furthermore, of what sort was it?
It was accompanied by cowherds whose qualities, character, age, amorous play, and dress were identical to His own, and who played flutes and lutes with enchanting, melodious sounds.
Accompanied by those skilled in the performance of graceful dances with their vine-like arms, moving in harmony with the singing of cloth banners in low, high, and shrill tones; Kṛd_3.21.

And surrounded by cowherds—of what kind? By those whose qualities such as excellence (*guṇa*), character (*śīla*), age (*vayas*), playfulness (*vilāsa*), and dress (*veśa*)—where "excellence" refers to qualities like nobility, "character" to traits like fortitude, "age" to childhood and so forth, "playfulness" to sporting, and "dress" to a particular mode of appearance—are all equal or similar;
by such [cowherds].

Furthermore, by what kind [of beings]? By those whose flutes and lutes possess a sweet, indistinct (*kala*), and resonant (*mūrcchita*) tone; that is, by those whose flutes and lutes have such qualities. As it has been said:
Where the blended notes attain the state of melody (rāga),
the poets call that a *mūrchanā* arising from the *grāmas*.
There are seven notes, three *grāmas*, and twenty-one *mūrchanās*.

Furthermore, by what kind of people? By those intent upon—that is, devoted to—a singing that is "clear" (paṭu), meaning distinct, through a particular modulation (yati-viśeṣa) characterized by being "low" (mandra), meaning soft, and "high" (ucca), meaning exceeding the limit, which is "sharp" (tāra). Furthermore, by what kind of people?
[He is] skilled in the performance—that is, the execution—of charming (*lalita*) dance (*lāsya*), which is captivating (*manohara*) by means of those tremulous vine-like arms (*dor-vallarī*).
Furthermore, of what nature [is he]?
He is one whose [dance] is fixed upon the slopes of his broad hips reaching down to his calves.

It was surrounded by playful young fawns wandering about, their necks adorned with ornaments fashioned from the claws of hyenas, making indistinct and sweet sounds as they tinkled with the jingling of swaying rows of small bells.
Surrounded and encircled by chubby children;

of what kind? By those wandering about with the sounds of a multitude of tinkling bells—a collection of small bells (*kiṅkiṇī-ghaṭā*) that are tied to and swinging from the region of the hips (*kaṭīra-taṭī*), which is thick and fleshy near the shanks.
Furthermore, of what kind?
Delusive and captivating.
Furthermore, characterized by what?
By those [beings] who have fashioned or prepared neck-ornaments—that is, neck-decorations—with the claws of hyenas and the claws of tigers;
for it is for the protection of children that the binding of tiger-claws is performed around the neck.
Furthermore, by what kind [of beings]?

Those whose speech is such—unmanifest (avyakta) yet indistinct, and at the same time charming (mañjula) and captivating (manohara)—are described as "those [whose speech is] thus"; by them. (KrdC 3.22)
Furthermore, of what nature was it?
Now, [the sound] of the very graceful cowherd beauties,
whose gait was slow due to their broad and firm hips.
[The women] possessed rows of body hair that were made prominent by the three folds of skin, which were curved due to the weight of their heavy breasts.

Immediately thereafter, the connection with the eighth verse is as follows: [the place] was constantly and eternally served on all sides and everywhere by the rows—that is, the lines—of the charming cowherd women.
Of what kind were they?
Their hips—the broad, large, firm, and dense posterior parts of the waist—[were such].
By him [he saw] those who were slow-moving and unable to walk;
furthermore, of what nature were they?
Their waists were slightly bent by the weight of their heavy breasts—the excessive burden of their bosoms.

Regarding "madhya-pradeśaḥ": those [women] whose rows of body hair (*roma-paṅkti*) have expanded and spread across the three folds of flesh (*bali-traya*) located there [in the middle region]. (KrdC 3.23)
Furthermore, of what kind are they?
Of those whose limbs and feet have been made to sprout with the nectar-like essence of the exceedingly sweet and beautiful music of His flute.
Their vine-like bodies were adorned with horripilation that had arisen, beautiful as the unfolding of flower buds.

Of those [women] for whom the tree of passion (kāma-vṛkṣa)— which sprouts and is ready to grow by means of that very nectar-like water, the sound of the flute which is the most sweet, most love-inspiring, beautiful, and heart-stealing music of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— has thus flourished.
The reading is *aṅgajāṅghripasya*.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?

Their vine-like bodies (*gātra-vallarī*) are adorned with a dense growth of bristling hair (*romodgama*), which has risen and increased, being as beautiful and captivating as a cluster of flower buds (*mukula-visara*). Of those [women] whose body-vines are thus embellished...
Likewise for those [feminine suffixes]. (KrdC 3.24)
Furthermore, of what nature were they?
Of those whose ocean of the water of passion was dried up by the moonlight of their exceedingly beautiful and gentle smiles.
Of those whose continuous streams of sweat-drops were like a multitude of fine droplets from the breaking of most tremulous waves.

Of that Kṛṣṇa, his exceedingly enchanting slight smile is itself the moonbeam; by it is expanded—that is, surged forth—the ocean of passion (*rāga-samudra*). From that ocean comes a wave, most restless in its motion; from that wave come droplets of water, and the collection of those droplets is equal to the beads of perspiration—those drops of sweat—which are continuous. Of these [beads]:
Of those that are pervaded.
Furthermore, of what nature were they?
[They were struck] by a rain of the sharp arrows of Māra, discharged from the bow of his exceedingly charming and slow-moving eyebrows.
Their limbs were overwhelmed by the piercing of every vital point,
and they suffered the agony of an unbearable, spreading trembling.
From that Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s exceedingly charming, gentle, and not very long bow-like brow-creepers,
there arose sharp side-glances which are themselves the arrows of Cupid; by the excessive falling of the rain of those glances,
all one's vital points (marmas) were shattered and pulverized, and thus an unbearable sensation of trembling spread through and pervaded the limbs that had become uncontrollable.
Of those [women], such as they are, for them [it is so].
Furthermore, of what kind [of beings]?
Of those who are longing for the method of drinking the nectar-essence of the beauty of the forms of their exceedingly lovely deeds.
From her two lotus-eyes, languid and tremulous, which carry a flood of the waters of affection.
Of those [women] who carry that very stream of water solely through affection—that is, through love alone;
by whom? By those whose lotus-eyes are half-closed due to bashfulness and so forth—or there is also a reading: "by those whose lotus-eyes are tremulous with graceful charm.
Of what sort are they?
The extremely beautiful activity of that Supreme Lord is a particular amorous gesture; His splendor of form is a radiance that delights the minds of loving women.
These two constitute the essence of nectar, and "the drinking" of them refers to the intense application of the eyes. [The couple] are longing for the performance of that [drinking].
There is an alternative reading: *subhaga-krama*.

According to those who maintain a threefold reading, the terms *subhaga* (fortunate) and *kamanīya* (desirable) are included as synonyms for *sundara* (beautiful) and *kamra* (lovely), because of the extraordinary nature of his physical form. (KrdC 3.27)
Furthermore, of what nature were they?
They were repeatedly attended by swarms of bees, greedy for the honey dripping from the full-blown flowers falling from their loosened tresses.
Of those whose soft voices falter with the intoxication of passion,
and whose hips are revealed as the silk garments slip loose from their shifting waistbands and fluttering girdles.
From that mass of hair which was loosening and slipping, there fell blossoming flowers;
from those flowers trickled honey, the floral nectar. Therein, by swarms of bees—bees who were intensely attached to it—the [trees] were repeatedly served, again and again.
Furthermore, of what kind [of women] is he the slayer?

They are those whose speech—clearly indistinct, soft, tender, and captivating—is faltering due to the intoxication produced by passion; such is their state. Intoxication (*unmāda*) and exhilaration (*mada*) are specific varieties of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
As it is said in the *Śṛṅgāra-tilaka*:
That in which activity arises through labored breathing, weeping, trembling, and various kinds of gazing is known as insanity (unmāda), as for example: [the following verse].
Some say that the characteristic of intoxication (*mada*) should also be understood in this way.
Furthermore, of what kind [of women]?
Of those whose girdle-string (*kāñcī-rasanā*) is swaying and restless, and whose knot of the lower garment (*nīvī*), which is being loosened, becomes tight again.
According to the lexicon, *nīvī* refers to the knot of a woman’s garment.

By that [knot], the Chinese silk (*cīna-sicaya*)—a fine cloth produced in the land of China—was becoming loose; those women whose hips possessed a manifest, radiant beauty (*nitamba-tviṭ*) in the middle of that [loose] garment were thus described.
Furthermore, of what nature were they?
Of those whose quarters were filled with the tinkling of jeweled anklets from the gentle impact of their stumbling, graceful lotus-feet,
and whose petal-like lips quivered as their eyelashes trembled like buds.
Of those with blossoming lotuses in their two lakes and shimmering earrings.

[The dust] from those lotus-feet—feet that are graceful, charming, and yet faltering due to lack of restraint; [the dust raised by] their gentle, slight impact, which causes the tips of the jeweled anklets to ring out, filling the faces of the quarters; [the dust from those feet whose] trembling petal-like lips, and the lotuses of their two lakes—the eyes with their long lashes—are budding; and [from those feet] where radiant earrings shine. (KrdC 3.29)
Furthermore, of what nature were they?
Their sprout-like reddish lips were withering due to the heat of the wind from the longest-drawn breaths.
He is constantly attended on all sides by rows of [goddesses] whose lotus-hands shine with various offerings.
Of those whose sprout-like red lips were withered by the heat caused by that long breath-wind;
furthermore, of what kind?
Of those whose lotus-hands were beautiful with various offerings. (KrdC 3.30)
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
Its entire body is worshipped by garlands of their wide, trembling, blue eyes— like blossoming blue lotuses— and it is the abode of manifold amorous graces.
He bears a captivating garland of bees— his eyes intoxicated with love— which tastes the honey-dew dripping from the lotus-face of his beloved.

He whose entire body was even more highly honored— that is, worshipped— with garlands made from the very eyes of those beautiful cowherd women, which were wide, long, tremulous, flickering, blue, and dark, like full-blown, blossoming blue lotuses; such is Mukunda.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is a place of various diversions.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?

"By those charming faces"—that is, that very captivating face of theirs is itself a cluster of lotuses; from that [cluster] flows—that is, drips—the *mādhvī* essence, which is nectar. She whose nature it is to taste that [essence], and who bears a captivating swarm of bees—which is actually her pair of eyes, intoxicated with passion through affection—is the one being described. (KrdC 3.31)

Now, following the meditation on the Supreme Lord, he describes the meditation on the deities beginning with the attendant gods: "One should visualize outside and in front of him a multitude of gods, along with the cowherd women, cowherds, and cattle."
Seeking wealth, she was preceded by Brahmā, the Three-eyed One,
and Indra, and was solely intent upon hymns of praise.
In front of this Supreme Lord, one should visualize the assembly of the goddesses of speech, the pitchers, and the gods outside the cowherd women and the cows.

Although the use of the ablative case is prescribed when joined with the word "bahiḥ" (outside), nevertheless, since what is established by a specific grammatical rule does not apply universally, there is no fault even in employing the genitive case.

Of what nature [is that assembly]? Is it seeking knowledge (*jñāna*), or seeking wealth (*dhana*), or else intent on stealing away the mind of the Supreme Lord, or seeking virtue, pleasure, and liberation (*dharma-kāma-mokṣa*)?
Furthermore, of what nature was she?
She was headed by Virañci (Brahmā), Īśa (Śiva), and Śakra (Indra).
Furthermore, of what nature was she?
Devoted to praise. (KrdC 3.32)
To his right, he saw a multitude of sages longing for the firm Dharma and devoted to the traditional teachings;
then, behind him, the lords of yogis who seek liberation.
Through meditative concentration, [he honors] Sanaka and the others who have subdued their pride.

To his right—that is, in the southern part from the Supreme Lord—one should likewise, according to the reading "tadvat," meditate upon the multitude of sages (*muni-nikara*), meaning a collection of sages.
Of what nature are they? Devoted to the *āmnāya*, meaning devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?

He whose desire for dharma is unwavering—since the term *muni* is derived from the act of reflecting (*manana*), such a desire for dharma would not be appropriate for them; therefore, the word *muni* here indicates the *ṛṣis*. This is because the word "dharma" here denotes the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-jñāna*).
As it was said by Yājñavalkya: "But this is the supreme dharma: that the vision of the Self occurs through yoga."
Immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon Sanaka and the other lords of yoga behind the Supreme Lord.
Of what nature are they? They are solely intent on liberation.
Again, of what nature are they?
Seated in meditative concentration.
Then, on his left side, he saw the Yakṣas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas,
along with the Kinnaras and the principal Apsarases, together with their consorts.
Those who seek sensual pleasure [should worship] with dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
Immediately thereafter, one should visualize the yakṣas and others together with their wives on the left side of the deity;
of what nature are they? Accompanied by kinnaras.
Again, of what nature are they?
One should likewise remember the principal Apsarases, headed by Urvaśī, who serve as the instruments for all dancing, singing, and instrumental music for those seeking their desired objects.
[He who is] white as a conch, the moon, or a kunda flower; who knows all the Āgamas;
whose mass of matted hair is tawny like a multitude of lightning flashes;
and [he who possesses] unwavering devotion directed toward his lotus feet.
Desiring [this], having utterly abandoned all other attachments.
One should meditate upon the Son of the Creator, the Son of Brahmā, in the sky—that is, in the ether.
Of what nature is he?
White and stainless, like a conch shell and the like.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
One who knows the complete Āgamas.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
[He is] one whose mass of matted hair (*jaṭā-kalāpa*) is a collection of locks that are tawny (*piśaṅga*), like the radiance or brilliance of a multitude of *saudāmanī* lightning flashes;
furthermore, of what kind?
One who desires devotion (*bhakti*).
Of what nature? Steadfast.
Furthermore, of what kind?
One who has utterly abandoned all connections distinct from the Supreme Lord. (KrdC 3.35)
Furthermore, of what kind?
It is endowed with enchanting *mūrcchanās* belonging to the three *grāmas* and the seven *rāgas*, which are accompanied by various collections of *śrutis*.
One should contemplate that son of the Creator, the Lord of Sages, in the vast sky, gladdening that [disciple] with his exalted words.

That collection of scriptures (*śruti-gaṇa*), which consists of thirty-six varieties and is composed of a multitude of sounds (*nāda*), is joined with the seven musical scales (*rāga*); these are the notes (*svara*) known as *niṣāda*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *ṣaḍja*, *madhyama*, *dhaivata*, and *pañcama*. Among them, the aggregate of the three scales (*grāma*) is called the "triad of scales" (*grāma-trayī*); those [notes] which have entered into or reached that triad of scales—[this is the meaning].
He who delights [the world] with the thirty-one types of *mūrchanās* that are captivating to the mind;
for there are seven notes (*svaras*), three scales (*grāmas*), and twenty-one *mūrchanās*,
wherein the blended note attains the state of a *rāga*.
The poets call that "mūrcchanā," which arises from the *grāma*.
Of what nature were they? They were those uttered, that is, raised up, by the great lute of Nārada, which was equipped with seven strings.
Now, concluding the subject at hand, he describes the sequence for self-worship:

"Having thus meditated upon himself as the son of Nanda before him with a sharp and clear intellect, [the practitioner], by means of the intellect alone, [should worship] with faultless offerings such as the arghya and so forth."
One should worship again with devotion, both within one's own body and with external resources;
we shall now describe that ritual procedure which brings about incomparable proximity [to the deity].

Thus, by means of the previously described method of meditation, one whose intellect is sharp, clear, capable, fit for discernment, and moreover stainless— such a person, having meditated upon the Self in the form of Nanda’s son, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa,
and having contemplated the non-difference between the Self and Nanda’s son, first, with the intellect alone and with the mind alone, [should offer] water for the feet and other such offerings.
One should worship according to the instructions with irreproachable offerings—namely, offerings such as *arghya* and *pādya*, and other blameless services.
As for the reading "abhinandya" (having greeted) found in the *Tripāṭhin* version, they explain that its meaning is "having taken [the deity] and then worshipping.
Furthermore, one should again worship within one's own body directly with external services such as *arghya* and so forth.
Immediately following that, we shall describe the procedure for the external worship of the manifestations (*bahiṣṭha-vibhava*).
Of what nature is it? It is that which grants the supreme proximity (*atyanta-sānnidhya*) of the Supreme Lord. (KrdC 3.37)
He demonstrates the procedure for filling the conch:
having prepared a small sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on the ground with cow-dung and water, [one should place] one's own seat (*viṣṭara*) there.
Having established his position there, he should purify the conch with water using the weapon-mantra.
On the ground— that is, on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or place of worship— having prepared it by sprinkling and smearing it with water mixed with cow dung,

one should place and settle upon that mound one's own seat (*viṣṭara*), such as a cloth or a woolen blanket; then, having taken one's position upon that seat, one should [purify] the conch with water using the *astra-mantra*, which is the weapon-mantra belonging to the root mantra.
Or one may smear it with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ."
There, the wise practitioner, reciting the heart mantra, should scatter perfumes, flowers, and unhusked grain, and fill [the vessel] with pure water.
With the syllables returned, ending at the head.
The wise practitioner, possessing excellent intelligence, having established a fire mandala as a support upon the left side, should recite the heart-mantra— which is indeed the root-mantra—
or simply "Hṛdayāya Namaḥ," and cast in perfume, flowers, barley, and rice; likewise,
he should fill it with pure water, that is, stainless water.

He states the mantra: "by those that have returned" (*pratigataiḥ*). This means by the letters of the *mātṛkā* read in reverse order (*pratiloma*), beginning with the letter *kṣa* and ending with the letter *a*, with the *śiraḥ* (the nasal *anusvāra*) at the end and accompanied by the *bindu*.
The author of the *Laghudīpikā* says "ending with the *bindu*" (*bindvantakaiḥ*).
The teacher of the Vidyādharas says that [the mantras] end with "svāhā," while those who follow the Tripāṭhin tradition say they end with "vikrāya svāhā."
Regarding the word "pīṭha":
the knower of mantras [should perform the rites] upon the pedestal, the conch, and the water,
during the day, the night, and the morning, respectively.
One should worship the mandalas with the syllables of the poison-mantra, preceded by the recitation of the face-mantra.

Upon the seat, the conch, and the water, one should worship in sequence the mandalas of Fire, Sun, and Moon; the syllable *viṣam* (the letter *ma*) is to be placed there as the head (*kaṃ*), the syllable *a* is to be placed there as the ear (*śravaḥ*), and the syllable *o* is to be placed there as the sense of hearing (*śrotra*). With these syllables, the practitioner who knows the mantra should worship in due order.

By what kind [of syllables]? By those "illuminated by the *bindu* preceding the face"—that is to say, by those preceded by the face, meaning placed upon the head (*śiras*), which is the *bindu*; the sense is that they are accompanied by the *anusvāra*.
The practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *maṃ vahnimaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane namaḥ* (Salutation to the fire-maṇḍala, whose self consists of ten digits);
*aṃ arkamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane namaḥ* (Salutation to the sun-maṇḍala, whose self consists of twelve digits).
Uṃ, homage to the lunar maṇḍala, whose nature consists of sixteen digits.
There, one should cause the sacred water (tīrtha) to descend from the orb of the hot-rayed sun,
and likewise cause Hari to descend from one's own heart-lotus.
And one should display the gālinī mudrā with the topknot.

There, in the water of the conch, one should invoke the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) of the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) using the *tīrtha-mantra* to be described; likewise, from the lotus of one's own heart, one should invoke Kṛṣṇa.

Immediately thereafter, with the *śikhā-mantra*, one should display the *gālinī-mudrā* to be described—and by the word "and" (*ca*), the *dhenu-mudrā* as well. Striking the palm of the left hand with the right index finger is the *prabodhana* [awakening]. (KrdC 3.41)
Having consecrated that water with the eye-mantra and covered it with the armor-mantra while holding both arms over it,
one should perform the sakalīkaraṇa with the root-mantra and then apply it.
And from the limbs and the digits [of the moon], the directions are indicated by the weapons.

That water—the water from the conch—is gazed upon with the *nayanamantra* (eye-mantra) while reciting "vauṣaṭ. Regarding this, Tripāṭhin maintains that gazing with the eye-mantra occurs only where such a mantra exists.

Having enveloped [the water] with the *varman*—that is, the *kavacamantra* (armor-mantra) while reciting "hum"—one should perform the *sakalīkaraṇa* (totalization) using the root-mantra, which consists of the connection between the root-mantra and its limbs (*aṅgas*).
The word "should place" (*nyaset*) is an explanation of this very process.
Rudradhara maintains that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the limbs of the deity constitutes the act of "making complete" (*sakalī-kṛti*).
Alternatively, the Tripāṭhins hold that it becomes "possessed of its deity" (*sadaivata*) through meditation on the root mantra.
Regarding the phrase "and one should place with the limbs," the meaning is that one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs of the root mantra.
Immediately thereafter, one should bind the ten directions of Śaṅkha with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) by snapping the fingers.
Touching the unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and other items that have been rendered imperishable (*acyutīkṛta*),
he should recite the mantra eight times;
furthermore, he should cast them into the water of the *vardhanī* vessel.
Then one should sprinkle one's own body with water.
Touching that water—which contains unbroken rice, sandalwood, and flowers, and has been transformed into the very nature of Viṣṇu—one should recite the root mantra eight times.
Immediately thereafter, one should pour a little of the *arghya* water into the water of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel placed on one's own right side. As it is said:
"Taking the *prokṣaṇī* vessel on the right, one should fill it with water."
"Taking a small amount of arghya water, one should add it to the prokṣaṇī water.
Immediately after that, one should sprinkle one's own body three times with the water from the arghya vessel;
however, the Vidyādhara Ācāryas maintain that this should be done with the water from the vardhanī jar.
Thus, the entire procedure for the preparation of flowers, sandalwood, and other materials, as well as the method for filling the conch shell with water, has been declared three times by Manu.
This foremost of sacrificers remains hidden here.
Likewise, with the root mantra and the right hand, one should sprinkle the flowers, sandalwood, and other materials for worship three times. He concludes with the word "conch":
this method for filling the conch has been proclaimed—that is, described.
Of what sort? Here, in this scriptural treatise (*āgama-śāstra*), he is the foremost of sacrificers, who is most excellent in the primary ritual procedure.
Now he shows the mantra for the sacred ford (tīrtha): "O Gaṅgā and Yamunā, O Godāvarī and Sarasvatī, O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī—be present in this water! (Kṛd 3.45)
This is declared to be the *tīrtha* that wards off the flood of misdeeds:
the little finger and the thumb of the two hands are joined with one another. (Kṛd 3.46)
The index, middle, and ring fingers joined together and bent;
this is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā, which is moved over the top of the conch.
This is the mantra for the invocation of the sacred sites (*tīrthāvāhana*), which destroys the multitude of sins such as *durita*.
Now, he describes the characteristics of the *gālinī* mudrā with the words beginning "the little fingers" (*kaniṣṭhā*) and so forth:

the little fingers and thumbs of the two hands should be joined together; likewise, having made the index, middle, and ring fingers compact, they should be slightly bent, contracted, and interlocked with one another.
This is the meaning.
And this being so, this is called the *gālinī* mudrā;
the meaning is that when it is moved over the conch, it brings about the satisfaction of the deity. // KrdC_3.45-47 //
Now he describes the sequence for the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) within one's own body:
"Then, having worshipped one's own lords and Gaṇanāyaka in the center of the root-cakra at the crown of the head..."
And by means of the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should worship with the mantras of the sacred seats (pīṭha) using water, scents, unbroken rice grains, flowers, incense, and lamps.

Immediately thereafter, having worshipped one's own lords (nātha), one's own gurus, and Gaṇapati in due order upon the crown of the head— that is, in the center of the *mūlacakra* at the *mūlādhāracakra*— one should worship with water, sandalwood paste, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), flowers, incense, and lamps, using the respective mantras from the *ādhāraśakti* up to the end of the *pīṭhamantras*, according to the previously mentioned sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
One should perform the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha-pūjana) within one's own body.
Then, one who meditates upon the triad— the splendor of the root mantra at the base of the spine, in the heart, and between the eyebrows— should contemplate their unification.
It has been made into a mass of bliss, resembling streaks of lightning.

Immediately thereafter, one should contemplate that triple radiance located in the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, and the space between the eyebrows—which consists of the essence of the root mantra—as having become unified with the supreme light through the seed-syllable of desire, *klīm*.
Of what nature is it? It is a mass of bliss, the bliss of consciousness (*cid-ānanda*).
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It has the brilliance of lightning.
Having made that splendor possessed of limbs by means of its parts,
and having performed the placement (nyāsa) starting from the seat and ending with the ornaments, one should worship it again with water, scents, and so forth.
The mantra-practitioner should perform [the rites] up to the prescription of the limbs, such as prosperity (bhūti) and so forth.

Having unified that light and made it possessed of parts by means of the five limbs, and having fashioned it as endowed with a body, one should perform the placement [of mantras] upon one's own body— beginning from the "Cage of Splendor" (vibhūti-pañjara), which includes the sequence from the beginning up to the end of the limbs, and concluding with the ritual placement of the limbs— and then worship the Deity with the services beginning with the seat and ending with ornaments.

Furthermore, once again, with water, fragrance, and so forth, one should worship by means of those very mantras, according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), upon the locations for the placement of the five limbs of the ten stages of creation and sustenance within the cage of the manifestation and the cage of the form.
Furthermore, one should offer the flute held in the mouth, the forest garland upon the region of the chest,
the two breasts, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha jewel.

Furthermore, one should again worship the flute held in the mouth and the forest-garland (*vanamālā*) in the heart—that garland made of leaves and flowers which begins at the neck and hangs down to both feet. As it has been said: "That garland made of leaves and flowers which stands beginning from the neck and hangs down to both feet is celebrated as the *vanamālā*."
One should worship the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem upon the breast.

Having anointed his limbs with the flowing paste of *śrīkhaṇḍa* (sandalwood), he should then draw diagrams on the forehead and other parts [of the body] using the root mantra; thereafter, [he should recite] the *pañjara-mūrti-mantra*.
The diseases themselves take on the form of lamp-flames.

Immediately thereafter, the worshipper, his limbs smeared with sandalwood paste, should—using the root mantra and the ring finger—apply decorative marks (*tilaka*) shaped like lamp-flames at the locations for the "cage of the forms" (*mūrti-pañjara-nyāsa*), such as the forehead and so forth, using the mantras of the cage of forms beginning with "aṃ oṃ keśava-dhātṛbhyāṃ namaḥ" and the others for the twelve forms; this is the meaning. (KrdC 3.52)
Now he shows the ritual for the offering of handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali):
one should then extend the puṣpāñjali five times with the root mantra over the pair of feet, using two tulasī leaves.
In the center with a pair of Hayāris, on the head with a pair of lotuses, and with all six [deities] upon the entire body.

Immediately thereafter, one should offer five handfuls of flowers five times with the root mantra. With two *tulasī* leaves—namely, the white and black *tulasī*—one should place two handfuls on the pair of feet, sequentially on the right and left feet; and in the middle, at the heart, one should offer with a pair of *hayāri* [karañja] leaves, namely the white and red *kara-vīra*. This constitutes one [offering].

With two lotuses—one white and one red—placed upon the head, there is another *añjali*; and with all [the flowers] upon the entire body, using all six—the two *tulasī*s, the two *karavīra*s, and the two lotuses—one should form the *añjali*;
this is the fifth *añjali*.
Now he shows the distribution for the offering of white *tulasī*, black *tulasī*, and so forth:
"White flowers, smeared with white sandalwood paste, [are offered] on the right side; red flowers, sprinkled with red sandalwood paste, [are offered] on the left side. (Krd 3.54)

White flowers such as *tulasī* and others, combined with white sandalwood paste, should be offered in the right portion; red flowers such as *tulasī* and others, combined with red sandalwood paste, should be offered in the left portion.
He shows the ritual procedure: "And likewise, having offered incense and lamps, one should satisfy Kṛṣṇa with nectar-like juices;
having given mouth-fresheners and so forth, one should worship him well with excellent perfumes and other offerings. (Krd 3.55)
Having offered incense and lamps, one should gratify and satisfy [the deity] with the nectar-fluids—the liquid nectar dripping from the lunar orb situated at the *brahma-randhra*.
Regarding "with nectar-fluids," Rudradhara says it means with water consecrated by mantras.
One should thus satisfy Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Immediately after, having offered a fragrant pellet (*gandha-vaṭikā*) such as mouth-perfume (*mukha-vāsa*), one should worship with fragrant flowers.
Having gratified [the deity] with betel, song, dance, and instrumental music, [one should offer] a handful of water while reciting the mantra known as *brahmārpaṇa*.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the offering of his own self.

The meaning is that immediately thereafter, the minister, the practitioner, and the devotee, having gratified Śrī Kṛṣṇa with betel, songs, and so forth, should perform the surrender of their own self as described below, using a handful of water and the Brahmārpaṇa mantra. (KrdC 3.56)
Reflection: The mantra concerning the offering to Brahman is as follows:
"The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him, through the concentration on action that is Brahman, Brahman alone is to be attained. Thus it is said.
Now, he speaks regarding those who are incapable:
"Alternatively, this procedure for those of contracted intellects is commenced with a cage of forms;
it is taught by means of the eighteen scripts, along with the syllables, words, and limbs, beginning with the flute. (Krd 3.57)

Alternatively, while the method of worship for worshippers of dull intellect has been described by means of the *mūrtipañjara* and so forth, this worship with the ten-syllable mantra now describes the worship with the eighteen-syllable mantra.

If the worship is performed with the eighteen-syllable mantra, then it is taught [to be done] by the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra’s syllables upon the forehead and other locations starting from the hairline (*kaca-bhuvi*), by the five-limbed placement (*pañcāṅga-nyāsa*), and by the flute and other [instruments].
He shows the procedure for recitation (*japa-vidhi*): [KrdC 3.57]...
Then, meditating upon the son of Nanda who is perfectly serene, one should recite the mantra with single-minded devotion,
accompanied by the recollection of its meaning, according to the prescribed rules and number.
The suffix *su* is applied after a verbal root ending in a long vowel to form a noun denoting the act of filling.
Immediately thereafter, preceded by the recollection of the meaning of the mantra, one should mutter the root mantra.
Doing what? Meditating in the heart upon Kṛṣṇa—who is exceedingly gracious, possesses the form previously described, and is non-different from oneself.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
"Undistracted and intent upon that": when the prescribed number of recitations has been completed, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) without envy;

and regarding the commencement of the recitation, the Teacher of the Vidyādharas says that if one lacks the capacity for external worship, one should perform the recitation after self-worship, but if one has the capacity, after [external] worship. (KrdC 3.58)
He states the preliminary practice for the application: "Having recited the seed-syllable encased within the *praṇava* one hundred and eight times,
the person of great intelligence should apply the yogas received from the mouth of his own guru."
Then, one whose self consists of the true nectar of consciousness-bliss should conclude the recitation;
thus has the rule for recitation, based on the two mantras, been correctly proclaimed.

Having recited one hundred and eight times the seed-syllable of Kāma enclosed by the Praṇava along with the eight [syllables], the one of great intelligence should apply—meaning perform—the yogas obtained from the mouth of his own guru, which are characterized by absorption into the Self and the Supreme Deity and will be described in the eighth chapter. He concludes the subject at hand with the words: "Immediately thereafter, he should conclude this recitation, being of the nature of true nectar and the bliss of consciousness."
In this manner, the method of worship based on the second *manu* (the *dvitīyā-manu*), which relies upon ten and eighteen syllables, has been correctly explained.
The person who follows this method will become beloved by all embodied beings,
even if they are merely the sole abode of a lotus-like voice.
That supreme majesty of yours approaches [him].
The person who practices this mode of worship will become beloved by all embodied beings;
at that time, he will become an abode for Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī. The meaning is that after the fall of the body, he attains splendor and becomes of that very nature.

The eternal one [becomes] a vessel for the rite—the performance characterized by the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*)—and very quickly becomes the sole, primary abode of Kamalā, that is, of all prosperity.
Alternatively, according to the variant reading *api vāk-kamalaika-mandiram*, he also becomes the sole abode of both Vāk (Sarasvatī) and Kamalā. (KrdC 3.60; HBV 17.15)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Kramadīpikā* composed by the venerable Keśavācārya.
(4) Fourth Chapter.
Now, regarding the recitation of mantras and so forth, only one who has received initiation possesses the qualification; as it is stated in another Āgama:
"Just as those twice-born who have not undergone the initiatory rite have no qualification here for their own rituals, Vedic study, and the like, until after the *upanayana* ceremony."
"Likewise, those who have not been initiated have no authority over the recitation of mantras, the worship of deities, and so forth; therefore, one should make oneself consecrated by Śiva.
Thus, he says: "Therefore, I shall explain initiation, which is the primary constituent of the recitation of mantras."
The practice for the two excellent mantras, which accomplishes all attainments, is now being told;
having performed which, the sages [attained] the state of the most exalted ones.
Nārada and others attained perfection here in this world.

"Immediately," [it is said] "now. "The means" (*sādhana*) is that by which the desired object of the two best of men—the ten-syllable and the eight-syllable [mantras]—is accomplished; thus it is called "initiation" (*dīkṣaṇa*).
Of what nature is it? It is the "means for accomplishing all fruits," having performed which the sages such as Nārada and others attained great perfection (*siddhi*) in this world. (KrdC 4.1)
-o)O(o- Since initiation is to be accomplished by means of a guru, he states the characteristics of a guru:
[One should choose] a brahmin whose host of enemies such as desire has been destroyed, whose limbs are stainless, and who is most venerable...
One who desires to fully understand true knowledge should take refuge in such a teacher— one who bears devotion for the pollen of the pair of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet,
who knows the stainless path of the Vedas, scriptures, and traditional teachings, who is esteemed by the virtuous, and who is self-controlled;
with body and mind inclined toward him, he should seek that instructor.
He who desires to fully understand the Vidyā and correctly know the Mantra should take refuge in and serve such a teacher (guru).
Of what kind? A *vipra*, that is, one born of the Brāhmaṇa caste, because those such as Kṣatriyas lack the authority for instruction. Furthermore, of what kind?

He whose body is purified by that [practice] which has thoroughly distanced the host of the six enemies, beginning with desire (*kāma*); for these enemies— desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy— are called "desire and so forth" (*kāmādi*), and because they arise continuously as obstacles in one whose mind is afflicted by greed and the rest, they are unfit to be cultivated.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is one who maintains an excellence of devotion characterized by passion for the dust of the pair of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet; for one who is not anointed with such devotion, the goals of human existence are not attained. Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is a knower of the stainless paths connected with the Vedas, the Śāstras, and the Āgamas, for otherwise the investigation of the Āgamas and Śāstras would be impossible.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?

He is one who is esteemed among virtuous people and renowned for his goodness; otherwise, due to his wickedness and unworthiness to be served, he would not even possess the meaning of the word "sat" (virtuous).
Furthermore, of what nature is he?

He is *dānta*, one who has brought his senses under control, because one whose senses are not controlled is averse to the deity. Of what sort is he? He is one whose body (*kāya*), mind (*manas*), and heart (*hṛdaya*) are bowed down, humbled, and disciplined; such is he. In this regard, more should be understood from my own work, the *Śārada-tilaka* (KrdC_4.2).
Sanātana (HBV 1.34)—
one whose limbs are stainless and free from disease,
the knower of those pure paths and ways which belong to the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Agamas.
Among the virtuous, the doctrine of the wise is highly esteemed.

One whose body and mind are inclined—that is, bowed down, disciplined, or solely devoted to the teacher—toward the *vidyā*, which is the mantra that serves as the means for crossing over the suffering of *saṃsāra* and so forth; being such a person [should listen].
The teacher is the guide.

Thus, the first mode of approaching the teacher should be understood as consisting of the state of having a body and mind inclined [toward him], as well as the carrying of sacrificial fuel in one's hand and so forth, as prescribed in the Śruti. (KrdC 4.2)
— o)O(o—
He states the manner of serving the Guru:
"One whose inner self is not crooked should satisfy [the Guru] at intervals."
Then, with his own wealth, his person, and agreeable speech,
and with the thought that he was the lotus-navelled Lord for three years, the exceedingly steadfast one,
when the Guru was pleased, desired to receive the initiation into the mantra.
Immediately thereafter, one who is wise and steadfast should satisfy for three years the Guru, whose characteristics have been described, with the thought that he is Padmanābha;
by what means? By his own wealth, as well as by his body and by pleasing speech.
What is he like? He is a learned scholar (sudhīra).
Furthermore, of what nature [should he be]?

One whose inner self—that is, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—is straight and exceedingly supple; then, immediately thereafter, when the Guru is pleased, the disciple alone should desire to speak—that is, wish to utter—the initiation (*mantra-dīkṣā*). As for that which has been stated elsewhere:
"In one year one becomes a Brahmin, in two years a king..."
"A Vaiśya [becomes purified] in three years, and a Śūdra in four years.
Otherwise, however:
"In three years for a Brāhmaṇa, and in six years for a Kṣatriya..."
It is recommended that one examine the subjects in nine years;
even within twelve equal years, those who are *vṛṣala*s and others [should be examined].
Thus it should be understood.
The prescribed lunar mansions and so forth are to be understood from my work, the *Śāradātilakodyota*. (KrdC_4.3)
— o)O(o—

Since initiation is of many kinds, distinguished by the *kalāvatī* and other types, he says: "But the initiation celebrated in the *Prapañcasāra* shall be demonstrated here by me in brief," referring specifically to the ritualistic (*kriyāvatī*) initiation.
She is now being recalled for the sake of accomplishing all things;
for without her, the multitude of mantras will certainly not grant success even to one who recites them continuously.
Now, the initiation (*dīkṣā*) consisting of ritual action (*kriyāvatī*) is being recalled; its mere recollection is performed here, but it is not fully described.
The reason for this is that it has already been explained in detail in the *Prapañcasāra*.
For what purpose is it described here?

For the attainment of all fruits, without which initiation (*dīkṣā*) the collection of mantras never bestows fruit upon a person who performs recitation (*japa*). As it is said: "When the Guru, according to the class of the mantra, causes the disciple to directly perceive the desired deity, that is called 'mantra-initiation' (*mantra-dīkṣā*)."
-o)O(o- Now, regarding the preliminary rites for the pavilion in the purified location such as the hall, he describes the *vāstu-bali* offering: "Then, one should prepare a mound of earth in front."
Then the wise man, having performed the ritual offering for the site according to the rules,
should construct here a pavilion measuring eight cubits, with a smooth altar-platform.
Immediately thereafter, the wise practitioner should first offer the *vāstu-bali* upon the ground on the surface of the earth, according to the rules and in the manner prescribed.
The procedure for offering the *bali* and so forth should be understood from my own work, the *Śārada-tilaka-uddyota*.
Then, following that, one should construct a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) here on this consecrated ground.
Of what kind? Measured by "immovable arms," that is, seven cubits in measure.
The word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned;
by this, it should be understood that [the measurement] may also be five cubits or nine cubits.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It has a smooth (*masṛṇa*) altar, meaning an oily (*cikkaṇa*) altar, that is to say, a well-swept (*utkṛṣṭa*) altar. // KrdC_4.5 //
It was encircled by a garland of kuśa grass joined with threads of the three qualities, adorned with the banner of primordial nature,
and featured four faces as its water-trees and archways.
Resplendent and radiant, adorned with a white canopy.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It is encircled by a garland of kuśa grass.
Of what nature is that [garland]?
[It is] joined with threads of white, red, and dark-blue color, or else joined with a triple-stranded thread. Furthermore, of what kind?
Adorned with eight banners; "nature" (prakṛti) [is indicated] by the number eight.

Furthermore, of what kind is it? It is such that at its four faces—that is, its four gates—there are archways (*toraṇa*) consisting of milk-trees (*payas-taru*), namely milky trees (*kṣīra-vṛkṣa*). These milky trees are known as the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *nyagrodha*.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
Adorned with the white radiance of the moon.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
Brilliant and stainless.

He states the procedure for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa): "In this [ritual], the wise man should prepare a fire-altar in the direction of the Lord of Wealth (the northeast), with a depth and width measured by eight times three finger-breadths."
One should draw a square with eight sides and four corners, marked by a source (yoni) resembling an elephant-girdle situated in the west.
Immediately thereafter, let the wise one construct the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), which is the hearth (dhiṣṇya) of Vasu, that is, of Agni, within this pavilion.
Of what kind? "Vasu" refers to the number eight, for it is well known that there are eight Vasus.
Twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) are three times those [eight] Vasus.
Measured by them—that is, such that its height and width of the excavated pit were equal to those [measurements].
Where? In the direction of Vasupati, Kubera; that is, in the north.
Furthermore, of what nature was it?
"Vasu-mekhalam.
Here, by the word *vasu*, fire is meant;
and that [fire] is threefold, consisting of the *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya*, and so forth.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It has four corners, being half of the group of eight corners.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?

Situated in the western direction, it is adorned with a vulva (*yoni*) resembling an elephant and measuring twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length. As it has been said: "Because its form consists of twelve finger-breadths, the vulva should be twelve finger-breadths [in length].
Another specific detail here is to be understood from the *Śāradā-tilaka*.
Now, regarding the procedure for the mandala of the zodiacal signs:
then, in the pavilion sprinkled with cow-products and fragrant water,
one should properly draw the mandala as an eight-petaled lotus.
It possesses three circular tiers, the pedestal of the zodiac, the feet, the pathways,
and is endowed with four gates, beauties, secondary ornaments, and corners.
Then, immediately after the pavilion, one should properly draw the mandala in this pavilion according to the manner described.
In what kind [of place]? Sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with water containing the eight Vaiṣṇava perfumes mentioned in the *Śāradātilaka*.
Of what nature is it? It is provided with an eight-petaled lotus.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It is endowed with three circumferences (*vṛtta*).

Moreover, the zodiac signs beginning with Aries are the pedestal (*pīṭha*), which is the place for installing the jar; its four-legged pedestal-base (*aṅghri-pīṭha-pātra*) consists of four paths (*vīthī*), four gates (*dvāra*), the primary ornaments (*śobhā*), the secondary ornaments (*upaśobhā*), and the corners (*asra*).
Which corner is joined with these?
This is the meaning: having prepared a level, square plot of ground measuring two and a half cubits, one should lay out seventeen threads extending from east to west.
When this is done, there will be two hundred and fifty-six squares.

Regarding the division of the squares: in the center, one should draw a lotus consisting of three circles formed by sixteen squares. (And upon that lotus, one should draw the remaining pedestal and its components.
Outside of that, one should draw the twelve zodiac signs using forty-eight squares.)
Outside of that, one should draw the thirty-six *pīṭhas* and the limbs of the *pīṭhas*. (Outside of that, one should draw it with eighty squares.
Here, this must be understood: one should apply four lines—east, south, west, and north—between the circle situated at the tip of the lotus petal and the *pīṭha*-power (*pīṭha-śakti*).
Immediately thereafter, one should draw the door-decorations, the secondary decorations, and the corners using one hundred and twelve squares.

In that [mandala], the door in every direction consists of six squares. Regarding the method there: on one side of the door, there is one [unit] consisting of four squares—namely, the two central squares belonging to the outer row and the two central squares belonging to the row situated within them.
Therein,
a single square situated in the outer row and three squares situated in the row within it— thus,
by means of these four squares, one *upaśobhā* (ornamental niche) is formed.

Here, three squares belonging to the outer row and one square situated within that [outer] row—thus, by means of these six squares, a corner is formed. In the same way, the ornaments (śobhā), sub-ornaments (upaśobhā), and corners are to be understood on the other side as well.
Thus, when combined across all four directions, there are one hundred and twelve.
What has not been stated here should be understood from the Śāradā-tilaka. (KrdC 4.8)
Then the preceptor, knowing the ritual procedure, having performed the rites beginning with the bath and ending with self-worship,
[should place] the conch shell for the water of honor (*arghya*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*) before him on his own left.
The vessels, beginning with those made of leather, were filled to the brim.
Having placed the flowers, perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and so forth elsewhere, as well as the vessel for hand-washing behind [the deity],
[one should perform] everything else in a place illuminated by rows of lamps.
And one should take up the means of accomplishment within the range of one's own vision.

Immediately thereafter, the preceptor (guru), the instructor who knows the ritual and understands the methods prescribed in the Āgamas, having completed the procedure beginning with the bath— namely, the bathing rites as prescribed in his own Gṛhya-sūtra up to the self-worship (ātma-pūjā)— should place before himself to his left the vessels for the conch (śaṅkha), the water-offering (arghya), the foot-water (pādya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya), filled with pure substances such as water.

Having performed these acts in successive order and set them aside, one should place flowers and other articles of worship on the right side; then, placing a single vessel for washing the hands behind [the seat], one should arrange all other ritual implements and requisites within the range of one's own vision, illuminated by a row of lamps.
In this regard, another specific detail is to be seen in the *Prapañcasāravivaraṇa* composed by Śrī Paramānandabhaṭṭācārya. (KrdC 4.9–10)
First, one should worship the northern row of the pedestal, starting from the northwest and ending at the northeast;
furthermore, Ambikeya is to be worshipped with his lotus-like hands even elsewhere.
Holding a noose, a tooth, and the fearsome *śṛṇi* weapon.
On the northern side of the *pīṭha*, that is, the *rāśi-pīṭha*, the row associated with the Guru should first be worshipped, starting from the northwest corner and extending to the northeast corner.
The ritual formula is: *oṃ gurubhyo namaḥ*.
Elsewhere, on the southern side, Gaṇapati, the son of Ambikā, is to be worshipped.
Of what sort? Holding his own tusk as a goad and the gesture of fearlessness with his lotus-like hands.
Now, he shows the method for the installation of the jar (*kalaśa*) with the words beginning "yato deśikaḥ":

"Then, in the central part, [one should place] the worshipful Foundation Power (*ādhāra-śakti*) and so forth, up to the feet of the Immortals; likewise, in the directions, one should place Dharma and the others ending with Fire, as well as Akṣa, Pavana, and Śiva, and [the opposites] Adharma and the rest."
In the center, one should worship the triad of the remaining lotus discs, the group of qualities beginning with the Self, and the filaments;
and in the center of the fire, one should again worship the nine Śaktis with the seat-mantra (pīṭha-mantra).
Immediately thereafter, in the central portion of the mandala, having propitiated and worshipped [the deities] beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with the Kalpavṛkṣa,
one should worship Dharmā and the others located in the corners starting from the southeast (Agni) according to the sequence of the Pīṭha-nyāsa,

as well as Adharmā and the others in the four directions starting from the east; likewise, in the center, the remaining lotus, and the three orbs of the Sun, Moon, and Fire pervaded by twelve, sixteen, and ten digits (kalās) respectively.
One should worship the three maṇḍalas as well as the fourfold [deities] beginning with Ātman.
Then, in the center of the filaments and upon the pericarp (karṇikā), one should worship the nine powers beginning with Vimalā in the sequence starting from the east.
Furthermore, once again, one should worship the pedestal (pīṭha) with the previously mentioned pedestal-mantra; this is the meaning.
Then, one should place pure, excellent grains of rice within a lotus; upon those, one should place *darbha* grass together with tufts (*kūrca*) and unbroken rice (*akṣata*);
and above that, one should place the ten digits (*kalā*) of Fire in a clockwise direction.
One should worship these goddesses, who begin with the letter *ya*, with fragrant substances and other offerings.

Immediately after that, one should place and set down non-glutinous rice (*śālī*) measuring one *āḍhaka* in the center of the lotus, and likewise excellent white rice grains measuring one-eighth of an *āḍhaka* within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the lotus.
As it has been said:
"Having indeed placed non-glutinous rice measuring one *āḍhaka* upon the pericarp..."
"And one should place rice and one-eighth part of that [weight] with *darbha* grass and *kūrca* bundles.
Thus, upon that—that is, upon the rice—one should place *darbha* grass together with *akṣata* grains and *kūrca* bundles.
According to Tripāṭhin, a *brahmagranthi* formed from three *kuśa* blades is denoted by the word *kūrca*, whereas others hold that *kūrca* means a handful of *kuśa* grass.

Above that, upon the *kūrca*, one should place the ten digits (*kalā*) of the fire *Kṛśānu*—those whose first [letters] are the ten syllables beginning with *ya*—in a clockwise direction; immediately thereafter, one should worship these ten digits with perfumes and other offerings. And they are as follows:
"Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavahā, and Kavyavahā. As for the ritual application, it is: "Obeisance to Dhūmrārcis. (KrdC 4.13)

One should place there a water-pot adorned with triple-stranded, shimmering threads, while muttering the *tāra* (OM) and perfuming it with incense made of *joṅkaṭa*. In this pot, one should arrange the pairs of syllables beginning with *ka-bha* and ending with *ṭha-ḍa*.
Likewise, after that, one should worship the twelve digits (kalās) of the jewel in the mouth of the other [deity].

There, upon the *kūrca* consisting of ten parts, one should place the water-pot (*kumbha*) while uttering the syllable *oṃ*, which is the shore [of the ocean of existence]. The pot, moreover, should be made of gold or other such materials. As it has been said:
"It may be made of gold, silver, or even clay, according to what has been prescribed."
"O Goddess of the Gods, one should properly consecrate the jar with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*).

Of what nature is it? It is encircled—that is, wrapped—with threads tripled around the neck, which are shining and beautiful, made of cotton spun by a maiden, [and] consecrated with the weapon-mantra.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?"

Immediately after that, it [the jar] should be well-perfumed with incenses made of *joṅkaṭa* wood and primarily *kṛṣṇāguru*. Then, the twelve digits (*kalā*) of the sky-mover, the sun, are to be placed within this jar and subsequently worshipped.
With what? With pairs of syllables.
Of what kind? Beginning with the letters *ka* and *bha*, that is, beginning with the letter *ka* and the letter *bha*.
Furthermore, by what kind [of syllables]?
By those ending in *ṭha* and *ḍa*, meaning those whose final letters are *ṭha* and *ḍa*.

This is the meaning: having joined each individual letter starting with *ka* recited in direct order (anuloma) together with each individual letter starting with *bha* recited in reverse order (pratiloma), one should associate them with the twelve digits (*kalā*) beginning with Tapinī.
The ritual of nyāsa and other rites should be performed. And they [the nāḍīs] are as follows:
Tapanī, Tāpanī, Dhūmrā, Bhrāmarī, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. Thus it is said.
The ritual application (prayoga), however, should be performed as follows: *kaṃ bhaṃ tapinyai namaḥ*, *khaṃ vaṃ tāpinyai namaḥ*, and so forth. //14//
Having thus conceived the fire as the form of the support (ādhāra) and the sun likewise as the form of the jar, those who know the ritual rules should install [the deity] within it,
accompanied by unbroken rice grains and other offerings.
The ritual broom (kūrca) is radiant with gold and the finest jewels.
Having thus conceived the fire in the form of the support (adhāra) in this manner, and likewise having meditated upon the sun in the form of the pitcher (kumbha),

the knower of the ritual— well-versed in the methods taught in the Āgamas— should place within that pitcher a *kūrca* (a bundle of grass) accompanied by unbroken rice (*akṣata*) and other offerings, using the root mantra; [the pitcher] being adorned with gold, excellent gems, and the nine precious jewels according to the previously mentioned characteristics.
Thus it was said by Bhairava:
"Having led these [deities] there, one should cast a white flower, white unbroken rice, the nine gems, and a tuft of grass into their midst, using the root mantra alone. (KrdC 4.15)
Then, one should fill it with decoction-water using the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*,
concluding with the recitation of one's own mantra three times, followed by milk.
[One should perform the purification] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with pure water alone.

Immediately thereafter, having contemplated the unity of the pedestal (pīṭha) and the jar (kumbha), one should [fill it] with the fifty letters, using water infused with medicinal herbs, water from the bark of the *palāśa* tree,

water from a decoction of the bark of milk-exuding trees, water containing all medicinal herbs, cow’s milk, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), pure water, water scented with camphor and other substances, or water from sacred bathing places (tīrtha), while reciting the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*.

One should complete [the recitation] in such a way that it ends with the triple recitation of one's own mantra using the *viloma-mātṛkā* (reverse alphabet), and concludes with the triple recitation of the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). KrdC 4.16.
In this water of the pitcher, one should likewise place the sixteen digits of the moon, preceded by the groups of vowels,
which are fragrant with the essence of the waters.
Thereafter, one should sacrifice with flowers that have been crushed.

In that water of the jar, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the sixteen lunar digits (*candrakalā*), numbering sixteen according to the "wealth-and-pair" count (*vasuyugasaṅkhyā*), preceded by the group of vowels beginning with the letter *a*. Immediately thereafter, one should worship those lunar digits with handfuls of flowers in that very same sequence. They have been described as follows:
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭī, Rati, and Dhṛti.
"Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā.
Now he states the eight Vaiṣṇava fragrances:
With *udīcya*, costus, saffron-water, iron, *sajjaṭā*, and *murā*, along with camphor—this is declared as the "Eight Fragrances Dear to Hari. (Krd 4.18)

Uśīra from the north, kuṣṭha, saffron, ambubālā, netrabālā, iron filings, black agallochum along with jaṭā, murā, jaṭāmāṃsī, and cool sandalwood—these together are declared as the "Eight Fragrances" (gandhāṣṭaka) that are dear to Hari. (KrdC 4.18)
Regarding the filling of the conch, he says:
having thoroughly stirred eight kinds of fragrant substances according to the prescribed method into the interior filled with decoction water;
One should sequentially employ the individual digits of the Moon, the Sun, and the Fire in the rite of sprinkling.

In the belly [of the vessel] and the conch, having filled them with the previously mentioned decoction-water according to the procedure prescribed in the Āgamas using the root mantra, one should stir in the eight fragrances while reciting the *namas* mantra and offer them; then, having separately invoked the digits (*kalās*) of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, one should sequentially perform the rite of sprinkling (*seka-karma*) and the rite of the installation of life-force (*prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā-karma*). // KrdC_4.19 //
In the same way, the vowels arising from the syllable *a* are produced by the *ka*-group and the *ta*-group; those born from the vowel *u* are produced by the *pa*-group;
and those born from the nasal dot (*bindu*) are produced by the *ma*, *la*, *pa*, and *ja* groups.
Those born from sound arise from the group of vowels beginning with *ṣ*.
In the manner previously described, the ten digits (kalās) born from the syllable *a*—that is, born from the syllable *a*—are accompanied by the ten letters beginning with *ka*;
furthermore, the ten digits born from the syllable *u*—that is, born from the syllable *u*—are accompanied by the ten letters beginning with *ṭa*;
likewise, the ten digits born from the syllable *ma*—that is, born from the syllable *ma*—[are accompanied] by the ten letters beginning with *pa*.
