Likewise, the four *kalās* born of the *bindu*—originating from the *bindu*—are accompanied by the four syllables beginning with *ṣa*;

and likewise, the sixteen *kalās* born of the *nāda*—originating from the *nāda*—are accompanied by the group of sixteen vowels; these are to be deposited in the water of the conch. And they are as follows:
Sṛṣṭi, Ṛddhi, Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Sthirā,
Sthiti, and Siddhi— these ten digits (kalās) arising from the letter 'A' have been proclaimed.
Old age, protection, peace, sovereignty, passion, and desire;
the granting of boons, joy, love, and longevity—these are the digits born from the syllable *ukāra*.
The subtle energies (kalās) born from the letters beginning with *ma* are Tīkṣṇā, Raudrā, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tantī, Kṣut, Krodhanī, Kriyā, Utkārī, and Mṛtyu.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti;
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and the supreme Mocikā.
"Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmāmṛtā, Jñānā, Ajñānā, Āyanī, as well as Vyāpinī, Vyomarūpā, Anantā, and Nādasambhavā.
And the ritual application (prayoga) is "Oṃ Kaṃ, salutation to Sṛṣṭi," and so forth. (KrdC 4.20)
After the invocation and before the formal seating,
a wise person should mutter the respective verses at each stage; having worshipped each of those [deities] individually, he should likewise recite that specific passage.
One should offer [the oblation] into the water-pot correctly with the root mantra. // Krd_4.21 //

At the conclusion of the invocation (*samāvāhana*) and prior to the firm installation (*susamsthāpana*), and before the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), the wise practitioner should maintain, recite, and chant [the following mantras] in their respective places.

This is the meaning: after the invocation of the sixteen digits (*kalā*) beginning with the letter *ka*, which originate from the syllable *a*, into the water of the conch, one should recite the verse "Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" before the consecration of the vital breaths.
After the invocation of the sixteen digits beginning with the letter *ṭa*, which originate from the syllable *u*, one should recite the verse "Pratad viṣṇuḥ."
Immediately after invoking the *kalās* beginning with the letter *pa*, which originate from the letter *ma*, one should recite the *ṛc* beginning with "tat savituḥ.
Immediately after invoking the *kalās* beginning with the letter *ta*, which originate from the *nāda*, one should recite the *ṛc* beginning with "viṣṇor yoniḥ.
Following that, one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) in reverse order over the water in the conch shell.

Having duly honored each of those various ritual arts (kalās) individually according to the prescribed rules, one should recite the root mantra over that water from the conch and pour it into the pitcher; [and] the pitcher [should be adorned] with clusters of mango, bodhi,
and jackfruit, entwined with the *śatamanyu* creeper.
May he cover it with an auspicious circular vessel filled with flowers, fruits, and grains.
The *sahakāra* is the mango tree;
*bodhi* is the *aśvattha*;
and the *panasa* is a thorny fruit tree.

With clusters and sprouts of these [plants], entwined with *śatamanyu* creepers and bound with *induvallī*, one should cover the mouth of the jar with the thought that it is the celestial tree (*suradruma*); likewise, one should cover it over with a beautiful shallow bowl (*śarāva*) adorned with a full, auspicious circular design (*cakrikā*) made of flowers and the like. (KrdC 4.22)
Thereafter, the wise one should wrap the mouth of the jar with a pair of fresh, stainless cloths,
and it should also be adorned here with flowers and other offerings.
And one should cause it to carry over to a further, greater glory.
Immediately thereafter, one should completely wrap the mouth of the jar with two new, stainless cloths.

Following that, once the jar has been adorned with flowers and other offerings, one should invoke the most excellent splendor—the very form of the deity to be worshipped—and perform the rites of invocation and so forth.
As it is said: "O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, come here, stay here, be present here! (KṛdC 4.23).
Having performed the sakalī-karaṇa rite upon this Hari residing in the water-pot through the placement of the mantras of the *arṇa-tattva*,
the Guru should then worship him with focused attention.
Accompanied by a retinue and groups of attendants.

Having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making the deity manifest) upon Hari residing in this jar, there should be the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*) upon the limbs of the deity; this is what is meant by *sakalīkaraṇa*.

Rudradhara states that after performing the *uttamāṅga* (the supreme limb), one should perform the placement of the *varṇa-tattva* (the principle of the phonemes) along with the placement of the *tattva-mantras* consisting of syllables.

Regarding the term *arṇa*, it refers to the arrangement of the phonemes of the mantra according to the distinction between creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and according to the distinction in the application of the fingers; thus, it means the *manu-nyāsa* (placement of the mantra) or the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* enclosed by the *manu* (mantra).
"By means of these and other such *nyāsas*, one should make the body complete (*sakala*) and endowed with qualities (*saguṇa*), bearing that form of light"—thus says Bhairava Tripāṭhin.
Vidyādhara also says this: "Even without the *pīṭha-nyāsa* and *kara-nyāsa*, [the body becomes complete] by means of the sets of *nyāsas* and so forth taught in the first and second chapters.
According to some, in the case of the eighteen-syllable [mantra], the placement of the mantra's syllables (*mantrākṣara-nyāsa*) should be understood as taking the place of the *tattva-nyāsa*.

Immediately thereafter, the preceptor, attentive and composed, should worship the deity together with his retinue and protective enclosures, using any of the ritual offerings consisting of either sixteen or five services.
He states the sequence of worship:
having offered a seat and uttered "Welcome," one likewise offers water for the feet and water for sipping.
First, the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and the sacrificial oblations (yūñji), ending with the water for sipping (ācamana), should be offered to the son of Nanda.
Then the minister, having assigned a place, a dwelling, and ornaments to that [deity] together with its limbs,
[honors] the body with purifying perfumes and flowers.
First, one should worship this [deity] according to the procedure for ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having offered a seat in the form of lotuses and other flowers to that Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, together with his attendants (Sāṅga),
and having uttered the words "Welcome," one should first offer the arghya,
pādya, and ācamanīya, along with the madhuparka; after giving the madhuparka, the final ācamanīya should be offered.
One should perform the bathing with scented water and other substances; a pair of garments should be offered upon the body, and ornaments such as earrings should be applied in their proper places.

Immediately thereafter, one should first worship this Supreme Lord on His limbs—that is, upon His body—with pure and sanctified perfumes and flowers, according to the method of ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
He describes the very manner of worship:
"Creation and maintenance, the pair of his own limbs, the flute, the garland, the primary [objects] such as the token of recognition and the excellent rays."
Having worshipped oneself with the root mantra as in the self-consecration, one should then worship the surrounding deities once more.
One should worship with the mantras for the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*) in their proper sequence:
*oṃ goṃ oṃ namaḥ*, and so forth.

The emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and maintenance (*sthitī*) rites consist of the previously mentioned pair of one's own limbs (*svāṅgayuga*), as well as the five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*) and ten-limbed (*daśāṅga*) placements. [The objects of worship are] the flute, the rosary, the forest garland (*vanamālā*), the token of recognition (*abhijñānavara*), the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem, which is preeminent among stones.

Having worshipped these with the root mantra (mūla-mantra) according to the procedure for self-worship— just as the worship of the Supreme Lord was performed within oneself five times with handfuls of flowers such as *tulasī* at the two feet and other locations— one should likewise worship that which is situated in the vessel; furthermore,
one should again worship the enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) that are about to be described.

In the case of the eighteen-syllable [mantra], it should be understood that worship must be performed for the placement of syllables (varṇanyāsa) and the placement of words (padanyāsa) at the locations of emanation and so forth. // KrdC_4.27 //
He states the sequence for the worship of the enclosures:
"Then Dāma, Sudāma, Vasudāma, and Kiṅkiṇī are to be worshipped in the directions; they consist of light-forms. One should also worship their external limbs upon the filaments. (Krd 4.28)
Immediately thereafter, within the pericarp, the four [deities] beginning with Dāma are to be worshipped in the four directions starting from the east.
Of what nature are they? They are of the form of brilliance, intensely radiant.
The ritual application is as follows: "Oṃ, obeisance to Dāma," and so forth.
He speaks of the second enclosure with the words "outside of that":
one should worship the limbs (aṅga) in the pericarp and the corners. (KrdC 4.28)
He states the procedure for worship:

"With a perfectly purified mind, one who possesses a pure intellect should, in sequence, [worship] from the Heart-mantra up to the Armor-mantra in the directions of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Śiva; then, in the directions starting from the East, [he should worship] the Weapon-mantra with perfumes and other offerings. (Kṛd 4.29)

In the four corners beginning with the southeast, one should worship the four limbs starting with the heart and ending with the armor; immediately thereafter, one should worship the weapon-limb in the four directions beginning with the east.
He describes the meditation on the limb-deities:
"The women have complexions like the released moon, the lovely *kuvalaya* lotus, emerald, and fire."
The limb-deities, with serene faces and hands radiating the gesture of granting fearlessness, should be recollected.
The limb-deities are to be meditated upon.
Of what nature are they? They are young women, possessing the natural characteristics of females. Furthermore, of what nature are they?
Those whose luster, radiance, and color were equal to pearl, moonstone (candrakānta-maṇi), blue lotus (kuvalaya), sapphire (harinīla), and fire (hutāśa);
what were they like? They were those whose hands were adorned with the boon of fearlessness (abhaya).
Of what nature were they? They had serene faces. (KrdC 4.30)
He states the third enclosure:
"Then, one should worship the eight queens, Rukmiṇī and the others, upon the petals."
Holding lotuses in their right hands,
their other hands are marked by excellent bowls filled with wealth.
Then, immediately after that, one should worship the eight principal queens, the great goddesses beginning with Rukmiṇī, upon the petals—that is, the leaves starting from the eastern direction.
Of what nature are they? They are those by whom lotuses are held in their right hands.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?
Those whose other left hands are sealed and filled with vessels brimming with *vasu* (wealth) are thus described.
He describes the eight [wives]: she named Rukmiṇī, Satyā, she called Nāgnijitī, and Sunandā; furthermore, Mitravindā, Sulakṣmaṇā, Ṛkṣajā, and Suśīlā. (Krd 4.32)
Jāmbavatī was born from a bear.
He shows their forms: these two are respectively the color of refined gold and emerald, and they wear very white and variegated garments.
Their limbs were languid from the weight of their broad breasts,
and they wore ornaments resplendent with various clusters of jewels.
These women, beginning with Rukmiṇī, are in pairs, sequentially; they are such that their luster is like that of gold and emerald respectively.
Furthermore, what are they like? They are such that they possess beautiful, white garments of various kinds.
Furthermore, of what nature were they?
They were such that their limbs were sluggish and motionless due to the weight of their firm breasts.
Furthermore, of what nature were they?
Their ornaments were especially resplendent among various kinds of gem collections, such as clusters of sapphire and other jewels. (KrdC 4.33)
He states the fourth enclosure: "Then one should worship Vasudeva and Devakī, Nanda-gopa and Yaśodā, Balabhadra and Subhadrikā, upon the tips of the petals."
The cowherds and cowherd girls, whose minds and eyes were absorbed in Govinda.
Then, immediately after that, one should worship Vasudeva and the others on the tips of the petals, starting from the east in due order.
Of what nature are they? They are those whose intellect and vision are dissolved—that is, joined—in Govinda. (KrdC 4.34)
He displays their weapons:
the Father and Mother have hands in the gestures of knowledge and fearlessness, and are yellow and pale-white respectively;
the Mothers, moreover, wear divine garlands, garments, ointments, and ornaments.
The two parents, Vasudeva and the cowherd Nanda, held in their hands the *jñāna-mudrā* and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).

Of what nature were they? They were respectively yellowish-green and white. The two mothers, Devakī and Yaśodā, were of what nature? They were such that they possessed divine garlands, garments, and ornaments worthy of the gods.
And the two [consorts], one ruddy and the other dark-blue, adorned with necklaces, gems, and earrings, hold a bowl filled with milk-rice and grant boons.

They hold the *varada* (boon-granting) and *varadāna* (bestowing boons) mudrās, as well as vessels filled with milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are reddish and dark-blue.
Furthermore, of what sort are they?
They are adorned with necklaces and earrings.
Balarāma is white as a conch or the moon, wielding a mace and a plow;
he is fond of the *hālā* liquor, wears blue garments, is full of playfulness, and sports a single earring.
Bala is Balarāma, white as a conch or the moon, bearing a plow and a pestle;
furthermore, how is he?
He is eager for and restless in drinking *hālā*—that is, honey-wine—and acts with impatience.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is clad in blue garments.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is full of sportiveness and grace.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is the wearer of a single earring.
Dark as a pea, auspicious, most auspicious, adorned with auspicious ornaments,
endowed with the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, clad in yellow garments, and in the full bloom of youth.
Subhadrā is dark-complexioned like a *kalāya* bean, auspicious, upright, adorned with beautiful ornaments, and resplendent with her finery.
Furthermore, of what nature is she?
She is endowed with the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).
Furthermore, of what nature is she?
She is one who wears yellow garments.
Furthermore, of what nature is she?
One who has reached full maturity.
The cowherds and cowherd girls, holding in their hands flutes, lutes, cane-staves, conchs, horns, and so forth, with their lotus-like hands grasping various offerings,
[should be worshipped]; and outside of that, one should worship the wish-fulfilling trees, such as the Mandāra.

The cowherds were distinguished by various objects in their hands— such as flutes (*veṇu*), bamboo pipes (*vaṃśī*), lutes with strings (*vīṇā-tantrī*), canes (*vetra-yaṣṭi*), conchs (*śaṅkha*), and horns (*śṛṅga*)— while the cowherd girls, moreover, had accepted various kinds of offerings (*prābhṛta*) presented to them.
"Those whose lotus-hands have been brought under control and mastered.
Regarding the fifth enclosure, he says "mandārādi" (mandāra flowers, etc.):
immediately outside of that [fourth enclosure], one should worship the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) beginning with the mandāra, which will be described further on. (KrdC 4.39)
The trees known as mandāra, santānaka, pārijāta, and kalpavṛkṣa, as well as karcandana,
[should be placed] in the center and in the four directions for the fulfillment of desired aims.
Skilled solely in giving, their branches were bent down by fruit.
He states those very [deities] as "Mandārī" and so forth. To the question of where and who is to be worshipped, he says "in the center.

Since there is no evidence for worshiping them first [elsewhere], they are to be worshipped in the center, that is, on the pericarp (*karṇikā*), just as they were first mentioned; and [the other deities] are worshipped in the four directions.

In the four directions beginning with the east, those [trees] which are peerless (advitīya) and skillful (dakṣa) in bestowing such desired and longed-for objects— those whose branches are bent by fruits— or alternatively, those who are uniquely capable in granting what is requested, and whose branches are likewise bent by fruits. (KrdC 4.40)
He speaks of the sixth enclosure: [One should worship] Indra, Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Soma, Śiva, Ananta, and Brahmā;
One of pure intellect, presiding over his own caste, should offer sacrifice in his respective directions, accompanied by weapons,
vehicles, and retinues.

One of pure intellect should worship these— Hari, Indra, Agni the carrier of oblations, Yama the swift one, Nirṛti the night-walker, Varuṇa the lord of waters, Vāyu, Soma, Īśa, Śeṣa the infinite, and Brahmā born from the lotus— in their respective directions, starting from the east. Here, because Ananta is mentioned as being between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, and Brahmā between Soma and Īśa, it is understood that the worship takes place in directions other than those conventionally assigned as east and so forth.
Thus it is said in another scripture:
"The teachers have declared that either in front of the deity or in front of oneself, the east is so called;
yet for the sake of liberation, the worship of the deity must be understood as being directed toward the true east alone."

Of what kind [are they]? Their own class (svajāti) consists of Indra and so forth; they are conjoined with their sovereign lord (adhīśvara), their weapon (heti)—whether a missile or a vehicle (patra), and their retinue (parivāra), which is their host (gaṇa). Furthermore, the seed-syllables (bīja) of these must be uttered. As for the ritual application (prayoga): "Laṃ! Salutation to Indra, the sovereign lord of all gods, together with his weapons, his vehicle, and his retinue. In this same way, it should be inferred for the others as well. (KrdC 4.41)
Now he states their colors: Vāsava and the others are, by color, brownish-red, tawny, blue, dark, white, smoke-colored, stainless-white, pure, and red.
Adorned with their own weapons shining upon their lotus-like hands, dressed in celestial raiment,
and enriched with ornaments sparkling with various clusters of jewels.

Kapiśa is golden-colored; kapila has the luster of copper; śyāmala is black; śveta is white; śukla is bright white; dhūmra is a variety of dark gray; amala-sita is pure white; śuci is also indeed white; rakta is red; and lohita is crimson—these are Vāsava and the others, according to their colors, in the sequence previously mentioned.
Furthermore, of what nature are they? They are those whose lotus-like hands possess resplendent weapons.

Moreover, they are distinguished by excellent attire; they are enriched and adorned with ornaments that flash and shine intensely with the radiance (*usra*)—the rays—of various kinds of gemstones, such as rubies (*padmarāga*) and others.
This is the meaning. (KrdC 4.42)
He describes the seventh enclosure:
the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose,
the fierce goad, the mace, the trident, the mountain, and the lotus.
They are to be worshipped externally, adorned with their own well-defined crowns,
and with their lotus-hands raised, brandishing their respective weapons out of fear.

The *dambholi*, the *vajra*, the weapon named *śakti* (the spear), the *daṇḍa*, the *kṛpāṇa*, the *khaḍga*, the one called *caṇḍāṅkuśa*, the one known as *ugrāṅkuśa*, the *gadā*, the three-pointed *triśūla*, the *ari*, the *cakra*, and the *padma*— these are to be worshipped outside, starting from the southeast (Vahni) and the east (Vāsava).
Of what nature are the *dambholi* and the others?
They are those whose heads are joined with their own well-marked crests, crowns marked with symbols such as the vajra;
furthermore, they are those whose lotus-like hands are raised and well-characterized by their respective weapons, missiles, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*). (KrdC 4.43)
He states the colors of the vajra and the others: they have the luster of gold, silver, a water-cloud, campaka, crimson, snow, blue, javā, and coral, respectively.
In sequence, however, they are resplendent with vajras first, and adorned with beautiful ointments, garments, garlands, and ornaments.
Those preceded by the vajra—beginning with the vajra—are to be known as having such forms in their respective order according to their luster and color.
Furthermore, what are they like?

Gold, silver, the water-giver (cloud), the cloud, the campaka flower, the crimson (red), snow (white), blue, dark-green, the javā flower, the auṇḍra flower, coral, and the fresh sprout; they are of such a nature.
Those who possess radiance are such;
furthermore, of what kind are they?
They are those who possess beautiful and captivating ointments such as sandalwood, as well as garments, garlands, and ornaments. (KrdC 4.44)
He concludes what was previously stated:
"The sevenfold enclosure has been described in the ritual for the worship of Acyuta; it brings all happiness."
Alternatively, this triple enclosure may be performed with the *Aṅgapurandara* and *Aśanimukha* mantras, recited with great effort.

Thus, in the manner previously described, the sevenfold enclosure (āvaraṇa-saptaka) has been explained in the ritual procedure for the worship of Viṣṇu. Of what nature is it? It is that which bestows all happiness and desired objects.
For one who is unable [to perform the full rite], he says: "one should sacrifice" (prayajatāt).
One who is unable to perform what was previously mentioned should worship the triad of enclosures together with the three enclosures.
By what means? By those headed by the limbs (aṅga) and Indra’s thunderbolt (vajra); that is to say, by these as the primary [deities]. (KrdC 4.45)
Concluding the current topic, he speaks of another form of worship:
"Having thus worshipped with water, fragrance, and flowers, one should then perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa by means of the 'Eight Verses on Kṛṣṇa'."
The wise one should perform those [mantras] which are called "invocations" (samāhvaya); I shall describe them as beginning with *tad* and ending with *namaḥ*.

Having worshipped in the manner previously described with water, fragrance, and flowers, immediately thereafter, the wise and learned practitioner should perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa by means of the eight names of Kṛṣṇa that will be mentioned hereafter—those names beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, such as "Oṃ Kṛṣṇāya Namaḥ" and so forth. (KrdC 4.46)
He shows those very names: Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, and he who is called Nārāyaṇa; the son of Devakī, the best of the Yadus, and also Vārṣṇeya. (Kṛd 4.47)
Following the word *asurāntaka*, the seventh is *bhārahārī*;
then *dharma-saṃsthāpaka*—these eight [names] end in the fourth case (*caturthy-anta*) in their respective order. (Krd 4.48)
The meaning of "asurāntaka" is "the bearer of the burden.
These words, beginning with "Kṛṣṇa" and so forth, should be understood respectively as being preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), ending in the dative case, and concluding with "namaḥ. (KrdC 4.47–48)
Regarding those who are utterly incapable, he says:
"Alternatively, with these very [means], the wise should perform worship of the Enemy of Kaṃsa for the sake of crossing the ocean of saṃsāra and for the attainment of all desires. (Krd 4.49)
Alternatively, with these very words beginning with "Kṛṣṇa," the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the enemy of Kaṃsa, should be performed by the wise—
that is, by the learned— for what purpose? For the sake of crossing over, for the transcendence of this very ocean of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, for what purpose?
For the sake of attaining all one's heart's desires.
He demonstrates the ritual procedure for offering incense:

having prepared incense with thick fragrances such as *guggulu* and other substances, which are crushed, scattered, and mixed with clarified butter upon glowing coals, the practitioner of mantra [should offer it].
Then, with his other hand, he should ring the bell while sounding it, having worshipped it with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers, as he offers it low to the Destroyer of the Danujas.
"Upon embers of *sāra* wood, embers of hard wood,
or embers of *khadira* wood— so say those who follow the three-fold recension—
[the offering is made] with scattered and cast *guggulu* and other substances, namely *guggulu*, sugar, honey, sandalwood, agallochum, and *śīra*, all blended with clarified butter."

Having prepared incense—consisting of substances that have been held, melted, crushed until worn away, ground into powder, and endowed with dense fragrance—the practitioner, the worshiper, should offer it low at the level of the navel to Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of demons.
What while doing so? Immediately thereafter, ringing a bell with his other left hand while reciting the mantra "Gajadhvani Mantramātaḥ Svāhā."
Of what nature was she? She was worshipped with perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, and flowers.

He shows the procedure for the offering of lamps: likewise, one whose intellect is exceedingly clear regarding sight and so forth should hold aloft a lamp ignited with a wick of camphor soaked in fragrant ghee, reaching as far as a lotus.
Having offered a handful of flowers, and having likewise presented water for washing the feet along with water for rinsing the mouth,
let her prepare an offering in a large golden vessel.

In the same way, one should prepare a lamp. With what? With a wick soaked and sprinkled with fragrant, sweet-smelling ghee and combined with camphor. Of what kind [should it be]? Blazing to the sight.
Rudradhara says it is "pleasing to the sight" (dṛṣṭi-manoharam).
Having placed [the hand] high above, reaching as far as the lotus (padma) or the head (mastaka), one turns it clockwise from the eyes and so forth down to the lotus;
Tripāṭhin says it reaches as far as the lotus-feet (caraṇa-kamala).
The reading "pāda-paryantam" occurs in some places.

Immediately thereafter, having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon the head and having provided water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), one should prepare—that is, arrange—the food offering (*naivedya*) in a vast golden vessel, a large golden bowl. "Along with sipping" (*sācāmam*) means that after first giving the water for sipping with [the verses] beginning with "vadane," one should subsequently give the food offering; this is the meaning. (KrdC 4.51)
He shows the nature of the food offering (naivedya):
with most fragrant milk-oblation well-cooked, along with white sugar and various delightful,
heart-pleasing, and manifold flavors provided by the instructors.
With curd, fresh butter, new snow (sugar), cakes, meat, ghee, molasses, coconut, plantain fruit, flowers, and juices; Krd_4.52.
With very fragrant milk-rice that is well-cooked and thoroughly prepared, along with sugar-based side dishes (*vyañjana*) accompanied by sugar;
according to those who read it as three words— *śarkarayā saha upadaṃśakaiḥ vyañjanaiḥ*—
in this alternative reading, the text is *śucitena sitā-samupadaṃśakaiḥ*.

With these substances—namely, pleasing, desirable, heart-pleasing, delicious, and various sweet flavors; fresh and excellent white sugar-candy and the like; and flower-essence honey—one should prepare the food offering (naivedya). KrdC_4.52 //
What kind of special offering (naivedya) should one prepare? To this he says:
"Sprinkled with the weapon-mantra (astra), protected by the 'enemy-seal' (ari-mudrā), and dried by the wind-mantra (vāyavya) with the hand of fire (agni)."
Having joined [the palms] and filled the left hand with the nectar of the moon,
which has been rendered into mantra-nectar, one should then recite the mantra while touching it.
One should worship Manu eight times with fragrant perfumes using a fragrant seal;
then, having formed a *prasava-añjali*, one should worship Hari.
And from his mouth, great light shall stream forth.

Having sprinkled [the site] with the root mantra or the weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*)— namely *astrāya phaṭ*— and having protected it with the wheel-gesture (*cakra-mudrā*), one should burn away defects by sprinkling water consecrated with the wind-seed syllable (*vāyu-bīja*) while reciting "vāyavya"; then, having touched it with the right hand consecrated with the fire-seed syllable (*vahni-bīja*)— namely *ram*— one burns away the defects and fills it with the nectar of the moon from the left hand.

Thus, having covered [the vessel] with the left hand and meditated upon it as being filled with the essence of nectar through the recitation of the *baṃ* seed-syllable, and having then meditated upon it as being of the nature of nectar by means of the root mantra, one should thereafter touch— that is, make contact with— this such food offering and recite the mantra eight times; having meditated upon the food offering as being completely full by means of the *surabhi-mudrā*, the cow-seal.
One should worship with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like.
By the words "Hari" and so forth, he shows the manner of giving:
having formed the añjali gesture of reverence, one should worship Hari and pray, "May your splendor issue forth for the purpose of accepting the food offering."

Immediately thereafter, one should contemplate that light shall issue forth and spread from the mouth of this Hari; thus says Tripāṭhin: "One should join it with the food offering (naivedya). (KrdC 4.53–54)
Then, reciting the root mantra ending with "vītihotradayitā," one should pour water and offer that oblation which is of the nature of nectar.
With his right hand, he plucks the *sukusuma* flower.
Immediately thereafter, while reciting the root mantra ending with *vītihotra-dayitā* and concluding with *svāhākāra*, one should sprinkle a little water over it.

Here, even though the mantra already ends in *svāhā*, the word *svāhā* must be employed once again; by the force of this very [repetition], lifting and raising it with both arms joined together, one should offer that oblation which has become the nature of nectar (*amṛta*). (KrdC 4.55)
He states the mantra for the offering of the food oblation (naivedya):
"I offer this to the Blessed One; O Hari, may You enjoy this sacrificial food.
This mantra for the offering of the food oblation is used with one's own name in all forms of worship. (Kṛd 4.56)

Regarding the phrase "by its own name" (*nijākhyayā*) in the context of all worship of the gods with this mantra: at the place where [the word] *hare* occurs, one should utter the name of whichever deity the offering is given; such is the meaning of the term *nijākhyā*.
Some, however, maintain that it means "by the name of the offering" (*nivedyākhyayā*). KrdC 4.56.

He shows the specific mudrā for partaking of food: one should display with the left hand the *grāsa-mudrā*, resembling a full-blown utpala lotus, and with the right hand, one should display the *prāṇa* and the other [winds]. (Kṛd 4.57)
With the left hand, one should display the *grāsa-mudrā*;
of what nature? Resembling a full-blown blue lotus.
Immediately thereafter, with the right hand, one should display the *mudrās* of *prāṇa* and the others, which will be described hereafter. (KrdC 4.57)
In this first mudrā, one should touch the little finger and the ring finger with the tips of the thumbs;
likewise, another [mudrā] consists of the index and middle fingers.
And the middle [finger] is between the ring finger and the middle finger. Kṛd 4.58.
The ring finger, the index finger, and the middle finger should be so; likewise, with the little finger added, that is the fourth;
and the fifth is declared to be the same as that.
The mudrās, beginning with Prāṇa, are joined with their respective mantras.
One should touch the two little fingers and the ring fingers with the tips of one's own thumbs;

this is the first mudrā here. Likewise, one should touch the index and middle fingers with the tip of one's own thumb, and one should touch the ring and middle fingers with that same [thumb]; thus is the vyāna-mudrā. One should touch the ring, index, and middle fingers with that [thumb].

The fourth belongs to Udāna; those three, together with the little finger, likewise touch the top of one's own thumb. If one should touch [them] in this manner, then it is the Samāna-mudrā. In this way, the mudrās of Prāṇa and the others are taught and described. Of what nature are they? They are accompanied by their respective mantras; the meaning is that they become mudrās through association with mantras, just like the Bilva-mudrā. (KrdC 4.58–59)
In response to the inquiry "What are those mantras?", he states the mantras of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth:
"Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna, ending respectively in the dative case; when ignited by the consort Tārādhārā, these are the mantras of the path of Kṛṣṇa. (Krd 4.60)
The five [breaths] beginning with *prāṇa*, joined respectively with the fourth case-ending, as well as the streams of *tārā* (the syllable *oṃ*), meaning they begin with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*);
likewise, being kindled—that is, ignited and connected—by the beloved wife of the fire of the black path (*kṛṣṇādhvan*), meaning they end with the word *svāhā*.
This being so, the meaning is that there are five mantras beginning with "Oṃ, svāhā to Prāṇa. (KrdC 4.60)
Displaying the *nivedya-mudrā*, he shows the mantra:
"Then, having displayed the *nivedya-mudrā* with both hands joined by the primary [thumb], while touching the ring fingers, one should display it while reciting one's own mantra. (Krd 4.61)
Then, immediately after that, one should display the *nivedya-mudrā*.
Doing what? Touching the ring fingers of both hands with the thumbs.
Again, doing what?
Reciting his own personal mantra.
He extracts the mantra:
Nandaja (Na), joined with Ambu (Va), Manu (Ra), and Bindu (M), followed by Nati (Ṅa);
then Pārśva (Pa), Ra, Marut (Ya), and Avātman (Ha), followed by Ni (Ña).
The self-born [Brahmā] is the object of offering (*nivedya*) when joined with the suffix *ṅe* (dative) and *yut*;
likewise, the wind (*anila*) is so when joined with *ami*. (Kārikā 4.62)

*Na* is born of *nanda*, which is the letter *ṭha*; *ambu* is the letter *va*; *manu* is the vowel *au*; and *bindu* is the nasal dot (*m*). Joined with these is *nati*, namely *namaḥ*. *Pārśva* is the letter *pa*;

*rā* is its own form; *marut* is the letter *ya*; and *avātmane* is the form of the vowel *a*. *Ruddha* is its own form. *Ṅe* is the dative case; thus, the meaning is that the word *aniruddha* is joined with the dative case.

Regarding the offering (*nivedyam*): there are three [syllables]. *Ātmabhūḥ* (the Self-born) is the letter *ka*; *māṃsa* (flesh) is the letter *la*; *pārśva* (side) is the letter *pa*. Joined with the letters *la* and *ya*, *anila* (wind) is the letter *ya*. Such is the essential form. Likewise, the mantra is: *Ṭhvauṃ namo paryāvātmane aniruddhāya naivedyaṃ kalpayāmi*. (KrdC 4.62)
The mantra-practitioner, having arranged vessels containing sprouts of seeds all around the mandala,
[should also place] lamps made of flour.
One should place [the lamps] filled with ghee, possessing brightly blazing flames.
Having arranged vessels containing sprouts of seeds all around the maṇḍala, one should likewise place lamps made of flour, filled with ghee and possessing blazing flames.
He shows the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) as an ancillary part of the initiation (dīkṣā): "Then, once the sacrificial fire has been consecrated, the one of pure intellect,
having duly invoked and properly worshipped Hari..."
One should perform the oblation with milk prepared from white rice and mixed with white ghee, using the [mantra] of the White-rayed One.
Having completed one thousand and eight oblations, one should again offer a *bali* to the presiding deities of the zodiac signs.
And likewise from the lunar mansions and from the karaṇas.

Immediately thereafter, having consecrated the fire with the purificatory rites prescribed by the scriptures, one of pure intellect should invoke Hari in His form as described, worship Him according to the rules with perfumes and other offerings, and perform one thousand and eight oblations. With what? With white-rayed [rice]; by what kind of devotee? By one who has prepared it with milk—that is to say, with *paramānna* (milk-rice) cooked in milk.

Furthermore, with what kind [of offering]? With that joined with white ghee—that is, accompanied by sugar and ghee. Immediately thereafter, having completed the aforementioned *homa*, one should offer the remaining *paramānna* to the presiding lords of the signs beginning with Aries, to the deities of the signs such as Maṅgala and the others, and to the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī.
One should offer an oblation (*bali*) to the planets beginning with Mars from the [signs] starting with Aries.
The ritual formula (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: "This oblation is for Maṅgala, the lord of Aries and Scorpio; likewise for Śukra, the lord of Taurus and Libra;
for Budha, the lord of Gemini and Virgo; for Candra, the lord of Cancer; and for Sūrya, the lord of Leo."
"Salutation to the Guru, lord of the sign of Pisces; salutation to Śani, lord of the signs of Capricorn and Aquarius.
Likewise, this offering is saluted to the Aries zodiacal sign, which consists of the constellations Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and the quarter of Kṛttikā," and so forth.
In this way, let there be this offering to Vava, Vālaka, Ilavata, Itila, Gara, Vaṇija, and Viṣṭi; homage!
He describes the procedure following the worship:
having prepared the nectar-water, having offered it,
and having given water for rinsing the mouth, one should remove the flame from the face.
Having set aside the food offering and presented it to Viṣvaksena, one should again smear the ground.

Having turned the water itself into nectar by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*, he should offer it for Kṛṣṇa’s drinking; then, having given water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), he should dissolve the splendor (*tejas*) brought down from the mouths of the gods— the faces of the fire— into his own mouth, and having deposited that splendor within the divine face, he should lift up the *naivedya* and offer it to Viṣvaksena and the host of deities, [and then touch] the earth.
Having smeared [it]. (KṛdC 4.66)

Having offered mouth-rinses, tooth-cleansing sticks, water for sipping, the wiping of the face and hands, ointments, mouth-perfumes, garlands, and ornaments— and even betel— along with excellent instrumental music and dance;
One should worship him once again, having fully gratified him with songs.

Furthermore, *gaṇḍūṣa* is water taken in the hollow of the palm; *dantadhāvana* is a tooth-stick (the variant reading *dantadhāvana* is found in the three recensions). *Ācamana* refers to the second sipping of water after the remainder has been consumed; *mṛjyam* is the cloth for wiping the mouth and hands.

Having offered unguents such as sandalwood paste, mouth-perfumes— so called because they make the mouth fragrant— such as camphor and the like, garlands of flowers, ornaments for decoration, and betel leaf (as well, in this inclusive sense), and having once again performed worship just as before, one should bow to and worship Hari, who has been thoroughly gratified by excellent instrumental music, dance, and song.
Then, having offered him an *argha* along with its retinue of perfumes and other offerings, having respectfully formed a handful of flowers,
and having praised him, one should bow with the head and offer water from the hollowed palms.
May he offer his very self at the base of those lotus feet.

With what? With fragrances and so forth, together with their attendants—that is, accompanied by the previously mentioned coverings—then immediately after offering this *arghya* to Hari, having offered a handful of flowers with devotion, having praised him, and having prostrated with his head, let him offer himself at the base of His true lotus feet with a handful of water from the remainder of the *arghya*. (KrdC 4.68)
He states the mantra for the self-offering with the passage beginning with "itaḥ" and ending with "svātma-samarpaṇe":

"Whatever was previously [done] by me—whether through the authority of the vital breath, the intellect, the body, or the qualities (dharmas)—in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, whether by mind, speech, action, the two hands, the feet, the abdomen, or the generative organ; whatever was remembered, whatever was spoken, and whatever was done."
"May everything be an offering to Brahman, Svāhā! I offer myself and all that is mine completely to Hari; Om Tat Sat"—this is the mantra proclaimed for the surrender of one's own self.

And these three mantras are not written here because they are clear: the wise person, recollecting the Imperishable One residing in the vase, should then mutter the mantra one thousand and eight times.
Then, having dissolved those veils of the one who has conquered the sons of Diti within his own body, he should lead even that [body] to the nature of nectar.

Immediately thereafter, the wise and learned practitioner, meditating upon Hari residing within the jar— that is, established in the water-pot and other vessels— should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times. Thereafter, having dissolved those aforementioned surrounding deities (āvaraṇa-devatās) into the body of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the conqueror of the sons of Diti, and having contemplated that they have become absorbed, he should then lead even that divine form to the state of nectar (sudhātmatā), that is, to immortality.

Having applied [the offerings] with flowers to the banner, the archway, the directional vases, and so forth, as well as to the pavilion, the mandala, and the sacrificial pit, one should apply them to the funeral pyre and the vase.
Having performed the worship, one should again recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.

Having projected the consciousness-form of the mantra-deity onto the *kalaśa* and having worshipped it with flowers, one should again recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Of what nature is that consciousness? It is the consciousness residing in the banner, the archway, the directions, the *kalaśas*, and so forth—not only residing in the banner and such, but also residing in the mandala, the pavilion, and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). (KrdC 4.70)
Then the disciple, having fasted, at dawn having performed his daily rites, wearing clean white garments and being well-attired,
[should offer] with land, wealth, grain, and herds of cattle—
May he revile the best of Brahmins for the sake of attaining devotion to Hari.
Immediately thereafter, the disciple, having fasted and observed the vow, at dawn during the morning time, having performed his daily obligatory rites, wearing white garments,

well-attired and adorned with beautiful ornaments, should satisfy and please the most excellent Brahmins with these things as appropriate: land (the earth), wealth (gold and so forth), grain (rice and so forth), a milch cow, and fine silk cloth.
For what purpose? For the sake of obtaining the grace of Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having further gratified and prostrated before the Teacher,
that Supreme Person who possesses a body,
he offered him a sacrificial fee, avoiding any stinginess regarding his wealth.
Having given his own body, the wise one should offer it completely.
Having again and once more fully gratified and satisfied the brāhmaṇas, he spoke further for the sake of ultimate satisfaction; in the reading *parītya*, the meaning is "having circumambulated.

Having prostrated before and offered obeisances to the spiritual master, the Guru, he—casting aside any stinginess regarding wealth and according to his means—offered to that embodied Supreme Person, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, that well-known portion consisting of half of his wealth, which is one-fourth [of his total possessions].

Or, having given [it], one should not—like a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)—immediately after receiving the mantra, out of that same impulse, offer up one's own body; rather, the wise person should offer it [at the proper time]. KrdC 4.72.
Then, while [the disciple] is seated comfortably on a throne in the consecration pavilion,
the Guru should purify him as before by means of the rites of drying and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, the Guru should purify this disciple—just as before, in the same manner—as by means of the drying [process] and so forth, beginning with the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*). Of what sort? One who is seated comfortably upon a seat in the consecration pavilion (*abhiṣeka-maṇḍapa*).

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) up to the *pīṭha* upon his body, the one of pure intellect worshipped that sword with mantras; then, having applied yellow pigment (*rocanā*) mixed with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and flowers,
he [proceeded] amidst the blessings of the twice-born and the clear, resonant sounds of songs and musical instruments.
Accompanied by auspicious objects, he, being confident, brought that jar covered [with cloth] into his presence.

Having performed the entire ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body of that disciple, up to and including the final *pīṭha-nyāsa*, and having worshipped the seat with the *āsana-mantra*, one should place yellow pigment (*rocanā*) on the head and apply a forehead mark (*tilaka*). Of what kind is this yellow pigment?
Accompanied by *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and flowers;
immediately thereafter, with the blessings of the twice-born (*dvijas*) and sounds such as songs and auspicious recitations—
of what kind were these?

Accompanied by clear and sharp sounds, distinct and excellent words, as well as other auspicious items suitable for a rite of consecration (*maṅgala*), the preceptor—having been chosen as the teacher (*ācārya*)—should bring that water-pot near him, that is, near the disciple. Of what nature [is he]? The meaning is: anyone who is recognized as belonging to the disciple and is endowed with trust. (KrdC 4.74)
Then, with that splendor which possesses the form of supreme nectar, in which jewels, mantras, and great medicinal herbs are absorbed,
he filled his body and expanded it.
May that state of perfect equilibrium duly consecrate [you].

Having placed the jars from the pond upon the head of the disciple, one should perform the consecration—that is, the act of sprinkling—with that water-pot, according to rule and in the manner prescribed. As it has been said:
"Having duly lifted the jar and placed the celestial trees situated at its mouth upon the head of the disciple, one should mentally recite the Mātṛkā."
By what kind [of person]?
By one in whom the jewel—the nine gems, the mantra, the *ṛk*, and the great medicinal herbs such as divine *pippalī*—is absorbed (*abhilīna*) and fully integrated (*saṃlīna*).
Of what nature is that? It is by means of the supreme splendor (*para-dhāman*), which is the very essence of supreme brilliance (*para-tejas*).
Furthermore, by what kind [of nectar]? By that which possesses the form of the supreme nectar, consisting of the nature of the supreme nectar.
What is he doing? Filling the body—the physical form—of this child.
Doing what? Immediately thereafter, expanding that state of aesthetic identity (sāmarasya) as a unity with the jar through each of those various forms of light.
He describes the consecration:

"With his body filled with the letters beginning with *kṣ* and ending with *m*, having recited the mantra three times at its conclusion, wearing a second white garment over his [usual] one, remaining silent, and having sipped water for purification. (Kṛd 4.76)

The disciple, whose body has been consecrated by means of the letters of the alphabet beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, as well as those ending in the vowel *a*, at the conclusion of three recitations of the root mantra; wearing a pair of fresh, exceedingly white garments; observing silence; and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice; [is thus prepared]. (KrdC 4.76)
Having prostrated many times before Hari, who bears the name of the Teacher, the disciple then approached him and sat down to his right, facing him with a one-pointed mind.

Having bowed many times to Hari, who bears the name of the Guide and appears in the form of a guru, and having thereafter clasped the feet of the guru by placing his two hands crossed over them, he should remain— that is, sit— with a one-pointed mind and a single-minded focus, facing the guru to the right of him, directly opposite the guru.
Having duly performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon him according to the rules,
he whose body was adorned with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings,
[the preceptor] then correctly applied the excellent mantra together with its seer (ṛṣi) and other components.
The Guru should say three times, "It is priceless," while holding [the substance] with his left hand.

Then, immediately thereafter, having duly established the disciple in the state of Acyuta through the ritual applications (nyāsa) as previously described— such as the five-limbed application (pañcāṅga-nyāsa)— and having transformed him into the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they [place] the priceless, most excellent mantra, accompanied by the sage (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), and deity, into his left and right ears, his body being adorned with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and flowers.
One should recite the supreme mantra three times—that is, three rounds—in the proper manner, according to the prescribed method. That method is as follows:

first, the Guru places water in the right hand, saying, "I give such-and-such a mantra," whereupon the disciple should say, "Please give it. Then he should bestow the mantra; in this regard, the mantra must necessarily be given by the Guru three times.
It should be recited; it should be recited until the mantra is mastered by the disciple and becomes under his own control. (KrdC 4.78)
After the reception of the mantra, he shows the duty of the disciple: having recited one hundred and eight times the mantra duly bestowed by the Guru, once again—
Then, having offered salutation, let him listen properly to the rules with his body bowed by a weight of devotion.

The Tripāṭhins maintain that the mantra has been obtained according to the prescribed rules through the Guru as its cause, perfected, and bestowed by way of grace. Having recited that [mantra] one hundred and eight times— meaning that which has eight more than one hundred— and having again saluted the Guru, paid homage, and prostrated like a staff, he should then properly observe the *samayas* (vows) and conducts from the Guru, and listen to what [is to be taught].
The injunction "one should recite the mantra eight times" is intended to prohibit recitation with a number of repetitions or durations less than that;
what kind of person [should do so]? One whose body is bowed down by an excess of devotion. (KrdC 4.79)
Regarding the duties of the guru immediately after the giving of the mantra, he says:

"Having given the mantra to the disciple and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the guru, having completed the procedure for self-worship (*ātma-yajana*), should recite it one thousand and eight times in order to avoid the loss of his own power. (Kṛtyakalpataru 4.80)

Immediately thereafter, the Guru, having given the mantra to the disciple, performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other rites, completed the procedure for self-worship (*ātma-yajana*), and performed the internal sacrifice (*abhyantara-yāga*), should recite the mantra given to the disciple one thousand and eight times in order to prevent the loss of his own power and to preserve that power. (KrdC 4.80)
He states the duty of the disciple:
having offered the entire collection beginning with the water-pot to the guru, he should also feed the best of the twice-born with various kinds of food.
Those who perform the consecration here according to this rite are indeed blessed, for they are the very abode of all prosperity.

Having offered and given all the items, beginning with the water-pot (*kumbha*) and including the entire mandala, as well as the materials situated within the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), to the Guru, one should satisfy the best of the twice-born with various kinds of food. He states the fruit of performing this: those who perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) in this world by means of this method and according to this sequence become the abode of prosperity—that is, of all forms of abundance.
Only they are truly fortunate, those who partake in the goals of human endeavor.
He summarizes the meaning stated:
"Initiation has indeed been described briefly for the recollection of those with clear intellects."
Having entered this [mandala], the practitioner should recite, offer oblations, and perform sacrifices with all the mantras.

Having condensed it slightly, initiation has been explained for those of clear intellect and pure understanding, so that they may remember it. Having entered—that is, having attained—this initiation, the practitioner (mantrin) and adept (sādhaka) should recite all mantras, perform worship, and offer oblations.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Worship of Initiation," in the *Kramadīpikā* composed by the venerable Keśavācārya.
**Fifth Chapter**
Now he shows the ritual procedure for the mantra of one who has been initiated:
"Having performed this rite in the month of Caitra during the bright fortnight under an auspicious constellation, [the disciple] should again receive initiation from the Guru."
Permitted by him, one should begin the preliminary service on the twelfth day of the second month, which is free from impurities.

In the month of Caitra, under an auspicious asterism (nakṣatra), a favorable lunar mansion (śubha-nakṣatra), during the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa) of the waxing moon, having performed this rite consisting of the initiation into the mantra,

and having again received from the preceptor, the spiritual guide (deśika-guru), the initiation and the instruction of the mantra, one should thereafter, authorized by that guru, begin the preliminary service (pūrva-sevā) or *puraścaraṇa* on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the second month, Vaiśākha.
The statement that "initiation in the month of Caitra leads to suffering" refers to initiations other than those for the Gopāla-mantra.

Having performed the rites beginning with bathing and ending with the worship of the body, following the path previously described, the chief of mantra-practitioners— pure, observing silence, celibate, and eating only at night— should proceed.
Through recitation, one whose self is tranquil [becomes so] by means of a pure garland of lotus seeds.
Having done this— the chief practitioner, the *sādhaka*, having performed the rites beginning with the bath and ending with the yoga of the self,

following the path previously described and relying on the mode of worship mentioned before— being pure through the recitation of the *gāyatrī* and thus free from sin, endowed with the external and internal purifications prescribed for Brahmins and others,

observing silence (*maunī*), restrained in speech, a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who has abandoned the eightfold sexual conduct, eating at night (*niśāśī*), being peaceful in soul and with an undisturbed mind.
One should perform the recitation with a rosary of white lotus seeds.
In this regard, what is stated in another scripture should be understood as follows:

on an auspicious day, having designated a field of one *krośa* or two *krośas* for the purpose of a monastery, [one should prepare] eight stakes made from the wood of a milky tree, each measuring one span (*vitasti*) in length.
Having recited [the mantra] ten or a hundred times for each [deity], or all at once, and having worshipped the deities of the eight directions,

one should offer a bali-oblation to the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla) in the center of the field; having performed the worship, one should bury those [objects] in the eight directions starting from the east, and in each respective place, having offered a bali-oblation to the Lord of that direction by his specific name and having also offered a lamp, on the day prior to the recitation—
One should observe a single meal or a fast, and gratify one's guru and Brāhmaṇas;
likewise, it is stated in the Sanatkumāra-kalpa:
"And one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with food, clothing, and other such provisions."

"Having honored one's own guru with many garments and ornaments, one should thereafter commence the recitation (japa), preceded by his permission. Thus it is said. Then, on the following day, having performed the ritual bath and other duties, one should make the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), uttering: "Oṃ, today, Oṃ, obeisance," and so forth, [for] the mantra of such-and-such.

Desiring success (*siddhi*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) as follows: "I shall perform the rite of *puraścaraṇa*, consisting of recitation (*japa*) of this many times, its tenth part as an oblation (*homa*) of such-and-such a substance, its tenth part as a libation (*tarpaṇa*) with such-and-such a substance, its tenth part as an ablution (*abhiṣeka*), and its tenth part as the gift of food to Brahmins.

Then, for the mantra, the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), and the deity (*devatā*), [one should state]: "The application (*viniyoga*) is in the recitation of the *puraścaraṇa* at the place of desire."
And this is the rule for recitation:
the prescribed method of continuity should not allow even a single day to pass;
one should sleep on a bed of *darbha* grass, pure and with a restrained mind.
If a day passes by, a fault arises that obstructs the accomplishment.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]:
One should perform the recitation day after day slowly and slowly, neither indistinctly, nor too fast, nor too slow; neither deficient nor excessive.
Likewise, in another place:
"With an undistracted mind, from morning until midday";
and similarly in the Nāradīya:
Neither speaking, nor sleeping, nor walking, nor recollecting anything else;
with a mind not impaired by hunger, yawning, hiccups, or other such conditions.
One attains the accomplishment of the mantra; therefore, one should be diligent in this regard.
Likewise, [one should practice] while wearing a turban, a bodice, naked, or with hair disheveled.
With his hands and feet extended, he should not sit on a seat with raised legs.
Likewise, in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā:

"Bathing at the three sessions of the day is prescribed; if one is unable, then twice or once. For one who does not bathe, there is no fruit, nor for one who does not offer libations to the ancestors."
One should not speak untruth, nor should one allow the senses to be seduced;
being pure and with a restrained mind, one should sleep on a bed of darbha grass.
One should always wash that garment; otherwise, it will bring about obstacles.
One should not recite a mantra while wearing only a single garment, nor ever while wearing many garments.
One performing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should worship [the deity] while wearing a garment above and below, and outside.
Likewise, in the Nāradīya:
"One should not converse with women or Śūdras at night, nor when intent on *japa*;
one should not perform *japa* during the *saṃdhyā* periods, nor at *pradoṣa*, nor during both [the morning and evening *saṃdhyās*]."
The ritual performer shall become pure with water from which a Brāhmaṇa has brought clothing. Thus [it is said]. (KrdC 5.2)
Furthermore, he states his duty: "While extending service to the cows, offering mouthfuls of fodder to them, and cherishing compassion for all living beings."
I pay homage to the deity who presides over the mantra,
Durgā, and to the Guru, who is a sun to the darkness that is difficult to penetrate.

Extending service to the cows—namely, cow-care in the form of scratching with smoke and so forth—while doing what? While offering mouthfuls of fodder to those cows; for it is the mantra of the cowherd himself that is understood here as the provider of fodder and such, since no other agent is mentioned. Furthermore, while maintaining compassion toward all living beings, and bowing to Durgā, the presiding deity of the mantra, and to the Guru, who is the sun to the darkness of ignorance. (KrdC 5.3)
Performing his own duty while remaining within the system of social classes and stages of life,

he should recite the mantra three times at the time of bathing and sprinkle himself; likewise, when sipping water for ritual purification (ācamana), he should do so after it has been consecrated by reciting the mantra as many times as there are principles (tattvas).
And while eating food, [one should consume] water and so forth over which the mantra has been recited seven times.

The meaning is: performing one's own duty as prescribed for one's caste and stage of life—that is, performing each specific action ordained for whichever caste (such as Brāhmaṇa and so forth) or whichever stage of life (such as studenthood and so forth) one occupies;
and at the appropriate time, one should sprinkle oneself three times with water over which mantras have been recited, having had them recited as many times as there are principles (tattvas).
Having consecrated the water thirty-two times or twenty-five times, he sips it while eating his food in this very manner.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is one for whom collyrium and the like—where "and the like" includes perfumes, garlands, and so forth—have been consecrated seven times.
In some places, the reading is "añjanādya" (beginning with collyrium).
He states the place for recitation (japa): on a mountain peak, on the bank of a river, at the root of a bilva tree,
in water reaching the heart, in a cow-pen, or in the temple of Viṣṇu.
Seated individually in these places— beneath an aśvattha tree and also on the shore of the ocean— Krd_5.5.
One should recite the excellent ten-syllable mantra four times ten thousand times, separately and in sequence;
if it is the eighteen-syllable mantra, the prescribed number is two times ten thousand. Krd 5.6.

Seated at eight locations— on a mountain peak, on a riverbank, in a place near a *bilva* tree, in water reaching the heart, in a cow-pen, in a house containing an image of Viṣṇu, in a place near a *pippala* tree, and on the shore of the ocean—
one should perform the ten-syllable mantra separately at each location, four times ten thousand times (*ayuta*) for each, in successive order.
When the eighteen-syllable mantra is to be recited, it is said that one should perform twenty thousand recitations; this is the number of recitations prescribed here.

It is not that there is a recitation of four *ayutas* at one location and two *ayutas* at another; rather, it must be recited in such a way that by means of that recitation, the total number becomes exactly that amount everywhere. Otherwise, if one were to recite at eight locations, there would be sixteen *ayutas* of recitations for the eighteen-syllable mantra.
In the *Prapañcasāra* it is also stated: "The recitation (japa) should extend up to twice ten thousand.
Although this number applies to the eighteen-syllable mantra, Rudradhara maintains that by the same logic, this very rule also applies to the ten-syllable mantra.
Regarding the aforementioned locations, he states the rule for food in successive order:

one who does not give [food] while staying at different locations in sequence— such as on a mountain peak and so forth— should subsist on vegetables, roots, fruits, curd produced from cow's udders, alms-food, grain-meal, and milk-rice.

And if one is unable [to perform all these], I have here described for them a preliminary method of service; once this is completed, the lord of practitioners should again recite [the mantra] according to the rule for the sake of accomplishment.
On specific locations such as mountain peaks and the like—the aforementioned mountain summits and so forth—one should, in due order, consume respectively:
leafy vegetables such as *vāstuka* and others; roots such as *śūraṇa* and others; fruits such as mangoes and others; milk produced from the udder of a cow and curds (as a copulative compound);
alms-food, which is food obtained from begging; and excellent winter rice that has not been steamed.
"One should perform the recitation while consuming barley-meal (saktu), roasted barley flour, milk-rice (pāyasa), or other food in moderation.
Desiring the accomplishment of the mantra, one should eat only recommended food; therefore, a person should always strive to eat only such recommended food. Thus it is said.
Regarding one who is incapable, he says: "one.

In the case of incapacity, among these eight locations beginning with a mountain peak, one should resort to a single location; and among the eight kinds of food beginning with vegetables, one should resort to a single meal and perform the recitation (*japa*).
This has been stated in the *Nāradīya*:
The practitioner should indeed take light food that is soft, lukewarm, and well-cooked;
he should eat in such a way that there is no increase in the [power of the] senses.
Whatever it may be, even that must be abandoned, as well as association with the wicked.

In this treatise, the procedure for preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*) has been declared and explained by me. When this is completed—that is, when the *puraścaraṇa* recitation is finished—one should recite again for the sake of accomplishment, for the sake of attaining the specific fruit, according to the rule, in the manner previously stated.
Here, some say that once this rite of commencing the preliminary service is finished and concluded, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* recitation once more.
Thus they say. (KrdC 5.7)
At the conclusion of the daily bodily worship, at the beginning of each day,
one should worship Kṛṣṇa in a secluded place, having adopted whichever procedure is prescribed in the teachings on initiation.
Seated at home, he eats the remains of the sacrificial offerings.

At the conclusion of the worship of the body—that is, at the end of the bodily worship—every day, at the beginning of the day in the morning, one should worship Kṛṣṇa by resorting to one or another of the paths mentioned in the initiation manuals, such as the sixteen or five services (*upacāra*). There is a distinction in the paths according to the distinction in the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇa*). Of what sort [is the worshipper]? Seated—that is, sitting—in a secluded house, a solitary place.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is an eater of the remnants of the oblation (huta-śiṣṭa-bhojī), that is, one who eats what remains after the daily recitation and the fire-offering consisting of one-tenth of that recitation.

Rudradhara states that there is also another method of *puraścaraṇa* for a great result, namely "ten lakhs. However, we observe that [the author] is here stating the *puraścaraṇa* as it was originally described.

Having recited the ten-syllable mantra one million times— which bestows imperishable fruit— one of disciplined intellect should perform oblations with fresh offerings saturated with jaggery, clarified butter, and honey.
One should offer ten thousand oblations into the fire with red lotuses.

The practitioner of pure intellect, having recited the ten-syllable mantra—which bestows imperishable fruit and the fruit of liberation—one million times, should offer oblations one hundred thousand times with reddish lotuses (aruṇāmbuja) into the consecrated fire; with what kind? With those soaked in molasses, ghee, and honey—that is, combined with molasses, clarified butter, and honey. (KrdC 5.9)

If the mantra consists of a pair of vowels, one who possesses a pure mind should recite it five hundred thousand times and perform oblations according to the prescribed method for half a hundred thousand; in the absence of lotuses, he should offer milk-rice.
One should perform the rite of homa with these very substances, together with ghee and sugar.
The "pair of hollows" (*śuṣira-yugala*) refers to the pair of two hollows—that is, two cavities or apertures—consisting of the number nine; one should mutter [the mantra] of eighteen syllables.

Then, one should mutter five hundred thousand [times] according to the stated procedure and the previously mentioned sequence, and one should perform oblations for fifty thousand [times]. Regarding the availability of other substances when the prescribed homa-substances are not obtained, he says "amalāmatiḥ," meaning one of pure intellect, [should offer] lotuses (*ambujānām*).
In the event that lotuses are unavailable or cannot be obtained, one should commence the fire-oblation (*homa*) with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), that is, with the finest rice-milk.
With what kind? "Accompanied by ghee and white [sugar]"—the meaning is: those [offerings] accompanied by ghee and sugar.

It should be understood that in all cases, the fire-oblation and worship conclude with the word *svāhā*. Furthermore, the method for performing the fire-oblation and other rites is to be understood from my own manual, the *Homānuṣṭhānapaddhati*.
As stated in the Nāradīya:

"The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed daily with a tenth part of the recitation (japa); or else, the wise man should perform the oblation until one hundred thousand [recitations] are completed. (KrdC_5.10)
Regarding one who is unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), he says:

"For those unable to perform the oblation, the recitation (japa) should be performed multiplied by eight, fourteen, or twenty-one; so say others concerning the twice-born, the kṣatriyas, and the vaiśyas."

If their recitation here is accompanied by fire-offerings, it is indeed equal; however, that which was prescribed for the social classes without fire-offerings is intended for those whose vision is unsteady.

Others, however, say that for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who are unable to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) due to the lack of materials and other necessities, the recitation (*japa*) should be performed according to their respective order, multiplied by these factors: four *nigamas* (Vedas), six *rasas* (flavors), and eight lords of serpents (*nāgendras*).
Regarding this, Rudradhara maintains that the recitation itself is already multiplied by these factors.
In reality, however—
when unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), the twice-born should perform recitation (japa) four times the number of oblations;
or six times, or eight times, according to their respective order.
Thus, we consider that which is stated in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā* alone to be appropriate:
"For Brahmins who are unable to perform the rite of fire-offerings (*homa*), the recitation (*japa*) is doubled;
for the other castes, however, it is ordained to be tripled."
In view of their opinion, it is said that "another [method] exists.

According to their view, the accomplishment of the *puraścaraṇa* occurs through the recitation (*japa*) itself—doubled from the root number—without the performance of libations (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth, because it is stated thus in another text. If the recitation for these castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, is accompanied by fire-oblations (*homa*), then for all three [castes], the count of forty thousand (*ayuta-catuṣṭaya*) and so on remains the same; whereas the recitation described as being without oblations applies equally to the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
Regarding this, Bhairava Tripāṭhin maintains that the fourfold recitation devoid of fire-oblation is prescribed for his wives who have unsteady gazes. *Kṛtyakalpataru* 5.11.

Sanātana: For Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who are incapable of performing the fire-oblation (homa), the recitation (japa) should be performed multiplied by these factors respectively: four according to the Vedas (nigama), six according to the tastes (rasa), and eight according to the lords of the serpents (nāgendra).

The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "alternatively. Another [teacher] says that this ritual of oblation (*homa-karman*) is indeed difficult to understand. He speaks thus with reference to the Śūdra:

Whatever social class a Śūdra may belong to, he too, full of faith and with his body bowed down by the weight of devotion, should perform the recitation according to the prescribed rule for those women with arched brows.

Among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, whichever caste a Śūdra has taken refuge in, he should perform the prescribed recitation (*japa*)—ordained for the women of those very twice-born (*dvijāti*) and other classes—in accordance with the rules, that is, in the manner described;
what kind of person? One endowed with faith (*śraddhā-yuta*).
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is one whose body (tanu) is bowed down by the weight of devotion—that is, by an excess of devotion.
And Rudradhara maintains that this recitation (japa) is devoid of fire-offerings (homa). (KrdC 5.12)
Regarding the duties following the *puraścaraṇa*, he says:

"Having been consecrated again by the Guru according to the rule, and having bestowed a sacrificial fee upon him, one should, endowed with devotion, feed the Brahmins and satisfy them with riches. (Krd 5.13)

Furthermore, having been consecrated again by the guru according to the prescribed rite as previously described, and having performed the consecration, he should bestow a sacrificial fee upon that guru; having fed the Brahmins and provided them with food, being filled with devotion, he should satisfy them and bring them joy with wealth, grain, and other such gifts. // KrdC_5.13 //
He states the function of the perfected mantra:
"Having thus accomplished either one of the two excellent mantras through recitation and so forth, with an unwavering mind..."
Then, with unwearied intellect, one should recite [the name] of Mukunda daily according to the rule throughout the three sessions of the day.

In this manner, having thoroughly accomplished— by means of recitation, worship, fire-oblation, libations, and so forth— one of the two mantras from among the pair, he whose intellect (*dhī*) is fixed on Acyuta, namely Śrī Kṛṣṇa, becomes one of steady mind.

Alternatively, he whose intellect is unshakable— that is, not fallen away from Viṣṇu— should, with a steady mind, that is, a pure mind, worship Mukunda, Kṛṣṇa, according to the prescribed method every day during the three libations, namely the three junctions of dawn and so forth. (KrdC 5.14)
Regarding the worship, he describes the morning meditation:
Now, within a pavilion shimmering with jewels that illuminate a golden ground, situated in a magnificent grove;
Seated upon a lotus throne situated on a radiant jeweled ground beneath a shimmering wish-fulfilling tree.

This is a *kulaka* consisting of seven verses. Immediately thereafter, being bowed down by devotion— his body bent low through the intensity of his devotion— he meditated upon Kṛṣṇa in the form previously described at daybreak (*prage*), and [worshipped] His limbs, such as the head and the thunderbolt, which were mentioned earlier.

Having worshipped the heart and other limbs, as well as the ten guardians of the directions beginning with Indra and their weapons beginning with the thunderbolt, the practitioner should gratify that Kṛṣṇa with white sugar, *mocā* (a specific variety of plantain), fresh butter (*haiyaṅgavīna*),
and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with curd— boiled milk combined with curds— using these together.

Of what kind? It was surrounded—encircled—by a glorious (*śrīmat*), beautiful garden or pleasure grove; and within that golden ground (*dhaima-sthala*), a shining floor of radiant gold, there was a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) resplendent with various jewels emitting rays of light, and [the Lord] was shining brilliantly in the midst of it.
Seated upon a lotus throne— that very lotus situated there, presiding over a jeweled abode from which light radiates beneath the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa). // KrdC_5.15 //
With the luster of a great sapphire, appearing exceedingly youthful, with hair falling over his face that is as glossy as molasses,
like a full-blown lotus surrounded by a swarm of bees.
With a face slightly smiling and glorious lotus-blue eyes.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It is dark blue, having a luster like that of a great sapphire (mahānīla) or an indranīla;
thus it is a dark-blue hue.
Furthermore, he is extremely young, about five years of age.
Moreover, his curls are crooked, glossy, and smooth; they hang down over the ears and cheeks, disheveled and tangled.
According to the reading *vaktrānte*, it refers to one whose hair hangs down, trailing from the face.

One whose face is as charming and beautiful as a blossomed lotus that is agitated, restless, or pervaded by a swarm (*ali-vrāta*) of bees; furthermore, how is he? One whose eyes resemble a glorious (*śrīmat*), faultless blue lotus (*indīvara*). // KrdC_5.16 //
Furthermore, of what kind?
With cheeks blooming and shimmering with moving earrings, with a beautiful forehead, with lovely red lips, and with a face of gentle smiles.
He bears a *pauṇḍarīka* nail that shines with throat ornaments sparkling with many rays of light from gems.
One whose cheeks are elevated, radiant, beautiful, fully blossomed, and opened by those two swinging earrings;
furthermore, one whose nose is beautiful;
and furthermore, one whose lower lip is very red and crimson.
Furthermore, he whose face was endowed with a beautiful smile—a slight laugh—and who was radiant with a neck-ornament shimmering with the rays and beams of many gems such as sapphires and others;
furthermore, he who bore and wore the claws of a *pauṇḍarīka* tiger. (KrdC 5.17)
Furthermore, of what kind was he?
His chest was grey with the dust from the cows,
his limbs were well-nourished, and he shone with ornaments of gold.
And upon the region of her hips and the pair of her beautiful calves,
it was bound with a cord of tinkling networks of small bells.
Whose chest was dusted—made greyish-white—by the dust of cows and the powder from cow-hairs; whose limbs were well-nourished from following after the cattle;
of what kind? Resplendent with ornaments fashioned from gold, shining like a checkerboard (aṣṭāpada);
and again, of what kind?

It was bound and fastened upon the region of the hips and the slope of the loins, at the pair of beautiful shanks, and above the two charming ankles, by means of a network of tinkling bells— a garland consisting of a multitude of small, resonant bells.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
