He is smiling, with the sublime splendor of his lotus-like hands and feet surpassing the luster of the blossoming *bandhūka* flower of living beings.
Holding milk-rice in his right hand and fresh, pure *haiyaṅgavīna* butter in his left.
With the magnificent splendor of his lotus-like hands and feet—the vast beauty of his palms and soles—he mocks the radiant glow of the bandhujīva flower while smiling.
Furthermore, what is he like?
In his right hand he holds *pāyasa* (milk-rice), and in his left hand he holds fresh, pure, stainless *haiyaṅgavīna*—that is, butter produced from yesterday’s milking of cows.
Holding [it]. // KrdC_5.19 //
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is one who has set out to slay the hosts of enemies who have become a burden to the earth, such as Aghāsura, Pūtanā, and others.
The Lord, who is surrounded by a multitude of cowherds, cowherd girls, and cows,
and who is worshipped by the hosts of gods led by Indra.

He is engaged in slaying those who have become a burden to the earth—the hosts of enemies, the multitudes of daityas who constitute the earth's burden, and the likes of Śakaṭāsura, beginning with Anaḥpūtanā.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is the Lord (prabhu), the capable Sovereign (īśvara).
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It is surrounded (vītam), that is, encircled, by a multitude of gopikās— cowherd women— and gopas— cows.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is one that has been saluted by Indra and the other hosts of gods.
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa at dawn and recollected Him with devotion, bowing low with His limbs, the lordly vajras, and so forth, [he should offer] white sugar, moca fruit, fresh butter, and curd.
One should satisfy him with milk that has been mixed [with other substances].

Although explained in the previous verse, it is explained here again for the sake of following the sequence: having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa at dawn (prage), that is, at the time of daybreak, in the manner described, and having worshipped Him with ritual offerings (upacāra)—worshipping Him together with the limbs and the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas)—one should present the food offering (naivedya). He states the materials for the food offering as follows: "white," and so forth.
White sugar, the plantain (mocā-kadalī), fresh butter (haiyaṅgavīna), and milk-rice (pāyasa) with milk.
He states the fruit of the morning libation worship:
"The man who, endowed with constant faith, worships Acyuta every day at the very dawn..."
One shall obtain complete prosperity here in this world without delay, and after death, one shall attain the pure, supreme abode.

In this manner, that man who, being endowed with faith, worships Acyuta every day at all times, especially in the morning— he certainly honors Him alone; he obtains and attains complete and perfect prosperity in this world in a very short time, and after departing from the body, he reaches the supreme, pure [state].
The meaning is that there shall be the great splendor called Brahman; he attains it, becoming of the same nature as it. // KrdC_5.22 //
He shows that the food offering (*naivedya*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) belong specifically to the morning worship: "Having worshipped Śauri every day at the beginning of the day,
one should then offer [the food] with curd or with water mixed with jaggery."
Having offered libations into the mouth of the Illustrious One with that same intent,
one should then recite it a thousand times, plus eight more, with devotion.

Alternatively, according to the previously mentioned method— that the word "atha" serves to complete the meter— one should daily, at the beginning of the day (prātaḥkāla), worship Śauri Kṛṣṇa; having offered an oblation (naivedya) of curd mixed with jaggery, one should then thoroughly satiate the mouth of the glorious Kṛṣṇa with water while perceiving it as being mixed with jaggery, and thereafter [recite] that mantra.
With reverence, one should recite it eight times, or a thousand times, or one thousand and eight times.
He describes the meditation for the midday libation:
At midday, one should meditate upon the Lord, whose form is distinguished by the rules of recitation, and who is worthy of worship by the hosts of chief gods, sages, ascetics, and celestial beings.
Surrounded by multitudes of cows, cowherds, and cowherd women,
his well-formed and enchanting body possessed the luster of a dense rain cloud.

The construction is with the action situated in the fourth verse: "In this manner, having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, who is born of Nanda, at midday—that is, at noon—one should worship Him for the sake of attaining Indirā, that is, Śrī.
Of what kind? One whose form is distinguished by the procedure of recitation (*japa-vidhāna*); that is, the meditation intended for the purpose of recitation.
Now, as for the phrase 'with manifest fragrance' and so forth, the Tripāṭhins maintain that the very meditation described in the third chapter applies here as well."
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is venerable and supreme.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?

It was surrounded—enveloped—by hosts and multitudes of the foremost and most excellent among the gods such as Indra, the sages such as Nārada, the ascetics such as Sanaka, and the sky-dwellers who reside in heaven; likewise, it was surrounded by groups and assemblies of cows, cowherds, and cowherd women; and its splendor was like that of a thick, dense cloud.
Moreover, his limbs are well-formed and free from defects; moreover, they are captivating, causing a festival for the eyes. (KrdC 5.24)
Furthermore, of what kind?
One whose beautiful braided hair is adorned with an ornament fashioned from peacock feathers, whose eyelashes are radiant, and who has eyes like lotuses.
His face is like the full moon and a bindu; his cheeks possess the beauty of jeweled earrings;
he has a beautiful nose and a most lovely, gentle smile.

This belongs to a peacock, thus it is *māyūra* (peacock); a leaf or wing is *patra*; and that which is both *māyūra* and *patra* is *māyūra-patra*. A crest (*vataṃsa*) is an ornament for the head that is decorated with that [feather]. According to the rule "Bhāguri desires the elision of the vowel *a* after the prefixes *ava* and *api*," there is the elision of the letter *a*. [The compound refers to] one whose beautiful braided hair (*dhammilla*), a mass of locks, possesses that [crest].
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He whose eyes are like an ambuja, that is, like a lotus (padma), is such; him [the Lord].
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He whose face—that is, his mouth—is like the orb of the moon, which is a full lunar disc;
furthermore, how is he?
He whose cheeks are endowed with beauty, being accompanied by the splendor of earrings made of jewels.
Furthermore, of what kind is he?
One whose nose is beautiful. Furthermore, of what kind is he?
Accompanied by a slight smile from the charming one.
Furthermore, of what kind is he?
He is clad in yellow garments, his limbs radiant with beautiful anklets, necklaces, waist-bands, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments.
His body was anointed with divine unguents, his forehead shone with a golden streak,
and he wore a variegated, unfading forest garland that seemed to blaze with the fire of the god of love.
One whose garment is yellow;
furthermore, of what kind?

One whose limbs are adorned with captivating anklets and so forth; [the list includes] a necklace (hāra), a string of pearls (muktāvalī), a girdle (kāñcī), small bells (kṣudra-ghaṇṭikā), an armlet (keyūra), a bracelet (aṅgada), a ring (ūrmi), a signet ring (mudrikā), a bangle (kaṭaka), a wristlet (kaṅkaṇa), and by the word "and so forth" (ādi-padena) [other ornaments are implied].
She is adorned with a crown and other ornaments;
furthermore, what is she like?
She shines upon her shoulder—that is, her shoulder—tawny-colored, dyed with divine unguents such as saffron and the like.
He who possesses a forest garland (*vanamālā*) made of leaves and flowers that is beautiful, unfading, untiring, variegated, of various kinds, and hanging down from his feet;
furthermore, of what nature is he?
Radiant like the bodiless one, Kāma. (KrdC 5.26)
Furthermore, of what sort?
Blowing a flute, or else holding it in his right hand, with a sacrificial staff in his left, and possessing a noble appearance.
Having thus meditated upon the Son of Nanda holding in his right hand a supreme jewel capable of granting desired boons, one should worship him for the attainment of prosperity.
Blowing and playing the flute;

or else, in another alternative, holding in his left hand—that which is other than the right—the staff for protecting cattle, and likewise holding in his right hand a jewel skilled in granting desired boons.
Furthermore, of what kind is he?
"Of noble appearance" or "of formidable appearance"—so says Rudradhara.
In reality, however, it shows him playing the flute; this is indicated by the word "then" (*atha*), referring to the left hand as the "left" (*savya*) and the right as the "right" (*dakṣiṇa*).

Because of this description, there is a synthesis of both [deities] here through the *tantra* method: therein, he holds in his left hand—the second from the left—a tethering post for bound souls (*paśu-yaṣṭi*), an axe for the sake of liberation, and likewise a staff; and in his right hand—the second from the right—he holds an excellent jewel, the most sublime gem, the *cintāmaṇi*.
Of what sort? It means a most excellent jewel, capable of granting desired gifts—that is, competent to bestow whatever object is wished for. (KrdC 5.27)
He describes the manner of offering the *āvaraṇa* (enclosure deities) and the *naivedya* (food offering):

"Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual with the noose and other [mudrās], the consorts of the limbs, the feet of the friends, the lord of serpents (*indra*), the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and so forth."
And having presented the various kinds of offerings prescribed by the rules for initiation,
let him duly offer them in an excellent golden vessel.
That which has Dāma as its first; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), Sudāma and others are included.

The limbs are the five previously mentioned; the beloveds are Rukmiṇī and others; the friends are Vasudeva and others; the trees are Mandara and others; the ten guardians of the directions are Indra and others as previously mentioned; and their weapons are the thunderbolt (vajra) and so forth.

Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa according to the previously mentioned [rites], in the manner and according to the method described, one should offer the collection of food-oblations (naivedya) as stated in the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā-vidhāna), into an excellent golden vessel made of gold; thus he describes the fire-offering (homa) and so forth.
Then one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with milk-rice mixed with ghee and well-refined sugar;
and one should present the *bali* offering in the directions of one's own [preceptor], the celestial sages (*surarṣis*), and the yogis.
With an uplifted mind, [he offers] to the hosts of deities belonging to the [respective] classes.

Immediately thereafter, one should perform a hundred and eight oblations (*homa*), offering milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with ghee and well-refined sugar, combined with exceedingly pure sugar. By virtue of association and for the sake of simplicity in ritual procedure, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the groups of deities presided over by the gods, sages, and yogis in their respective directions using the very same materials prescribed for the *homa*.
Among them, the gods beginning with Virañci (Brahmā) are stationed in the eastern direction, and the sages beginning with Nārada are stationed in the southern direction.

The group of yogis beginning with Sanaka and others reside in the western direction; the groups of secondary deities (upadeva-gaṇas)—namely the yakṣas, siddhas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and so forth—reside in the northern direction, according to Tripāṭhin.
Rudradhara, however, maintains that the groups of secondary deities are the guardians of the ten directions (daśa-dik-pālās).
"Udagra-cetas" means one whose mind is exalted, that is to say, one who possesses enthusiasm.
At the conclusion of the worship, having satiated his mouth with water while perceiving it to be milk-rice mixed with fresh butter,
the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] one thousand times, or even one hundred and eight times.

At the end of the worship, at the conclusion of the ritual, the practitioner (mantrī), having offered libations with water while perceiving it as the milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with fresh butter that was [offered] into the mouth of that deity, should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times.
He states the fruit of this:
"That foremost of men who would daily worship with devotion that Beloved of the cowherd girls at midday [attains this fruit]."
All the gods constantly pay homage to him;
indeed, all the worlds would abide under his authority.

One should always, at all times, with devotion and a sattvic disposition, worship that beloved of the cowherd girls, the lover of the gopīs, who is the foremost among men, the best of men, at midday during the middle of the day.
All the gods pay homage to that best of men;
likewise, forever and at all times, all people would abide under his control—that is to say, they would become subject to him. (KrdC 5.31)
Endowed with intelligence, long life, fortune, beauty, and good luck,
he shall be enriched by sons, friends, cattle, land, jewels, grain,
and many other enjoyments.
That abode, called the Immutable (acyuta), is ever greater and more vast.
Likewise, in this world, *medhā* is intelligence endowed with retentive power; *āyus* is life; *śrī* is prosperity;
and *kānti* is the beauty of the body.
Good fortune is being beloved by all people.
Endowed with these—that is, connected with them—as well as with legitimate sons, friends, and well-wishers; and with cows, the earth, jewels, and grain such as rice;
and further enriched and augmented by these and other abundant pleasures, he becomes at the end of the body one whose nature is that very splendor and majesty known as Acyuta, named Kṛṣṇa.
The meaning [is as follows]. (KrdC 5.32)
He states the arrangement for the third-period worship:
"Regarding the third-period worship, there is a distinction of time;
some wise ones say here that it may be either in the evening or at night. (Krd 5.33)

Regarding the third time of worship, there is a conceptual distinction concerning the specific hour; he states that very point: "in the evening, at twilight, or during the night. On this matter, some learned ones say: "If [the mantra] consists of ten syllables, it should be performed at night; if it consists of eighteen syllables, it should be performed in the evening."
"Others have declared that one should perform both [types of rites] by means of both [methods]. (KRD 5.34)

If the worship and so forth are performed with the ten-syllable mantra, then [it is done] at night; if they are performed with the eighteen-syllable mantra, then [it is done] in the evening—this is the opinion of some. Others, however, say that one should perform both types of worship with both mantras, namely the ten-syllable and the eighteen-syllable; thus, the sense is that there is an optional choice. // KrdC_5.34 //
"At eventide," and so forth.
Here, the section ending with the ninth verse forms a *kulaka*.
At eventide, in Dvāravatī, which was adorned with wonderful gardens...
It is completely surrounded by dwellings numbering sixteen thousand.
In that supreme dwelling, surrounded by lakes of pure water filled with lotuses and water-lilies, and teeming with swans and cranes.
In a pavilion of jewels, illuminated by the radiance of rising lamps,
Hari sat comfortably on a golden lotus throne with a soft cushion.
Surrounded by Nārada and others for the sake of determining the true nature of the Self,
he was bestowing upon those sages his own abode, the supreme and imperishable.
In the evening, one should meditate upon and worship Hari wearing such an attire as this.

Of what sort? Seated—that is, sitting—upon a golden lotus throne, which has the form of a soft seat with a gentle cushion; situated where? In a pavilion of jewels; of what kind? [It is] distinguished by... [as follows].
In that [palace] which possesses a splendor equal to the light of the sun, which rises as a radiant illuminator; where? In the most excellent abode, the best of houses; what is it distinguished by?
Adorned with colorful gardens and frequented by many groves—
furthermore, characterized by what?— it was situated in Dvāravatī.
Furthermore, what is it qualified by?
It is surrounded by palaces, that is, houses;
of what kind? Numbering two times eight thousand (sixteen thousand).
Furthermore, by what is it distinguished? It is surrounded by lakes (*saras*), that is, by ponds.
Of what kind are they? By those possessing pure water (*amala-ambhas*), that is, by those with stainless waters.
Furthermore, of what kind?
"Filled with swans and cranes," meaning pervaded by flocks of birds such as swans and the like.
Furthermore, of what kind?
With lotuses and water-lilies—meaning together with red and blue lotuses—and surrounded by sages such as Nārada; of what kind [is Hari]? He is encircled by these sages.
For what purpose? For the sake of determining the reality of the Self—that is, for the purpose of ascertaining the true nature of the Self.
Furthermore, of what kind [was He]?
Speaking of His own abode—His very self whose nature is knowledge—to Nārada and the others.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is devoid of supreme ignorance and its effects.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
The syllable is indestructible.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
Resembling a blue lotus, gentle, with eyes as large and red as lotus petals,
radiant with a crown and tiara interspersed with glossy locks of hair.
Resembling an *indīvara*, like a blue lotus, and gentle, meaning devoid of ferocity;
furthermore, of what nature? One whose eyes (*īkṣaṇe*) are long and wide like the petals of a lotus.
Furthermore, it is radiant and brilliantly shining with a *kirīṭa* and a *mukuṭa* that are joined together by glossy, smooth locks of hair (*kuntala*).
In this context, by the word *kirīṭa*, a specific ornament consisting of three prongs resting on the forehead is meant;
and by the word *mukuṭa*, a specific ornament shaped like a flame of a lamp resting on the central part of the head is meant. (KrdC 5.39)
Furthermore, of what sort is he?
He has a beautiful and serene face, shimmering makara-shaped earrings,
the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, the radiant Kaustubha gem, and a garland of forest flowers.
One whose face is beautiful, captivating, serene, and bestowing of fruit; furthermore, one whose two earrings, shaped like sea-monsters (*makara*), are shimmering and resplendent;
and furthermore, one who has the *śrīvatsa*—a particular mark produced by the blow of a brahmin’s foot—upon his chest.
Furthermore, he is the one who possesses the *kaustubha*, a particular gem that is radiant and shining intensely;
furthermore, he is the wearer of the forest garland (*vanamālā*).
With a chest like that of a Kashmiri antelope, clad in yellow silk garments,
and adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, girdles, and other ornaments.
One whose chest has the color of saffron from Kashmir;
furthermore, one who wears yellow garments;
furthermore, one adorned with a *hāra* (a pearl necklace), a *keyūra* (an armlet), and *bāhv-alaṅkāra* (arm ornaments).

A bracelet (*kaṭaka*) is a ring (*kaṅkaṇa*). A girdle (*rasanā*) consists of small bells; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), items such as finger-rings are included. Adorned (*pariṣkṛta*) means beautified by these. (KrdC 5.41)
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He has removed the immense burden of the earth, his mind is joyful,
and his four arms shine with the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
He by whom the immense burden—characterized by asuras and other such beings—of the Viśvambharā (the Earth) has been removed and taken away;
him whose mind is again gladdened and joyful;
and him whose four arms are adorned with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. (KṛdC 5.42)
Having meditated thus, the practitioner of mantra should worship the first enclosure with the [mantra] limbs;
he should worship the second with the principal consorts, and the third he should worship likewise.
He saw Nārada, Parvata, Jiṣṇu, Niśaṭha, Uddhava, Dāruka,
Viṣvaksena, Saineya, and the son of Vinatā at the forefront in the various directions.
In this worship, the first enclosure consists of the five previously mentioned limbs (*aṅga*).
The second enclosure consists of the queens, Rukmiṇī and the others.
In the third enclosure, one should worship Nārada and the others—who will be described—in the cardinal directions starting from the east, and in front, Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā.
Parvata was a particular sage;
Jiṣṇu is Arjuna;
Niśaṭha was a particular Yādava.
Uddhava was likewise [his minister]; Dāruka was Kṛṣṇa’s charioteer;
Viṣvaksena was the treasurer; and Saineya was Sātyaki.
"Then, with the Lokīśas and their weapons, one should again worship the two obstructions;
having thus worshipped according to the rule, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa). Kṛd 5.45.

The first enclosure consists of the world-protectors, Indra and the others; the second enclosure consists of their weapons, the thunderbolt and so forth. Having thus worshipped with the fivefold enclosure in this manner and sequence, one should duly offer the milk-rice (pāyasa) prescribed for initiation.
He shows the method of libation and the number of recitations:

"Having offered libations with water mixed with sugar-candy, perceiving it as milk, the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times while meditating upon Puruṣottama. (Kṛd 5.46)

The practitioner (mantrin), contemplating and meditating upon Puruṣottama, should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times after offering libations (tarpaṇa) with water, perceiving that milk mixed and combined with sugar-candy (khaṇḍa) as [the offering itself].

Although the suffix -ktvā in the word "tarpayitvā" indicates that the libation occurs prior [to the recitation], nevertheless, the recitation must first be performed and the libation thereafter; this is because such is the sequence according to the tradition (sampradāya).
Rudradhara. (KrdC 5.46)
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) during all worship ceremonies, or at midday;
having performed the rites from the seat up to the water-offering (arghya), the wise one should offer praise and bow down.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in all three types of worship.
He states an alternative: "or else" (athavā); the meaning is that one may perform the homa during the midday worship at noon.
"From the seat" means:
having performed everything from the mantra of the seat up to the *arghya* offering, and having offered praise—that is, having performed a hymn of praise—one should bow, prostrating like a staff.

Having set aside the final *arghya*, and having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the middle, one should then offer the remaining *arghya* of the worship, which is designated as the "final *arghya*" and has the synonym "the *arghya* for turning away. This is the meaning.
Having offered oneself and withdrawn that [deity] into the lotus-lake of one's own heart, and having placed it there, becoming one with it, one should worship oneself once again. (Kṛd 5.48)

Having offered oneself to the Supreme Lord with the mantra of self-surrender, one should withdraw that splendor of the Supreme Lord from the place of worship, transfer it into the lotus of one's own heart, become absorbed in that [divinity], and then worship oneself once again. KrdC 5.48.
He states the fruit of the evening worship:
"The man who always worships Vāsudeva in the evening, having attained all desires, goes at the end to the supreme goal. (Kṛd 5.49)

The man who, at evening, always and at all times worships Vāsudeva in the manner described— satisfying Him through worship, libations, fire-offerings, and so forth— attains all desired objects and, at the end of his body's life, reaches the supreme goal, which is union with Viṣṇu.
If at night one should worship the son of Devakī, whose mind is overcome by the god of love,
who is weary from the *rāsa* dance and situated in the midst of the circle of cowherd girls.

If the worship is performed at night, then one should worship the Son of Devakī, who is exhausted by the *rāsa*—a particular kind of play—and whose mind and heart are overcome by love (*manmatha*), and who stands in the midst of a circle (*maṇḍala*) of gopīs, which is a particular kind of assembly. (KrdC 5.50)
He demonstrates the *rāsa*-dance:
having fixed a peg into the ground that is broad, well-rounded, smooth, and one span high;
Having stepped upon one another with their feet, while clutching each other’s hands, this indeed is the circular dance of the rāsa assembly.
With their hands grasped one by another—that is, with their hands held by each other—they performed this *bhrama*, which is a circular dance, in the *rāsa* assembly.

Having done what? Having firmly planted in the earth (*kau*) a wooden peg (*śaṅku*) that was broad (*pṛthu*), thick (*sthūla*), well-rounded (*suvṛtta*) and circular in shape, smooth (*masṛṇa*) and glossy (*snigdha*), rising to the measure of a span (*vitasti-mātra*), and standing twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*) high.
Furthermore, having done what?
Having stepped upon the stake with both feet and restrained it. // KrdC_5.51 //
He speaks of meditation:
[The mind is filled] by the multitude of droplets from the waves, which carry the pollen of flowers growing on the land and in the water.
On the vast and stainless bank of the Yamunā, where the heat was removed by the Maruts, he took up residence.
This is a *kulaka* consisting of twelve verses.

Having meditated upon the unborn one whose essential nature consists of auspiciousness, one should worship him with effort according to the rules— that is, according to the prescribed ritual— in the excellent seat of worship (*pūjā-pīṭha*) previously mentioned in connection with initiation, specifically at the best of seats, on the bank of the Yamunā, where a multitude of women with hands joined together are engaged in the performance of the *rāsa* dance pastime.
In the course of a particular game devised by a group of women with their hands bound together, [the ball] was caught upon a jeweled peg situated in the midst of jeweled stakes.

On what kind of place? On a sandy bank (*pulina*) occupied and swept over by the wind. By what kind of wind? By one laden with the pollen of land-lotuses—that is, land-lotuses—meaning it was joined with the floral dust from flowers in close proximity to their filaments.

By this, its fragrance is described; furthermore, "laharī-taraṅga" refers to a mass of droplets—that is, a collection of drops—and by their abundance (bhareṇa), meaning with excellence, for the virtuous (satām).
According to Tripāṭhin, it means "endowed with the most eminent."
By this, coolness is expressed; furthermore, by the phrase "removing the heat" (*paritāpahṛtā*), which destroys exhaustion, languor is expressed. Moreover, of what kind is the sandbank?
Furthermore, in that which is vast, extensive, stainless, and pure.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is one agitated by hundreds of millions of women who have been mangled by sharp, bodiless arrows.
In which the expanse of the quarters was illuminated by the rays of the Lord of Stars, and swarms of female bees were wandering about.

In that place which is agitated and pervaded here and there by hundreds of millions of women who have been overwhelmed and distracted by his desire— which is bodiless— yet whose arrows are sharpened and keen;
and again, of what kind is it?
In that [place] where the expanse of the quarters— the spatial extent of the directions— is illuminated and made bright by the rays (karas) or beams of the Lord of Stars, namely the Moon;
furthermore, of what nature is it?
In that place where there is a swarm—that is, a multitude—of female bees wandering and roaming about.
Furthermore, of what kind [is it]?
By the Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Suras;
by the Gandharvas, Bhujaṅgamas, and Cāraṇakas.
Seated in well-constructed celestial palaces, accompanied by their wives, they remained composed while showering down heaps of exquisite flowers.

Just as the Vidyādharas and others are well known, so too is the *bhujaṅgama*—a serpent belonging to the world of Nāgas (*nāga-loka*) who possesses a body with hands, feet, and other limbs. By these [beings], accompanied by their wives and mounted upon beautiful celestial chariots (*vimāna*), the sky was filled with masses of showers of flowers they had released. KṛdC 5.54.
Furthermore, what is Kṛṣṇa like?
He is engaged in the performance of the rāsa-dance pastime, arranged by throngs of women whose hands are intertwined with one another.
Even Maṇiśaṅku,
having assumed his own divine body in many ways through this very form.
With this body—this physical form adorned with jeweled pegs—he manifested his own divine body in various ways.
Furthermore, of what nature was it?
It was situated between the two well-behaved women, with the pair of arms of his beloveds entwined around him.
For those whose bodies are joined with a multitude of horripilations, shining as their limbs are set ablaze by the fire of passion expanding through contact with their own [beloved].
Of the beautiful women, the two arms of each pair— interposed between the two [men] in a sequential manner of pairs—
were again such that their two arms were bound together by the group of beloveds, the multitude of women, being interlaced with one another by their own hands.

By this it is said of Him: among two lovers, the Supreme Lord has his hand grasped by the very hand of the beloveds; this is also understood through the conjunction [of the verse] as being appropriate even between the beloveds alone, who are situated upon the stake (śaṅku). Of what sort are they? They are those in whom the fire of the bodiless god (Anaṅga) is burgeoning—that is, blazing—through their own union, namely, through union with Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.

The fire of desire is ignited by that [embrace]; on that limb which is thus set ablaze and glowing, there shines—that is, is beautiful—the row of horripilation (pulakālī), a series of bristling hairs;
those who are joined with that are called "tadyujaḥ" (those possessed of it). KrdC 5.56.
Furthermore, of what kind?

[It is characterized] by groups of scales (*mūrcchanā*), rhythms (*tāla*), and musical measures (*gaṇa*), consisting of the seven notes (*svara-saptaka*) which are more pleasing due to being differentiated by various traditional melodies (*śruti*).
It was exceedingly beautiful with the tinkling of magnificent ornaments made of bright jewels as it wandered about with them.

Wandering together with these cowherd girls, causing them to whirl about— with what? With that group of seven notes (*svara-saptaka*) beginning with *niṣāda*, which is most charming and captivating to the heart, being diverse— that is, of various kinds— and distinct through its association with *śruti*, which is a specific sound consisting of the constituent parts that initiate names and vowels.
It is accompanied by twenty-one types of melodic modulations (*mūrcchanās*), such as *bhāgatāla*, *aśvatāla*, and *paritāla*, numbering forty-nine;
furthermore, by what kind [of sound]?
It is most beautiful and heart-pleasing due to the tinkling—the resonant sound—of the ornaments of a magnificent, highly lustrous gem that has been set upon it. //57//
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It has a body divided by jewels, appearing as if composed of refined gold.
Seated in the center of a large, radiant, red lotus, which is situated upon a central pivot fashioned from jewels.

Thus, with his body divided; in this manner, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, whose body was joined by the gopīs, resembled what? He was like an emerald gem set and strung together with jewels made of *tapanīya*, that is, gold.
Furthermore, of what nature was he?
It is situated in the center of that large, broad, and radiant red lotus which is fixed upon the central shaft fashioned from jewels.
Furthermore, of what kind is he?
His body has the luster of an *atasī* flower; he is youthful, with eyes like the petals of a fresh, reddish dawn lotus.
Her mass of hair was bound with peacock feathers shimmering with variegated clusters of fresh sprouts.
Whose body has a luster like the flowers of the *atasī* plant, which is well-known;
how else is he described?
He whose eyes resemble the petals of a fresh, reddish lotus.
Furthermore, of what sort is it?
It is one whose mass of hair is bound with peacock feathers, which are beautified by various clusters of blossoms and fresh sprouts. (KrdC 5.59)
Furthermore, of what sort?
With tremulous eyebrows, a face equal to the moon,
and a pair of cheeks adorned with jeweled earrings.
His lips were like the blood of a hare,
and he wore various ornaments with many kinds of excellent jewels.
With tremulous eyebrows— that is, possessing moving vine-like brows—
furthermore, of what nature?
With a face resembling the full moon of the bright fortnight.
Furthermore, of what kind? With both cheeks adorned by jeweled earrings. Furthermore, of what kind?
With lips like the blood of a rabbit;
furthermore, of what kind?
Adorned with various types of ornaments shining with jewels.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is a dwelling-place of exquisite grace, radiant with garments made of leaves, flowers, and foliage.
His palms and soles of the feet are like auspicious new coral,
and his body shines with a garland swarming with bees.
The *āsana* is a particular kind of tree; its *prasava* is its flower, and its *chedana* is its leaf. [He is the one] whose garment is similarly radiant, shining, and captivating.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is the locus of beautiful and variegated play.
Furthermore, of what sort is he?
He whose palms and soles of the feet are auspicious and captivating like fresh, new coral (*vidruma*).
Furthermore, of what sort is he?
He whose two arms are resplendent with a garland of flower-wreaths crowded with and pervaded by bees; or, he whose body is resplendent with such a garland.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
His chest is reddened by the saffron mingled from the embrace joined with the breasts of a young woman; his gait is like that of a bull.
[He saw] the sole teacher of the world, who was overwhelmed by passion and intent on singing as prompted by Śiva’s flute.
Whose chest was reddened by saffron from embracing the pair of breasts of young women;
furthermore, of what nature was he? He possessed the gait of a bull, the movement of a vṛṣabha.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is intent upon—that is, devoted to—that song which was produced and performed on a flute (veṇu), that is, a bamboo pipe, by Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
Agitated and rendered helpless by Smara, the god of love;
furthermore, of what nature was he?
The sole, peerless teacher of the three worlds.
One should worship, according to the rule, the formless and unborn [deity] in the most excellent seat first mentioned;
having first worshipped that, one should perform the ritual service of its limbs.
Then one should worship the couples that reside in the [six] flavors.

Thus, one should worship the formless, attribute-less [Reality] within the unborn Form in the most excellent seat—the seat fashioned by the previously mentioned deities—when [the deity] has first arisen.

He shows the enclosures (āvaraṇas): "First" means that having first fully worshipped the previously mentioned enclosure of limbs (aṅgāvaraṇa) as the function of those limbs, then immediately after that, the couples such as Keśava-Kīrti and others who are engaged in the *rāsa* dance, that is, those involved in the *rāsa*-play.

Upon the sixteen petals are the vowels together with the group of *ūti* syllables and their respective powers (*śakti*), situated in the supreme *rāsa* dance, along with Saramā, Madana, and his own digits (*kalā*).
Then [he offered] those called Mithuna, headed by Indrapavi.

On the sixteen petals—that is, the sixteen-leaved [lotus]—one should worship the pairs (mithuna). He explains this as "the group of forms arising from the vowels" (*svara-mūrti-gaṇa*); these are the sixteen forms beginning with Keśava, which arise from the vowels, that is, from the phonemes beginning with *a*.
Of what nature is this group of forms arising from the vowels?
It is "accompanied by the Śaktis," meaning it is joined with the Śaktis beginning with Kīrti.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is that which has gone to the supreme *rāsa* dance;
in some places, the reading is "gone to the northern *rāsa*" (*uttara-rāsa-gata*).
In that regard, one should worship the Supreme Lord in the central *rāsa* circle, and in the northern and other circles, one should worship Keśava and the others.
Furthermore, of what nature [is this]?
It is accompanied by these two: *Ramā*, which is the *Śrī*-seed syllable (*śrīṃ*), and *Madana*, which is the *Kāma*-seed syllable (*klīṃ*).
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is accompanied by its own sixteen digits (*kalās*), which are the sixteen vowels.
And the practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *Śrīṃ Klīṃ Aṃ Keśava-Kīrtibhyāṃ Namaḥ*, and so forth.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is called "the pair" (*mithunāhvam*), meaning it bears the name "pair.
Then, immediately thereafter, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the thunderbolt and the other [weapons], headed by Indra and the thunderbolt; this is the meaning. (KrdC 5.64)

Having thus properly worshipped Hari, who is encompassed by the four enclosures (āvṛtis), with a moistened mind, he describes the food offering (naivedya) preceded by the number of the aforementioned enclosures:
And let her serve him milk that is well-cooked and mixed with sugar, in a cup fashioned of silver.

Having thus properly worshipped this Hari, who is surrounded by the four enclosures, according to the prescribed ritual, a person endowed with faith [should offer] into a cup or vessel made of silver— that is, fashioned from silver— to this Hari [an offering] together with sugar and ghee (or, according to another reading, together with white [sugar]).
Let him offer well-boiled, fresh milk.
If available, having offered milk with sugar to the couples in sixteen separate bronze cups in successive order, one should proceed.
Then one should perform everything just as before.

If such prosperity exists when wealth is available, then one should offer milk with sugar, sequentially for each pair [of deities], into sixteen individual cups made of bell-metal; thereafter, one should complete the entire specific worship according to the manner previously described, beginning with the words, "I now offer before the Blessed One. // KrdC_5.66 //
He states the fruit of the Rāsa-pūjā: "The noble-minded person who, with a disciplined mind, daily performs this rite which enchants all the worlds at night— "
He indeed, being honored by the entire world,
attains incomparable glory and goes to the infinite.

He who, being noble-minded and serene of heart, regularly and without obstruction performs this ritual— the method of Rāsa-worship which enchants all worlds and brings all worlds under his control— every night, throughout every day, shall become worshiped by all the world and, having attained incomparable and transcendent prosperity and abundance, [attain] the infinite.
He goes to, that is, he attains Viṣṇu.
One should always worship Acyuta with devotion either at night or at the end of the day;
for both of these yield equal fruit.
He who desires to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra.

The man who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra should worship Acyuta with devotion either at night or at the end of the day during the twilight (saṃdhyā), for he should do so constantly, every single day. Since the two-fold worship—both at night and at the twilight—is equal in its fruit, for that reason the meaning is that one should worship either at night or at the end of the day. (KrdC 5.68)
He concludes what has been said:

"Thus, whoever worships at the three times the enemy of Madhu, who possesses a human form and whose abode is the daughter of the ocean, he [attains the fruit] of that very one who is beloved by all classes of living beings."
In their hands are the trees of Dharma, happiness, wealth, and liberation, longed for by the assembly of the virtuous;
from them flow the great essence of intense bliss, and they bear rows of excellent fruits.
In this manner, for that person who worships Madhusūdana— the embodiment of mantra— three times a day,

the four aims of human existence beginning with dharma become as if in the palm of his hand; such is the implication, for He is beloved by all multitudes of living beings, His abode is the daughter of the ocean (Lakṣmī), and He is the dwelling place of Lakṣmī herself.
Of what kind? They are those requested by the *satāṃ vargaḥ*, the assembly or multitude of the virtuous.

Regarding the reading *saṃsargibhiḥ*: although there is no fruit of liberation for those who merely associate with or remain near [the virtuous], nevertheless, by the word "liberation" (*mokṣa*), the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) which is the cause of that liberation is indicated. The rows of fruits of those trees are the eternally blissful Brahman.
They bestow the flowing nectar of the great essence of one's own true nature.
Now it is said that at the conclusion of the worship of those [deities] previously invoked, there is a ritual procedure for this Supreme Person;
furthermore, in rites for specific desires, there is also the ritual of libations (tarpaṇa).
Indeed, even without worship, those [who possess it] obtain that fruit.

Now, immediately following that, after the worship of the Supreme Person, Śrī Gopāla Kṛṣṇa, is concluded, the ritual procedure for the daily libations (nitya-tarpaṇa) previously mentioned— namely those described starting with "O fair-faced one"— is stated; this is also the method for optional libations (kāmya-tarpaṇa), by means of which one obtains the fruit of worship even without performing the formal worship itself, just as in the case of the worship.
In the same way, the libation (tarpaṇa) [is performed].
Having first satiated Acyuta there once with the *pīṭha*-mantras,
one should invoke him and worship him with all the water offerings and ritual gifts.

First, having gratified the deities who constitute the limbs of the pedestal (pīṭha)— beginning with the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) and so forth— once each with the mantras of the pedestal, one should thereafter invoke Acyuta upon that water-filled pedestal and worship him with water alone,
consisting of all the ritual services such as perfumes and the rest.

Then, having formed the *dhenu-mudrā* and prepared the liquid for libation with water, he should offer it as a libation with that [liquid] held in his cupped hands, which he should mentally transform into a golden goblet. (Kṛd 5.72)

Then, having formed the *dhenu-mudrā* and performed an abundant libation (*tarpaṇa*) with water, one should contemplate that water as being of the nature of those [offering] substances; with that perception—that is, with the perception of the specific substances prescribed for the libation—one should satisfy that Kṛṣṇa. With what kind of handful? The meaning is: with a handful conceived of as a golden goblet. (KrdC 5.72)
The number twenty-eight is prescribed for the libations performed at the three times of day;
furthermore, one should repeatedly satisfy the retinue as ordained for their own specific times.

Regarding the libations at the three times (*trikāla-tarpaṇa*)—that is, during the offerings made throughout the day—at one time, twenty-eight libations endowed with eight [qualities] are prescribed as the number for the libation. Furthermore, one should satisfy those retinues (*parivāra*), i.e., the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇa-devatā*), who are ordained for their own specific times—such as morning, midday, and so forth—once each, at their respective occasions. (KrdC 5.73)
Regarding the substances for the libation at the three times of day, he says:
"At dawn, curd mixed with jaggery; at midday, milk-rice with fresh butter; at the third time, milk with sugar-candy—these are the stated substances. (Krd 5.74)

Curd with jaggery at the morning time, milk-rice with fresh butter at midday, and milk with sugar-candy and its preparations at the third period—in this manner, the substance for satiation has been described. (KrdC 5.74)
He states the mantra for libation: "The word 'tarpayāmi' (I satisfy) should be joined at the end of the mantras with one's own names in the accusative case;
thereafter, one should complete the remainder of the worship. (Krd 5.75)

At the end of the mantra— that is, at the conclusion of the root mantra— one should append the word "tarpayāmi" (I satisfy) immediately after one's own names of the deities to be propitiated, which are placed in the locative case near those [mantras] and in forms such as "amuka-devatām" (the deity so-and-so). Thereafter, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
He states the subsequent duty:
Having sprinkled himself with the water from that [consecrated vessel], being purified, he should recite that [mantra];
then, having dismissed it, being absorbed in that [deity], he should mutter the mantra. (Kṛd 5.76)
Having sprinkled one's own body with those waters of grace—the waters used for the propitiation of the Supreme Lord—and having recited that mantra, one should drink the water.
Immediately thereafter, having dismissed that deity and merged him into one's own heart, being absorbed in Him, one should recite the mantra. (KṛdC 5.76)
He states the optional libation (tarpaṇa) together with its varieties and constituent substances: "Now, the substances for the optional libations will be described;
one should resort to one or another of those [substances] based on the prescribed rules. (Krd 5.77)
Immediately thereafter, those substances which have been described by Nārada and others for optional libations (tarpaṇas) shall be stated.
Following the aforementioned procedures and the procedures prescribed for the three times of day, one should perform the rite of optional libation by resorting to a single procedure.
One should satisfy this [deity] with sixteen substances, four times each;
and with devotion, one should satisfy Acyuta once with the four milk-products and so forth, ending with water and so forth.
One should satisfy this Śrī Kṛṣṇa with sixteen substances, four times each, using water alone while perceiving it as those specific substances.
Of what kind [of water]? That which has the four milks as its first;
the meaning is that there are four handfuls of milk at the beginning of the sixteen substances and four at the end.

The phrase "sakṛj-jalādy-antam" (ending with water once) is an adverbial modifier of the action. Thus, it results in this sequence: first once with water, then four times with milk, and then once again with water. (KrdC 5.78)

He states the sixteen substances as follows: "Milk-rice, curd-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, rice with jaggery, milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, plantain, banana, *rajasvalā*, coconut, sweetmeats, and cakes. (Krd 5.79)
In this context, sixteen substances including parched grain and fried rice are prescribed;
having offered these with heaps of white sugar from the end of the fried rice up until the final milk, Krd_5.80.
Pāyasa is milk-rice;
dādhika is food prepared with curd;
kṛsara is rice mixed with mung beans; gauḍānna is food cooked in molasses-water.

*Milk* (*payas*) is *dugdha*; *curd* (*dadhi*) is well known; *fresh butter* (*navanīta*), *clarified butter* (*ājya*), and *ghee* (*ghṛta*) are synonymous. *Kadalī* refers to the banana tree; *campā-kadalī*, *mocā*, and *svarṇa-kadalī* are specific varieties of the *kadalī*, while *rajasvalā* is also a particular species of *kadalī*. *Coca* is likewise a specific variety of *kadalī*. A *modaka* is a sweetmeat ball (*laḍḍuka*).
"Cake," "sweet roll," "flat cake" separately, and "with parched grain"—thus, including the parched grain, sixteen substances are described here in this text as "lāja.

After the parched grain libation (*lāja-tarpaṇa*) and before the final four milk libations, one should perform a single libation with heaps of white sugar (*sitopalā*), that is, masses of white granulated sugar, which have been transformed into water through meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*). He states the fruit of the aforementioned libation for the fulfillment of desires:
The man who, with undistracted mind, daily gratifies Hari at dawn by reciting this [mantra] seventy-four times,
shall possess all prosperity.
Situated in the hand, they are desired from the mandala.

In this manner, if a person, with single-minded devotion and an undistracted mind, should satisfy this Lord Hari, Kṛṣṇa, seventy-four times every day at dawn, then for that man— according to Tripāṭhin, within forty-nine days from the beginning of the maṇḍala,
or according to others, within forty-eight days— [the result follows].
The author of the *Laghudīpikā* states that [the result occurs] within thirty-five days;
Rudradhara says it is within thirty-five days.
Here, the desired and longed-for prosperities and all accomplishments (*siddhis*) come to rest in the palm of one's hand; there is no need to count heaps of white sugar-candy. (KrdC 5.81)
After the optional libation (kāmya-tarpaṇa), he says:
"With these nine—warm milk, boiled milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, rice cooked with milk, sugar-candy, honey, and nectar—one should perform the libation twelve times. (Krd 5.82)

*Dhāroṣṇa* is milk that has been produced at that very moment; *pakva-payaḥ* is boiled milk. These two—*dhāroṣṇa* and *pakva-payas*—as well as curd (*dadhi*), the well-known fresh butter (*navanīta*), clarified butter (*ghṛta*), *dauḥgdhānna* (rice cooked in milk), *pāyasa* (milk-rice), *matsyaṇḍī* (a specific kind of sugar), *sa-śarkara* (sugar with spoiled milk)—so says Tripāṭhin—and honey (*madhu*), the well-known nectar (*amṛta*): with these nine substances, one should satisfy [the deity] twelve times. (KrdC 5.82)
He states the fruit of this:
"This other rite of libation (tarpaṇa), numbering eight [times], has a result equal to that previously mentioned;
it is specifically prescribed for the performance of magical acts (kārmaṇa), for fame, and for winning over people. (Krd 5.83)
This method of libation (tarpaṇa) is distinct from the previously mentioned method of libation. Of what nature is it? It yields a fruit equal to the fruit of the previously described libation.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It consists of one hundred and eight [recitations]. Then, by means of nine substances, through twelve rounds of libation (*tarpaṇa*), the count becomes one hundred and eight.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?

It is specifically prescribed for the rite of *kārmaṇa*, the rite of subjugation (*vaśya-karaṇa*), as well as for fame, virtuous discourse, winning over people, bringing the world under control, or through being beloved by the world. (KrdC 5.83)
After the libation, he says:
"Having satisfied Mukunda with thoughts of [Him] possessing fragments, streams, and heat, even while traveling through cities and villages."
The minister shall obtain delicious food for himself and his servants,
as well as garments, grain, and wealth.

Even if he travels through cities and villages, a minister who offers water with sugar-candy, pieces of sugar, and warm milk to Mukunda will obtain delicious food along with his servants, as well as garments, grain, and wealth.
He demonstrates that the act of offering bestows all fruits and shows the ritual duties subsequent to the offering:
"As many times as the minister satisfies [the deity], for that same number of times he should mutter the mantra."
By means of libation alone, one should accomplish all tasks whatsoever.
One should accomplish all desired tasks in their entirety—even without worship or fire-offerings—by means of libation alone.
In this regard, for as many times as one performs the libation, for that many times one should recite the mantra. (KrdC 5.85)
He states another practice:
"The twice-born man who here subsists on alms, having himself become the son of Nanda day by day, wanders about begging while sporting with the beautiful-eyed cowherd women."
With his own minds made exceedingly playful through various modes of jesting,
he obtains abundant alms enriched with curds, milk, and clarified butter.

That twice-born member of the three higher castes whose means of livelihood is the practice of begging wanders here daily, day after day, having personally become the son of Nanda and contemplating himself in that form, to beg for alms.
What is he doing? He is doing so by means of his own most charming and exceedingly captivating methods of jesting and playful activities.
Sporting together with the minds of the cowherd women of beautiful appearance, the word *amā*—meaning "together with"—obtains abundant alms consisting of plenty of curds, milk, and ghee. (KrdC 5.86)

In the center and in all six corners of the fire-receptacle, one should draw Kāmadeva together with the person to be accomplished (sādhya) within the pericarp; the six syllables situated in the cavities [of the mantra] twice upon the filaments;
and the letters of the two nine-syllable mantras, preceded by Śakti and Śrī, upon the petals.
In the center, one should place the ten letters of the ten scripts and the syllable of the best of mantras, each within a lotus.

Having drawn a ten-petaled lotus, one should draw a hexagon—the abode of fire—within the pericarp (karṇikā). One should write [the mantra] in the middle of the pair of fire-abodes, that is, within the hexagon.

Regarding the method of writing, he says: in the center of the pericarp, one should write the *kandarpa* or *kāma-bīja* (the seed-syllable of desire) together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), using the formula "Oṃ, let such-and-such of such-and-such a person be accomplished.
Likewise, one should write the six syllables located in the cavities—that is, the six letters to be described as residing in the hexagon—and so forth.

On the filaments, at the bases of the ten petals, one should write the eighteen syllables of the mantra consisting of two nines (the *dvinavali*)—namely, the syllables preceded by the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī and the seed-syllable of Śrī, beginning with *Śakti-Śrī*—two by two.

Likewise, in the center of the ten vessels, one should write the letters of the most excellent ten-syllabled mantra (*daśākṣaramantra*), the best among the ten-lettered mantras, one by one. Then [one should draw] the lotus (*abjam*).
That [charm], surrounded by the earth-dwelling mantra, inscribed with a golden needle by the god of love who was devoid of blood,
and fashioned into a pellet upon a plate made of gold— this was it.
This Gopāla-yantra, which bestows all goals, has thus been described.
One should encircle it with a square representing the orb of the earth.
Of what kind? With the "abode of the earth," which is the seed-syllable of Kāma (the god of love) located at the corners; this Gopāla-yantra is said to bestow all desired objects. How is it prepared?
It is written with a golden stylus and yellow pigment (gorocanā) and the like upon a cloth plate fashioned from gold.
Immediately thereafter, it was made circular.
This [mantra], sprinkled with the *sampāta* offering and consecrated by recitation (*abhijapta*), should be maintained by the great ones; it is uniquely skilled in subjugating the three worlds,
and [bestows] protection, fame, sons, earth, wealth, grain, and prosperity.
By those desiring good fortune, [this] of priceless potency should be practiced incessantly.

This mantra— sprinkled with the remains of oblations (*āhuti*), preceded by the offering of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) placed before it, and likewise consecrated (*abhimantrita*) by the mantra— is for those great ones who desire to obtain these: the warding off of fear from protection, fame, the manifestation of virtuous renown, a son (a male child), the earth (the world), wealth such as gold and the like, fortune (all prosperity), and good fortune (being beloved by all people).
It should always be worn by those endowed with purity.

This is the meaning: having prepared the yantra as described, performed the consecration of life-force (*prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā*), sprinkled it with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth, drenched it with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) poured over it one hundred and eight or one thousand times, and recited the mantra the prescribed number of times, one should wear it. Of what kind [should it be]?
It is uniquely skilled in bringing the three worlds under its control;
furthermore, it possesses priceless vigor and great power.
He shows another application of the *yantra* through its retention:

For those afflicted by possession by spirits, insanity, epilepsy, poison, fainting, delusion, or fever, one should meditate on [the deity] at the head and recite this mantra in order to immediately pacify the disorder. (Kṛd 5.90)

A *bhūta* is one who dwells in cremation grounds, possesses an invisible form, and performs undesirable acts; *unmāda* is mental derangement; *apasmṛti* is the affliction of epilepsy; *viṣa* is poison, both stationary (*sthāvara*) and mobile (*jaṅgama*), which causes fainting; *mūrchā* is a state of unconsciousness or delusion; *prasāda* is clarity; and *jvara* is a specific type of disease. For those afflicted and tormented by these, this [mantra] in the form of a *yantra* is placed upon the head, above the skull.
Meditating [on this], one should recite this Gopāla-mantra; for what purpose? To pacify—that is, to quickly and immediately destroy—the transformation (vikṛti). // KrdC_5.90 //
He extracts the six-syllable mantra from the yantra:
"Smara-trivikramākrāntaś cakrīṣṇāya-hṛt. This six-syllable mantra is proclaimed to be the bestower of all accomplishments (siddhi). (Kṛd 5.91)

Smara is the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), and Trivikrama is the letter Ṛ; he is "traversed" (krānta) by that, meaning joined with it. Cakrī is the letter Ka, and likewise "Kṛ" [is the next]. "Ṣṇāya" is its essential form, followed by "Hṛt" and "Namaḥ. In this manner, this six-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as the bestower of all perfections and the granter of all desires. (KrdC 5.91)
He extracts the seed-syllable of Śakti:
"The lap [K], blazing with fire [R], possessing Māyā [I] as its mark on the head [with a dot], this is that supreme, subtle, eternal Śakti, whose nature is consciousness. (Krd 5.92)
The breast is the letter *ha*.
Of what nature is it? It is illuminated by fire, which is the letter *ra*;
furthermore, it is joined with the illusory power (*māyā*), which is the long vowel *ī*.
Furthermore, he whose head is marked by a *lava* (a small portion) and a *bindu* (dot) is thus one accompanied by the *anusvāra*; this is the meaning.

This power (*śakti*) is supreme, excellent, subtle like a lotus fiber, eternal, devoid of birth and destruction, consisting of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*), and consisting of self-luminous nature. (KrdC 5.92)
He extracts the seed-syllable of Śrī:
"The seed-syllable of Lakṣmī is said to consist of the elements of bone (th), fire (ra), Govinda (go), and a fraction (la).
From these two [syllables], there arises the eighteen-fold script, a mantra of twenty syllables. (Krd 5.93)

The letter *śa* is bone, the letter *r* is fire, *go-vinda* is the long vowel *ī*, and the nasal dot (*bindu*) is the moment (*lava*). When these are joined together, the seed-syllable of Śrī (*śrī-bīja*) is thus proclaimed.

When this is combined with the previously mentioned eighteen-syllable mantra and these two—the seed-syllable of Power (*śakti-bīja*) and the seed-syllable of Śrī—it becomes a twenty-syllable mantra. (KrdC 5.93)
He shows the rule regarding the place for the worship of the Supreme Lord:
"Worship of Hari should always be performed upon a *śālagrāma* stone, a gem, a yantra, a mandala, or in images, but never on bare ground alone. (Krd 5.94)

In a well-known *śālagrāma* stone, in gems such as *gomeda* or *padmarāga*, in this very *gopāla-yantra*, in a *maṇḍala* such as the *sarvatobhadra*, or in the *maṇḍalas* of the Moon, Sun, and Fire—so says Rudradhara—or in images, such as an image of Gopāla made of gold and other materials:
here, the worship of Hari must always and at all times be performed, but never upon the bare ground alone. (KrdC 5.94)
He shows the fruit of the aforementioned modes:
"Thus, he who here worships Mukunda constantly by resorting to one of us, through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, libations, and so forth,"
Having attained extraordinary enjoyments effortlessly for a very long time,
he then proceeds once more to that most stainless abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Kramadīpikā* composed by the venerable Keśavabhaṭṭācārya. In the manner described above, he who constantly serves Mukunda through recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), worship (*pūjā*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), and—by the word "etcetera"—consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth; having taken one of the two mantras consisting of ten or eighteen syllables, he does so effortlessly in this world for a very long time, at all times.
Having obtained all enjoyments, he finally attains the celebrated, stainless splendor; the meaning is that he becomes one with that abode.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Kramadīpikā-vivaraṇa* composed by Śrī Vidyāvinoda Govinda Bhaṭṭācārya.
**Sixth Chapter**
Now, he shows the applications and so forth for the two mantras thus established:
"Next, I shall declare the common applications of both mantras, as well as certain mantras of infinite power that accomplish their respective purposes. (Krd 6.1)

Immediately thereafter, I shall describe certain mantras that possess ten or eighteen syllables, which have identical applications through specific meditations, as well as some mantras of infinite power that accomplish those purposes and bestow abundant fruits. (KrdC 6.1)
He states the meditation on the [mantras] of ten and eighteen syllables for the purpose of practice:
I bow to that son of Devakī, who was born at once with the splendor of the sun, wearing yellow garments, and with his hands shining with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. (Krd 6.2)

I bow down and offer salutations to the son of Devakī, whose form has been described above; who is renowned, born at once as a child, possessing the splendor of the sun, with a complexion as dark as the sky, clad in yellow garments, and in whose hands shine the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. KrdC_6.2 //
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the Brāhma-muhūrta;
and with sweet-smelling palāśa flowers, one should offer ten thousand oblations.

In this manner, during the *brāhma-muhūrta*—that is, two *daṇḍas* before sunrise according to some, or four *daṇḍas*—one should recite one hundred thousand repetitions of the mantra for both [deities].
Immediately thereafter, one should perform ten thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers soaked in sweet substances and accompanied by ghee, honey, and sugar. (KrdC 6.3)
He states the result:
"Whoever, being well-composed, should perform [this] in this manner with either of the two *mantras*,
having obtained memory, intelligence, and the power of intellect, shall become a supreme poet."
It may be that another [person] obtains the fruit of recitation, meditation, and fire-offerings equal to that of a human being.
Being well-composed and well-restrained, whoever should perform this with either of the two mantras consisting of eighteen syllables shall obtain memory (smṛti),
recollection (smaraṇa), intelligence (medhā) characterized by retention, intellect (mati), right knowledge (samyak-jñāna), and strength (bala) consisting of great vitality;
having attained all this, he becomes a kavirāṭ, a preeminent sage— thus says the following mantra which will be spoken hereafter.
One obtains results equal to those of the recitation, meditation, and fire-offerings of the two previously mentioned mantras.
He states the mantra:
"The glorious feet of Mukunda, always my refuge; I take refuge [in them]. Thus is declared the eighteen-syllable Maukunda mantra.
"Śrīman-mukunda-caraṇau sadā" is its essential form; then "iti śaraṇam" is its essential form;
and "ahaṃ prapadye" is its essential form—in this manner, the eighteen-syllable mantra related to Mukunda has been described.
The extraction of the mantra:
"I always take refuge in the feet of Śrī Mukunda.
He states the seer and other details:
Nārada, Gāyatrī, and Mukunda are the seers (ṛṣis) of this [mantra].
A man who drinks water every morning after reciting it one hundred and eight times will,
within six months, become a possessor of the Veda (śrutadhara).

Regarding this mantra: Nārada is the sage (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), and Mukunda is the deity (*devatā*). The phrase "preceded by the seer" (*ṛṣipūrvaka*) means the seer, meter, and deity; these are Nārada and the others.
He states the application: every morning, one should drink water over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times.
By this method, that person shall become a bearer of what has been heard within six months.

He states another practice: "Having withdrawn the divine limbs, one should recite the mantra while recollecting the blue-hued child as before, resting on his mother's lap, with moving arms and feet. (Krd 6.7)

One should remember Him— the dark-complexioned child, the infant with moving hands and feet, resting on His mother’s lap in Devakī’s embrace, His divine limbs withdrawn, having abandoned His four-armed form and assumed two arms, just as He was when, out of fear, His divine limbs were withdrawn in the house of Vasudeva. KṛdC 6.7.
One should likewise offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter into the sacrificial fire;
thus, one shall obtain unwavering devotion, faith, and eternal peace.

One should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times and likewise offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire; he who does so attains a firm and pure conviction regarding the Supreme Lord as the object of worship, a certainty concerning the goal taught by the scriptures that is inevitably realized, and eternal, perpetual peace in the form of liberation. This specific meditation on the ten and eighteen-syllable mantras is for the purpose of practical application.
Thus says Bhairava Tripāṭhin. (KrdC 6.8)
He states another mantra:
"At the end of this entire [mantra], preceded by *manu* (the seed-syllable), there is that which is called 'bowed to by Marut' (*marunnamita*);
or else, with this: *bālalīlātmane huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. (Kṛd 6.9)
Alternatively, one should accomplish this collection of practices by means of the mantra that will be spoken. He states the mantra: "samasta...
At the end of its essential form (svarūpa) is "marunnamita," which constitutes its essential form.
From this word, "bālalīlātmane huṃ phaṭ" is its essential form, and "namaḥ" is its essential form.
This too consists of eighteen syllables and is equal to the [mantra] of eighteen syllables.
The extraction of the mantra: *samastamantrunnamita bālalīlātmane hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
He speaks of the seers and so forth:
Nalakūvara, Gāyatrī, and Bālakṛṣṇa are thus declared;
by means of this [mantra], all perfections (siddhis), beginning with those of the seers (ṛṣis), shall be attained here through recitation (japa) and other such practices.
The seer (ṛṣi) and other [constituent elements] of this mantra are as follows: the seer, the meter, and the deity are Nalakūvara and others.
Specifically, in this case, the sage is Nalakūvara, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Bālakṛṣṇa.
In this world, all accomplishments (siddhis) are attained through the recitation (japa) and other practices of this mantra. (KrdC 6.10)
One who satisfies with food the [child] who is lying on a cradle, crying and being watched by the cowherd women with the thought that it is milk, attains his nourishment.
On his cradle in the infant’s bed, he remains suspended, crying and wailing, watched and beheld by the cowherd folk— the gopīs— and, according to the reading "preryamāṇam," being moved,
meaning being rocked; one should satisfy him with water, thinking it to be milk.
Food is that which is to be eaten; it is so called because one partakes in or attains it. // KrdC_6.11 //
He states another mantra:
"With this [mantra], one should say the word 'of the nature of taste' at the end of 'of the nature of food';
then 'O you whose form is contented, homage,' followed by the dual [vocative] 'to the Lord of Food, for me.'"
"Give food, svāhā!"—this thirty-syllable mantra is the giver of food.
One should perform the previously mentioned rite with this mantra.

He states the mantra: at the end of the word *annarūpa*, [add] *rasarūpa* as its own form; *tuṣṭarūpa* as its own form; *namo dvandvam* as the own form; *namo nama* as the own form; then *annādhipataye mamānnaṃ prayaccha svāhā*. This consists of thirty syllables.
The *annada* mantra is equivalent to those consisting of ten, eighteen, or twenty syllables.
The extraction of the mantra:
*annarūpa rasarūpa tuṣṭarūpa namo namaḥ annādhipataye manānnaṃ prayaccha svāhā*.
He speaks of the seers and so forth:

One should recite the Nārada-anuṣṭubh mantra, preceded by its seers and ending with "the lord of food," while remembering it upon the head of one afflicted by disturbances such as spirits, infantile seizures, insanity, or loss of memory, or by one seized by a *pūtanā* who has begun to suckle at the breast. (Kṛd 6.13)
For this mantra, Nārada is the sage (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas),
and the Lord of Food is the deity (devatā).
He states the application [of the remedy]: "bhūta" refers to a child-seizing spirit such as a *piśāca* or the like, which is a specific type of disease;
"unmāda" is a derangement of the mind, a loss of memory, and a state of delusion.

When one's head is seized by these calamities and afflictions, and the crown of the head is tormented, one should recite the mantra while remembering Kṛṣṇa, who drank from the breast of Pūtanā. (KṛdC 6.13)
One should visualize that Pūtanā weeping and crying out, her entire body pierced by the sucking [of the child];
and having entered her, all the seizing spirits (grahas), leaving him, flee away swiftly. (Kṛtyakalpataru 6.14)
Furthermore, of what nature is she?
She is one whose every limb is stretched out and torn asunder by that sucking—that drawing in—accompanied by breath (*prāṇa*).
Having become what, should one mutter [the mantra] in such a manner?

Having entered [the victim] and meditated, "I am indeed Hari," immediately thereafter all the seizing spirits (grahas) and afflictions, having released and abandoned that [victim] who has been swallowed, flee and run away swiftly and quickly.
Regarding this, the Tripāṭhins maintain that this special meditation on the ten and eighteen-syllable [mantras] is for the purpose of the ritual application (prayoga). KrdC 6.14.
He states another ritual application:

"Having bathed well with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should offer oblations into the fire with the blossoms of the *khara* plant into the mouth of the slayer of Pūtanā. (Kṛd 6.15)

One should offer oblations into the fire—the mouth of Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of the one who obstructs worship—using the tips of the flower-clusters of *kharamañjarī* and *apāmārga*, sprinkled with the waters of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should have the subject consume the remains of the cow-products and consecrate him with the water from that jar,
over which the mantra has been recited a thousand times, for the pacification of all calamities.

One should have [the patient] consume the remainder of the *pañcagavya* prepared during the *homa*, or one should consecrate them with an ablution using a jar prepared according to the previously mentioned procedure and empowered by a thousand recitations, for the sake of removing all afflictions.
He states another mantra: "Or else, by means of this twelve-syllable [mantra] ending in *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*..."
The seer and so forth for this [mantra] are Brahmā, Gāyatrī, the Graha-demons, and Hari; it is a destroyer of planetary afflictions.
One may perform these two previously mentioned applications either with the aforementioned [methods] or with the mantra that is about to be stated.

He states the mantra: "Twelve"—that is, at the end of the previously mentioned twelve-syllable Vāsudeva mantra, one adds *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*; this sixteen-syllable mantra is equivalent to the ten- and eighteen-syllable [mantras].
He states the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituent elements]: "The seer and so forth."
The "sages and so forth" refers to Brahmā and the others;
therein, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi),
and the Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas).
The deity is Hari, who has the form of the destroyer of planetary afflictions.
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
One should recite this while meditating upon the cart overturned by the lotus feet of one’s own [deity].
One should recite ten thousand repetitions of each of the two mantras for the pacification of all obstacles.
One should meditate upon Hari, who has set down His cart at His own lotus feet.
One should mutter one of the two mantras—the former or the latter mantra—ten thousand times (*ayuta*).

For what purpose? For the sake of pacifying all obstacles; specifically, for the sake of quelling all obstacles, this is the special meditation (*viśeṣa-dhyāna*) on the two mantras consisting of eighteen and ten syllables, according to the Tripāṭhin tradition.
The worship of the limbs of these mantras with the wheels and so forth, along with Indra and the others, and Vajra and the others, is always taught for the sake of accomplishment. (Kṛd 6.19)

For these aforementioned mantras, the limbs (aṅga) should be performed using the ten-syllable [mantra] as taught for the wheels and so forth; furthermore, worship (arcanā) and ritual offerings (pūjā) should always be performed for the sake of prosperity with the limbs, as well as with Indra and the others, along with their weapons. // KrdC_6.19 //

He shows the ritual procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya: "May Hari—the child with a blue body, holding curd-rice with his two arms, and adorned with a network of leopard-claw amulets and small bells—protect you. (Krd 6.20)
Regarding the specific meditation for the sake of health in the mantras of ten and eighteen syllables, the followers of the Tripāṭhin tradition say "bāla" and so forth:
may Hari protect you (yuṣmān).
Of what nature is Bāla?
Five years old.
Again, of what kind? Blue-bodied.
Again, of what kind?
With his two hands he should hold fresh butter produced from curds and milk-rice, that is, *paramānna*.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is adorned with a pair of tiger-claw ornaments and a cluster of small bells. (KrdC 6.20)

Having meditated thus, one should offer oblations into the fire with three hundred sprouts of *śatavīryā* soaked in milk and clarified butter; meanwhile, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

Having meditated upon Hari in this manner, one should offer oblations into the fire with three hundred sprouts of *durvā* grass—one hundred each—sprinkled with milk and clarified butter; one should perform one hundred thousand oblations and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. (KrdC 6.21)
Having given a sacrificial fee to the teacher, one should feed the best of the twice-born;
for he shall live for a hundred years, free from disease—of this there is no doubt.
Immediately thereafter, having given a sacrificial fee to the preceptor and fed the Brahmins, he shall live for a hundred years free from disease; of this there is no doubt.
He states another mantra: "In this regard, O Puruṣottama, there is another mantra consisting of twelve syllables at the end:
'O Viṣṇu, the all-powerful one, grant me long life,' having thus addressed him. (Kṛd 6.23)
This mantra, ending with "namas," consists of thirty-two syllables; its seer is Nārada, its metre is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Hereafter, I shall state its limbs (aṅgas). (Kṛd 6.24)
For such a task, there is another mantra.

He states the mantra: at the end of the twelve-syllable Vāsudeva mantra, the form "Puruṣottama," the form "dehi me āyuḥ" (grant me long life), and the form "Viṣṇave prabhaviṣṇave. With "namaḥ" at the end, this thirty-two-syllable mantra consisting of thirty-two letters has been declared.

Furthermore, for this mantra, Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and Śrī-Kṛṣṇa is the deity; immediately following this, I shall state—that is, I will speak—the ancillary limbs (aṅgas). KrdC_6.23-24.
The extraction of the mantra:
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person; grant me long life, salutation to Viṣṇu, the All-pervading Lord.
[This is formed] by the syllables equal to the sun (12), the elements (5), the senses (5), the Vasus (8), and the eyes (2), joined with the word *ātmane*.
The light of the state of great bliss [is attained] through the stages of *māyā* and *vidyā* in succession.

The five limbs [of the mantra] are formed in sequence with twelve, five, five, eight, and two syllables respectively, ending in middle-voice (ātmanepada) verbal suffixes, together with the words "mahānanda" and so forth;
in some places, the reading is also "sahānanda."
Regarding the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth for this [mantra], he says:
"Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, one should offer ten thousand oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
By offering [oblations] with *dūrvā* grass as before, one shall obtain an exceedingly long life. (Kṛd 6.26)
Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, one should perform ten thousand oblations with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).

Having thus accomplished the mantra, as before, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass mixed with milk and ghee. Through these recitations, one attains an exceedingly long and superior lifespan. (KrdC 6.26)

Having grasped Kṛṣṇa by his two beaks as he was tearing at Baka with his arms, one should practice with intense concentration while recollecting [the Lord’s] protection of children in times of distress;
through anointing with sesame seeds consecrated by that mantra, they shall become happy. (Krd 6.27)
When fear or danger has arisen for children or infants, one should touch those children, remember Kṛṣṇa, and practice—that is, recite—one of the mantras mentioned. What kind of Kṛṣṇa?
One who, grasping the demon named Baka by his two snouts with His two hands, was tearing him apart.
By anointing with oil over which that mantra has been recited, those children become happy.
"Remembering" means remembering Kṛṣṇa by the name Śuśu;
