it should be understood that one should recite [the mantra] while touching the head. Regarding the difference between the ten-syllable and eighteen-syllable mantras, the Tripāṭhins maintain that this constitutes a specific visualization (viśeṣa-dhyāna).

He says that for this very purpose of protecting children, there is yet another mantra: "In this case too, there is another mantra: *vahni-vallabhā* [O Beloved of Fire] for the child's body; likewise, [one should visualize] him tending cattle while playing his resonant flute during the protection of the cows. (Krd 6.28)
"Bālavapuṣe" refers to his form, and "vahnivallabhā" refers to Svāhā; regarding this meaning and for the protection of cattle, he describes the specific meditation with the words "kvaṇat":
one should recite the mantra while remembering Kṛṣṇa, who is intent on playing the flute and tending the cattle. (KṛdC 6.28)

Regarding this very purpose of protecting children and protecting cattle, he states another mantra: "Having uttered the word *gopālaka*, and again for *veśadharāya*, [then] *vāsudevāya*, the armor (*varma*), the weapon (*astra*), and the head (*śiras*)—this is the eighteen-syllable [mantra]. (Krd 6.29)

Having said "Gopālaka," and having again said "Veśadhārāya," one should say "Vāsudevāya. Then one should utter the armor-mantra "Hūm" and the weapon-mantra "Phaṭ. Finally, one should utter "Śiraḥ Svāhā. When done in this way, it becomes eighteen syllables long.
The extraction of the mantra: *gopālaka-veśa-dharāya vāsudevāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Or, by this [mantra], Nārada, Gāyatrī, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth are the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituent elements] of the mantra.
The wise practitioner should perform the protection of the cowherd using the limbs beginning with the discus.

For this aforementioned mantra, the sage is Nārada, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Śrī-Kṛṣṇa; by means of this mantra, or with the previously mentioned materials and so forth, one should perform the protection of the cowherds.
With what kind [of mantra]? With that which is joined with the limbs (aṅgas) beginning with the discus (ācakra). (KrdC 6.30)
He states the practice for removing poison:

"In cases of suffering from the venom of the *kumbhīnasa* and other such snakes, one should practice [this] while remembering Hari dancing upon the stage of Kāliya’s hoods, with his head placed upon the bitten spot. (Krd 6.31)
Sprinkling his body with a glance that showers nectar,
the wise man quickly releases him from poison by threatening him with his left index finger.

In cases of suffering from the venom of *kumbhīnasa* snakes and the like, or when afflicted by the poison of serpents—where *dharaṇi* explains that *kumbhīnasas* are those snakes whose poison is potent through their very glance—the practitioner should meditate on Kāliya, a specific serpent, as he dances upon his own hood, which is described as a stage (*raṅga-bhūmi*), having touched the head of the victim who is suffering at the site of the bite. (Note: The term *ādi* in *kumbhīnasādi* includes scorpions and other such creatures; *daṣṭa-mūrdhni* refers to the head of the bitten person; *ārta-mastake* means "on the head of the one in pain"; and *tasya phaṇā saiva raṅga-bhūmiḥ* identifies the serpent's hood itself as the performance arena.)
One should practice and recite a certain mantra.
Of what kind? [One that depicts] Hari sprinkling his body with a nectar-showering gaze.
What while doing so? While threatening with the left forefinger.
This being so, the mantra-practitioner shall immediately and swiftly release the poison from that which has been bitten.
Regarding this, the followers of the *Tripāṭhin* tradition maintain that there is a specific visualization for the ten and eighteen syllables.
He states another application:

"Having visualized a previously unfilled jar being filled with waters while recollecting the subduing of Kāliya, and having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should sprinkle it upon the victim; he shall become well. (Krd 6.33)

Having filled a water-pot with water, and having subsequently meditated upon the Lord who subdues Kāliya and recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should sprinkle that which is possessed of poison with that pot;
immediately thereafter, one becomes free from the poison and happy. // KrdC_6.33 //

He states the mantra for the subduing of Kāliya: having uttered the letters "kā-vya-ma-dhya-li-yasyān-te-pa-hā-ma-dhye-di" in the middle of the verse, one should then immediately say "nṛtyaṃ karoti. (Kṛd 6.34)
"Having said 'I bow to the son of Devakī,' one should say 'to King Acyuta' with a sound like dancing; such is the instruction on dental articulation according to Manu. (Kṛdanta 6.35)
One should utter the form *kāvyo* between the two syllables; then the form *liyasīti*; then at the end, the form *phaṇāmadhyādi*; immediately after that, one should say *nṛtyaṃ karoti tam*;
then immediately after, one should say *namāmi devakīputram*;

and finally, from the word *nṛtya*, at the end of the word *nṛtya*, one should say *rājanaṃ acyutam*. In this manner, the thirty-two-syllable mantra of the "Tooth-Writing" (*dantalipi*) has been described.
The extraction of the mantra:
"I bow to that son of Devakī, who performs a dance in the midst of the hoods of Kāliya; he is called the King of Dance."

He shows the limbs and other components of this mantra: "The sage of this [mantra] is Nārada, with all his feet placed [as syllables] for its limbs; the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Kṛṣṇa, the crusher of Kāliya. (Kṛd 6.36)

The sage Nārada has declared that for this mantra, the five limbs are formed by its four individual feet taken separately and by the entire mantra taken as a whole; the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Kṛṣṇa, the crusher of Kālīya.
He states the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
"This mantra is to be recited one hundred thousand times, and ten thousand oblations are to be offered with clarified butter;
its worship is declared to consist of the limbs [of the mantra], the guardians of the directions, Vajra, and so forth. (Kṛd 6.37)
This mantra is to be recited one hundred thousand times; furthermore, ten thousand oblations are to be offered with clarified butter (ghṛta).
Worship and adoration are said to consist of three enclosures: the limbs, the guardians of the directions, and Vajra and the others.
He states the practical application:
"And every action previously described as destroying poison must be performed;
for there is no mantra in this world equal to this for removing venom. (Krd 6.38)

Since all anti-venom rituals previously mentioned in the mantras must indeed be performed with this very mantra, there exists in this world of saṃsāra no other remover of poison equal to or like this mantra.
He states another application for neutralizing poison:
"A pill prepared from the ground parts of the *śukataru* tree with cow's urine, when used as an ointment or an application to the mouth by this method, destroys poison. (Krd 6.39)
Bhairava Tripāṭhin says it refers to the *śukataru* and the *karañja* tree;
the author of the *Laghudīpikā* says it refers to the *kiṃśuka* tree;
and Rudradhara says it refers to the limbs, that is, the bark.

According to those who recite the three versions [of the text], it is prepared with five ingredients: pills made from cow urine and the urine of a cow with its calf, ground together. When these pills have been consecrated with this mantra, they become a destroyer of poison through various methods such as applying them as collyrium or ointment to the face.

Now he shows another visualization: [One should meditate on Him] holding the Govardhana mountain with His left arm raised like a staff, His face resting upon a flute held between the fingers of His other hand. (Kṛd 6.40)
Meditating on Hari and chanting one of the two mantras, he may travel even without an umbrella;
for him, there shall never be any fear from rain, wind, or lightning.

One who, while meditating upon Hari— who held up Mount Govardhana with his uplifted left arm-staff, whose flute has its mouth applied to that [arm] which resounds clearly through the fingers of his other hand—
should wander without an umbrella while chanting one of the two mantras consisting of eighteen syllables, shall be protected from rain, wind, thunderbolts, and other such calamities.
No fear exists anywhere at all.
He states another application:
"Recalling him who has caused Indra to abandon his efforts against the futile mass of clouds, one should offer ten thousand measures of salt; there will be no rain, without a doubt. (Krd 6.42)

One should offer oblations with ten thousand *lavaṇa* seeds while meditating upon Hari as one from whom the moon has departed due to the effort of that fruitless mass of clouds; immediately thereafter, a drought occurs—of this there is no doubt. (KrdC 6.42)

He states another visualization: [One should meditate on Him] sporting in the waters of the Yamunā by means of immersing and swimming, and being sprinkled by His beloveds with showers of droplets from those waters. (Krd 6.43)
Having meditated thus, one should offer ten thousand oblations with *vānīra* twigs sprinkled with milk;
then, even at a time when it is not the rainy season, a great rain will fall—of this there is no doubt.
Sporting—playing—by means of plunging in and emerging from the waters of the Yamunā;
again, of what sort?
By his beloved women, Rukmiṇī and others, with showers of water-sprays in the form of streams of Yamunā water.
Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa in such a state as being drenched [by rain], one should offer ten thousand oblations with *vānīra* twigs, *vetasa* fuel-sticks, and water-drenched milk-soaked offerings.
When this is done, even out of season there will be a great downpour; of this there is no doubt.

By means of this very meditation, he describes another application: "Remembering this very [mantra] over the head of one afflicted by poison, eruptions, fever, and so forth, along with burning sensations and delusions, one should recite it; peace will occur in an instant. (Kṛd 6.45)

For one afflicted by burning sensations, delusion, pustules, fever, and so forth, one should meditate upon this very form previously described on the head of that person and recite [the mantra]; immediately thereafter, peace and recovery shall occur for that sufferer.

Regarding this very affliction, he states another method: "Alternatively, [one should meditate on] Acyuta mounted upon Garuḍa, accompanied by Balarāma and Pradyumna, praised by the fever-afflicted who have been crushed by his own fever. (Kṛd 6.46)
Having meditated, one should practice [the mantra] upon the head of the person overcome by fever;
even an incurable fever, along with its complications, shall be pacified in an instant.
Alternatively, for one overcome by fever, having meditated upon Acyuta on the head, one should practice—that is, recite—one of the two mantras.
Of what kind? Acyuta mounted upon Garuḍa.
Furthermore, of what kind?
Accompanied by Bala and Pradyumna;

furthermore, of what nature is He? He is praised by the Raudra-jvara (the fever of Rudra), which takes the form of the weapon called Uṣṇa (the hot one), after that Raudra-jvara has been crushed—that is, pulverized—by His own Vaiṣṇava-jvara, known as Śīta (the cold one), which likewise takes the form of a weapon.
Immediately thereafter, even an incurable fever is swiftly destroyed.
What kind of fever?
One accompanied by complications (*upadrava*), such as bodily pain and the like. (KrdC 6.47)
By means of this very meditation, he states another application:
"Having meditated thus and worshipped in the fire, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *amṛtā* stalks, four finger-breadths long and unbroken, for the pacification of fever. (Kṛd 6.48)

Having thus meditated upon Kṛṣṇa in the form previously described and having worshipped him in the fire, one should offer ten thousand oblations of pieces of *amṛtā* (guḍūcī) stalks, each measuring four finger-breadths and sprinkled with milk, for the purpose of pacifying fever.
He states another application:

"Having remembered Hari, who dispels the torment of Bhīṣma pierced by sharp arrows, one should touch the afflicted person with both hands and recite [the mantra] for the pacification of disease. (Krd 6.49)

One should meditate upon Hari as one who removes the fever—the affliction—of Bhīṣma, who was pierced and struck by a sharp, whetted arrow; having thus visualized Him, one should touch the afflicted person suffering from fever and other ailments with both hands and mutter one of the two mantras for the sake of destroying the fever. (KrdC 6.49)
He states another application:

"For the destruction of untimely death, having meditated upon [the deity] as the bestower of Sāndīpani’s son, one should offer ten thousand oblations of pieces of the nectar-creeper smeared with milk. (Krd 6.50)
Sāndīpani was the preceptor of Kṛṣṇa.

Meditating upon Kṛṣṇa as the one who restores his son, one should offer ten thousand oblations (*juhuyāt*) of pieces of *amṛtalatā* (immortality-creeper) and pieces of *guḍūcī* (guduchi), sprinkled with milk.
To whom? For the destruction—that is, the cessation—of *apamṛtyu*, which is untimely death. (KrdC 6.50)
He states another application:

"For the sake of increasing one's offspring, having meditated upon [the deity] as giving sons to a brahmin whose children have died—along with Arjuna—one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. (Krd 6.51)
For the sake of a brahmin whose sons have died, one should meditate upon [Viṣṇu] together with Arjuna—that is, accompanied by Arjuna—and recite one hundred thousand times either of the two *mantras*;
for what purpose? For the sake of the increase of his offspring. (KṛdC 6.51)
He states another ritual application:
"One should offer ten thousand oblations into the fire with *putra-jīvaka* fuel and its fruits smeared with honey; by this, his sons shall become long-lived. (Kṛd 6.52)

For one who is renowned as "Jīvāputra," when fire has been prepared together with fuel, he should offer ten thousand oblations (*ayuta*) with the fruits of the *jīvā* tree—which are sweet and smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*)—using either of the two mantras.
Immediately thereafter, the sons of this performer of the *homa* become long-lived. (KrdC 6.52)
He states another application:

"Having worshipped a jar filled with the decoction of milk-tree (*kṣīradruka*) at night, and having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times, one should sprinkle a woman in the morning for twelve days. (Krd 6.53)
Even a barren woman, by consuming clarified butter over which this mantra has been recited, obtains sons who are long-lived and free from disease; of this there is no doubt. (Kṛd 6.54)

Having worshipped a jar filled with a decoction of milk-tree (kṣīravṛkṣa) according to the ritual for filling a jar, and having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times at night, one should sprinkle a woman desiring a son at dawn, extending over twelve days.
Thereafter, even if she is barren, once consecrated she becomes fit for the time of giving birth; and even if she has not yet given birth, she obtains sons who are long-lived and free from disease.
Being of what nature?
She is one who consumes the clarified butter (ājya) resulting from the recitation of mantras;
there is no doubt regarding this matter. (KṛdC 6.53–54)
He states another application:

"In the morning, a woman who restrains her speech, having consecrated water with the mantra one hundred and eight times while holding it in the hollow of her hands made from *bodhi* leaves, will certainly obtain a son. (Kṛtya 6.55)

In the morning, remaining silent and observing a vow of silence, a woman desiring a son—one who wishes for a son for herself—should drink water that has been consecrated one hundred and eight times with either the *manu* mantra, using a cup made from a leaf of the *bodhicchada* (the tree of awakening) or a leaf of the *pippala* (fig tree), for the duration of one month.
Thereafter, she obtains a son; this is the remainder [of the meaning].

He states the mantra for drinking water: *devakīputra*. Here, by way of context, the *santāna-gopāla* mantra—which, though not mentioned in this particular work, is nonetheless well-known—is also recited. It is as follows:
*devakīputra govinda vāsudeva jagadguro*.
Give me my son, O Kṛṣṇa; I have come to you for refuge.

The sage of this mantra is Nārada, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of progeny. The five limbs [of the ritual] are formed by the individual words [of the mantra]. The visualization is as follows: Kṛṣṇa, bearing the conch and the discus, four-armed and seated upon his chariot.
Blazing with all ornaments, clad in yellow garments, and infallible.

Adorned with peacock feathers and augmented by the splendor of Viṣṇu, he was returning the lost children to the brahmin; and he gazed upon that twice-born man with a look filled with the nectar of compassion. Thus [it is said]. (KrdC 6.55)
He states another practice:
"Having cut down the *kṛtyā* sent by the King of Kāśī with his own weapon, one should meditate on Hari burning that city with its fiery power. (Krd 6.56)
One should offer oblations at night for seven days with mustard seeds smeared with one's own fat;
thus, the enraged *kṛtyā* will certainly destroy the performer herself. (Kṛd 6.57)
Having cut with his own discus that malevolent spirit (*kṛtyā*) sent and dispatched by his enemy, the Lord of Kāśī, as a slayer,

one should then meditate upon Kṛṣṇa burning that king’s city with its splendor; for seven days, using mustard seeds smeared with oil and anointed with one's own affection, one should offer oblations at night with either of the two *mantras*.
Immediately thereafter, that *kṛtyā*, being enraged, will certainly and inevitably destroy the performer himself.
He states another visualization:
"Seated in a divine hermitage adorned with groves of jujube trees, [one should visualize him] touching the body of Ghaṇṭākarṇa with his two lotus-like hands. (Kṛd 6.58)
Having meditated upon Acyuta, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds soaked in the three sweets,
for the liberation from all sins, for peace, and for the beauty of the body.

Having meditated upon Acyuta, seated in a divine and excellent hermitage adorned with a grove (*badarī-ṣaṇḍa*)— a cluster of *badarī* trees— and touching with his lotus-like hands the body (*kalevara*) of Ghaṇṭākarṇa, who is a form of Mahādeva, or the body of some devotee of Mahādeva, [one should offer] sesame seeds soaked in the "three sweets" (*tri-madhura*), that is, mixed with clarified butter, honey, and sugar.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations with each mantra.
For what purpose? For liberation, as well as for the destruction of all sins, and likewise for the luster—that is, the radiance—of the body.
He states another application:

"Remembering Hari while [the two] Rukmin and Bala are engaged in gambling and causing hatred, one should offer pellets made from cow dung into the fire for the purpose of creating enmity between those two who are fond of each other. (Krd 6.60)

While Rukmin and Balabhadra are engaged in gambling and performing the act of dice-play, one should remember Hari— who causes them to feel mutual hatred— and offer a pellet made from cow dung into the fire with either of the two *mantras*;
here, it should be understood that a thousand oblations are to be performed.

Because of the statement, "But when no number is mentioned, one should specify a thousand there," for what purpose? For the sake of causing enmity—that is, for the purpose of creating hatred—between two friends who are otherwise well-disposed toward each other. (KrdC 6.60)
He describes another practice:
[one should meditate on] Acyuta, who rains arrows with flaming tips from his mouth, and who pursues a host of enemies as they flee, while he himself bears the Garuda-banner.
Having meditated thus, one should practice one of the two mantras seven thousand times;
this shall effect the eradication of enemies within seven days.

Having meditated upon Hari— who is mounted upon Garuḍa, who pursues the host of enemies running behind him, and who strikes while raining down arrows whose tips blaze like a fiercely flaming fire— one should practice and recite one of the two mantras, either the ten-syllable or the eighteen-syllable, seven thousand times.
When this has been performed, the eradication of his enemies occurs within seven days, and their departure from his own country takes place.
He states another application:
"Meditating on one who has carried off the kapittha fruit along with the young calf, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times; that very moment, the target is eradicated. (Krd 6.63)

Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa as one who has tossed upward and thrown away Vatsakāsura—who was in the form of a calf—and who steals the fruit of the wood-apple (kapittha), one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times between the two *manus*;
immediately thereafter, at that very moment, he swiftly effects the expulsion (*uccāṭana*) of the person to be acted upon.
He states another application:

"Having meditated upon himself as Kaṃsamathana (the Slayer of Kaṃsa) having been thrown down from the bed, and drawing out the enemy who is the very self of Kaṃsa as one whose life has departed, one should recite the mantra. (Krd 6.64)
If one performs ten thousand oblations with the *janmanakṣatra* tree as the sacrificial offering, the enemy will die even if he has consumed nectar; of this there is no doubt.

Having meditated upon oneself as Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of Kaṃsa, and having contemplated the unity of one's mind with that destroyer of Kaṃsa; and likewise, having meditated upon the enemy in the form of Kaṃsa as being deprived of life— meaning, having contemplated the non-difference between the enemy and Kaṃsa—
one should recite the mantra ten thousand times while contemplating the act of pulling [the enemy] down from the platform and dragging him away, thereby unifying the two minds.
One should offer oblations for this enemy with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) that are extremely pleasing to the birth-place [of the foe];
these are the *kāraskara*, the *dhātrī*, the *udumbara* tree, and furthermore the *jambū*, the *khadira*, the one called *kṛṣṇa*, the *vaṃśa*, and the one named *pippala*.
The two trees named Nāga and Rohita, those known as Palāśa and Plakṣa,
the one called Ambaṣṭha, Bilva, and Arjuna, and the Vikaṅkata tree;
Bahala, Savala, Kharjū, Bhaṇḍila, Panasa, Arkaka, Śamīka, Damba, Āmra, Nimba, Madhuka, Ṛkṣa, and Śākhin.
Thus are the trees of the twenty-seven lunar mansions.
When the tree of one’s birth-mansion is treated in this manner, even one who has drunk the nectar of immortality will die; of this there is no doubt.
He shows that this purpose can also be achieved by another method:
"Alternatively, one who is self-restrained should offer ten thousand oblations at night with the seeds of the *akṣa* tree smeared with neem oil;
[this brings about] the death of the enemy in an instant. (Krd 6.66)

Being disciplined and pure, one should offer ten thousand oblations at night with fuel-sticks of *vibhītaka* produced from *akṣa* trees and sprinkled with *nimba* oil, using either of the two mantras;
for what purpose? For the swift destruction of the enemy. (KrdC 6.66)
Regarding this very point, he states another ritual application:

"Standing in a cremation ground at night, one should offer oblations for the pacification of enemies, using the husks of *ariṣṭa* seeds, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and cotton seeds, smeared with castor oil. (Krd 6.67)
Regarding the term *doṣā*, Rudradhara says it is the leaf of *haridrā* (turmeric) or the leaf of *ariṣṭa*; Rudradhara also says it is the leaf of *bhallātaka*;
and Bhairava Tripāṭhin says it is the leaf of *nimba*.

One who stays at a cremation ground—the site for the funeral rites of the deceased—should, during the night, offer oblations with one of two mantras, using a mixture of *vyoṣa* (the three pungents), cotton seeds (*kārpāsāsthi*), and *kaṇa* (pepper), soaked in castor oil (*eraṇḍa-taila*).
For what purpose? For the destruction of enemies.
Regarding the expiation for the practice of killing out of passion, he says:
"If one should perform the act of killing that is not sanctioned, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times;
or, for the sake of pacification, one who is peaceful by nature should offer milk-rice oblations that many times. (Krd 6.68)

The act of killing is not praised for a learned person; nevertheless, if one should perform it out of passion, then for the sake of pacification and the destruction of evil, one should—with a peaceful mind and free from envy—recite one of the two mantras ten thousand times, or offer ten thousand oblations of *paramānna*. (KrdC 6.68)
He states another practice:

"One who desires victory should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while meditating on Hari, the remover of the *pārijāta* tree; for him, there shall be no defeat from any quarter. (Krd 6.69)

A man desiring victory should, while meditating upon Kṛṣṇa—who by his power seized the Pārijāta tree from Indra as it stood in heaven—recite one hundred thousand repetitions of one of the two mantras. When this is done, he shall suffer no defeat from anyone whatsoever. (KrdC 6.69)
He states another practice:

"One should recite [the mantra] while meditating on Hari, who stands upon his chariot, teaching the meaning of the Gītā to Arjuna and making the gesture of exposition (vyākhyā-mudrā), for the increase of Dharma and for tranquility. (Krd 6.70)

One should meditate upon Hari as He is seated upon His chariot, instructing and speaking the meaning of the Gītā to Pārtha (Arjuna), with His hand in the *vyākhyā-mudrā*—that is, the gesture of exposition formed by the upturned index finger joined with the thumb—and while so meditating, one should recite one hundred thousand repetitions (*lakṣa*) of either of the two mantras.
For what purpose? For the sake of the arising of righteousness (*dharma*) and for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*). (KrdC 6.70)
He states another ritual application:
"Whoever should offer a hundred thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers soaked in honey, he shall become a poet, a sovereign of debaters, and an expounder of all scriptures. (Krd 6.71)

He who should offer one hundred thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar, while reciting either of the two mantras, shall become a commentator on all the scriptures, a sovereign among poets, and the most excellent of poets.
He states another practice:
"One should meditate on Hari, who assumes all forms, whose splendor is equal to ten million rising suns, who resembles molten gold, and whose nature consists of both fire and moon. (Kṛd 6.72)
The lotus-feet of the servant of the sun and fire are radiant, adorned with divine ornaments,
bearing various weapons, and pervading every space within the universe.
For the protection of the kingdom, cities, villages, dwellings, and the body,
one should recite either of the two mantras with devotion while meditating in this manner.
This [verse] explains the "Bearer of Universal Forms" (viśvarūpadhara): [His form] possesses a splendor equal to ten million rising suns, is like molten gold, and has the nature of fire and moon;
according to those who recite three lines, it is "consisting of the sun and moon.
Likewise, His face and lotus-feet are as radiant as the sun and fire.

Having thus meditated upon Hari—who is adorned with beautiful ornaments, who wields various weapons, and who pervades the interior of the space of the entire world—one should recite one of the two mantras with devotion.

For what purpose? [To protect] the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*), the country (*deśa*), the city (*pura*), the town (*nagara*), the village (*grāma*)—which is a place inhabited by few people—or the dwelling (*vāstu*) of a single householder.
Govinda Miśra explains that "field" (kṣetra) refers to land;
however, if the reading is "thing" (vastu), it refers to gold and so forth. These, along with the body, are for the purpose of protection—that is, for the sake of guarding them. (KrdC 6.72–74)
He states another application:
"Alternatively, [one may perform] the rite of the sage Arjuna, whose limbs are formed by all the feet [of the verse] arranged separately;
its meter is Triṣṭubh, and its presiding deity is Viṣṇu in his universal form. (Kṛd 6.75)

One should recite the Gītā-mantra at that place, or one should offer oblations of clarified butter to Hṛṣīkeśa and the others for the sake of all protection and the pacification of all suffering. (Krd 6.76)
Alternatively, in a sacred place, one should mutter the Gītā-mantra beginning with Hṛṣīkeśa. Of what nature is this mantra?
It is composed of five limbs (*pañcāṅga*), where each individual quarter (*vyasta*) and all the quarters (*samasta*) together constitute the four feet (*aṅghri*) that form its body.

Where Arjuna is the seer (ṛṣi), that [verse] where all the limbs and feet are arranged separately; and "Arjuna-ṛṣika" is a *dvandva* compound; that which has the *triṣṭubh* meter and Viśvarūpa Viṣṇu as its presiding deity (*adhidevatā*).
One should offer oblations with clarified butter (*ājyaka*), or—with the word "or" (*vā*) used in a conjunctive sense—one should offer them.

In other commentaries, regarding the aforementioned ritual applications, where the number for recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) is not specified, the number mentioned in proximity is taken; in the absence of that, one thousand and eight, or one hundred,
or eight thousand— so say some— in the *Jaganmohana-tantra*.
Whether it be one hundred thousand, ten thousand, a thousand, or even a hundred,
the mantra-practitioner should perform the corresponding fire-oblation (homa) for each of the tasks according to its gravity.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Kramadīpikā* composed by the venerable Keśavabhaṭṭācārya.
**Seventh Chapter**
He begins the seventh chapter for the purpose of explaining various mantras, starting with the words "I shall speak" (*vakṣye*) and so forth:

"I shall speak of the practice of the Lord of Śrī, which is well-guarded by the fortunate ones such as Dhaneśvara and others, and which is performed constantly for the sake of attaining inexhaustible wealth. (Krd 7.1)

I shall describe the practice of Gopāla, the Lord of Śrī—namely, the method of meditation, mantras, worship, and so forth—that practice which is performed by the lords of wealth and others, such as Kubera and other great riches;
for what purpose? For the attainment of that wealth which is imperishable and indestructible.
The meaning is that she is well-guarded, not excessively exposed by the twice-born.
The middle *kulaka* consists of seven verses beginning with "In Dvāravatī":
"In Dvāravatī, within a most excellent pavilion surrounded by many supreme mansions as radiant as a thousand suns and by numerous wish-fulfilling trees... (Kṛd 7.2)
Where is Acyuta to be meditated upon?

In Dvāravatī, in a jeweled pavilion, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne lotus. That is, situated in the city of Dvārakā, he is seated upon a jewel-encrusted lion-throne located within a jeweled pavilion.
Of what sort is that pavilion? It is surrounded by the finest of dwellings and the most excellent of houses, as well as by wish-fulfilling trees (kalpa-vṛkṣas).
Of what kind?
Like a thousand suns, they were radiant, blazing, and extensive.
In a place with walls, doorways, and arches made of blazing jewels,
where pearls hang from variegated canopies shimmering with garlands of blooming flowers.

Furthermore, of what kind? It is that in which the pillars—which serve as the support of the house—are composed of or dominated by blazing, radiant jewels; and wherein the door-arches and walls are adorned with blossoming, expansive flower-garlands that shine with splendor.
Various kinds of purifying canopies, adorned with pearls, were suspended here and there.
Furthermore, what was that jeweled pavilion like?
It was situated between a ruby-paved ground and a river of gems,
beneath its own tree from which nectar-like jewels were incessantly dripping.
Between that ground made of ruby and that river consisting of radiant jewels, beneath his own tree—the *pārijāta*—of what kind was his own tree?
It was one from which jewel-like nectar (*sudhā*) or ambrosia (*amṛta*) flows incessantly at all times. (KrdC 7.4)
Furthermore, what was that jeweled pavilion like?
Its interior was illuminated by rows of jewel-lamps;
it resembled the rising sun, and contained a jeweled lion-throne in the form of a lotus.
The space between the directions was illuminated and made radiant by rows of jewel-lamps consisting of blazing gems, upon that jeweled lion-throne;
of what kind [was it]? Like the rising, appearing sun. (KrdC 7.5)
Of what nature is Acyuta?
Seated, Acyuta is the object of meditation, resembling molten gold;
his splendor is equal to ten million rising moons, suns, and lightning flashes.
He whose splendor is equal to that of ten million moons, ten million suns, and even ten million flashes of lightning, all rising simultaneously like molten gold—that is, like liquid gold.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is beautiful in every limb, gentle, adorned with all ornaments,
clad in yellow garments, and his arms shine with the discus, conch, mace, and lotus.

He is beautiful, lovely, and gentle in all his limbs, including his face, being free from arrogance; he is adorned with all ornaments, such as earrings and other decorations; he wears yellow garments (*pīta-vāsas*);
and his arms are radiant and blazing with the discus, conch, mace, and lotus. (KrdC 7.7)
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He touches with the tip of his left lotus-foot the jar from which flows an incessant stream of jewels, robbing it of its verdant hue.

The compound *vāma-pādāmbujāgreṇa* means "with the tip of the left lotus-foot. It touches that which is both a jar (*kalaśa*) and a mass (*ogha*)—that is, a continuous flow (*pravāha*) of a stream of jewels (*ratna-dhārā*) which is constantly and perpetually surging upward. With what kind of [foot] does it touch? [With one that is]... [as follows].
Stealing the luster of new shoots and robbing the beauty of tender sprouts.
He describes the meditation on the eight queens:
Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā, stationed to his right and left respectively, drench his head with a stream of jewels arising from the vases held in their own hands.
Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā are to be meditated upon;
of what nature are they? They are sprinkling the head—the crown—of this Hari with a stream of flowing jewels. Of what kind [is that head]? It is situated on the right and left [sides].
Here, Rukmiṇī is on the right and Satyā on the left;
by what kind of stream? By one arising from a jar held in her own hand.
One should meditate upon Nāgnajitī and Sunandā. Of what nature are these two?
Nāgnajitī and Sunandā are bestowing two water-pots;
and by them [are supported] Mitravindā and Sulakṣmaṇā, situated on the right and left respectively.
One should meditate on Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā as being in the positions of two jeweled jars, bestowing—that is, giving—[offerings].
Of what sort? They are situated on the right and left.
Likewise, Mitravindā and Sulakṣaṇā, situated on the right and left, are to be meditated upon.
Of what nature were they? They were *tābhyām*—by those two, Nāgnajitī and Sunandā—who were *diśantībhyām*, i.e., bestowing a water-pot, giving a water-pot.
Having drawn two jars filled with jewels from the river of jewels,
Jāmbavatī and Suśīlā stand at their right and left sides, bestowing them.
Likewise, Jāmbavatī and Suśīlā are to be meditated upon on the right and left [sides];
what are they like? They are lifting up two jars filled with jewels from a jewel-river and bestowing them upon Sulakṣmaṇā and Mitravindā.
Outside, sixteen thousand women in number should be visualized all around,
radiant with jars joined by streams from a multitude of every kind of jewel.
Outside of that, sixteen thousand beloved ones are to be meditated upon.

Of what nature are they? They are radiant with a jar (*kalaśa*) joined to a stream (*dhārā*) of a flood (*ogha*) consisting of gold—meaning fine gold—and jewels such as lotuses and the like. (KrdC 7.12)
Outside of that, the eight treasures (nidhis) are to be meditated upon. Of what sort? Outside of that, the eight treasures fill the earth with wealth.
Outside of those, all the Vṛṣṇis and the gods and others are as previously described.
One should meditate upon the Vṛṣṇis and Yādavas outside of that, filling the earth with wealth.

Immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon the gods and others—such as the celestial sages (devarṣis), perfected beings (siddhas), vidyādharas, and gandharvas—standing in the directions like a city, performing the jewel-consecration.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self, one should recite the twenty-million-syllable mantra;
one should offer oblations of clarified butter four hundred thousand times, and forty thousand times [with other substances].
Having thus meditated upon the form of the Supreme Self as bodiless, one should recite the twenty-syllable mantra four hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations with clarified butter forty thousand times. KrdC_7.14.
He extracts the twenty-syllable mantra:
preceded by Śakti and Śrī, it consists of eighteen syllables and thus becomes twenty syllables in total. There is no mantra in the three worlds equal to this mantra. (Krd 7.15)

The meaning is as follows: preceded by these two seed-syllables—the seed of Śakti, which is Bhuvaneśvarī, and the seed of Śrī—this previously mentioned eighteen-syllable mantra becomes twenty syllables.
There is no mantra equal to this mantra in the three worlds. (KrdC 7.15)
He shows the seer and so forth:
"The seer is Brahmā, the metre is Gāyatrī, and Kṛṣṇa is the deity;
the assignment of its seed-syllable, power, and so forth is exactly as previously stated. (Kṛd 7.16)

The conceptualization of the seed-syllable, power, and so forth for this mantra is as previously stated, like that of the ten-syllable [mantra]; thus, the meaning is that whatever seed-syllables and so forth belong to the ten-syllable [mantra] belong to this one as well. (KrdC 7.16)
He states the method of worship:
"Now the ritual manual for this mantra, as spoken by Sanatkumāra, is being declared;
having performed the placement [of mantras] on the seats (pīṭha-nyāsa) and so forth according to the previously mentioned sequence, the wise one [should proceed]. (Krd 7.17)
The method of worship for this mantra, as taught by Sanatkumāra, is now being described by me:

having performed the placement of the seat (pīṭha-nyāsa), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and so forth, according to the previously mentioned sequence and the manner prescribed for the ten-syllable mantra. (KrdC 7.17)
One should place the six limbs upon the palms and fingers of both hands;
having performed the pervasive placement with the mantra, one should enclose the Mātṛkā with the mantra.
One should arrange the ten principles (tattvas) by way of dissolution and emanation;
then, having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka), one should place the syllables of the mantra upon the body.

One should sequentially place the six limbs upon the fingers of both hands and the palms of both hands. Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) over the entire body with the twenty-syllable mantra, one should perform the placement of the *mātṛkā*— the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* encapsulated by the mantra— where each individual letter of the *mātṛkā* is encased within the twenty-syllable mantra,
at the previously mentioned locations of the *mātṛkā*.
And the ritual application (prayoga) begins with *hrīṃ aṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* and so forth;
thus there is a double repetition up to the letter *bha*.
Then: *hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ*.
"Klīṃ krīṃ paṃ klīṃ krīṃ namaḥ," and so forth;
one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the ten principles (*tattva*), beginning with earth (*mahī*) and water (*salila*), according to the path of dissolution and emanation (*saṃhāra-sṛṣṭi*).
Then, having again performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the twenty-syllable mantra, one should place the twenty mantra-syllables upon one's own body. (KrdC 7.19)
He states the locations for the placement of the syllables (akṣara-nyāsa):
on the crown of the head, the forehead, between the eyebrows, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the mouth, the chin, the throat, the base of the arms, the heart, and the navel. (Krd 7.20)
One should place [the mantras] at the navel, the linga, the foundation (ādhāra), the hips, the knees, the shanks, the ankles, and the feet; this is declared to be the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi).
One should place each syllable individually on the head, the forehead, the brow, between the eyebrows, and so forth;
at the *ādhāra*, in the triangular location below the *liṅga*—this is the method for the placement (*nyāsa*) of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) as described.
Stability begins with the heart and ends at the top of the head; withdrawal begins with the feet and ends at the heart.

Having thus performed the "cage of the form" (mūrti-pañjara) five times, ending with stability, and having performed the rites of emanation and stability, one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa).

The "stability" (sthiti) consists of the placement starting from the heart and ending at the shoulders; the "withdrawal" (saṃhṛti) consists of the placement starting from the feet and ending at the head. Having thus performed the placement up to the stage of stability five times—this being intended for householders—and having likewise performed the previously mentioned placement of the "cage of the form" (mūrti-pañjara), one should again perform the creation and stability placements, assigning the syllables of the mantra according to the method of creation and stability, and then perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa).
One should practice.

He shows the six ancillaries: having bound the mudrā called Kirīṭa with the syllables of Manu— namely the qualities (guṇa), fire (agni), the Vedas (veda), the instruments (karaṇa), the organs of action (karaṇākṣi), and the vowels (akṣara)— one should perform the binding of the directions as before.
Having meditated and recited the mantra, one should worship [the deity] within one's own body, preceded by the "cage of forms" (mūrti-pañjara).
The mantra of Manu has three qualities (*guṇas*), three fires (*agnis*), and four Vedas; the instruments (*karaṇas*) are the four internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇas*).
Furthermore, with these syllables arising from the mantra—the four instruments and the two eyes—the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgas*) are to be performed; this is the meaning.

Having formed the *mudrā* called the *kirīṭa* (the crown), or having made it known as the *kirīṭa*, if the reading is *kirīṭādyām*, it includes the *kaustubha* and *śrīvatsa* *mudrās*. As before, the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) is performed with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).

One should perform the self-worship. Regarding this, he says "having meditated": having performed the meditation previously described and having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, preceded by the *mūrti-pañjara*, one should worship within the body.

Thus, within [the ritual], first comes the propitiation of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara), followed by that of the pentad of forms (mūrti-pañjara), followed by the placement (nyāsa) of emanation and maintenance, and finally that of the six limbs (ṣaḍ-aṅga). //23//
He describes the method of external worship:
"Alternatively, one should indeed worship Viṣṇu; for that purpose, a maṇḍala is prescribed.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should place a pedestal there. (Krd 7.24)
Now, after the self-worship, one should worship Viṣṇu externally.
For the sake of that worship, the place of worship is described:
having smeared the ground with cow-dung and water, one should place a seat—a vessel dear as the support for worship—upon that smeared spot. (KrdC 7.24)
Having smeared [the ground] with fragrant paste, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus;
in its pericarp, however, one should draw a six-pointed star containing the Manmatha-mantra together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).

Immediately thereafter, having smeared that pedestal with sandalwood paste and drawn an eight-petalled lotus there, one should draw a lotus in the pericarp; in the central space, one should draw two fire-cities (triangles) joined at their apices by a hexagon.
There, in the middle of the hexagon, one should write the seed-syllable of Kāma (the "manmatha"), together with the ritual action to be accomplished and the name of the person to be acted upon.
The followers of Tripāṭhin maintain that because of the inclusion of the word "sādhya," this [suffix] should also be understood as having the sense of "holding" (dhāraṇa).
One should encircle that Smara with the remaining seventeen syllables;
[one should place] Śrī in the east, the southwest, and the northwest corners, and Saṃvit in the remaining [spaces].
One should encircle that *kāma-bīja* with the remaining seventeen syllables.
In the eastern, southwestern (*nairṛti*), and northwestern (*vāyavya*) corners of the hexagon, one should write the goddess Śrī and the three *śrī-bījas*.
In the remaining three corners—the western, northeastern (*aiśāna*), and southeastern (*āgneya*)—one should write Saṃvid and the *bhuvaneśvarī-bīja*. (KrdC 7.26)
One should write the six-syllable Smara-gāyatrī at the joints and on the filaments three by three, and the garland-mantra on the eight petals. (Krd 7.27)
Having drawn six lotuses, one should encircle them on the outside with the letters of the Mātṛkā;
and on the exterior, one should draw a circle of the earth, as well as the syllable Śrī-Māyā in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
In the joints—specifically the six-cornered joints—one should write the six-syllable mantra "Kṛṣṇāya namaḥ," preceded by the Kāma-bīja.
In the place of the filaments, one should write the Kāma-gāyatrī to be described hereafter, arranging it by three syllables at a time.

On the eight petals, one should write the Mālā-mantra to be described hereafter, dividing the six syllables into groups of six. Outside the lotus, one should encircle it with the letters of the Mātṛkā.

One should draw the form of the earth-circle (*bhū-bimba*), whose nature will be described below, immediately outside the enclosure of the *mātṛkā*s. The meaning is that one should write the syllable *Śrī-Māyā* in the cardinal directions of the earth-circle, the seed-syllable *Śrī* in the intermediate directions, and the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī in the corners.
Having inscribed this yantra on plates of gold or other materials as before,
whoever wears it once consecrated shall indeed be honored even by the gods.
This yantra is also useful for worship; whoever wears it is honored even by the gods.

Having done what? Having written it, as previously described, with the appropriate substances on plates of gold, silver, copper, or other materials, and having performed the rites such as the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā*) as before during the acts of worship. Or else, [having performed] the rites such as the installation of the vital breath as was done previously with the mantra.
Of what kind? Accomplished (*sādhita*) and consecrated (*prajapta*) in the manner previously described. // KrdC_7.29 //
He extracts the *gāyatrī* of Kāmadeva:
"May there be the *gāyatrī*; [the names] Kāmadeva and Puṣpabāṇa, ending in the dative case (*ṅe*);
joined with *vidmahe* and *dhīmahi*; may that limb (*aṅga*) impel us."
From the recitation of the Gopāla mantras at the beginning of the *japa* and other rites, one wins the favor of the people.
The words *kāmadeva* and *puṣpabāṇa* are in the dative case respectively;
what are they like? They are accompanied by the words *vidmahe* and *dhīmahi*.
Following that is the essential form: *tan no anaṅgaḥ pracodayāt*.
This being so, there is the *kāma-gāyatrī*.
Regarding the phrase "one should recite" (*japyāt*): at the beginning of the recitation of the Gopāla mantras—that is, at the commencement of the *japa*—one should recite this *kāma-gāyatrī*.
For the meaning is that this [mantra] is one that delights people and brings them under control (*vaśyakarī*). (KrdC 7.30)
He extracts the garland mantra with the words beginning "naty-ante" and so forth:
having uttered "naty-ante kāmadevāya" ending in the dative case (ṅe), which means "dear to all people," and then after "sarvajana," likewise the word "saṃmohana. (Kṛdanta 7.31)
"Jvala jvala prajvala" is proclaimed for all people;
one should then utter "my heart," followed by the pair "vaśaṃ kuru" as the head.
This Madana mantra is said to consist of forty-eight syllables. (Krd 7.32)

At the end of the word *namaḥ*, one should utter the essential form *kāmadevāya*; thereafter, having pronounced the word *sarvajana-priya* in the dative case (*caturthy-ante*), and then having spoken the word *sarvajana*, one should say the word *saṃmohana*. Thereafter, having uttered the essential form *jvala jvala prajvala*, and having uttered the essential form *sarvajanas ya hṛdayaṃ mama*, and having uttered the essential form *vaśam*, and then having uttered the essential form *kuru kuru*— [The mantra is: *Namaḥ kāmadevāya sarvajana-priyāya sarvajana-saṃmohana jvala jvala prajvala sarvajana-hṛdayaṃ mama vaśaṃ kuru kuru svāhā.*
One should say "Śiraḥ svāhā.
This being the case, the Madana mantra consists of forty-eight syllables.
He shows the application:
"In recitation and other rites, [the mantra] beginning with the seed-syllable of Māra brings the three worlds under control.
The earth-pavilion should be square, adorned with vajras at the corners and so forth. (Krd 7.33)

In whatever [mantra] it arises in such a manner—whether in recitation (japa), worship (pūjā), fire-offering (homa), and so forth—if it begins with the seed-syllable of desire (kāma-bīja) and the like, then it is capable of subjugating the three worlds; this occurs when this mantra is recited independently (*svatantra*), according to the Tripāṭhin school.
"The earth-cellar" (*bhū-gṛha*) refers to the extraction of the earth-cellar.
Or rather, the reading is: "a square adorned with eight vajras joined at the corners, together with the four corners, hanging down from the ground. (KrdC 7.33)
Regarding the method of worship in the yantra, he says:

"Having worshipped the pedestal as before and having conceived the anthropomorphic form (pauraṣī-mūrti), one should invoke Acyuta there with devotion, perform the ritual of the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), and worship him. (Krd 7.34)

As before, having performed the worship up to the adoration of the Guru’s seat (*gurvāpīṭha*) with the ten-syllable mantra, one should meditate there upon the supreme form of the Lord (*pārameśvarī mūrti*), which is the *pauruṣī* [form] in human shape. Having invoked Acyuta into that form and performed the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should worship with devotion.
Then, by means of the channel of the flow of the *suṣumṇā*, one should unite the splendor (*tejas*) of the form residing in the heart with the flower held in the upturned hands.

Having visualized the deity Tejas as having entered the body of the god through the *brahma-randhra*, and having established [the deity] externally with its respective mudrā, having caused it to be present (*sannidhāpya*), having bound it firmly (*sanniruddhya*), and having veiled it (*avaguṇṭhya*), one should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa*) upon the limbs of the deity and worship it with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*); such is the meaning. (KrdC 7.34)
One should again worship [the deity], from the seat up to the ornaments, according to the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa):
the emanation and maintenance [mantras], the six limbs, the crown, and the two earrings.
Having worshipped the discus, conch, mace, lotus, garland, śrīvatsa, and kaustubha with perfumes, unbroken rice, and flowers using the root mantra as before, [verse 7.36].

One should worship in such a way that [the sequence] begins with the seat and ends with the ornaments; the meaning is that one should worship with the services (upacāras) starting from the seat and ending with the ornaments.
Furthermore, one should worship the [deities] beginning with Creation (sṛṣṭi) according to the order of placement (nyāsa);
having first performed the placement of Creation and the others, one should then worship them.
Alternatively, "by the sequence of placement" means according to the order in which their placement was performed. Regarding "scented unbroken grains":

*akṣatāḥ* are barley; having worshipped Kṛṣṇa as before with scented unbroken grains and flowers using the root mantra, one should worship him with seven circumambulations—this is the meaning. // KrdC_7.36 //
He states the obstructions:
"First, one should worship the limbs in the corners of the fire and the two cities, in sequence as follows: the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the eye, and the weapon. (Krd 7.37)

The meaning is that one should first worship the six limbs, beginning from the southeast corner, within the six corners associated with the pair of fire-puruses (the two triangles). He states the limbs: "With the heart" (*sahṛd*).
"With the heart" means the heart repeats [at the beginning]; thus, the heart, head, crest, armor, kavaca, eye, and weapon constitute the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*).
He speaks of the second enclosure, beginning with "Vāsudeva":
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
at the base of the petals starting from the southeast [are] Śānti, Śrī, and Sarasvatī. (Kṛd 7.38)
Rati is to be worshipped in the petals of the directions; thereafter, one should worship the eight queens—Rukmiṇī and the others—in due order on the tips of the petals to the right and left.

The meaning is that Vāsudeva and the others are to be worshipped at the bases of the petals in the corners beginning with Agni (the southeast), in the locations of the filaments; likewise, Śānti and the others are to be worshipped at the bases of the petals in the four directions beginning with the East. He speaks of the third enclosure: "Then eight," which means that immediately after that, the eight queens (mahiṣīs) are to be worshipped.

Regarding the phrase "those beginning with Rukmiṇī," he states the place of worship: "on the right and left. The meaning is that four [consorts] on the right side of the Supreme Lord and four on the left side are to be worshipped in sequence.
He states the fourth enclosure: "Then," etc.
Then one should worship at once sixteen thousand beloved ones—Indranīlas, Mukundas, and so forth; Makaras, Anaṅgas, and Kacchapas. (Krd 7.40)
One should also worship the eight treasures in sequence, beginning with the lotus and the conch;
outside of that, one should fully worship the enclosures beginning with Indra and Vajra.
At the tips of the petals in the east and other directions, one should worship the sixteen thousand beloved wives of the gods all at once, in a single sequence.
Regarding the fifth enclosure, he says: one should worship the eight treasures, beginning with Indranīla, in the order starting from the east.
Here, after each word such as "Indra" and so forth, the word "treasure" (nidhi) should be added in the dative case.
The ritual application (*prayoga*) begins with "Oṃ, homage to Indra-Nidhi," and so forth.
Regarding the two outer enclosures, the sixth and seventh, he says: "Outside of that.
One should worship Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and the other [emblems], on the exterior of that. (KrdC 7.40–41)
Having displayed the veils, he shows the food offering:
"Thus, having worshipped Acyuta with devotion seven times around, one should gratify him with milk-rice mixed with curd, sugar-candy, and ghee. (Kṛd 7.42)

In this manner, having worshipped Kṛṣṇa—who is encircled by the seven veils—with due reverence, one should gratify him with milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by curds, sugar, and ghee; such is the meaning. Then, having offered royal honors, and having praised and bowed to Keśava, one should dissolve him into one's own heart along with his retinue.

Having offered the parasol, fly-whisks, and other [emblems], and having immediately thereafter performed a hymn of praise, one should bow with either the eight-limbed or five-limbed prostration; then, together with the assembly of attendants, one should dissolve Keśava into the heart—lifting him up, that is, establishing him there.
Having established oneself [in the deity] and worshipped thoroughly, one who is absorbed in that [deity] should recite the mantra;
this is declared as the twenty-syllable [mantra] based on the meditation and worship of the jewel-consecration (ratnābhiṣeka).
The house of one who worships this mantra through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and meditations is incessantly filled with jewels, gold, and grain.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] as previously described, having performed the placement beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), and having conducted the self-worship (*ātmapūjā*), one should become absorbed in that—becoming identical in nature with the deity to be worshipped—and recite the mantra that is a limb of worship.
He concludes what has been discussed with the word "jewel" (*ratna*);
the meaning is meditation (*dhyāna*), sacrifice (*ijyā*), and worship (*pūjā*).
And thus, in that worship wherein there is the meditation on the gem-consecration of Kṛṣṇa, this worship of Kṛṣṇa described by means of the twenty-syllable mantra is taught.
He shows the fruit [of this practice] with the words "by recitation" (japa):
the house of one who serves this mantra through recitation and other such means is filled incessantly—that is, without interruption—with rubies and other gems, gold, and grain. (KrdC 7.44–45)
The earth becomes vast for him, filled with all kinds of grain;
endowed with sons and friends, he goes at the end to the supreme goal.
He shows the ritual application:
having worshipped Govinda in the fire with white flowers together with rice grains,
and having offered ten thousand oblations of them soaked in clarified butter, one should apply that ash to the crown of one's head.
He shall possess an abundance of food and other provisions, and all women shall be under his control.

Having established the fire in the manner described and having worshipped Govinda there according to the prescribed method, one should offer ten thousand oblations of white flowers mixed with rice grains soaked in ghee. That man who bears the ashes of this sacrificial fire upon his head shall attain manifold prosperity and wealth, and all women shall become subject to him.
He states another practice:
"One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter, or of red lotuses soaked in the three sweets;
by this, his sovereignty equal to that of Indra will certainly become like a mere blade of grass. (Kṛd 7.48)

For that practitioner who offers one hundred thousand oblations with pure ghee, or with red lotuses combined with ghee, honey, and sugar, his sovereignty—which rivals that of Indra—will certainly become like a blade of grass through the power of Śrī, the Goddess of Fortune; this is a certain metaphorical comparison. (KrdC 7.48)
He states another application:

"To obtain white garments and the like, one should perform oblations with white flowers and the like, smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), a thousand times; or else, smeared with clarified butter (*ājya*), eight hundred and eight times. (Kṛd 7.49)
For the purpose of obtaining white garments and the like, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with white flowers mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar, or with flowers smeared in ghee.
He states another practice:
"One should daily offer one thousand and eight oblations with white flowers sprinkled with honey for six months; he shall become the domestic priest of a king. (Krd 7.50)
He who offers one thousand and eight oblations daily with white flowers mixed with honey becomes the royal priest after six months have passed.

One should perform the rites such as recitation, meditation, and fire-offerings as prescribed in the ten and eighteen classes [of tantras], and by this [method] as well; these are also proclaimed here in relation to those two.
One should perform the recitation, meditation, fire-offering (homa), and so forth, which were prescribed for the ten- and eighteen-syllable [mantras], by means of this mantra;
and one should also perform the ritual applications (prayoga) and other rites mentioned here in this mantra by means of those two.

He states another mantra: "Obeisance to Śrī, Śakti, Smara, and Kṛṣṇa, to Govinda"—this is the *śiras* mantra, consisting of twelve syllables, with Brahmā as the seer and the Gāyatrī meter; now follows its [application]. (Kṛd 7.52)

The seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Śakti, and Smara—the seed-syllable of Kāma; "kṛṣṇāya govindāya" is the essential form (svarūpa), and "svāhā" is the essential form. The mantra consists of twelve syllables. "Those whose ṛṣis and so forth are at the beginning" means that the ṛṣis and others are Brahmā, Gāyatrī, and Kṛṣṇa;
the meaning is that for this [mantra], Brahmā is the ṛṣi, Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), and Kṛṣṇa is the deity (devatā).
The seed, power, and so forth are as previously described.
The six limbs (aṅgas) are here declared with seed-syllables (*bījas*) consisting of twenty-four syllables;
the rites of recitation, meditation, fire-offering (*homa*), and worship are said to consist of twenty syllables.
This mantra should be practiced by the wise who desire all-encompassing sovereignty. (Krd 7.53)

In this mantra, the six limbs (ṣaḍ-aṅga) are said to consist of three seed-syllables (bījas); likewise, three limbs are formed by three groups of syllables consisting of three Vedas (nine), two (four), and two; and the remaining three limbs are formed by [the other] twenty [syllables].
Thus [it is said].
"Twenty" refers to the total count.

Let this mantra, together with the recitation, meditation, fire-offering, and worship prescribed for the twenty-syllable mantra, be practiced by scholars who desire all forms of sovereignty. (KrdC 7.53)

He states another mantra: "The ten-syllable [mantra] beginning with Śrī, Śakti, and Kāma, and ending with Aṅgajanma, Śakti, and Ramā, should be placed at the beginning of the vessel (sarāva) if it is joined with Śakti and Ramā."
These two mantras are modifications consisting of non-vowels, having the wheels and so forth as their primary components.

The seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī, and the seed-syllable of Kāma—these precede the ten-syllabled mantra; likewise, the birth of the limbs [is formed by] the Kāma-bīja, the Śakti [is] the Bhuvaneśvarī-bīja, and the Ramā-Śrī-bīja—these follow at the end of that ten-syllabled mantra. Thus, the ten-syllabled mantra, distinguished by these elements at its beginning and end, becomes a sixteen-syllabled mantra; and so too does that same ten-syllabled mantra [become one].
If the mantra is joined at the beginning with Śakti (Hrīṃ) and Ramā (Śrīṃ), and is further accompanied by the seed-syllables of Bhuvaneśvarī and Śrī, then it becomes a twelve-syllable mantra.

This being the case, these two modified mantras—consisting of sixteen and twelve syllables respectively—should be understood as having the limbs (aṅgas) such as Ācakra and the rest, which were previously described for the ten-syllable mantra, as their constituent parts.

Then, during the ritual of worship described in the *Viṃśaty-arṇa*, one should meditate upon Acyuta as he embraces his beloved seated on his lap with both hands— bestowing boons and fearlessness— while she,
holding a lotus and a blue water-lily, embraces him; he is radiant with the discus and the sword.
These two modes of worship have been described using twenty syllables; immediately after this, one should contemplate Acyuta.
Of what kind? He who is embracing—clinging to—the two beloved ones, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, who are situated upon his own lap; or alternatively, Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā.

By which two? By the two hands that grant boons and fearlessness. "Varada" means one who gives a boon (*vara*); "abhaya" means that from which fear (*bhaya*) does not exist; and those two being the hands (*hasta*) are "varadābhaya-hastau. The meaning is: by those two. Of what kind is the beloved?
A *padma* is an ordinary lotus, and an *utpala* is a blue lotus; those [hands] in whose two palms these are found are of such a kind.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?
They are embraced—that is, clasped—by those two beloveds.
Furthermore, of what kind is it?
It is radiant with a conch and a discus.
He states the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), such as the recitation (*japa*), and so forth:
"One should recite [the mantra] one million times and perform one thousand oblations (*homa*) with clarified butter (*ājya*) that many times;
once these two mantras are mastered, they bestow all prosperity and good fortune upon men. (Krd 7.56)

One should recite these two mantras one million times; through a thousand oblations of clarified butter for each hundred-thousand recitations—that is, ten thousand oblations—these two mantras become perfected for men, bestowing all sovereignty and the love of all people.
Now he extracts the mantra in sequence:
preceded by Māra, Śakti, and Ramā; preceded by Śakti, Śrī, and Māra; and preceded by Śrī, Śakti, and Māra—these are the three ten-syllable mantras. (Krd 7.57)

The first ten-syllable mantra is preceded by the *anna* syllable, the *Kāma-bīja*, and the *Bhuvaneśvarī-śrī-bīja*. The second is that which has *Bhuvaneśvarī*, *Śrī*, and *Māra* preceding it. The third is the ten-syllable mantra preceded by *Śrī*, *Bhuvaneśvarī*, and the *Kāma-bīja*.
Among these foremost of Manus, in the period of Aṅgārṣi and the others,
Kṛṣṇa should be meditated upon at midday as being ruddy in hue, bearing a conch, a discus, a bow, an arrow, a noose, and a goad, while blowing a flute held with his two arms. (Kṛd 7.58)
In the first mantra, meditation is performed in this way; in the second, with twenty syllables;
and in the third, with ten syllables, there is worship along with the limbs, the guardians of the directions, and so forth.
One should recite [the mantra] five hundred thousand times and then perform ten thousand oblations with milk-rice;
thereafter, the mantras become effective for men, bestowing prosperity and splendor.
The phrase beginning with "of these" (eteṣām) and so forth is easy to understand.
Regarding "in the maker" (divākare), it refers to the solar disc (sūrya-maṇḍala). // KrdC_7.58-60 //
He clearly extracts another mantra:
"The eighteen-syllable mantra ending with *bhāra* bestows sons and wealth;
its seer and other [limbs] are stated as eighteen syllables, [arranged] by means of the vowels mounted upon the *māra*s in their proper order."
O dear one, the limbs of this mantra are worshipped by the guardians of the directions and others.

The previously mentioned eighteen-syllable mantra, with the *kāma-bīja* at its end, bestows sons and wealth. Its six limbs are formed, respectively, by the six long vowels (*krāṃ*, *krīṃ*, etc. combined with the *kāma-bīja*—which is devoid of neuter vowels and mounted upon the *māra* [syllables]. (KrdC 7.61)
He describes the meditation:
joyfully bearing in his right hand a vessel containing milk-rice with its flavor infused,
and in his left holding fresh butter resembling the orb of the autumnal moon;
May the Divine Child of Yaśodā, who bears an unrestrained radiance and whose toenails are fashioned like lotuses upon his throat, and who is clothed in the celestial directions, grant you happiness.
"In his hand" refers to the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) that has been well-cooked; "well-cooked" means very delicious. "Exceedingly intense radiance" means exceedingly brilliant splendor.
Regarding the term "divya," it is a compound meaning one who is both divine (*divya*) and sky-clad (*digambara*).
"Having the nature of a divine deity. (KrdC 7.62)
Having worshipped Govinda daily for thirty-two hundred thousand times according to the prescribed measure,
one should perform the fire-oblation with sugar, clarified butter, and milk, using a tenth part of the recitation count.
With milk-rice mixed with sugar and ghee, and with *paramānna* accompanied by sugar and clarified butter.
Having worshipped the deity seated upon a lotus, one should offer libations into his lotus-like mouth with milk,
ripe plantains, curd, and fresh butter.
One seeking a son should likewise perform this libation; within a year he obtains a son.
Whatever one desires, all that is accomplished through this very libation.
The libation (tarpaṇa) that was mentioned with the words "with milk" and so forth should be performed using water itself, while maintaining the mental conception of it as substances such as milk.
He extracts another mantra:
Vāgbhava, the seed-syllable of Māra, Kṛṣṇāya, Bhuvaneśvarī, Govindāya, Ramā, and the word "Gopījanavallabha" followed by the dative case-ending (ṅe) and the head-portion (śiras). Krd 7.66.

The seed-syllable *vāgbhava* is *aim*; the seed-syllable of Māra is *klīṃ*; the essential form is *kṛṣṇāya*; the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī is *hrīṃ*; the essential form is *govindāya*; the seed-syllable of Ramā-Śrī is *śrīṃ*; the essential form is *gopījanavallabha*; the dative singular case-ending is *ṅe*; the head-mantra is *svāhā*; and in the reading "Śukra," it refers to the white letter *śa*, endowed with the fourteenth vowel (*au*) and accompanied by the vowel *au*.
The dental *sa*-kāra is "saṃ," which means "salutation to the self of semen" (*śukrātmane namaḥ*).
According to the rule for ritual placement (*nyāsa*), it is accompanied by the *sarga* (the vowel *i*) and the *visarga*.
Regarding the phrase "above that" (*tad-ūrdhvataḥ*), Rudradhara explains that it means "above that"—namely, above that twenty-first syllable—this is the first seed-syllable (*bīja*). KrdC_7.66.
Established upon fourteen [vowels], white and creative,
with twenty-two syllables above that, this mantra is the means for accomplishing mastery over speech.
The seed-syllable *vāgbhava* is *aim*; the seed-syllable of Māra is *klīṃ*; the essential form is *kṛṣṇāya*; the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī is *hrīṃ*;

the essential form is *govindāya*; the seed-syllable of Ramā is *śrīṃ*; the essential form is *gopījanavallabha*; then the dative singular case-ending *ṅe*; then the head-mantra *svāhā*. In the reading "Śukra," the letter *śa*, which is white, is endowed with the fourteenth vowel and accompanied by the letter *au*.
The letter *sa* produced from the dental [place] is "saṃ," which is for the self of semen (*śukrātmane namaḥ*).

According to the rule of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), it is accompanied by the *sarga* (the *visarga*) and is situated above that; Rudradhara says this means "above that" twenty-first syllable, while the author of the *Laghudīpikā* says it means "above the *svāhā*-syllable."
Together with this seed-syllable, it becomes a mantra of twenty-two syllables. Of what nature is it? It is the bestower of mastery over speech. (KrdC 7.66–67)
Its entire system, including the limbs, the ṛṣis, and so forth, consists of eighteen syllables;
the worship has been described as consisting of twenty syllables, and now the practical application is being explained.

The meaning is that all its components—the seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-devatā*), seed-syllable (*bīja*), power (*śakti*), and limbs (*aṅga*)—are like those in the eighteen-syllable mantra; it is just as it was there, so it is here too.
Furthermore, the worship (*pūjā*) should be understood as described for the twenty-syllable [mantra], and the practice (*pratipatti*) is further explained as meditation (*dhyāna*).
In her upper left hand she holds the book containing the entire essence of knowledge,
and in her upper right hand she holds a crystal rosary composed of the *mātṛkās*.
He is dark-complexioned with a tender luster, wearing yellow garments, and singing while playing with his two lower hands a flute composed of the Word-Brahman (śabda-brahman).
One should always worship Hari, who has a peacock feather as his crest-ornament, who is omniscient, and who is attended by hosts of sages and all-knowing seers.

With these three verses, there is an *ādikulaka* here. One should worship and meditate upon Hari as holding in His upper left hand the book that is the entire essence of knowledge— the Vedānta manuscript— and in His upper right hand, a rosary of fifty crystal beads, equal in number to the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā.
Wearing a rosary of beads;
furthermore, of what nature?
With his two hands positioned below, he holds a flute-hole that is sounded and played, consisting of the Sound-Brahman (śabda-brahma) and having the Sound-Brahman as its very essence.
Furthermore, of what sort?
Singing with a flute itself.
Furthermore, of what sort?
He whose [clothing] is yellow and who is dark-complexioned;
furthermore, of what nature is he?
He whose complexion is tender and charming is such, and him [he saw].
Furthermore, of what kind?
He by whom a crest-ornament—a head-adornment—made from the *barha*, or tail-feather, of a *barhin*, or peacock, has been fashioned.
Furthermore, of what kind?
The witness of all;
furthermore, of what nature is he?
He who is worshipped at all times.
By whom has it been practiced? By the hosts of sages such as Sanaka and others, who are all-knowing—that is, those who know the past and the future. (KrdC 7.69–71)
Regarding the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa), he says:

"Having thus meditated upon Bhuvaneśvara, who possesses the playful grace of entering into a woman, the practitioner of mantra, well-restrained, should recite this mantra four hundred thousand times. (Krd 7.72)

Thus, one who has performed the previously mentioned *puraścaraṇa* should, being well-restrained, meditate upon Śrī-Kṛṣṇa—the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśvara*)—who possesses the delight (*vilāsa*) or joy arising from the attire (*veśa*) and particular posture (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) of a young woman (*pramadā*), meaning he assumes the form of a maiden; or rather, having meditated on Him as bearing the form of a woman and possessing feminine grace, one should recite this mantra four hundred thousand times. (Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta 7.72)
Regarding the fire offering (homa), he says:
One should offer forty thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers mixed with honey; by this rite, the mantra will certainly become perfected (*siddha*). (Kṛd 7.73)
One should perform forty thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar;
by this rite, the mantra will certainly be accomplished.
He demonstrates the fruit [of this practice]:
"The speech of that minister whose intellect is proficient in this [tantra], as it issues from the cavern of his mouth, consists of prose and verse and flows like the current of the Gaṅgā. (Kṛd 7.74)

From the cavern of the mouth—the interior of the face—of that practitioner who dwells with an intellect perfected in this mantra and whose mind is fully dedicated to it, speech consisting of prose and verse issues forth; it is compared to the flow of the Gaṅgā because of its purity and uninterrupted nature, just like the current of the Gaṅgā. (KrdC 7.74)
Learned in all the Vedas, the scriptures, and the arts of music,
and having attained supreme realization, may he reach the highest state in the end.

Being a learned scholar endowed with discriminative intelligence regarding all the scriptures beginning with the Ṛgveda and including the Vedāntas, one attains supreme knowledge (*saṃvitti*) and, at the end, upon the dissolution of the body, reaches the world of Viṣṇu.
He states another mantra: "The *tāra* (Om), the heart (*hṛt*), the Lord (*bhagavān*), ending with *ṅe*, and likewise the word *Nandaputra*."
At the end of bliss, for the body that is entering the fire of the bones, there is the ten-syllable mantra.

This [mantra] consists of twenty-eight syllables; I shall now speak of the thirty-two-syllable version: the word *nandaputra* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), likewise the word *śyāmalāṅga*, the word *bālavapuḥ* ending in the dative case, and the ten-syllable sequence *kṛṣṇagovinda*. (Krd 7.77)

The *tāra* is the *praṇava* (oṃ). The heart-mantra is "namaḥ" followed by the Lord's name in the dative case ending in *-ṅe*. The essential form is "bhagavate. Then "nandaputraṃ," likewise in the dative case ending in *-ṅe*, becomes "nandaputrāya" at the end of the word. At the remainder of the words, "ānanda" is used, and the essential form is "vapuṣe. The letter *śa* is "asthi," the letter *ra* is "agni," and the long vowel *ī* is "māyā"; thus, this is the seed-syllable *śrī*. At the end of this is the ten-syllabled mantra (*daśārṇaka*). By this, this mantra consists of twenty-eight syllables.
Now he extracts the thirty-two-syllable mantra:

*nanda*, the word *putra* in the dative case (*nandaputrāya*), the word *śyāmalāṅga* also in the dative case (*śyāmalāṅgāya*), and the words *bālavapuḥ*, *kṛṣṇa*, and *govinda*, each also in the dative case (*bālavapuṣe*, *kṛṣṇāya*, *govindāya*).
Following these is the previously mentioned ten-syllable mantra.
By this, the mantra consists of thirty-two syllables.
Vimarśa: Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the son of Nanda, whose form is bliss, Śrīṃ, the beloved of the cowherd women; svāhā! (KrdC 7.76)
Svāhā to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, the dark-limbed one, the youth with a child’s body, Govinda, the beloved of the cowherd women!
He shows the seer and so forth:
"For these two, Nārada is the seer; the meters are Triṣṭubh and Anuṣṭubh;
the limbs [of the mantra] are worshipped with Ācakrā and others, and the guardians of the directions and so forth. (Kṛd 7.78)
For these two, the seer is Nārada;

the meters are Triṣṭubh and Anuṣṭubh respectively. The five limbs are performed with the previously mentioned [mantras] beginning with *ācakrāya*, and the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjana*) is performed with the limbs, the guardians of the directions, and the [deities] beginning with Vajra. The worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*), however, is as before.
Now he shows the visualization (*dhyāna*):
One should meditate upon Hari, holding a jeweled cup in his right hand and a golden cane in his left, embraced by two goddesses.
One should meditate upon Hari.
Of what sort? Holding a jeweled vessel in his right hand and a cane fashioned of gold in his left hand.
Furthermore, of what sort?
Embraced by the two goddesses Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, or by Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā.
One should recite the excellent mantra one hundred thousand times and perform ten thousand oblations with milk-rice;
thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall become a possessor of sovereignty over the three worlds.
One should recite each of the two supreme mantras one hundred thousand times.

Immediately thereafter, one should perform ten thousand oblations with *paramānna* (excellent food). By this, the mantra becomes perfected, and the practitioner of that mantra becomes a recipient of sovereignty over the three worlds.
