He states another mantra: enriched with the seed-syllables of Tāra, Śrī, and Śakti; the word *namo bhagavate*;
the word *nandaputra* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*); and [the name] Bhūdhara joined with the face-circle (the vowel *u*).
At the end of the month, for the sake of the body, there is a mantra consisting of nineteen syllables.
The syllable *tāra* (om), the *praṇava*, the *śrī-bīja*, and the *bhuvaneśvarī-bīja*—this mantra is enriched by these three seed-syllables. Then follows the essential form: *namo bhagavate*.

After that, the word *nandaputra* in the dative case (*caturthy-anta*), followed by the letter *ba* (the "earth-bearer"), the letter *ā* (the "face-circle"), and the letter *la* (associated with "flesh").
At the end of this is the essential form *vapuṣe*. By this, the mantra consists of nineteen syllables.
It becomes extracted.
The extraction of the mantra: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the son of Nanda, who possesses the body of a child.
The seer is Brahmā, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the rest has been declared as before;
this [mantra] should be practiced by the wise for the sake of attaining all prosperity and success. (Kṛd 7.82)

The meaning is that for this mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) and the metre (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh; everything else has been stated [elsewhere], and all other points are to be understood as being the same as previously mentioned. (KrdC 7.82)
He extracts the mantra:

*Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), the heart (*hṛt*), the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) ending with *ṅe*, and likewise *rukmiṇī-vallabha* ending with the head (*śiro 'nta*). This sixteen-syllable mantra is called *Rukmiṇī-vallabha*. (Kṛd 7.83)
*Tāra* (the syllable Om), *praṇava* (the syllable Om), *hṛt* (Namaḥ), the word *bhagavān* ending in the dative case, and likewise the word *rukmiṇī-vallabha* ending in the dative case;
[these constitute] the head ending with the word *svāhā*. By this, the sixteen-syllable mantra known as *Rukmiṇī-vallabha* has been described. (KrdC 7.83)
Vimarśa: Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the Beloved of Rukmiṇī; svāhā!

This mantra bestows all prosperity; Nārada is remembered as its sage (ṛṣi). The meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Hari, the beloved of Rukmiṇī. Its five limbs consist of one, four, three, four, and seven syllables respectively. Kṛd 7.84.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is Nārada, the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity (devatā) is Hari, the beloved of Rukmiṇī.
Regarding the word "eka":
there are five limbs (pañcāṅga) of this mantra.
By what? By one, two, four, seven, or two syllables of the mantra.
He describes the meditation:

[The practitioner should visualize] his beloved, who possesses the hue and color of the *tāpiccha* flower, whose entire radiance is all-pervading, and whose left arm emerges from a lotus; she embraces him with her own left arm, which holds the *cintāmaṇi* jewel.

May Hari— clad in yellow garments like the flowers of the *āsana* tree, adorned with various ornaments, and holding a golden staff that shines in another’s hand as he embraces her— protect you for a long time.
May Hari—possessing the luster of the *tāpiccha* tree and the beauty of the *tamāla*—protect you;
what is he doing? Embracing with his hand, which holds the *cintāmaṇi* jewel, his beloved fair-limbed lady who rests in his lap;
[or rather,] embracing her as she embraces him, the Lord, with her right hand.
What kind of Hari is he? He is one who holds a golden staff in his other hand while embracing [her]. Furthermore, what kind is he?
He whose garments are yellow like the flowers of the *āsana* tree;
furthermore, of what nature is he? He who possesses ornaments of various kinds. (KrdC 7.85)
Regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), he says:
"Having thus meditated upon the Lord of Rukmiṇī, one should mutter this mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations with ten thousand reddish lotuses soaked in honey. (Kṛd 7.86)
Having thus meditated upon the previously described beloved of Rukmiṇī, the Lord of Rukmiṇī, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should also perform ten thousand oblations with red lotuses soaked in ghee, honey, and sugar. (KrdC 7.86)
He shows the worship:

"A person should constantly worship Him with His limbs [the deities], with Nārada and the other lords of the directions, and also with Vajra and the others, for the attainment of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. (Kṛd 7.87)

The worship of the *pīṭha* is as before. Now the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*) is described: one should worship Hari daily with the limbs beginning with the *ācakra*, as mentioned in the evening worship, as well as with Nārada and the others, the lords of the directions beginning with Indra, and their weapons beginning with the thunderbolt (*vajra*).
Of what nature is it? It bestows the fourfold aims of human life.
He extracts another mantra:
the word *gopī-jana-saṃsakta-doḥ* ending with *līlā-daṇḍa*, then at the end of *daṇḍa* the word *bāla-rūpa*, and after that the word *megha-śyāma*. (Kṛdanta 7.88)
Having stated "Bhagavān Viṣṇu," followed by the wife of fire (svāhā) and the end-maker (namaḥ), this mantra consists of twenty-nine syllables; Nārada is declared to be its sage.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh and the deity is Hari bearing the playful staff;
the limbs and ritual actions are considered to consist of syllables numbering fourteen, four, eleven, and four respectively.

The meaning is as follows: after the word *līlā-daṇḍa*, at the end of the word *līlā-daṇḍa*, one should place the word *gopī-jana-saṃsakta-doh*; immediately after the word *daṇḍa*, the word *bāla-rūpa*; and after that, the word *megha-śyāma*.
The word "also" (*api*) is connected [to each preceding term] like the eye of a crow (i.e., it applies to all).
Then, having uttered the vocative ending *bhagavān viṣṇo*, at the end of the word *svāhā*, the mantra consisting of twenty-nine syllables should be extracted. This is the sense.
For this mantra, Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and Hari, the wielder of the play-staff, is the deity (devatā). Regarding "manv-abdhi":
for this mantra, the limbs (aṅga) are fourteen (the Manus), the actions (kriyā) are four (the oceans), the instruments (karaṇa) are five, and the fires are three.
The four oceans are considered and agreed upon by those mantra-syllables numbering that much; the meaning is that these are the five limbs.
The extraction of the mantra: *Līlā-daṇḍa-gopī-jana-saṃsakta-dor-daṇḍa-bāla-rūpa-megha-śyāma bhagavan Viṣṇo svāhā*.
He states the meditation (*dhyāna*):
May He, whose right hand is joined with His own beloved, grant blessings— He who bewilders the young cowherd women and the celestial beauties with the playful staff held in His own left hand.
May the Lord of wide strides, who slew Kaṃsa, bestow prosperity upon you.

May the Lord Urukrama—having slain Kaṃsa—grant you prosperity; he who, with his left hand holding his playful staff, bewilders the young cowherd girls and the celestial beauties, while his right hand is joined with that of his own beloved.
Regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), he says:

"Having meditated thus, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times or ten thousand times; one should offer oblations of sesame and rice grains smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*); and one should worship the limbs [of the deity], the guardians of the directions, and so forth. (Krd 7.92)
Having thus meditated upon Kṛṣṇa as previously described, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Following that, one should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar. Thus it is said.
The worship of the seat (pīṭha-pūjā) is as before, along with the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇa-pūjā) by means of the five limbs and [the worship] of Indra and the others.
He states the fruit of the daily worship:
"Whoever indeed worships Hari with constant devotion as the playful staff, he is honored by all the worlds; Indirā always worships him. (Kṛd 7.93)
That man who daily serves Hari, who holds the staff of divine play (Līlā-daṇḍa), is honored by all people;
Lakṣmī, the goddess Indirā, always attends upon him. (Kṛdanta 7.93)
He extracts another mantra:
"The Śārṅgin, joined with the thirteenth vowel, along with Bheda and Keśava;
likewise, the pair 'Māṃsa', 'Bhāya', and 'Śiras'—this is the seven-syllable mantra. (Krd 7.94)
The thirteenth vowel is the syllable *oṃ*; joined with that is the letter *ga*, which is Śārṅgin; the letter *va* is Medas. Of what nature is he? He is Keśava, accompanied by the letter *a*.
Likewise, "the pair of flesh" refers to the two *la* letters; thus [the mantra is] *bhāya śiraḥ svāhā*.
By this, the seven-syllable mantra has been stated.
The nature of the mantra:
Svāhā to the Beloved of the Cow.
He states the seer and so forth:
"The formation of the limbs [of the mantra] begins with *ā* and *ca*; Nārada is remembered as its seer (*ṛṣi*); the meter is *uṣṇih*, and Govallabha is declared to be its deity. (Kṛd 7.95)
The five-limbed ritual is performed with [the syllables] beginning with *ā* and *ca*.
For this mantra, Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*) and *uṣṇih* is the meter (*chanda*).
Kṛṣṇa is the deity beloved by cows.
He describes the meditation: "The object of meditation is Acyuta, seated in the midst of the group of Kapilās,
calling out to them while holding a flute in his left hand."
Elsewhere, he is dark as a rain cloud, wearing yellow garments, with a noose and a staff, and adorned with a crest made of peacock feathers— the enemy of serpents.

The infallible Kṛṣṇa is to be meditated upon. Of what nature is he? He is one who dwells within a herd of Kapilā cows, which is a collection of a specific kind of cattle. What is he doing? He is calling out to those Kapilā cows, drawing them toward himself.
Furthermore, of what sort is he?
Carrying a bamboo flute with its holes in his left hand upon his right shoulder,
and holding in his other, the right hand, the rope used for tethering cattle together with a staff.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is as dark as a rain-cloud, with garments of yellow.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
The enemy of snakes is the peacock;
its tail-feathers are the crest.
He by whom an ear-ornament or head-ornament has been made from that [feather] is thus described.
He states the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
One should recite this [mantra] one hundred thousand times for a sage; to remove [obstacles], one should recite it seven thousand times.
In the midst of the guardians of the directions, colored with cow’s milk, one should worship the eight groups of cows.
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times for a sage (muni-lakṣa) or seven hundred thousand times.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) seven thousand times with cow’s milk.

Regarding the limb-worship (aṅga-pūjā), before the worship of the guardians of the directions (dikpāla-pūjā), a group of eight cows should be worshipped; and that group of eight cows should be positioned starting from the east (the first direction).
The first is golden-colored; the second is tawny;
the third is fair with reddish-brown eyes; and the fourth is brown like molasses.
The fifth is cloud-colored; these are the most excellent among cows.
The fourth is tawny (piṅgalā), the sixth is the same, and the seventh is reddish-brown at the hooves (khura-piṅgalā).
The eighth is tawny (kapilā); this is to be known as the group of tawny cows (kapilā-gaṇa).
This has been stated by this [verse]. (KṛdC 7.97)
He states another application:

"Whoever offers one thousand and eight oblations daily with milk, after a fortnight he becomes enriched with herds of cattle; or this same procedure may be performed with *daśārṇa* [honey]. (Kṛd 7.98)
He who offers more than one thousand oblations daily with cow’s milk becomes endowed with a herd of cows within fifteen days;
the meaning is that this ritual application may be performed with the ten-syllable mantra.
He states another mantra: "Vāsudeva with the suffix -salava, the word *bhagavat* ending in *-ṅe*, and likewise the word *śrī-govinda*; this is declared to consist of twelve syllables. (Krd 7.99)
The letter *la* is the *bindu*.
Accompanied by that, Vāsudeva is the syllable *oṃ*, that is to say, the *praṇava*.
Then there is the word *namaḥ* ending in the dative case, as well as the word *bhagavat* ending in the dative case, and likewise the word *śrī-govinda* ending in the dative case.
By this, the twelve-syllable mantra has been extracted.
The nature of the mantra: Oṃ namo bhagavate śrī-govindāya.
He states the seer and so forth:
"Manu, Nārada, Gāyatrī, Kṛṣṇa, and the seers; then the ancillary parts [are formed] with one, three, four, and five syllables, or even with all of them combined. (KRD 7.100)
In some places, the reading "muniḥ" is not appropriate, because it lacks grammatical connection and involves tautology; rather, the reading must be "manuḥ.
Rudradhara maintains that the reading "ayam" is obtained through logical reasoning. (KrdC 7.100)
He describes the meditation:

I bow to Murāri, who is seated upon a jeweled lion-throne at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree; he has a blue luster, wears yellow garments, and holds in his lotus-like hands a conch and a staff that shines.
Surrounded by cows of great renown, bathed by the pure streams flowing from the jar held in the hand of the exalted Lord of the Immortals, and possessing eyes with the luster of fresh lotus petals.
I bow to Murāri.
Of what nature is he? He is seated upon a lion-throne fashioned from rubies, situated at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He who has a dark-blue luster and is dressed in yellow garments, whose lotus-hands shine with a conch and a staff, who is surrounded by cows with flowing udders and milk-filled teats,
and who stands upon a jar placed on the hand of Indra, the lord of the immortals, which is mature and most powerful— [him I salute].
Therefore, he is one whose eyes possess a luster and beauty like the petals of a fresh, newly blossomed lotus that has been bathed by streams of flowing nectar.
Regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), he says:

"Having thus meditated upon Acyuta and performed the recitation (*japa*) one hundred thousand times, one should then offer oblations (*homa*) with milk twelve thousand times daily; in this manner, one should worship him. (Krd 7.102)
Having thus meditated upon the previously mentioned Acyuta and having recited [the mantra] twelve hundred thousand times, one should offer oblations with milk twelve thousand times;
or else, one should worship him every day.
He shows the distinction in worship regarding the sacred sites and so forth:
"Whether established in a cow-pen, in one's own home, or in images and the like, those attendants of Viṣṇu are to be worshipped together with their entire retinue. (Kṛd 7.103)
At the front of the door, on the offering pedestal (bali-pīṭha), the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is to be worshipped;
in front of him are Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa to the east, and Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ to the south.
One should worship Jaya and Vijaya in the west, Bala and Prabala in the north,
and having worshipped Dvāraśrī above, one should worship the door-guardians in pairs.
There, the Vāstupuruṣa, situated in the middle of the door-sill, is to be worshipped;
likewise, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the two Treasures (Nidhis) are to be honored on the inner sides of the doorway.
In the corners, one should worship Vighna, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Kṣetreśa;
with a concentrated mind, the wise man should worship Vāstupuruṣa in the center of the house, or according to the requirements of the deity worship, in the southwest.

In the cow-pen—that is, in the place where the cows stay—he should worship Viṣṇu installed there; likewise, he should worship Viṣṇu installed in his own home within images fashioned from gold and other materials—this is the connection with what precedes.
Those very same complete offerings to the retinue mentioned previously are to be performed.

Likewise, the attendants of Viṣṇu who are about to be described should be worshipped in pairs on the offering pedestals at the front of the four doors starting from the east; here, according to the Tripāṭhin tradition, this should be understood as a specific requirement for the worship of the four doors starting from the east—both in the previously mentioned initiation worship (*dīkṣā-pūjā*) associated with the twelve-syllable Govinda mantra, and in the daily single-time worship (*ekakāla-pūjā*). [The mantra is: "Salutations again and again to Acyuta together with his entire retinue."
"Salutations again and again to the attendants of Viṣṇu.
By means of these two mantras, one should worship on the offering-platform at the front of the four doors, starting from the east; this is the meaning.
The Lord of Birds is Garuḍa.
He is to be worshipped in front of that, at the front of the pedestal for the offering of the *bali*.
Regarding the instruction "first [he] shows the attendants of Viṣṇu":
having worshipped the Door-Glory (*dvāra-śrī*) in the upper portion of the four gates of the square [mandala], one should worship Caṇḍa and the others, two by two.

In due order, beginning from the eastern door, one should worship the Vāstupuruṣa between the door and the offering pedestal with the mantra: "Obeisance to the Vāstupuruṣa. At the end of each door—that is, on both side-panels in the middle of the four doors—one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā, as well as the Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi treasures.
Thereafter, having entered the pavilion, one who is self-restrained should again worship the Vāstupuruṣa in the corners beginning with the southeast.
He invokes the weapon-mantra:

having uttered "Tāra" (Om), the word "Śārṅga" in the dative case, followed by "Sa-pūrva-śarāsana" (the bow together with its string), and "Huṃ Phaṭ Namaḥ," he stands before Hari with the weapon-gesture (*astramudrā*). (Krd 7.108)
Then, one should scatter flowers and consecrated rice-grains (akṣata) in all directions while seated upon the seat;
this should be performed everywhere, especially when [the deities] have been installed.
Having uttered "Tāra" (Oṃ), the Praṇava (Oṃ),

the word "Śārṅga" with the dative ending (Ṅe), followed by "Sa-pūrva-sa-śarāsana" with the dative ending, and then "Huṃ Phaṭ Namaḥ," one should scatter flowers and consecrated grains (akṣata) in the four directions using the Astra-mudrā with a snap of the fingers.

Of what kind [is he]? He stands before Hari; thereafter, he should sit upon his appropriate seat. All of this must be performed at the beginning of every worship, and it must be performed especially so in the case of installed images and the like. (KrdC 7.108–109)
He states the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā):

"Then, having performed the self-worship up to its conclusion, [one should worship] the lineage of gurus as previously described, as well as the venerable gurus beginning with the Supreme One (Paramādya), and all our great predecessors. (Krd 7.110)

Having worshipped the *pīṭha* within one’s own body according to the previously described form, and having worshipped the Lord in the heart, one should thereafter worship the lineage of gurus (*guru-paṅkti*) upon the external *pīṭha*, as before, in the northern direction as mentioned in the previously cited section on initiation.
He states the lineage of gurus itself with the words "the venerable gurus" (*śrī-gurūn*).
Those preceded by the word "Śrī" are the gurus and the supreme gurus;
and the formula is: "Homage to the Śrī-gurus," and "Homage to the Śrī-parama-gurus."
Homage to the glorious great gurus! Homage to our glorious gurus!
Homage to all gurus! KrdC_7.110 //
Immediately after worshipping the sandals of that [deity], Ārādhya, and the other previously established [deities],
and then the Bhāgavatas, one should worship Vighna on the right side.

Regarding that [salutation], the author of the *Laghu-dīpikā* says it is "to the sandals of Nārada and others who were previously perfected and devoted to the Lord" (*bhāgavata*). The *Tripāṭhin*s say: "Obeisance to the sandals of the venerable Guru; obeisance to the sandals of the venerable Supreme Guru, the sandals of the Original Guru, the sandals of the Great Guru, the sandals of our own Guru, and the sandals of all Gurus."
Having thus worshipped the row of gurus on the seat to the north, one should worship Gaṇeśa to the south.
Having worshipped the pedestal as before, one should then worship Śrī Govinda,
with Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā at his sides and Indra in front.

Having worshipped Surabhi behind [the central deity], one should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅga-devatās) upon the filaments, beginning with the Heart-mantra and ending with the Armor-mantra; the Weapon-mantra is to be worshipped in the cardinal directions and in the intermediate corners.
Having worshipped, according to the previously described method, from the *ādhāra-śakti* up to the *pīṭha-mantra*, one should invoke the Deity and worship Him with the *arghya* and other offerings.
Regarding the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*), he says: "Rukmiṇī.
Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā are to be worshipped on the right and left sides of Govinda, respectively, upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) in front of the Deity.

Having worshipped Indra, one should worship Surabhi behind the deity; then, on the filaments in the four cardinal and intermediate directions starting from the east, the limb-deities beginning with Hṛdaya and ending with Varma are to be worshipped.
Furthermore, on the filaments in the corners, one should again worship the weapon-limb.
The six Śaktis—Kālindī, Rohiṇī, Nāgnajitī, and so forth—are to be worshipped on the petals;
and the bells (kiṅkiṇīs) are to be worshipped with fire and the other [elements] in the corners of the pedestal.
One should then worship the cords, the staff, and the bamboo in front, followed by the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem,
and the forest garland in front, and then [the deities] in the eight directions.
Pāñcajanya, the mace, the discus, Vasudeva, and Devakī;
Nanda the cowherd, Yaśodā, along with the cows, the cowherds, and the gopīs.

The Śaktis beginning with Kālindī, who are the wives of the gods, are to be worshipped on the petals; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), Sunandā, Mitravindā, and Sulakṣmaṇā are included. One should worship the small bells, garlands, and so forth in the corners of the seats starting from the southeast (āgneya).
Among those, one should place the small bell of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa in the southeast corner.

For the purpose of protecting the cows, [one should place] ropes in the southwest (Nairṛta); for the purpose of driving the cows, a staff in the northwest (Vāyu); a bamboo pole in the northeast (Īśāna) corner; the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha gem in front of the Deity;

the forest garland (vanamālā) in front of the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha; and above that, the Pāñcajanya conch and others in the eight directions. These should be worshipped with mantras ending in "Obeisance to Pāñcajanya" and "Obeisance to the cows, cowherds, and gopīs. By the word "and others" (ādi), the inclusion of the mace (gadā), the discus (cakra), Vasudeva, Devakī, Nanda, and Yaśodā is intended. (KrdC 7.114–116)
Indra and the others, as well as Kumuda and the others, [should be placed] with Viśvaksena in the north;
namely, Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita.

Indra and the other deities are to be worshipped in their respective directions; their weapons, such as the thunderbolt (vajra) and others included by the word "and so forth" (ādi), as well as the eight elephants beginning with Kumuda, are likewise to be worshipped above them in their respective directions. Outside of that, one should worship Viṣvaksena in the north among the deities.
He states the fruit of worship:
"One should constantly worship Śrī Govinda at the cow-pen once, twice, or thrice a day, and provide fodder to the cows. (Krd 7.118)
Long-lived and free from fear, enriched in this world with cattle, grain, wealth, sons, and friends, he at the end attains the supreme state.
One should worship Kṛṣṇa, who resides in the cow-pen and the cow-shed, once, twice, or thrice every day.

By providing mouthfuls of fodder to the cows while remaining present in their world, one becomes long-lived, fearless, and endowed with cattle, grain, gold, sons, friends, and so forth; and at the end of the body's fall, one goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
He states another mantra:
"The letter Ū, joined with the letter at the end [of the alphabet] (Ḥ), followed by Śārṅgin, Cakrin, and the right ear (R);
then Māṃsa, ending with Nāthāya and the word of salutation (Namaḥ). This is the eight-syllabled root mantra. (Krd 7.120)

The syllable *oṃ* with the vowel *u* at its end; joined with that is the syllable *ga*, which is "the wielder of the Śārṅga bow" (*śārṅgī*); the syllable *ka*, which is "the wielder of the discus" (*cakrī*), joined with the right ear, i.e., accompanied by the vowel *u*;

the syllable *la*, which is "flesh" (*māṃsī*); followed by the form *nāthāya*; ending with the act of bowing, i.e., the word *namaḥ*. This eight-syllabled mantra is known as the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). (KrdC 7.120)
He states the seer and so forth:
"The seer is Brahmā, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Kṛṣṇa;
the five limbs are declared by means of the colors of the ages and by the whole [mantra]. (Kṛd 7.121)

For this mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda), and Śrī-Kṛṣṇa is the presiding deity (devatā). By the word "and" (ca), which implies an unmentioned collection, the seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), and the presiding deity are included, just as in the case of the ten-syllabled mantra. Furthermore, for this mantra, the five limbs (pañcāṅga) are to be understood through four pairs of syllables arising from the mantra, along with the complete mantra itself as the fourth limb. (KrdC 7.121)
He speaks of meditation: [one should meditate on] a five-year-old child, exceedingly proud, running about in the courtyard with eyes disheveled by tresses.
Remember the cowherd boy adorned with tinkling bells, bracelets, necklaces, and anklets.
Bow down to the cowherd child.

Of what nature is he? He is five years of age, exceedingly strong, running about in the courtyard, with extremely restless eyes, and adorned with tinkling bells, small bells, bracelets, armlets, and pearl necklaces.
Ankle-ornaments and the tips of the scales; by these it is anointed and adorned.
Regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), he says:
"Having meditated thus, one should mutter [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times, or at least one thousand;
one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree or with milk-rice (*pāyasa*). (Kṛd 7.123)
Having thus meditated upon what was previously described, one should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
Thereafter, one should offer oblations eight thousand times with fuel-sticks of the *palāśa* tree or with *paramānna* (milk-rice).
He states the manner of worship:

"One should constantly worship Kṛṣṇa installed in the temple by means of this [rite], having performed the worship of the door and so forth, ending with the worship of the pedestal, according to the prescribed path. (Krd 7.124)
One should worship Kṛṣṇa, who has been installed in the white palace, every day in the manner that will be described hereafter;
one should perform the worship, beginning with the worship of the door and ending with the worship of the pedestal, according to the path of the mantras previously mentioned. // KrdC_7.124 //
In the center, one should worship Hari with the *arca*-mantras; in the cardinal and intermediate directions, the limbs (*aṅga*) in sequence:
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Lakṣmaṇā, and Jāmbavatī—
one should worship these outside in the cardinal and intermediate directions, along with Indra, Vajra, and the others.
One should worship Hari in the center of the lotus;
one should worship the four limbs beginning with the Heart on the filaments in the cardinal directions starting from the East,
and the Weapon limb on the filaments in the intermediate directions starting from the Southeast.
Regarding "Vāsudeva":
one should worship Vāsudeva and the others on the petals of the cardinal directions, starting with the east;
one should worship Rukmiṇī and the others on the petals of the intermediate directions, starting with the southeast.
The meaning is that one should worship Indra and the others in their respective directions outside of that, and thereafter worship the vajra and the other [emblems]. // KrdC_7.126 //
He states the result:
"Whoever should constantly recite this mantra and worship Hari according to the prescribed rule, he, filled with all prosperity, shall eternally attain the pure state. (Krd 7.127)

The person who worships Hari according to the prescribed method and recites this mantra, being endowed with all sovereignty, attains the eternal, imperishable, pure state called Brahman, which is free from ignorance and its effects. He states another mantra:
At the end of *tāra* (om), *śrī*, *śakti* (hrīṃ), and *māra* (kṛṣṇāya), one should utter the word *śrī-kṛṣṇāya*;
above that, *śrī-govindāya*, and then *śrī-gopī-jana*;
then *vallabhāya*, and finally three times *śrī-siddhi-gopālaka*. This is the mantra.

*Tāra* (the syllable Om), *praṇava*, *śrīḥ*, the *śrī-bīja*, and the *śakti-bīja*; at the end of the *kāma-bīja*, the essential form "Śrī-Kṛṣṇāya," followed by the essential form "Śrī-Govindāya," followed by the essential form "Śrī-Gopījana-Vallabhāya," and the three *śrī-bījas*—
thus is the Siddhi-Gopāla mantra extracted.
He speaks of meditation:
"Seated in a bower of mādhavī vines, protected by Garuḍa. (Krd 7.129)

One should recite the mantra while remembering Rāma and Kṛṣṇa as they delight in divine sports. The single-syllable mantra is considered to be the Discus (Cakra) joined with the eighth vowel and the letter *s*. (Kṛd 7.130)
One should recite while remembering Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Of what sort are they? They are situated together in a bower of Mādhavī creepers and likewise served by Garuḍa.
He shows the Gopāla mantras beginning with the single syllable (Ekākṣara) as "Cakrī" and so forth.

The letter *ka* is the *vasu-svara*, which is the eighth vowel; accompanied by that is the letter *ṛ*, according to the author of the *Laghudīpikā*. It is accompanied by the *muni-svara*, which is the seventh vowel, according to Rudradhara. Together with the *sargī*, meaning the visarga, this constitutes the single-syllable mantra. (KrdC 7.129–130)
The two-syllable [mantra] is "Kṛṣṇa"; that same one, preceded by "Kāma," is three syllables;
that same one with the dative ending (-ṅe) is four syllables; and another is four syllables [as "Kṛṣṇāya"].
It will be stated that [the mantra] may consist of five syllables, such as "kṛṣṇāya namaḥ";
furthermore, there is another five-syllable [mantra], "kṛṣṇāya," situated between the two [names of the] Smara couple.
*Kṛṣṇa* is the essential form (*svarūpa*), a two-syllabled mantra.

If that same two-syllabled form is preceded by the *kāma-bīja*, it then becomes a three-syllabled mantra. If that same three-syllabled form ends in the fourth case (*caturthī-vibhakti*), it then becomes a four-syllabled mantra. Another [form] is *kṛṣṇāya*, which is the essential form of the pair of *smara*-mantras and the pair of *kāma*-bījas.
When it occurs in the middle, then there is another five-syllable mantra.
The six-syllable mantra is declared as "gopālāya" ending with the wife of fire (svāhā);
another is "kṛṣṇāya," enriched with the seed of desire (klīm), ending with the wife of fire.
The six-syllable mantra previously mentioned, as well as "Kṛṣṇa" and "Govinda" ending in the dative case, consist of seven syllables; another such seven-syllable mantra was mentioned earlier.
The six-syllable mantra is said to consist of the two words "gopālāya" (for Gopāla) and "svāhā," which is the wife of Fire (the *svāhā* syllable).

Another six-syllable mantra is extracted by her [the Goddess] with the two words "kṛṣṇāya" accompanied by the Kāma-bīja and "svāhā"; that other six-syllable mantra was already mentioned previously as "klīṃ kṛṣṇāya namaḥ."
If the words *kṛṣṇa* and *govindaka* end in the dative case, then there is another seven-syllable mantra; that other seven-syllable mantra previously mentioned is *go-vallabhāya svāhā*.

*Śrī-śakti-māraḥ* (Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ) followed by *kṛṣṇāya māraḥ* is another seven-syllable mantra. *Kṛṣṇa* and *govindaka* ending in the dative (*ṅe*) and enriched with the seed-syllable of Smara (klīṃ) constitute an eight-syllable mantra.

The syllables *śrī-śakti-mārāḥ* (the seed-syllable of Śrī-Bhuvaneśvarī) followed by *mārāntaḥ* ending with *kṛṣṇāya*, constitute another seven-syllabled mantra. The words *kṛṣṇa* and *govinda* are in the dative case (*ṅe*-anta), and how are they characterized? They are "enriched by the seed-syllable of Kāma. Thus, this is an eight-syllabled mantra consisting of eight letters (*vasu-varṇa*). (KrdC 7.135)
Another group of eight [suffixes] consists of *dadhi*, *bhakṣaṇa*, *ṅe*, *vahni*, and *jāyā*;
another group of eight consists of *suprasannātmane* followed by *mama*.

The word *dadhibhakṣaṇa* ending in the dative case, followed by the syllables *vahni-jāyā* (the wife of fire), namely *svāhā*—this is another eight-syllable mantra. Having spoken one's own nature as "to the well-pleased Self," one should say *namaḥ*;
this is another eight-syllable mantra.
The nine-syllable root mantra previously mentioned is joined with the word *smara*;
another nine-syllable mantra consists of *kṛṣṇa* and *govinda*, both ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), followed by *namaḥ*.
The previously mentioned eight-syllabled root mantra, when conjoined with *smara*—that is, joined with the *kāma-bīja*—becomes nine syllables.
That is: *klīṃ gokulanāthāya namaḥ*.
Furthermore, if *kṛṣṇa* and *govinda* are both in the dative case, ending in *-ṅe*, and are conjoined with *smara*, then it becomes a nine-syllabled mantra.
If these two alone end with "namaḥ" and have the word "namaḥ" at their conclusion, then the subsequent mantra consists of nine syllables.
*Klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ śyāmalāṅgāya namaḥ* is the ten-syllable mantra;
*klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* ending with the word for the head (*śiraḥ*) is known by the wise as the mantra for the one with a youthful body.

It has been stated that the meter is Gāyatrī and the deity is the praised Kṛṣṇa; one should then meditate upon Hari, whose limbs are formed by the syllables *ka*, *la*, *ṣa*, and *ḍga* with long vowels.

"Klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ śyāmalāṅgāya namaḥ" is the ten-syllable mantra ending with "namaḥ. "Bālavapuṣe klīṃ kṛṣṇāya svāhā" is the eleven-syllable mantra as remembered by the wise. Regarding these [mantras], he states the seers and other details: for these twenty-two mantras, beginning from the one-syllable up to the eleven-syllable, Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), and Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the deity (devatā).
He states the limbs: "with *kala*.
This means by means of the syllables *ka* and *la*, together with the six long vowels excluding the neuter [vowels], namely: *klāṃ klīṃ klūṃ klauṃ kalaḥ*. (KrdC 7.139)
He describes the meditation:
May Mukunda protect you— he who possesses the luster of an unblemished blue lotus, whose lotus-eyes are red,
who stands upon a lotus, and whose calves, hips, and waist are adorned with tinkling bells.

May He who is worshipped by the entire universe, who is surrounded by cows, gopīs, and cowherds, whose neck is adorned with a shimmering necklace of deer claws, and who holds in His two hands the fresh butter and the most pure milk-rice, protect you for a long time.
May Mukunda— the child who possesses the luster of a blue lotus in agitation, whose lotus-eyes are like red lotuses, who wears tinkling bells upon his calves and hips,
who holds with both arms the most pure fresh butter and milk-rice, who is worshipped by the universe, who is surrounded by cows, gopīs, and cowherds,
and whose neck is adorned with the shining claws of a deer— protect you for a long time.
Regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for these, he says:

"Having thus meditated upon one of these, one should then recite the mantra a hundred thousand times; thereafter, one should offer ten thousand oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee and white sugar. (Krd 7.141)
Having performed the meditation as described, one should recite one of these mantras one hundred thousand times.
Following that, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *paramānna* mixed with ghee, sugar, and the essence of grain.
One who worships with a well-concentrated mind should always perform the libation for other Manūs according to the number of oblations offered; such is the prescribed daily libation.
One should worship the limbs beginning with fire (the heart) and ending with peace (the armor), from the heart up to the armor;
then one should worship the eye in front and the weapon in the directions, and again fire.
Indra, Vajra, and the others are to be worshipped; this is declared to be their ritual service (*saparyā*).
Thus, the best of those who know the *mantras* should devote himself to one of these *mantras*.
Accumulated by the hand from all objects, he is worshipped by the immortals;
I shall now speak another four-syllabled mantra that bestows immediate fruit. (Krd 7.145)
He is addressed by the black syllable situated between the pair of Māras;
furthermore, the six limbs beginning with the seer (ṛṣi), which were previously mentioned, are prescribed for him.
Thereafter, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) ten thousand times.

When a single mantra has been mastered in this manner, for the other twenty-one mantras whose preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) have already been performed, the prescribed *puraścaraṇa* consists solely of the libation—without the need for the specific counts of recitation (*japa*) or fire-oblation (*homa*)—performed ten thousand times. This is what must be done.
For these mantras, the propitiation (tarpaṇa) is prescribed by means of exactly ten thousand (ayuta) oblations (homa).
Regarding worship, he says "constantly" (nityam):
one should worship constantly, at all times, being well-composed and self-restrained.

One should worship the four limbs, beginning with the heart-mantra and ending with the armor-mantra, starting from the southeast corner (āgneya-koṇa), which is peaceful with fire and the other elements, and extending to the northeast corner (īśāna-koṇa). One should worship the eye and the weapon in front, at the very forefront.
One should worship Indra and the others in the four directions, starting from the east.
Following that, one concludes by mentioning the vajra and the other [implements].
The worship and ritual service (*saparyā*) of these mantras has been explained.
He states the result:

"In this way, one"—meaning that by this method, whichever supreme practitioner (*sādhakottama*) among these mantras should devote himself to (*bhajet*) or practice (*upāsīta*) even a single mantra, for him all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) are within reach of his hand, and he is honored by the gods.
He states another mantra with the words "sadyaḥ" (immediately).
I shall now declare another four-syllable mantra that bestows immediate results. This four-syllable mantra is described by the word "Kṛṣṇa" situated between two *kāma*-bījas.
Its seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*daivata*), and the six-limbed ritual (*aṅga-ṣaṭka*) are to be understood as having been previously stated in the collection of earlier mantras.
He describes the meditative absorption (dhyāna):

He who is seated upon the shimmering pericarp of a lotus arisen from the root of the glorious wish-fulfilling tree, and who is consecrated by countless jewels trickling from the interior of that very lotus upon which he rests.
May that Vāsudeva, golden-hued, illuminating the entire three worlds with his own radiance,
who eats milk-rice and constantly partakes of fresh butter as nectar, and who is self-controlled, protect you.
May Vāsudeva protect you!
Of what nature is he? He who is seated upon the pericarp (karṇikā) shining within a lotus that has emerged from the root of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) endowed with Śrī;
likewise, he who is consecrated by the countless jewels trickling forth and spreading from the interior of the lotus hanging from the branch of that wish-fulfilling tree.
Likewise, golden-hued and illuminating the entire three worlds with his splendors, he subsists on milk-rice; likewise,
illuminating the entire three worlds with his own radiance, he constantly and at every moment eats fresh butter as if it were nectar.
Regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), he says:
"Having meditated thus, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; thereafter, one should perform oblations forty thousand times with bilva fruits smeared with the three sweets."
Having performed the meditation as described, one should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times.
Thereafter, one should offer forty thousand oblations of *bilva* fruits mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar.
Regarding the worship, he says:
"Worship is declared to be performed with the limbs, the treasures, Indra and the others, and the thunderbolt and the others;
one should satisfy Kṛṣṇa daily with water, perceiving it as the three sweets. (Kṛd 7.149)

The worship (pūjā) consisting of the offering of non-blue [substances] has been described as being performed with the six limbs, the eight treasures beginning with Indra, the deities beginning with Indra, and the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt (vajra).
He states the libation (tarpaṇa): "One should satisfy" (tarpayet).
Every day, one should worship Kṛṣṇa with water, perceiving it through the three sweet substances—the notion of clarified butter, honey, and sugar. (KṛdC 7.149)
He states another mantra:
"If there is blood from the flesh-eating Māra of this [deity], there is another mantra;
for this crest-jewel of mantras, the six limbs are formed by the six vowels with the long [vowels]. (Krd 7.150)

If, in this previously mentioned four-syllable mantra, there is a red *repha* (the letter *ra*) beneath the letter *la* which is below the *māṃsa* [syllable], situated between the two *kāma-bījas* at the beginning and end, then another four-syllable mantra arises:

*klīṃ kṛṣṇa klīm*. Regarding this crest-jewel of mantras, this head-jewel of mantras, one should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*) using the six long vowels (*kala-ṣaṭ-dīrgha*)—this is the remainder [of the instruction]. (KrdC 7.150)
The nature of the mantra:
klīṃ klūṃ kleṃ kloṃ klauṃ klaḥ.
He describes the meditation:
mounted upon a golden swing shimmering at the top of a wish-fulfilling tree in a slightly reddish garden,
being rocked by two cowherd girls, and glowing with the hue of a blooming fresh bandhūka flower and vermilion.

I worship Mukunda, who is lovely as a dark-blue child, richly adorned with a cluster of tiny bells dangling from his hips, and radiant with a neck as beautiful as the "elephant-hook" (kāmāṅkuśa) mark.
I bow to Mukunda—
of what nature? Seated upon a beautiful golden swing that shines atop the peak of a wish-fulfilling tree in a grove reddened by the dawn, and being rocked there by two cowherd girls.
He was like a young child with black hair, whose nature was like that of fresh *bandhujīva* flowers— swaying, blooming, and fully blossomed— and who was like vermilion;
he was bound at his waist by a cluster of tiny bells (*kṣudra-ghaṇṭikā*) moving here and there, and likewise [adorned] with a tiger’s [skin].
It was resplendent with that neck-ornament which shone as if it were the goad of desire belonging to a tiger.

Having meditated thus and having recited this [mantra] according to the previously established procedure, one should offer oblations with fresh red lotuses soaked in the three sweets, and then worship Hari as before.

Having meditated upon Mukunda as previously described and having recited this mantra the same number of times as before, one should offer oblations with fresh red lotuses mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar the same number of times as before, and worship Hari according to the previously mentioned method. (KrdC 7.152)
It shows the application of the two mantras from afar:
"One should daily offer four hundred and fifty sprouts of red *śāli* rice mixed with the three sweets, using either of the two mantras. (Kṛd 7.153)
From that mandala, the earth becomes filled with various crops,
and his house quickly becomes full of heaps of śāli rice.

If a person offers as a libation into the fire one hundred and eight stalks of red winter grain mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar, using either one of these two mantras every day, for that man [the result will appear] within forty-nine days from the mandala; according to the author of the *Laghudīpikā*, it will be within twenty-six days.
Rudradhara states that this occurs after forty-five days;
just as the great earth becomes filled with a multitude of grains and other crops, so too does that house quickly become filled with a multitude of śāli rice.
He states the result:
"But he who, possessing perfect devotion, would certainly resort to one of these two paths through recitation, worship, oblations, and so forth,"
May he be illustrious like Manmatha among women and eloquent; and may that [name] of the Great Acyuta be his when his body falls into calamity.
That man who, being self-controlled, should constantly practice one of these two by means of recitation, worship, fire-offerings, and so forth— he,
having attained devotion, becomes endowed with prosperity and, like Kāmadeva among women, becomes a recipient of excellent speech.
In the event of the body's calamity, immediately after the fall of the physical frame, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Kramadīpikā* composed by the venerable Keśavabhaṭṭācārya.
Now begins the eighth chapter; next, the ritual application for subjugation (*vaśyakara*) is described.
Now, the ritual for subjugation (vaśya-vidhi) is explained, based on the previously mentioned ten-syllable and eighteen-syllable mantras;
by the mere recollection of which one attains the state of being beloved by the entire world.
He always ordains the human state for one who has been permitted by Manu.

The two mantras previously mentioned—the ten-syllable and the eighteen-syllable—constantly bring about the state of being beloved by all people for the practitioner through mere recollection. (KrdC 8.1)
He who, at the beginning of the day, having worshipped Mukunda with reddish wild flowers during his daily rites, and then, throughout the day,
having performed the prescribed duties, recites the mantra of ten syllables one thousand and eight times, is a true practitioner of mantra.
One should certainly bring under control the circles of circles belonging to those whose faces are talkative.

Having daily and at all times worshipped this Mukunda— who is exceedingly red with blossoming forest flowers— with the prescribed method of midday worship at the beginning of each day, the practitioner who recites the ten-syllable supreme mantra one thousand and eight times;
From the *maṇḍala* itself, within fifty days, one will certainly bring under control—that is, subjugate—the assemblies or groups of learned Brahmins whose faces are eloquent.
[The author] now shows the three applications even for a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra:
with *jātī* flowers, [one should fashion] the form of an excellent cowherd...
Having visualized him as before, intent on play with red *hayāri* flowers and intent on song with blue lotuses,
one shall gradually bring kings and others under control.

Having meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who wears the excellent attire of a cowherd and assumes the form of a preeminent gopa, and having worshipped Him with *jātī* flowers according to the previously described method, one should recite the ten-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times to bring a Kṣatriya under control; then, visualizing Him as intent on play,
having worshipped Him with red *karavīra* flowers according to the previously described method, [one should recite] the ten-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times.

Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times and having meditated upon a Vaiśya who is devoted to song and attached to singing, and having worshipped him with blue lotuses according to the previously mentioned method, one should subjugate a Śūdra by reciting the ten-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times; the meaning is that in this manner one may subjugate kings and others.
He states another application: "Then,
having offered a thousand oblations daily for seven nights with white flowers combined with rice grains sprinkled with clarified butter,"
And by applying that ash on the surface of the forehead and the eyes, a person brings three women under his control; likewise, those women also bring men under their control in the same way.
Having offered one thousand oblations with white rice grains accompanied by white flowers, using the ten-syllable mantra mixed with ghee,

constantly for a period of seven days; thereafter, that person who wears the ashes of that homa on the hair, on the ground, on the head, and on the forehead— whether he be a man or a woman (manuja-nārī)— is called a "bearer of Rudra" (rudra-dhara).
According to the threefold reading, "it subjugates a young woman";
the meaning is that by this same ritual application, that woman may likewise subjugate men. (KrdC 8.4)
He states another application:
"Betel, clothing, flowers, collyrium, sandalwood, and so forth,
having been consecrated three thousand times with either one of the two mantras."
To whomever the knower of Manu gives [a gift], his companions shall quickly become his servants; indeed, there is no need for deliberation in this matter.

Be it betel, clothing, flowers, collyrium, sandalwood, or whatever other object it may be— whichever of these two mantras, consisting of eighteen or ten syllables, the practitioner has consecrated three thousand times with one or the other; to whichever person he gives that object, that person quickly and immediately becomes subject to the will of this practitioner.
The meaning is that there is no doubt in this matter.
He states another application: "At the king's gate, in legal proceedings, in an assembly, at gambling, or in debate, [one should employ] one hundred and eight."
Having recited [the mantra], he should utter his first word;
thus he shall proceed toward those who are seated there in various places.

In the presence of a king, in buying and selling, in an assembly, in gambling with dice, or in debate, if one first recites one hundred and eight repetitions of either of the two *mantras*, then by whatever speech he utters, he shall prevail over those seated in that debate or other activity; this is the meaning. (KrdC 8.6)
He describes another visualization:
"One should meditate on the Destroyer of Mura seated at the foot of a Kadamba tree,
singing most sweetly with the women of Vraja."
Having remembered [the deity] and offered oblations into the fire with peacock-wood fuel mixed with honey, that knower of mantras brings the three worlds under his control.
Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Mura, seated at the foot of a Kadamba tree and being sung to most sweetly by the gopīs, the practitioner,
having offered oblations into the fire with peacock feathers dripping with honey and fuel-sticks of Apāmārga, brings the three worlds under his control.
He states another practice:
"One who, while recollecting Acyuta situated in the midst of the rasa, should mutter the ten-syllable mantra one thousand times."
Whether constantly or instantaneously, within a month, that man shall obtain his desired maiden.

The man who, meditating on Kṛṣṇa situated in the midst of the previously described rāsa dance, recites the ten-syllable mantra one thousand times every day, will very quickly obtain his desired maiden within a single month. [He] states another application:
Having meditated upon Acyuta as mounted upon a lofty white lotus,
she who recites [the mantra] one thousand and eight times every day from the mandala— she indeed [attains success].
The maiden obtains her desired boon.
Any maiden who, meditating upon [the deity] residing in a tall kadamba tree, recites the ten-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times every day,
will certainly obtain her desired boon within forty-nine days from the commencement of the mandala rite.

He describes another practice yielding the same result: the knower of mantras, having meditated upon Him who is eighteen syllables long and having held the lotus-hands of the beautiful women of Vraja as they dance, should recite the excellent mantra one hundred thousand times.
Or, having offered ten thousand oblations of parched grain or powders saturated with honey,
one should recite the mantra until the desired maiden is soon won over.

To marry the desired maiden soon or quickly, the practitioner who knows the mantras should grasp and hold the lotus-like hands of the cowherd girls, meditate upon the famous Śrī Kṛṣṇa as He dances, and recite one hundred thousand times this most excellent eighteen-syllable mantra.

Alternatively, [one may offer] with the powders of parched grain (*lāja*) that have been quickly melted with honey and are abundant with ghee, honey, and sugar; Rudradhara says they are "liquefied by honey. Having offered ten thousand oblations, one should recite the mantra that same number of times—this is the meaning. (KrdC 8.10)
He states another application:

"With eighteen syllables, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *dvija* (rice) and *taruja* (plant-derived substances) smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), or with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, or rice, in order to bring the twice-born under control. (Krd 8.11)

To bring the twice-born Brahmins under one's control, one should offer ten thousand oblations (*ayuta*) with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) produced from the *palāśa* tree (*dvija-taru*), which are smeared with the "three sweets" (*tri-madhura*)— that is, mixed with clarified butter, honey, and sugar— or alternatively, one may offer oblations with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, or rice grains smeared with the three sweets, using the eighteen-syllable mantra.
He states another application:
"One may bring kings under control by means of *kṛtamāla* flowers from the current existence, as well as with buds produced from *kuruṇṭaka*."
With *ikṣuraka* flowers, or even with those of the *pāṭala*, one may likewise subjugate others as well. (Kṛd 8.12)

Having offered oblations with buds and calyxes (*mukula*) produced from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree and belonging to the *kṛtamāla*, one shall bring kings and *kṣatriyas* under control. Having offered oblations with buds produced from the *kuruṇṭaka* and the *jhiṇṭī*, one shall bring courtesans (*veśyā*) under control.
Regarding "with sugarcane juices" (*ikṣu-rasaiḥ*), if the reading is *ikṣurakaiḥ*, the meaning is "with *kokilākṣa* [plants]. Alternatively, it means "with *mathī*."
Or, by offering oblations with buds produced from the *pāṭala* tree, one may bring other Śūdras under one's control.
Regarding the number of oblations not explicitly stated, it should be understood that this very [number] applies here, as it is the subject matter of the context. (KrdC 8.12)
He states another ritual application:
with fresh lotuses and red water-lilies, as well as sweet-scented campakas and pāṭalas;
One should perform ten thousand oblations in sequence to quickly bring under one's control excellent women, such as those born from the mouth [of Brahmā] and others.

To swiftly bring under one's control women born from the mouth [of Brahmā] and other such excellent women, as well as the wives of Brahmins and others, one should perform ten thousand oblations (*pratihoma*) by offering two thousand five hundred of each of four substances— each mixed with honey and combined with the "three sweets"— in successive order.
He states the substances: with fresh white lotuses, red water-lilies, campaka flowers, and pāṭala flowers.
He states another ritual application:
A wise person should daily offer a thousand oblations at midnight during the day of a sage (*ṛṣivāsara*), using fresh *hayāri* flowers soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
He forcibly and instantly makes that woman of noble intellect— though afflicted by the arrows of Love— his own servant.

With fresh *karavīra* flowers— the "enemies of horses"— mixed with the three sweets, a wise practitioner should offer oblations by the thousands every day for seven days, or for a "sage-day" (forty-nine days), at midnight during the night; thus,
he shall forcibly and swiftly bring under his power that proud courtesan who is tormented by the arrows of love.
He makes her his own maidservant.
He states another ritual application: even with mustard seeds that are pungent, combined, sweetened with the three sweets, and very moist, one obtains ten hundred [times] three.
For when he offers oblations at night, even Śacī’s husband, though self-controlled, becomes subject to his will; what need be said of others?

In the reading "combined with salt" (*lavaṇa-saṃyutaiḥ*) and "combined with pungent" (*kaṭu-saṃyutaiḥ*), the meaning is "combined with pungent substances" (*kaṭuka-saṃyutaiḥ*). [The substances are] very sweet and moist, being unctuous with ghee, honey, and sugar. The word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction. For a person offering oblations at night during the three periods of the night—namely one hundred, ten hundred (one thousand), and three thousand—with mustard seeds, even Indra, the beloved of Śacī, becomes subject to his will against his own will; how much more so [others]?
Others. // KrdC_8.15 //
He states another application: "Then,
by means of oblations consisting of bilva fruits, sacrificial fuel, blossoms, and leaves, quickly melted with honey..."
With lotuses accompanied by white unbroken rice grains, one shall individually bring Kamalā under control for a long time before long.

With fruits, sacrificial fuel-sticks, flowers, and leaves produced from the *bilva* tree, with white lotuses thoroughly saturated with honey, combined with white unbroken rice (*akṣata*), mixed with sugar and rice, and accompanied by white [sugar] and clarified butter (*ājya*)— according to the reading "accompanied by white sugar and clarified butter" (*sitā-śarkarā ājyam ghṛtam*)— by performing three thousand oblations (*homa*) for each individual item separately, one attains results after a long time or even immediately.
One will quickly bring Kamalā-Lakṣmī under one's control; the number [of recitations] for this is that which was just mentioned. KrdC_8.16 //
He states another practice:
"Having stripped the cowherd women of their garments, Acyuta was mounted upon the Kadamba tree by them with their hearts."
Reciting this while remembering [the deity] at night, one shall quickly bring even Urvaśī herself by force within ten days.

Having forcibly snatched away and taken the garments of the cowherd girls with his own heart (intent), one should remember Kṛṣṇa as he has climbed a *kadamba* tree and recite the mantra a thousand times at night; within ten days—that is, during the course of ten days—he shall, by the power of the mantra, forcibly bring even Urvaśī, the celestial courtesan, under his control, that is, into his presence. (KrdC 8.17)
He speaks of the majesty of the two mantras:
"What is the use of saying more here? For there is indeed no other superior means for bringing [beings] under control than these two mantras."
In this world, for women skilled in the art of attraction, their very bodies consist of the weapons of the flower-armed god [Kāmadeva].
What is the use of much speaking in this treatise?

In this world, there is no other equal to these two mantras of ten and eighteen syllables for the purpose of subjugation. Of what nature are they? They are like the very bodies of the arrows of the God of Love in the act of attracting the women of the city.
He states another practice for accomplishing liberation:
"I bow to the Youthful One, white as jasmine or the moon, with eyes possessing the luster of the petals of a red lotus,
holding a discus, a conch, a mace, and two lotuses with his long, club-like arms."
Mukunda is resplendent with divine ornaments and body-unguents, adorned with a garland of shimmering fresh lotuses, clothed in radiant yellow garments, seated upon a lotus, and surrounded by sages.
I bow to Mukunda,
who is as white as a jasmine flower and the moon, likewise youthful, with eyes resembling red lotuses,
and who holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in His own long, club-like arms that are shaped like hammers.

He was holding a lotus, adorned with divine ornaments and bodily unguents, and was radiant with a shimmering, brilliantly shining garland made of fresh lotuses; likewise, he was clothed in garments with the luster of glowing turmeric,
surrounded by Nārada and others, and seated upon a lotus.
Having thus meditated upon the Person seated within the blossomed lotus of the heart—

possessing the complexion of a dense lotus or like molten gold— one should recite the mantra one million times. Then, interspersed with two *tārās* (oṃ), one should offer fuel-sticks into the fire one thousand times while reciting either of the two mantras.
Or else, with milk-porridge prepared with substances that cause the liquefaction of [impurities], along with honey, ghee, and sugar.
Having thus meditated upon Mukunda as previously described— seated upon a lotus-throne with a blossoming heart-lotus,
the primordial and first one, dark like a water-laden cloud, or according to the reading "sāndrābhojacchavim," possessing the smooth luster of a lotus—
one should meditate on him situated between the two *div* syllables in the midst of the two mantras consisting of ten and eighteen syllables.
One should recite one hundred thousand or twelve hundred thousand [mantras] for the sun.

Then, immediately after the recitation, one should offer oblations with a thousand pieces of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from any of the following trees—*aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, or *nyagrodha*—which have been soaked in milk; or alternatively, one should offer oblations with milk-rice (*paramānna*) mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar. KrdC 8.20.

Then, with a pure mind, meditating every day upon the Lord of the World— who possesses a body of eternal consciousness and bliss, and who is like the sun that dispels the darkness of worldly existence— within the lotus of his own heart as one with himself, he recited the mantra.
One should recite it three thousand times, performing the sacrifice according to the ritual for the evening.

Then, immediately thereafter, with a pure mind— that is, with a stainless internal organ— one should daily meditate upon this Kṛṣṇa within the lotus of one's own heart as being non-different from oneself, through identity; [meditating on Him] as the Overseer of the worlds, the Lord of the worlds, possessing indestructible knowledge, whose body is the very nature of bliss, and who is the sun that dispels the darkness of saṃsāra.

One should offer oblations three thousand times, that is, three times one thousand; likewise, one should perform worship according to the previously described method for evening worship and also carry out the fire sacrifice.
He who, with steady and firm intellect, constantly worships this ritual method with devotion,
crosses the terrifying ocean of worldly existence, which is vast and filled with the high waves known as birth and death, and teeming with swarms of crocodiles in the form of perilous sense-objects.
Having crossed over the infinite, he goes to the supreme abode of Hari.
That man of steady intellect, who constantly and with devotion follows this rule— that is, this method—
crosses over the ocean of existence, the sea of saṃsāra, and attains the supreme abode of Hari, which is non-dual (ananya), meaning there is nothing else besides it, and which consists of all things.

Of what sort? Terrifying like the ocean, with multitudes—that is, collections—of crocodiles, sharks, tortoises, and the like, which are the sense-objects such as sound and so forth, or rather garlands, sandalwood, women, and so on, that are treacherous and difficult to ward off;
and likewise, vast with towering—that is, great—waves known by the names of birth and death. (KrdC 8.22)
Constantly chanting His names, hearing His stories, and recollecting His forms,
one should bow to His lotus feet, humbled by devotion.
He alone is always worthy of worship by the wise; he alone is ever-yoked [to the goal].
That person is worthy of worship by the wise and the learned; he alone is constantly disciplined and partakes in eternal yoga.
What does he do? Chanting the names of this Śrī Kṛṣṇa and narrating His stories.

Constantly meditating upon the forms and images of that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he serves His lotus feet—the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—bowing down in devotion; the repetition [of the word "namra"] is for the purpose of expressing an exceeding degree of humility. (KrdC 8.23)
Now he speaks of the two supreme mantras: "I shall describe another, most secret pair of mantras,
known by the name 'Deluder of the World,' in brief."
The first [number] is divided by the moon, the eye, the eye, and the moon; that preceded by it is divided by the sky, the ṛṣis, the joined lord, and the horn.
Immediately thereafter, I shall briefly describe another pair of mantras, which are extremely secret and known as the "Deluder of the World" (jagan-mohana).
*Brahmā* is the letter *ka*;
*Indra* is the letter *la*.
The left eye is the long vowel *ī*;
the moon is the *anusvāra*.
Combined with these, the first mantra, which is the form of the seed-syllable of Kāma, has been extracted.

Preceded by that [seed-syllable], the form is *viyat* (the letter *ha*) and *ṛṣīka* (the letter *ī*); joined with these two, the word *īśa* forms the form *hṛṣīkeśa*. The suffix *ṅe* is the dative singular case ending; *hṛt* and *namaḥ* follow.
Thus, *klīṃ hṛṣīkeśāya namaḥ* is the second mantra.
Regarding this, Bhairava Tripāṭhin maintains that it is the Puruṣottama-mantra. (KrdC 8.24)
He states the seer and so forth: "But for the mantra, the sage is Saṃmohana-Nārada; the meter is declared by the wise to be Gāyatrī."
Now I shall state the deities for the Trailokyasaṃmohana and Viṣṇu retas mantras, along with their six-limbed ritual application.
For these two mantras, the sage is Sammohana-Nārada; the meter is Gāyatrī;
and it is declared by those who know the mantras that the deity is Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds.
Now I shall describe the six ancillaries (ṣaḍ-aṅga): with syllables that are neither neuter nor long, and likewise mounted upon the musical notes (kalāsana);
one should then perform [the rite] as previously stated, up to the placement of the seat (āsana-vinyāsa). Krd 8.26.

With the six long vowels excluding *ṛ* and *ṝ*, joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*) and bound to the two syllables "kala," namely: *klāṃ klīṃ klūṃ klaiṃ klauṃ klaḥ*—by these, its six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*) are declared.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the rites up to the worship described previously for the ten-syllable mantra. (KrdC 8.26)
Having placed the six limbs upon the palms and the fingers of both hands as arrows,
one should assign the limbs to the body using the letters of the alphabet encased by the mantra, and likewise assign the arrows.

Having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*) upon the branches of the hands, the fingers, and the palms of both hands; having again placed the arrows of desire (*kāma-bāṇa*) upon the fingers; and having performed the placement of the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet—situated at the beginning and end of the mantra—upon the locations of the Mātṛkā; one should then perform the placement of the six limbs upon one’s own body using the seed-syllables of desire (*kāma-bīja*) conjoined with the long vowels, and likewise perform the placement of the arrows (*bāṇa-nyāsa*). // KrdC_8.27 //
He states the locations for the placement of the arrows:

"One should [place] the [mantras] ending in *namaḥ* and ending in the dative case (*ṅe*)—namely Śoṣaṇa, Mohana, Sandīpana, Tāpana, and Mādana—respectively upon the mouth, heart, liṅga, feet, and the fingers of the hands. (Krd 8.28)

One should sequentially place the five arrows to be described later—each accompanied by the fourth word "namaḥ"—upon the head, face, heart, genitals, and feet, using each finger individually from the thumb to the little finger. (KrdC 8.28)
He states the names of the arrows: "These five, beginning with *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *klūṃ*, and *saḥ*, are declared to be the arrows.
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon Puruṣottama as the one who completely deludes the world. (Krd 8.29)

*Hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *klūṃ*, *sa*: these five seed-syllables (*bīja*), each placed at the beginning [of the respective mantras], are thus declared to be the five arrows, beginning with *śoṣaṇa* (drying).

As for the ritual application (*prayoga*): with the thumb, one says *hrāṃ śoṣaṇāya namaḥ* on the head; with the index finger, *hrīṃ mohanāya namaḥ* on the mouth, and so forth. Immediately thereafter, with a restrained mind, one should meditate upon Puruṣottama, who brings the three worlds under his control. (KrdC 8.29)
Regarding meditation, he says:
[It is for one] who sits upon a seat of auspicious lotuses shimmering on a ground made of jewels, beneath a great kalpa-tree rising up from a divine garden of trees. (Kṛd 8.30)
Seated upon the lofty shoulder of Suparṇa— the life-breath of the universe, whose splendor is like the rising sun—
[the Lord] rests with limbs as beautiful as coral, his body tormented by the god of love.
Holding a discus, sword, goad, and noose, as well as a flower, arrow, sugarcane bow, lotus,
and mace with his own arms, he possesses a pair of large, reddish, wide, and rolling lotus-eyes.
He was resplendent with a crown, earrings, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and a bow made of jewels;
he was radiant with reddish garlands and ointments, and was clothed in yellow garments.
Seated upon his own left thigh, she embraces him while holding a lotus in her left hand;
her womb throbs with desire, and the vine of her limbs glows, agitated by the intoxication of passion.
A young woman, adorned with beautiful ornaments, garlands, and ointments, draped in white garments, her restless,
bee-like eyes intent upon the lotus of her own face.
Embracing with his staff-like left arm, which firmly holds the sugarcane bow,
his heart overflowing with the supreme bliss produced thereby, he is the sole preceptor of all that moves and is stationary.
It was surrounded by thousands of women— goddesses, daughters of the Daityas, serpent-nymphs, Guhyakas, Gandharvas, and others—
their limbs languid with intoxication and passion, and radiant with divine ornaments.
Having thus meditated upon the single syllable or the eight-syllable mantra as non-different from oneself,
one should recite it one million times while offering *kiṃśuka* blossoms sprinkled with the three sweets.
A collection of nine verses.

Having meditated upon Vāsudeva in this very manner, one should recite either the single-syllable seed-mantra of desire (*kāma-bīja*) or the eight-syllable mantra twelve hundred thousand times—that is, one million two hundred thousand times. Of what kind? Having meditated [upon Him] at the foot of the enchanting Pārijāta tree, which is growing and flourishing in a celestial grove of wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpa-vṛkṣa*), upon the lofty shoulder of Garuḍa...
Seated.

Of what kind of Garuḍa? One seated upon a magnificent lotus-throne shining with ground fashioned from rubies and other gems; likewise, because he is a portion of the Supreme Lord who is the soul of all living beings, he possesses a luster equal to the rising sun.
Of what nature is Vāsudeva?
His limbs are as beautiful as coral;
he is agitated by desire; and with his own arms—right and left in sequence—he bears the discus, conch, goad, noose, flower-arrow, sugarcane bow, lotus, and mace, and is likewise red in hue.
He whose lotus-like face has the form of two eyes;

who is resplendent with head-ornaments, ear-jewels, and other decorations fashioned from rubies and other gems, as well as pearl necklaces, armlets, bracelets, finger-rings, small bells, and so forth, along with red garlands and perfumes; and who wears yellow garments as both undergarment and upper robe.
In such a manner, with his staff-like left arm holding the sugarcane bow so firmly, he embraced Śrī;
how was she? Seated upon the region of his own beautiful thighs, and likewise embracing him.
Likewise, she holds a lotus in her left hand; likewise, her secret parts have become moist; likewise, her creeper-like limbs are agitated and rendered helpless by desire;
she possesses charming ornaments, garlands, and sandalwood paste; and likewise, she is clothed in white garments.

Her dark, swarthy eyes—which are intent upon the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa, perfectly engaged in their function, tremulous, charming, and restless—are themselves like bees; she who possesses such eyes is thus described. Furthermore, what is she like? A young woman (*taruṇī*). How else is she characterized?

Having meditated upon the Teacher of the World—whose heart is filled with the supreme bliss born from the embrace of his beloved, and whose limbs are rendered motionless by intoxication and desire amidst thousands of women of the gods, daityas, serpents, celestial musicians, and vidyādharas—and who is surrounded by those radiant with ornaments worthy of the gods, by what method [should one meditate]? By means of identifying oneself with him (*ātmaikya*). (KrdC 8.30–38)
One should offer a thousand oblations with pure waters and satisfy [the deity] with as many;
when the twenty-millionth mantra has been recited, one should worship this [deity] daily with devotion in the prescribed yantra.
After meditation and recitation, one should perform twelve thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers mixed with ghee, honey, and sugar.
Following the fire sacrifice, one should perform twelve thousand libations with pure water.
This is called "the twenty-syllable [rite]."
One should worship this Kṛṣṇa with devotion every day upon a yantra extracted from his mantra, according to the previously mentioned procedure for the twenty-syllable seat (pīṭha).
He describes the manner of worship with four and a half verses.
He states the mantra of Garuḍa:
"In the ritual of the pedestal, at the end of the wings, one should worship the enemy of the serpent-king with this [mantra], beginning with the word *rājāya*."
Having invoked Hari onto his shoulder and worshipped him with offerings such as *argha* up to the ornaments;
He placed his limbs and arrows according to the sequence of ritual deposition (*nyāsa*), as did the crown upon his head,
the earrings upon his ears, and the weapons, foremost among them the enemy-slaying ones, upon his hands.
One should also [place] the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha above the two breasts, the forest garland on the neck,
the yellow garment on the hips, and Śrī on the left side, using their respective seed-syllables.
Having performed the sacrifice in the pericarp, one should worship the limbs (aṅgas) in the intermediate directions and the ten arrows in the cardinal directions;
then, in the corners, the fifth [limb] is worshipped again, and the powers (śaktis) are to be worshipped on the petals starting from the southeast.

In the ritual of worship, at the end of the word for "bird" (*pakṣin*), one should append *rājāya* as the name-form, followed by *śiraḥ* and *svāhā*. Having worshipped Garuḍa, the enemy of serpents, in the center of the pedestal in this manner, one should invoke Śrī Kṛṣṇa upon the back of that Garuḍa, perform the rites of invocation and so forth according to rule, worship Him with the services beginning with the water-offering (*argha*) and ending with ornaments, worship His limbs, and [worship] the five arrows.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "having worshipped the ornaments, and having worshipped them, the Śaktis are to be worshipped in the petals of the directions.
He clarifies this very point with the words beginning with "in the order of the ritual placement" (*nyāsa-kramataḥ*).
This refers to the specific part of the body of the Supreme Lord upon which the placement (*nyāsa*) of each [Śakti] occurs.
His worship is to be understood as follows: a crown upon the head; earrings for the two ears;
the faces of his enemies and weapons such as the discus and others in the hands; the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha gem above the heart;
a forest garland hanging from the neck down to the feet; a lotus garland on the hips and waist; and yellow-hued garments on the left side of the body.

Having worshipped Lakṣmī with her own seed-syllable (*sva-bīja*) and the *śrī*-seed-syllable (*śrī-bīja*), and having performed worship in the pericarp, one should worship the limbs (*aṅga*) as before in the cardinal and intermediate directions and the corners. Then, one should worship the arrows in the cardinal directions and the fifth arrow in the corners starting from the southeast (*agny-ādi*).
Furthermore, the eight Śaktis are to be worshipped on the petals starting from the southeast.
He states the colors of the Śaktis:
Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī are gold-colored; Rati and Prīti are deep red;
Kīrti and Kānti are white; and Tuṣṭi and Puṣṭi resemble emeralds.
In one with the luster of gold, yellow-colored, deeper than dawn-red, intensely red, white, pure white, resembling emerald, or the color of turmeric.
Of what nature are these Śaktis?

Their creeper-like limbs are adorned with divine unguents, ornaments, garlands, and silken garments; their faces are smiling, and the palms of their beautiful hands hold fly-whisks for those afflicted by the god of love. Krd_8.45.

Their bodies were adorned with divine unguents, ornaments, woven flowers, and fine garments; the word *aṅga-latā* here denotes their physical form; likewise, they had slightly smiling faces, were tormented by the arrows of Love, and were captivating as they held yak-tail fans.
It has been stated that the worship of the Lords of the World (Lokeśas) is performed externally; thus, this mode of worship arises from two [preceding] mantras.
Generally, it is the procedure for Puruṣottama alone that is described in this way, for it is not mentioned here because of its great abundance.

Outside of that, Indra and the others, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons, are to be worshipped; thus has the worship arising from the two mantras been described in general—that is, for the most part. Furthermore, although the method described for the Puruṣottama mantra is also like this, it is not explicitly stated here because there is much to be said; generally, the ritual procedure for Puruṣottama should be understood from other sources in this manner.
An alternative reading accepted by another commentary. KrdC_8.46.
He states the *sammohana-gāyatrī*:
having said "to the one who deludes the three worlds," he says "we know" and "to the god of love"; "may we meditate upon that," and at the end, "may Viṣṇu impel us toward that. (Kṛd 8.47)
