Having stated the essential form as "trailokyamohanāya," immediately thereafter one should say "vidmahe" for "smarāya," then "dhīmahī," and finally state the essential form "tan no viṣṇuḥ pracodayāt.
He describes its power:
"For this [mantra], when recited at the beginning of a recitation and so forth, removes evil and brings prosperity through recitation, worship, and fire-offerings."
May he sprinkle these substances for the self-sacrifice upon the ground for the sake of purification during the worship.

This Gāyatrī should be recited prior to the recitation [of other mantras]; furthermore, through the recitation of one's own mantra, worship, and fire-offerings (*homa*), it becomes the destroyer of sins and the bestower of prosperity (*lakṣmī*).

With this Gāyatrī, for the sake of purification during worship, one should sprinkle (*prokṣayatu*) oneself, the sacrificial ground, and the ritual materials—namely, the self-sacrifice, the site, and the substances. (KrdC 8.48)

He states the common propitiation for the two mantras: "He who daily at dawn propitiates [the deities] one hundred times with water mixed with *mohanī* flowers using either of the two mantras, obtains his desired objects without effort. (Krd 8.49)

Whoever offers libations every day, one hundred times each, with water mixed with *mohanī* flowers and combined with *śakrāsana*, *padmāsana*, and *puṣpa* flowers using either of the two previously mentioned mantras, shall effortlessly attain their desired wishes. (KrdC 8.49)
He states another application related to the two mantras:

"Having offered ten thousand oblations, with the remainder of the offering mixed with clarified butter over which that many recitations have been performed, let the master feed his beloved woman in order to bring her under his own control. (Krd 8.50)

With clarified butter in the fire, one should offer ten thousand oblations; with the remaining clarified butter, consecrated by the recitation of the mantra, the woman should be fed, and the lover should be made to feed his beloved, in order to bring her under one's own control. The ritual procedures prescribed for the eighteen-syllable [mantra] should be performed by these two for the sake of subjugation.
Of these two mantras, the latter is equal to the former in the matter of subjugating the three worlds in this world.

The ritual applications for subjugation taught in the eighteen-syllable mantra should certainly be performed with these two mantras; for in this world, regarding the task of bringing the entire universe under one's control, there is no other mantra equal to these two.

In this context, during the recitation of the Ekārṇava mantra and so forth, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa holding a flute; or else, one may meditate upon Kandarpa, whose limbs and attire possess a reddish luster, holding a noose, a goad, and a bow.

In this context, between the two [options] just mentioned, when performing the recitation (*japa*), worship (*pūjā*), fire-offering (*homa*), and so forth of the single-syllable mantra, Kṛṣṇa should be meditated upon.
Of what nature? He is "one whose gait is accompanied by the flute," meaning he is intent on singing produced from the bamboo;
likewise, his body and ornaments are red and enchanting.

Alternatively, in this very context of mantra-recitation and so forth, one should meditate upon Kāmadeva bearing the noose, the goad, the bow, and the arrows; the underlying sense is that the mantra is of the nature of the primordial deity. // KrdC_8.52 //
He concludes the subject at hand:

"But the practitioner of mantra whose intellect is pure, who always resorts to one or the other of these two mantras, attains vast accomplishment both in the hereafter and exceedingly so in this world. (Krd 8.53)
The practitioner who constantly serves one of these two supreme mantras through recitation and other means attains exceedingly vast accomplishment in this world and the next.
Now, he extracts the mantra of Rukmiṇī’s Beloved:
"Then *satya* and *śauri*, with the third and fourth [vowels],
adorned by the fire, the left eye, and the crescent moon."
The letters are joined by *jaya*, *kṛṣṇa*, pairs (*yugmaka*), *nirantara*, *ātma*, *bhū*, *śikhi*, *śakti*, *ḍā*, *asya*, *vṛta*, and *sakta*.
From the middle of the *praṇava* (oṃ), for one whose mind is joyful, there arise the syllables of the Guru’s wind (*māruta*)— the letter *ya*, followed by *tya*, *parakta*, and *dṛg*—
together with the word *kṛṣṇa* in the dative case, and the word *ikṣukārmuka*.
And that excellent Manu is indeed ten-fold.
Encased by the syllables *sa-la-vā-dha-r-rā-ca-la-su-tā-ra-mā* arranged in forward and reverse order like a casket, this [mantra] consisting of thirty-two syllables—
namely, the teeth (32), the sun (12), and the Vasus (8)— is thus extracted.
He who delights in poetry, the source of Ramā, and the remover of sin.
The letter *da* is Satya;
the letter *dha* is Śauri;
and the third and fourth [of the gutturals] are the letters *ja* and *jha*.

These four syllables are each adorned by the "crest" (śikhī), which is the letter *ra*; the "left eye" (*vāma-netra*), which is the vowel *ī*; and the "moon-fragment" (*śaśi-khaṇḍa*), which is the nasal dot (*bindu*).
The meaning is that they are beautified and joined with these.
Thus, they are: *drīṃ*, *dhrīṃ*, *jrīṃ*, and *jhrīṃ*.
Following that, there are "Jaya-Kṛṣṇa" and others such as Tripāṭhi-Govinda-Miśra.

In reality, the form [of the mantra] consists of the pair of words "Jaya-Kṛṣṇa," followed by "Nirantara"; then the syllable *ka* which is the Self-born (Brahmā), the fire (*śikhī*) which is the letter *ra*, and the power (*śakti*) which is the vowel *ī*.
Thus, it has the nature of the syllable *krī*.
Following that, the nature of the syllable *ḍa* is the letter *ā* enclosed by the mouth (*āsya-vṛtam*), which is the nature of *ḍā*.

"Attached" (*sakta*) is its nature; "in the middle of the two syllables" (*pranimadhyato*) means between the two syllables. Then, for one whose mind is joyful (*mudita-cetase*), after the word *ni*, the nature of *tya* follows, and after that, the nature of *pa*.
The letter *ra* is the "passionate one" (*rakta*).
The letter *i* is the "vision" (*dṛk*); because there is no reason to skip the first [vowel], the short *i* is obtained.
Thus, *pri* is its own form; then *ya* is its own form, with the long *ā* as the guru;
and *yā* is its own form.
Following that is the letter *ya* with the *māruta* (vowel *u*).
Following that is the word "Kṛṣṇa" in its actual form (*svarūpa*) with the fourth case ending, namely *kṛṣṇāya*. Following that is the sugarcane bow, which is the seed-syllable of Kāma (*klīm*).
Following that is the previously mentioned ten-syllable mantra.
Following that is *lava*, which is the nasal dot (*bindu*); together with that, *dharā* is the vowel *ai*. Thus, its essential form is *aiṃ*.
*Acala* means "mountain," and its daughter is Pārvatī; the meaning is that she is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhuvaneśvarī.
*Ramā* is the *śrī-bīja*.

With these three *bījas* recited in reverse order at the end of the mantra—namely, *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* at the beginning and *śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ* at the end—it becomes encapsulated like a casket (*samudga*) or a box (*sampuṭa*). This fifty-two-syllable mantra thus becomes perfected.
He states the number of syllables in the mantra with the word "iti":
*danta* = 32, *sūrya* = 12, *vasu* = 8. When these are combined, the total number consists of fifty-two syllables (52).
The meaning is that it becomes a mantra.
Of what kind? It is that which brings about the fortune of the splendor of poetry and the world, and likewise, it is the remover of evil, the destroyer of sin.

The nature of the mantra is: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Drīṃ Jrīṃ Jhrīṃ Jaya Kṛṣṇa Jaya Kṛṣṇa, O You whose mind is delighted and attached to incessant play, to Kṛṣṇa who is eternally beloved, Krīṃ, to the Beloved of the Gopīs, Svāhā, Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Aiṃ.
Regarding the seer (ṛṣi) and other details of this mantra, he says: The sage is Nārada, who possesses a face and the number nine; the metre is said to be Virāṭ, beginning with Amṛta.
Hari, indeed called the "Deluder of the Three Worlds," is declared by the sages to be his deity.
The face is the *vṛtta* (meter) and the form is *ā*; Nārada is endowed with these two.

Thus, the sage Ānandanārada has declared that the *virāṭ* meter consists of [the syllables] beginning with *amṛta*, its presiding deity is Hari who deludes the three worlds, and it was taught by sages such as Nārada. (KṛdC 8.57)
He shows the method for the limbs: with the syllables of the mantra consisting of eight, six, seven, eight, four, ten, and five [units], arranged separately in three groups.
That which is prescribed for one's own caste consists of six limbs;
indeed, it is through ritual action alone that one truly wins over people.
Vasu = 8, Mitra = 12, Bhūdhara = 7, Gaja = 8, Ātman = 1, Diś = 10.
With this number of mantra syllables arranged in three groups— namely:

*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ drīṃ vrīṃ jrīṃ jhrīṃ jaya-kṛṣṇa aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* and *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ jaya-kṛṣṇa-nirantara-krīḍāsakta aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth— by means of this very ritual of the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*), one generates affection in all people.
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa): "Then, having thoroughly purified [the body] from the path that releases the form, and having fashioned a seat by means of one's own body..."
One should place upon the two hands the sequence of the ten-syllable rite,
along with the six-limbed [mantra], the five arrows, and the five bodiless ones.
Then, immediately after purifying the body (*tanu*)— the physical form— by means of the previously described method of elemental purification (*bhūta-śuddhi*),
one should arrange the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with one's own form, that is, one's own body. Then, in both hands— that is, in the pair of hands—

one should perform the sixfold application of the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-ṣaṭka*) according to the method stated for the ten-syllable mantra, as well as the arrows, namely the [five] acts of withering and so forth, and the five "bodiless" ones (*anaṅga-pañcaka*) known by the names Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makaradhvaja, and Manobhūta.
One should place the five objects of desire.
Having analyzed this very point, he demonstrates it:
"One should perform the placement three times all over the body with the syllables of the Mātṛkā, encased by the Smara-mantras."
Then, one should perform the ritual beginning with the ten principles (daśatattva) and the recitation of the ten syllables, concluding with the "Cage of the Embodiments" (mūrtipañjara).
First, one should perform the three-fold pervasive placement (*tri-vyāpaka*) upon the body with the root mantra according to Manu.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) three times using the letters of the Mātṛkā, each encased by the Kāma-bīja.
One should then place the ten principles (*tattvas*) as proclaimed by the ten syllables, as described in the Daśākṣara.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with the principles (tattva) and ending with the cage of forms (mūrti-pañjara).
He creates and maintains the sixteen limbs and the five arrows;
thereafter, he deposits everything else as previously described,
having established the sole witness of all worlds.
One of faultless and steady intellect should remember Mukunda.
One should perform the creation and maintenance [of the mantra], and place the ten limbs, the six limbs, and the arrows upon the body.

Immediately thereafter, having performed everything beginning with the worship of the Self as before, the practitioner—whose intellect is stainless and steady—should remember and contemplate Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the witness of all the worlds. (Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta 8.61)
He speaks of meditation:
Now, in that city adorned with mountains and oceans, possessing lofty *śāla* trees and great gate-towers, and wide thoroughfares;
In a place crowded with palaces resounding with loud, passionate laughter, and with gateways and balconies spread across jeweled mansions; Krd_8.62.

Immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon Acyuta seated upon a lotus-throne with a pedestal shaped like the face of a massive lion, featuring broad lion-like faces at its feet, situated on a ground of jewels beneath a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) in a jeweled pavilion within his own city.
In what kind of city?

In one adorned—that is, surrounded—by mountains (bhūdhara), by peaks, and by the ocean (udadhi); likewise, in one where there are very high (mahonnata) ramparts (śāla), gate-towers (gopura), and outer gates; and where there are vast (viśālā) and great (mahatī) streets (vīthikā) or paths.
In various places there were *karmadhāraya* compounds: likewise, it was pervaded by houses that were extremely pure and white, touching the clouds;
likewise, in the jewel-made houses, there were wide door-panels, as well as railings and decorated ground in various places.
Furthermore, what was that city like?
It was filled with various dwellings belonging to the twice-born, kings, merchants, and those born of service, as well as the houses of diverse artisans.
And with thousands of shining elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, cows, buffaloes, goats, and sheep.

It was adorned by thousands of worlds consisting of various kinds of dwellings for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as the houses of artisans, and the enclosures for elephants, horses, sheep, donkeys, cows, buffaloes, and goats.
Furthermore, of what kind was it?
It was filled with accumulations of wealth brought by great crowds of people from various marketplaces for the purpose of buying and selling.
And it was adorned with beautiful mansions belonging to lovely women, skilled in captivating the minds of people.
It was filled with the accumulation of wealth from buying and selling brought by great crowds, resting upon various kinds of market stalls;
furthermore, of what sort?
It was adorned with the beautiful houses of courtesans who were skilled at captivating the hearts of people. (KrdC 8.64)
Furthermore, what kind of city was it?
One whose vast and long, stainless waters were filled with bees greedy for the nectar of blooming, radiant lotuses.
In his own city, the quarters were made resonant by birds bearing names such as *vara*, *haṃsa*, *sārasa*, and *rathāṅga*.

In which [place] the quarters were made resonant by birds known as excellent swans (*haṃsa*), cranes (*sārasa*), and ruddy geese (*cakravāka*), who were greedy for the nectar called the juice of the radiant, blooming lotuses in the pure waters of the Sthūla lake.
Furthermore, what was that jeweled pavilion like?
It was filled with celestial trees (*surapādapa*)— trees that grant various desires to human beings and are swarming with bees greedy for their fragrant blossoms.
In a jeweled pavilion, radiant with the splendor of a thousand suns, which was surrounded by peaks swaying in the gentle breezes of Śiva;

It was surrounded by wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) that grant various desires to human beings, filled with bees greedy for fragrant flowers, their upper branches swaying in an auspicious, gentle breeze;
it possessed a radiance equal to a thousand suns.
Furthermore, of what kind?
Its interior was illuminated by a multitude of jewel-lamps, and it was graced by slender, variegated, and wide-spreading canopies.
In Lalitā, where the ground is sprinkled with fragrant scented water and adorned with garlands variegated by the songs of cuckoos; Kṛd_8.67.
The jewels themselves were the lamps; in their multitude, the central portion was illuminated.
Furthermore, of what kind [was it]?
It was joined with a subtle, variegated, and extensive moonlight.
Furthermore, of what kind?
Adorned with garlands of various kinds of blossoming flowers, it was a place sprinkled with exceedingly fragrant water.
Furthermore, of what kind?
[It was] with hundreds of young women whose eyes were rolling with intoxication, whose faces were flushed with wine, and who brandished chowries with their hands.
They were attended by those who, with faltering and sweet speech,
possessed slender waists that curved under the weight of their breasts.

It was attended on all sides by hundreds of women whose eyes rolled with intoxication, who were accompanied by the languor born of wine, holding flickering fly-whisks in their hands, whose charming speech was slightly faltering, and whose slender waists were bent low by the weight of their breasts.
Of what kind of celestial tree?
Of that which pours forth a continuous stream of excellent jewels, even though it drips with the nectar-like essence that destroys fatigue.
Upon the jeweled ground of the celestial tree, he sits upon a broad lion-throne whose lotus-feet are lion-faces shimmering with jewels.
Furthermore, of what kind [is it]? It pours down a stream of excellent jewels without ceasing;
moreover, it flows with the nectar-like essence that destroys fatigue. (KrdC 8.69)
Of what nature is Acyuta?
One should meditate upon Acyuta as established in bliss,
with a complexion as tender as a fresh blue lotus.
His crown shines with locks of hair curling at the tips,
and his ear-ornaments are fashioned from flowers and jewels amidst his smiles.
Possessing the lovely splendor of a fresh blue lotus;
furthermore, of what kind? Him whose crown shines upon his hair with curled tips.
Furthermore, of what kind?
He by whom a crest-ornament (*avataṃsa*) has been fashioned from smiles—which are slightly blossomed flowers—and from jewels. (KrdC 8.70)
Furthermore, of what kind was he?
He had a beautiful forehead, a prominent nose, and upturned eyebrows;
his large, reddish, long, and tremulous eyes were wide.
His cheeks were brilliantly illuminated by his jeweled earrings,
and his lips were as red as the fresh bandhujīva flower.
Thus his forehead was radiant, thus his nose was high, and his creeper-like eyebrows were arched; thus his long, flickering eyes were thick and of a reddish hue,
thus the regions of his cheeks were adorned by the rays of jeweled earrings, and thus his lower lip was as red as a fresh bandhujīva flower.
Furthermore, of what nature is the Supreme Lord?
His face illuminates the quarters of the sky with the moonlight of his smile, and it is adorned with beads of perspiration from fatigue and shimmering horripilation.
His shoulders were adorned with excellent necklaces and strings of ornaments, radiant with clusters of gems whose rays were flickering.
With the quarters of the sky whitened by the rays of his moon-like smile, and his face adorned with drops of perspiration born from the thrill of horripilation;
furthermore, what was he like?
His shoulders were graced by excellent necklaces and garlands, which shone with a multitude of jewels whose radiant rays were intensely gleaming. (KrdC 8.72)
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
His body is anointed with the finest essence of saffron,
and he is resplendent with twelve broad and long arms.
His body is churned by the auspiciousness of his two lotus-feet, as beautiful as fresh lotuses, while his two lotus-hands rest upon his lap.

Furthermore, his body was smeared with sandalwood and saffron; he was resplendent with twelve thick, long arms; his lotus-feet resembled fresh, reddish-colored lotuses; his body was afflicted by desire;
and his two hands were placed upon his own lap.

[He saw Kṛṣṇa] embracing with his two lotus-like arms that woman of glistening golden hue, who was seated upon the broad space between the thighs of Bhīṣmaka’s daughter resting on his own lap, while she in turn embraced him, her hips moist with passion.
[He embraced] himself with his two long, shimmering, sprout-like hands.
Furthermore, he is embracing Rukmiṇī— who possesses the luster of molten gold— with His two lotus-like hands as she sits upon His own lap, nestled between His two thighs. Of what nature is she?
Again, she embraces herself, her hips moist with passion, as Śrī Kṛṣṇa with his long and enchanting sprout-like hands.
With her lotus-like eyes closed due to the overflow of bliss, her limbs relaxed, her body adorned with pearls in the form of beads of perspiration born from intense exertion and dense horripilation,
she has withdrawn the entire host of her external and internal faculties into herself, her limbs becoming motionless.
She is immersed in the ocean of the mass of incomparable great bliss, wherein various mental conceptions have dissolved.
Again, she is pervaded by the overflowing bliss of her own self;
again, her eyes are sealed with blue lotuses;
again, her body is adorned with pearls in the form of dense drops of perspiration produced by the horripilation arising on her skin.
Furthermore, she whose entire collection of external and internal senses was completely dissolved into Śrī Kṛṣṇa within herself;
furthermore, she who was submerged in an ocean of an abundance of supreme bliss with her bodily limbs devoid of all activity;
furthermore, she whose mind was free from flickering restlessness. (Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta 8.75)
Furthermore, of what nature is the Supreme Lord?
He is accompanied by Satyā and Jāmbavatī, who are adorned with divine silken garments, ointments, and ornaments.
By those two restless-eyed bees of the lotus-face, who were tormented by the arrows of the God of Love.
The embrace by Satyabhāmā and Jāmbavatī; by what kind of women?
By those two who possessed excellent silk garments, ointments, and ornaments.
Again, by those two who were tormented by the arrows of desire;
again, by those two whose restless eyes, like bees, hovered over the face of Kṛṣṇa.
Embraced by a pair of serpents with dark and reddish, lovely, and tender vine-like bodies,
he embraced his own right [side].
With two lotuses shining from his left hands.
Furthermore, by those two creeper-like limbs of the Supreme Lord which are embraced by his two arms—
limbs that are, respectively, blue and crimson in color, charming, and tender; furthermore,
by those two situated on the right and left of the Supreme Lord.
Again, with two lotuses flickering from his hands.
Furthermore, of what nature was he?
He was embraced from behind by the daughter of Kalinda, who held a pair of lotus-hands,
who possessed the luster of collyrium, and who was tormented by love.
His two arms bear a lotus, a mace, a discus, and a conch;
upon his two forearms rests a flute, which shines like a lotus upon his face-lake.
He was embraced by Yamunā, who stands behind the Supreme Lord and holds a lotus in her hand; of what nature was she? Dark-complexioned, and moreover, tormented by love.
Furthermore, of what nature is the Supreme Lord?
His four hands are joined with a lotus, a mace, a conch, and a discus; his lotus-face shines as it rests upon two hands held like a flute.

[He is] being constantly served from all directions by celestial sages, ascetics, and lords of the sky-dwellers, whose bodies are bowed down by the weight of devotion and whose mouths are resonant with hymns of praise— [the Lord] who is beyond the sphere of mind and speech.
This [mantra], which bestows the fourfold aim and is the progenitor of the three worlds.
The meaning is "according to the sequence stated in the third chapter.

Furthermore, it is constantly served by gods, sages, and ascetics—the foremost of sky-goers—whose bodies are bowed low with excessive devotion, by these preeminent leaders with mouths eloquent in hymns of praise; and furthermore, [it is served] by the mind.
Furthermore, it is beyond the range of words; moreover, it bestows the fourfold fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; and furthermore, it is the progenitor of the three worlds.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Person, who is immersed in a great ocean of intense bliss and established in His own stainless abode, and having received initiation from a faultless Guru,
one of pure intellect should diligently recite this mantra one hundred thousand times for the sake of women.
A minister who is devoid of hearing news, seeing [the situation], and so forth, [is ineffective] even for his teachers.

Furthermore, having meditated upon the Supreme Lord in the form described above— immersed in the great ocean of dense bliss and abiding in His own pure splendor in that very form— the one of sharp intellect, having obtained from a sinless guru the ritual for initiation and the instruction on the mantra, and having received this mantra, should recite it with devotion one hundred thousand times.
What kind of practitioner is he?
One who turns his back on listening to and looking at even the talk of old women. (KrdC 8.80)
He describes the fire sacrifice (homa) and its service:
"And one should offer a tenth part as an oblation into the fire with milk-rice mixed with sugar, honey, and ghee."
One should constantly worship this [deity] on the most excellent seat first mentioned, for the sake of liberation from impermanence.
In the sacrificial fire, one should offer ten parts— that is, ten thousand oblations— of *paramānna* (excellent rice) mixed with sugar, honey, and clarified butter. Furthermore,
one should constantly worship this [deity] upon the most excellent *pīṭha* described previously in the context of the ten and eighteen-syllable mantras.
For what purpose? Because cyclic existence is impermanent, in order to abandon it.

Then, having begun with the sequence of the placement of the manifestations (*vibhūti-nyāsa*) up to the arrow, and having worshipped [the deity] from the form (*mūrti*) down to the limbs (*aṅga*), one should [worship] oneself within the excellent diagram (*yantra*) arising from twenty syllables.
Having written the central seed-syllable and, surrounding it, the four seed-syllables in the directions of Varuṇa, Indu, Yama, and Indra,
one should then [arrange] those forty-two syllables.

Having caused the learned ones to enter, one should then sequentially inscribe the mantras of Vāk, Māyā, and Śrī upon the [remaining] corners starting with those of Śiva, Hari, and Vasu; likewise, one should inscribe them on the corners of the Rakṣas, Water, and Wind.
Having performed the remaining rites as previously described and having duly worshipped the pedestal,
one should mentally construct the form, invoke it here, and worship it within the central seed-syllable.

Having begun with the "Vibhūti-pañjara" (the cage of manifestations) and worshipped up to the "Bāṇa" [mudrās] by means of the sequence of placement (*nyāsa*), and having fully worshipped his own form starting from the placement of the *mūrti* up to the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*), one should worship within the center of the middle seed-syllable, situated in the middle of the pair of fire-cities located at the center of the pericarp of the excellent *yantra* described in the previously mentioned twenty-syllable mantra.
According to the natural sense of the reading *bījam*, Rudradhara, Govindamiśra, and others maintain that it refers to the *hal-lekhā-bīja*.
However, according to the reading *parastān madhyama-bījam*, one should write the *kāma-bīja* and, surrounding it in the western, northern, eastern, and southern directions, write the four seeds—
namely the fourfold seed-mantra *drīṃ trīṃ jīṃ jhrīṃ*— and then [surround] those four seeds as well.
One should surround the upper part with the remaining mantra syllables, beginning with the forty-two *japa*s and ending with *svāhā*.
Immediately thereafter, the directions starting from the east are as follows: Śiva is Īśāna; Hari is Indra;
Vasu is Agni; and likewise, [the others] are in the south-eastern (Āgneyī) and subsequent directions, namely the south-western (Nairṛtī), western (Vāruṇī), and north-western (Vāyavī) directions.
In these corners, one should write the seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Bhuvaneśvarī, and Śrī, repeating them three times in sequence.

Having completed the remaining arrangement of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) as before, and having worshipped the pedestal according to the rules, one should visualize the form of Rukmiṇīvallabha upon that pedestal—conceiving it within the *kāma-bīja* situated in the center of the pericarp—and having meditated upon it and invoked it, one should worship it. (KrdC 8.82–85)
The Śaktis, beginning with Rukmiṇī, are to be worshipped in sequence within the seed-syllables located at the front, right, left, and back;
then the limbs (aṅgas) in the six corners, and the arrows on the filaments.

Immediately thereafter, one should worship the powers (śaktis) beginning with Rukmiṇī in the four seed-syllables located at the front, right, left, and back regions of the Lord; one should worship the limbs (aṅgas) in the six corners and the arrows (śaras) on the filaments (keśaras).
Lakṣmī and the others are in the middle of the petals; outside of those, in the directions starting from the southeast (Agni), are the deities headed by Dhvaja.
At the front is Ketu, dark blue; at the back is Vipama, reddish and of stainless red luster.
On both sides are the Lords of Treasures (Nidhīśau), with heaps of wealth showered by continuous streams;
and in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, one should place Heramba, Śāstṛ, Durgā, and Viṣvaksena.
Having visualized [the deities] outside with the luster of coral, emerald, dūrvā grass, and gold— beginning with Indra, Vajra, and the others—
the procedure for worship of Mukunda, accompanied by the seven enclosures (āvṛtis), has thus been described.
Within the lotuses beginning with the one for Agni, Lakṣmī and the others are to be worshipped;
there, on the outer part, one should worship the [emblems] beginning with the banner.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship the Gaṇa named Śyāmavarṇaketu in front of the deity.
One should worship Garuḍa, who is of a reddish hue, on the back of the deity.
On both sides of the deity, the two Lords of Treasures (Nidhīśvarau), possessing the luster of pure red, are to be worshipped; what are they like?
They are those upon whom masses of wealth have been rained down by continuous streams.
One should worship Heramba and the others, colored like coral and so forth, in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (vahni).
Immediately thereafter, one should worship Indra and the other world-protectors (lokapālas) in the cardinal directions outside, as well as their weapons, such as the vajra and so forth.
Thus, the procedure for the sevenfold enclosure (āvaraṇa-saptaka) worship of Mukunda, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, has been described according to the previously stated method. (KrdC 8.87–89)
Thus, he who— having conquered his own self— worships Acyuta with devotion while reciting this supreme mantra, shall,
after being honored by divine beings, [attain the state] of all people.
The fierce sun within the lotuses of his heart and eyes.

Thus, in this manner, that person who, having conquered his senses, worships Acyuta Kṛṣṇa with devotion and serves this most excellent mantra, is honored even by the gods. Of what nature is he? He is the sun for the lotus-eye and the lotus-heart of the worlds; [an alternative reading states: "he is the mantra capable of bringing all people under his control. (KrdC 8.90)
At the beginning of the day, one should satiate [the deity] with milk mixed with white sugar, which is prescribed for the day; by means of these waters,
he attains the splendor of Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
He makes himself a mere drop of water in the ocean of his own sovereign power.
With the practice centered on white sugar, perceiving it as milk, one should satisfy him every day at the break of dawn, during the morning time, a hundred times with water alone.
Thereafter, the practitioner [perceives] the fortune of Indra in his own sovereign ocean like a drop of water. (KrdC 8.91)
With *sumanas* flowers ground by means of stone mortars and immersed in abundant liquid sandalwood and camphor,
[the rite is performed] ten thousand times by this sage through oblation.
He shall become beloved by the three worlds, a knower of the Manu-mantras, and a sovereign among poets.
With this mantra, using *sumanaḥ* flowers— namely *jāti*, *mālatī*, and *adheya* blossoms—

and with those flowers combined with camphor and sandalwood paste, when one performs ten thousand oblations (*ayuta-homa*) with many drops [of the paste], that practitioner becomes beloved by the three worlds and the best of poets;
moreover, by mere meditation upon him, the deer-eyed women of the gods will certainly come under his control immediately.
What is not easily obtained for a man through this mantra— even from the japā flower afflicted by the god of love?
Having cast aside even their own innate rivalry, it is truly marvelous that both Sarasvatī, whose abode is the lotus, and the Mistress of Speech constantly serve this preeminent counselor.
By meditating upon this beloved of Rukmiṇī, the celestial women—the deer-eyed goddesses—will certainly and swiftly attain a state of submissiveness.
Of what nature are they? They are tormented by desire.
Immediately thereafter, what is not easily obtained by the practitioner from this mantra through recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth?
Rather, the meaning is that everything indeed becomes easily obtained.

Moreover, this too is a great marvel: that Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus, and Sarasvatī, the sovereign of speech, having abandoned their natural envy, [reside] eternally with this best of practitioners.
They serve. // KrdC_8.93 //
For a long time, he has been completely and eternally freed from mental anguish, physical disease, old age, death, and all malevolent spirits; from all poisons, misfortune, poverty, and the like;
and he is always attended by virtuous sons, excellent daughters, and a multitude of good friends.
Abounding in prosperity and possessing praised renown, he shall live for many years.

Furthermore, this practitioner shall be free from mental suffering, disease, old age, untimely death, grief, and poverty; he shall be utterly abandoned by all living beings, by poisons, by adverse fortune, and by such things as destitution for a long duration; he shall be endowed with distinguished sons, attended by a circle of virtuous daughters and friends, ever-prosperous, and possessed of celebrated and praised fame.
May he live for many years.
He states its superiority over other mantras:
"Among all mantras, the Vaiṣṇava mantras are indeed powerful and rich in highly honored fruits; among those, the Gopāla mantras [are supreme]."
Among these, this mantra called Sammohana is exceedingly powerful here;
it is a kalpa-tree for the imagination of incomparable prosperity.

Among all mantras, the Vaiṣṇava mantras are preeminently powerful; among those Vaiṣṇava mantras, the Gopāla mantras possess most highly honored fruits; and among those Gopāla mantras, this mantra known as Sammohana is the most potent, endowed with supreme strength.
Furthermore, he is the unique wish-fulfilling tree for the gift of incomparable sovereignty.
The foremost of mantra-practitioners who, humble with devotion, meditates upon this heart-entrancing Manu while performing recitation, fire-offerings, sacrifices, and other rites,
shall have all the knots of karma severed and his consciousness awakened.
He indeed goes to that state of Murāri, which is eternally pure.

That chief of mantrins, the best of practitioners, who is absorbed in meditation and worships with devotion through the knowledge of the object of worship, should revere this captivating mantra by means of recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and so forth; he goes to— that is, attains— the well-known state of Murāri, the state of the destroyer of *mura*, which is ignorance.
Of what nature is that state?
It is indestructible and free from all impurities.
Of what nature is he [who attains it]? He is one whose bonds of all karma have been destroyed.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? One whose mind is awakened, with a consciousness intent upon grasping the object. // KrdC_8.96 //
Now he describes yoga:

"Having undertaken one of these mantras, and then, through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, having driven away the enemies by means of the eight limbs of mantra, with an inner self that is joyful, purified, and serene..."

The yogi should practice yoga with appropriate conduct regarding walking, sleeping, and waking; first, he should sit facing east on his own very soft seat, seated with his face forward and his eyes closed.
Among these *manus* (mental states) and *mantras*, having mastered one through the recitation of mantras, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth, and having brought it under control;

being one by whom the enemies such as desire and anger have been driven away and abandoned by means of the eightfold path characterized by restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and absorption (*samādhi*)— that yogi, with a joyful, stainless, and serene mind, faces the east as before.
Let him practice the yogas, such as the cessation of mental fluctuations;
what kind of yogi? One whose dwelling, sleep, waking, and food are appropriate.
Again, he sat down upon his own very soft seat.
Furthermore, of what nature was he?
He was one by whom the eyes were closed—that is, shut—easily and without effort. //97//

Having led this entire universe— consisting of the elements, senses, and internal organs, and taking the form of the sun, moon, and fire, and composed of the phonemes— into the eternal seed-form consisting of the *kalās* and the two eyes (*kala-nayana*) within *pradhāna*;
then having led that into the *puruṣa* who is the nature of the *bindu*, and that too into the Supreme Self, and finally into the principle of Time (*kāla-tattva*).
One should indeed lead that [consciousness] into the conscious self (cid-ātman), and lead that [self] into the solitary, peaceful abode.

Having brought this entire universe—consisting of these phonemes, comprising the elements, the senses, and the internal organ, and taking the form of the sun, moon, and fire—into the *pradhāna*, which is the seed of desire (*kāma-bīja*) in the form of *praṇava*, one should contemplate it as dissolved therein. Then, one should contemplate that seed of desire within the *bindu*, which is well-known as the *anusvāra*; and that *bindu* itself within the *nāda*, which is the *kāla-tattva*, the Supreme Self.

One should withdraw even that reality of time into the power whose nature is consciousness; one should then withdraw that power as well into the solitary, luminous abode of light, which is self-manifesting, tranquil, and free from all afflictions. One should lead [the soul] there.
In what kind [of state]?

In the eternal Self, which is free from dualities, devoid of distinctions, dense with unsurpassed great bliss, free from any end, and the ultimate reality beyond the words of even Kṛṣṇa and others that are free from impurity; in this way.
Having withdrawn and practiced the supreme seed-syllable, then, with his breath and mind gradually dissolved,
and with both merit and demerit exhausted, may he become the very nature of incomparable, supreme consciousness.

In this manner— having performed the withdrawal by dissolving [the universe] into his own essential nature, which is free from duality (nirdvandva), devoid of specific dualities such as cold and heat, free from all distinction or heterogeneity (vaidharmya), a mass of absolute bliss, infinite, and the referent of pure terms such as Kṛṣṇa and Govinda— one should mutter the seed-syllable of desire (kāma-bīja).
Immediately thereafter, having himself become one whose breath and mind are motionless, and having exhausted both sin and merit, that incomparable yogin becomes composed of supreme consciousness.

[He perceives] the Desire (Kāma) flickering within the triangular Mūlādhāra, radiant with the luster of the rising sun, shining with a brilliance equal to ten million rising suns, fires of cosmic destruction, and the moon.

Having meditated upon Him who is as delightful as a blossoming bandhujīva flower smiling with the brilliant luster of thousands of garlands of lightning, who possesses the point (bindu) pervaded by the three qualities (guṇas), and who is the sole cause for the arising and dissolution of the world; Krd_8.100.

In the Mūlādhāra, which consists of a triangle and shines like the rising sun, there revolves the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), possessing a luster equal to ten million rising suns, the fire at the time of universal dissolution, and the moon; furthermore, it possesses the brilliance of a thousand streaks of lightning and is as enchanting as a grove of newly blossomed *bandhūka* flowers. It is that [syllable] which is pervaded by the three qualities beginning with *sattva*—namely, the *bindu* known as the *anusvāra*—and which is the sole cause for the creation and destruction of the universe.

Above that, following the path of the Suṣumṇā, one should contemplate the digit (kalā) that flashes upward, radiant with the luster of a mass of clearly beautiful lightning, reaching as far as the orb of the moon upon the forehead;
it consists of pure consciousness, is subtle in form, encompasses the entire universe, and is accessible through the primordial sound (nāda).
May he, whose chest is uplifted by the sound of "Hūṃ," remember that which is the incomparable root of all abodes.
Upon that seed of desire (kāma-bīja), one should contemplate the Kuṇḍalinī power situated within the Bindu as blazing;

of what nature? Possessing a radiance shining like a thousand clearly manifest and enchanting flashes of lightning, and furthermore, proceeding toward the aperture of the Suṣumṇā as far as the orb of the moon at the forehead.
Furthermore, it is that in which the flame of the fire-tongue—which follows after and is inherent in the nature of the seed-syllable—is present;
and furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is of the very essence of consciousness (*cit*).
Again, she is difficult to perceive;
again, she is the one who has attained the entirety of the universe;
again, she is the form of the arts.
Furthermore, she is inferable through sound;
furthermore, she is the root of all splendors.
What kind of person is the qualified practitioner?
One by whom the *ira*—the wind known as *apāna*—is raised upward (*udañcita*) and drawn up (*ūrdhvam utpāṭita*) by means of the syllable *huṃ*, is so described.
Having slowly led her [the goddess] from there— [her who is] like the orb of the full moon shining within the interior of a thousand-petaled red lotus with its face turned downward—
one should enter, having drunk that stream of nectar, which is red, consists of mantra, and takes the form of a flow of ambrosia.
Furthermore, having risen once more from one's own abode and having drunk [the nectar], one should enter again.
Having slowly led that Kuṇḍalinī Śakti to the full lunar orb shining in the center of the red thousand-petaled lotus with its face turned downward,

one should cause her to drink from this lunar disc a rain of nectar-streams— red in color, consisting of the phonemes, and having the nature of flowing nectar— and then cause her to enter the abode of the Self at the Mūlādhāra.
Furthermore, immediately thereafter, having raised her up in that same manner and performed it likewise, he should again cause her to reach her own place in that same way. // KrdC_8.102 //
He states the fruit of such practice:
"He who thus practices daily until reaching the end of himself—
the Lord of the Seed— [destroys] misfortune, old age, death, and disease."
Having conquered [him], may he himself, like the God of Love incarnate,
live on for a long time with his mass of hair as dark as a cloud.

The practitioner who daily practices the seed-syllable of desire (kāma-bīja) within the body in this manner— practicing it until the end of the self, which is the dissolution of the mind (mano-laya)— overcomes misfortune, old age, untimely death, and disease; having himself become the very Cupid who inhabits a body, he lives for a long time.
Of what kind? A mass of hair as dark as the color of a bee.
The stream of his speech— composed of a sequence of words and syllables that are both clear and sweet, and possessing most wondrous meaning— flashes forth instantly from his lotus-like mouth;
moreover, all mantras are swiftly accomplished for him.
He abides as the sole locus of the dense bliss of complete cessation.
From the lotus-face of this practitioner, Sarasvatī swiftly emerges.
Of what nature is she? She consists of a collection of clearly articulated and captivating words and syllables, and is an object of great wonder;
moreover, other mantras also quickly attain accomplishment for this practitioner, and furthermore, that practitioner abides solely in an uninterrupted and dense state of bliss.
Having come into being, it persists.
Having visualized Anaṅga, whose form is whirling from the root-cakra,
filling the entire expanse of space with his own rays of light consisting of pairs of red nectars;
Those who are to be brought under control should be made to enter [the deity] therein for the sake of subjugation.
Whether women or men, cities or even assemblies,
once they have been introduced there by one of sharpened intellect,
they would instantly and incessantly become his servants.
For a long time, those whose intellects are devoted to that [object] have no doubt [of its reality].

From the root-cakra at the *mūlādhāra*— here the ablative case is used in the sense of the locative— one should meditate with a sharpened mind and keen intellect upon the form of the wheel of rotation, the Kāma-bīja, being filled within the region of the middle of the universe by its own radiant splendors joined with red nectar; therein, for the purpose of bringing the target under control, women and others should be projected and cast in.

Immediately thereafter, the women and others who have been made to enter and have entered there—with their intellects submerged in him and their minds captivated by him—quickly become obedient to that practitioner for a long time; of this there is no doubt.

In this dark-complexioned one with tender limbs, who resides within the heart-lotus— supported by petals like the sun's rays, crimson as a *śakragopa* insect, and possessing a beautiful center shimmering with the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire— [one should meditate].
One should remember that Vāsudeva as being seated in perfect bliss.

In that heart-lotus endowed with twelve petals, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva— dark-complexioned, with tender limbs and delicate body— seated in a state of ease within its lovely center, which is as red as the insect known as the indragopa (coccinella beetle) and adorned by the orbs of the sun, fire, and moon. KrdC_8.107 //
Upon her two lotus-feet with their stainless sprout-like toes,
upon her calves as beautiful as the noble shell of a tortoise, upon her shanks adorned with anklets,
upon her knees and thighs, upon her excellent new saffron-colored garment, upon her girdle-string, and upon her navel—
Upon the line of hair, on the broad ground of her noble belly, and upon her expansive chest adorned with a full necklace; Kṛd_8.108.

Beginning from the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the primeval Person, one should gradually, as the case may be, fix one's own mind upon the places to be described hereafter— in due order, according to the sequence of those places. Thus, first one should fix the mind upon His two lotus feet.
Immediately after that, having set aside each preceding part, one should fix the mind upon the subsequent locations: first upon those very fingers which are like stainless sprouts and pure shoots;
then upon the row of shining nails; then upon the two feet joined with the foreparts of the toes.
Of what nature are they? Their upper portions are elevated like the back of a tortoise.
Thereafter, upon the two brilliantly shining shanks;

thereafter, upon the two knees, the two thighs of golden hue, the pair of excellent fresh garments, the garland of tiny bells, the region of the navel, the line of body hair resting there, and the expansive area of the broad belly adorned with a great necklace.
On the chest.
Upon the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, upon the garland of lotuses shining clearly bound to His chest, upon the two arms radiant with armlets at their roots and skilled in protecting the world,
upon the two hands enriched with bracelets, and upon the flute held by the fingers of both hands which captivates the entire universe with its exceedingly sweet sound— [I bow].
With two fine earrings upon his neck, and a pair [of marks] clearly and beautifully situated on his cheeks; // Krd_8.109 //
Upon the *śrīvatsa*, which is characterized by hair standing erect where the forefinger strikes the feet of Brahmā; upon the *kaustubha*, a special jewel set in the heart;

upon the garland of blooming lotuses; upon the two arms, beautiful with armlets at their roots and adorned with bracelets on both hands, capable of protecting the world from the cycle of existence; and upon the flute, by whose exceedingly sweet sound the three worlds are immersed—[in all these places].
Thereafter, at His throat, the pair of charming cheeks were illuminated by the radiance of beautiful earrings.
Upon the pair of ears, the two nostrils, the lotus-eyes, the play of the eyebrows, the forehead,
and the hair with its shimmering plumage— hair radiant with exceedingly fragrant and beautiful flowers;
upon the crimson lower sprout where a flute is placed, and upon the row of teeth known as a smile.
And let him gradually fix his own mind upon the sequence of the Primordial Person within the moonlight.
Upon her two ears, the pair of nostrils, the two lotus-eyes, the play of her eyebrows, and upon her forehead;

upon her hair, which was adorned with a restless peacock’s tail and radiant with exceedingly fragrant and enchanting flowers; upon her red lips, where a braid was fastened, and upon her row of teeth, which bore the name "smile"; and upon that moonlight-like moonstone which was equal to the moonlight itself.
Strike! (KrdC 8.110)
Until the mind reaches dissolution in the noble, gentle smile of Hari, one should practice the seed-mantra of the Bodiless One (Kāma),
consisting of either eighteen or ten syllables.
Then the practitioner, with his breath composed, slowly [performs the practice].

While the mind attains dissolution—indeed, a special absorption—in Hari’s noble and radiant gentle smile, one should recite either the eighteen-syllable or the ten-syllable seed-mantra of Anaṅga. What is his state? His vital breath (prāṇa-vāyu) has been withdrawn and brought under control, like a well-regulated wind. (KṛdC 8.111)
Having repeatedly fixed the mind upon [the objects] beginning with the lotus feet and ending with the gentle smile,
and having dissolved it therein, when the consciousness is exhausted, one becomes the self that is bliss, consciousness, and existence.
Having projected the mind, starting from the lotus feet up to the slight smile [of the deity],

and subsequently having dissolved it there— having made it absorbed— when the consciousness is exhausted and purified, the practitioner becomes one whose nature consists of bliss, knowledge, and existence.

By means of this very *Dīpikā*, I have elucidated the sequence of the applications (*viniyoga*) for the entire collection of mantras taught [herein], including their placement (*nyāsa*), recitation (*japa*), fire-offering (*homa*), worship (*pūjā*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), and consecration (*mantrābhiṣeka*). (Krd 8.113)
The sequence for the ritual placements (*nyāsa*), recitations (*japa*), and so forth, which are taught in the collection of *Kṛṣṇa*-mantras, has been elucidated precisely by the *Kramadīpikā*.
This very *Kramadīpikā*, which cuts through the darkness of doubt,
should be held by the virtuous in their hands with affection, day and night, like a hand-held lamp, for the attainment of all happiness.
This very *Kramadīpikā* should be held by virtuous people with affection, just as one holds a hand-lamp.

Of what nature is it? It is the cutter of the darkness consisting of doubt. Just as any other [lamp] is held with oil and other such lubricants so that it may destroy the darkness, so too is this work to be maintained. For what purpose is it to be held?
For the sake of attaining all happiness.
This world is permeated by Him; from whom it is produced, by whom it is eternally pervaded, and under whose governance He protects it;
and whom the cowherd girl worships with vast, great, and blazing splendor.
I bow to that Kṛṣṇa, the light of the awakening to the bliss of immortality.
This world is permeated and woven through by that light, from which Supreme Lord this world of living beings—known as *saṃsāra*—is produced; the meaning is that it attains its origin.
There is also a reading "in which" (*yasmin*).
Likewise, having taken refuge in the Supreme Lord as its presiding controller, the world remains perpetually and eternally expanded.

I praise and extol that Uktānanda, the self-luminous one, whose vast thigh—the great majesty of the Supreme Lord—is possessed of blazing splendor; being itself radiant with that splendor, she bears him in the form of a reflection. KrdC_8.115 //
The Lord, though established in his own abode, wields that discus— the instrument of his own sport—
which was given by the enemy of Manmatha for the sake of protection and which has withdrawn from the world;
it shines brilliantly with its new splendor, dispels sins, and certainly destroys all illusion.
I praise the Yādava, who crushes the bodies of those who commit slaughter and who devours the day of his enemies.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "I bow to that Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa who bears the discus whose characteristics are about to be described.
Of what nature is that discus?
It is the instrument for His own pastimes, the means for His own playful battles.
What is the Supreme Lord like?
He is established in the foundational substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) and established in meditative absorption (samādhi);
or alternatively, even while remaining in the external world, he is the sovereign lord (prabhu).
Furthermore, by what kind [of qualities]?
It was bestowed upon the earth by Mahādeva, the enemy of Manmatha, for the sake of protection—that is, for the purpose of guarding all the worlds.
Moreover, it is free from calamities such as excessive rain, drought, and so forth.
Furthermore, it was beautiful and resplendent as if with fresh radiance.
Of what nature was that black one? It was free from sin, yet possessed of Māyā; furthermore, it was eternal and indestructible, [the destroyer] of those who commit slaughter and cause affliction.

"Kāya-vimardanaṃ" means that which destroys the body; "punaḥ bhuñjad-dukhaṃ" means experiencing suffering again; and "bhuñjat-svarga-lokaṃ punar jāty-ādy-avaḥ" means falling back again to birth and so forth in the heavenly world—this is the meaning.
It should be understood that in this verse, the author of the work has inserted his own name within a *cakrabandha* (wheel-pattern) arrangement. KrdC_8.116.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Kramadīpikā*, composed by the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya, Śrī Keśava Kāśmīri Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī. //8//
This work is completed.
